Here, we introduce a framework that bridges statistical physics and analytical chemistry to deconvolute complex self-assembled mixtures from partial spectral data. Inspired by Potts models of protein folding, we express the chemical potential of each compound as a function of a reduced set of parameters-intrinsic building-block energies and pairwise coupling terms between neighboring building blocks in the sequence. Coupling this model with the law of mass action yields equilibrium concentrations across the entire reactive network. The model parameters can be infered by fitting predicted spectroscopic signals to experimentally measured partial data. We demonstrate this approach using dynamic combinatorial libraries (DCLs) of peptides as a model system. Applied to a DCL of 81 peptides, our method resolves the full mixture composition from just 13 overlapping peaks, revealing that lateral couplings dominate the assembly energetics. Beyond DCLs, this strategy offers a general route for analyzing self-assembled systems from partial data and extends naturally to target-driven identification of high-affinity binders.

Title: Paper-Faithful Federated Learning: Scientific Checks for Practitioner and Agent Development
Author: Ali Dadras, Alp Yurtsever
Text_Content: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.

Title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models
Author: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
Text_Content: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.

Title: STeP-C: Real-Time Neural Compression for Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing at Scale
Author: Tingfeng Li, Ming-Fang Huang, Shaobo Han, Yue Tian
Text_Content: Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) generate continuous, high-resolution spatio-temporal data at rates exceeding hundreds of megabytes per second, creating severe challenges for real-time storage and transmission. While neural compression methods can achieve strong rate-distortion performance on sensing data, prior approaches either require per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming, or have only been validated offline. None have been demonstrated end-to-end on a continuously streaming DAS acquisition system at scale. We present STeP-C (Spatio-Temporal Predictive Compression), a neural compression framework that decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective motivated by conditional entropy reduction. Critically, we identify entropy coding as the dominant bottleneck for streaming deployment. We address it through GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, and parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, together with FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, enabling a full real-time pipeline built around a GPU ring buffer. We validate this pipeline on a live DAS testbed, achieving a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and an average throughput of 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s requirement for 1 kHz, 81 km DAS streams. We further show that STeP-C substantially outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates, can be applied to unseen channel ranges within the same acquisition system without retraining, and largely maintains downstream detector consistency, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.

Title: Graded Intersection Types
Author: Rémy Cerda, Ugo Dal Lago
Text_Content: We introduce graded intersection types, in which arrow domains are multisets of types with coefficients in a semiring. Boolean and natural number grades recover idempotent and non-idempotent intersection types. We give algebraic conditions on the semiring for subject reduction and expansion in finite systems and in locally finite systems with guarded infinite types. We construct a lifting to multisets of grades corresponding, in this general setting, to lifting the idempotent system to the non-idempotent one. We recall the main existing operational characterisations from the literature, and show some general extensions.

Title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
Author: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu
Text_Content: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.

Title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
Author: Boris P. Belotserkovskii, R. Edward Watts
Text_Content: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

Title: Bellman Contraction under MMD: A Unified Framework
Author: Baptiste Debes, Tinne Tuytelaars
Text_Content: We introduce a mathematical framework for studying contraction of the distributional Bellman operator under Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). We show that contraction reduces to conditional positive definiteness of an associated kernel constructed from the base kernel, which we call the Bellman difference kernel. Focusing on radial kernels, we use Schoenberg's theorem to connect this condition to Bernstein functions. This gives contraction criteria that hold in any dimension and can be verified analytically or tested numerically. Our framework unifies known results for the Gaussian RBF, power-distance, and multiquadric kernels. A numerical search identifies 11 new kernels that induce contraction. We also propose chaining, a general construction that produces kernels inducing contraction with any prescribed factor. To reconcile theory with practice, we show that contraction on a set only requires conditional positive definiteness on that set. This explains why the RBF kernel can remain a valid choice when rewards are bounded, despite its lack of global contraction. Finally, we identify a fundamental tradeoff between contraction rate and discriminative power, where kernels that contract faster tend to discriminate less between distributions. Code is available at https://github.com/BaptisteDebes/BellmanContractionMMD

Title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
Author: Zimo Xu, Wenzhuo Liu, Hideki Nakayama
Text_Content: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

Title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
Author: Petter Törnberg
Text_Content: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

Title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
Author: Zhuangzhuang Ma, Rukuan Chai, Qianqian Ma, Yanghua Wang, Branko Bijeljic, Martin J. Blunt
Text_Content: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

Title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
Author: Jiachun Jin, Zetong Zhou, Haonan Wang, Xiao Yang, Jun Zhu, Zhijie Deng
Text_Content: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

Title: Near-Optimal Regret for Oracle-Efficient Adversarial Contextual Bandits
Author: Kiarash Banihashem, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Text_Content: We study contextual bandits with $K$ actions, a class of $N$ policies, and i.i.d.\ contexts from a distribution that the learner can sample. For any sequence of loss functions fixed before play, we give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret $O(\sqrt{KT\log(2N)}\,\log(2KT))$ against the best policy in hindsight on the realized contexts. This improves the $T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon in prior oracle-efficient bounds and achieves the optimal regret rate in this setting up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm perturbs policy scores using a Poisson sample of auxiliary contexts. At each sampled context, the perturbation assigned to an action is a Laplace noise draw multiplied by a scale specific to that context and action. We show that choosing these scales to minimize a convex objective determined by past observations yields the stated regret bound. We further approximate the minimizing scales by projected stochastic gradient descent using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimization oracle that returns the optimum value. Since the table of scales can be large, the algorithm represents the SGD iterates implicitly by storing the random draws that determine each update and evaluates the scales only at queried contexts. Both the oracle complexity and the remaining resource bounds are polynomial in $T$, $K$, and $\log(2N)$.

Title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
Author: Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
Text_Content: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

Title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification
Author: Paul Grunenwald, Benoît Crabbé, Guillaume Wisniewski, Pirmin Lemberger
Text_Content: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.

Title: Mathematical foundations for symmetric programming and reasoning
Author: Ohad Kammar, Matija Pretnar
Text_Content: We develop a mathematical abstraction for uniformly exploiting symmetries in programming and reasoning based on the mathematical proof principle `without-loss-of-generality' (w.l.o.g.). Given: group actions that describe symmetries of the input and the output; and a canoniser, which captures how arbitrary inputs get sent to canonical ones, our construction extends any function from the canonical inputs to the whole domain. We characterise the conditions on the canonisers which guarantee that the construction gives the unique equivariant (i.e. symmetry-preserving) extension. Furthermore, we adapt the construction to a dependently-typed setting, where it captures traditional symmetric w.l.o.g. arguments via the Curry-Howard correspondence. Finally, we extend the construction to algebraic data types, where the symmetries of the constructors both uniquely determine the symmetries of the data type and pave the way for efficient execution.

Title: Predicting Ethanol Drinking Status from Nonhuman Primate Liver Histology: A Proof of Concept for Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning in Few-Shot Vision-Language Modeling
Author: Amirmohammad Mohammadi, Rupak Khadka, Kathleen A. Grant, Mary Lauren Benton, Joshua Peeples
Text_Content: Combining vision-language models (VLMs) with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a promising approach to few-shot whole-slide image (WSI) classification in computational pathology. This study evaluates this approach for predicting ethanol drinking status from nonhuman primate liver histology. Adapters are evaluated against non-PEFT configurations on a subset of the Monkey Alcohol Tissue Research Resource (MATRR). All evaluated PEFT configurations achieve higher mean balanced accuracy than the non-PEFT baselines. For example, in the four-shot setting, attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) alone achieves 43.5% mean balanced accuracy, compared with 78.1% after adding an adapter. Qualitative attention analysis shows that textual pathway adaptations produce localized attention heatmaps, while visual pathway adaptations produce more diffuse ones. A pathologist's review identified similar histological features across adaptations.

Title: TuMAP: A Dual-View, Morphotype-Aware Pathomics Pipeline for Quantifying Renal Tubular Remodeling
Author: Ruijie Wu, Yuechen Yang, Yanfan Zhu, Yu Wang, Shilin Zhao, Ming-Tsun Tsai, Szu-Yuan Li, Shuo-Ming Ou, Tz-Heng Chen, Haichun Yang, Yuankai Huo
Text_Content: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous. We introduce TuMAP (Tubular Morphotype-Aware Pathomics), a pipeline combining (1) dual-view foundation-model representations and provisional morphotype annotation, (2) compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and (3) patient-level statistical inference. From 456,158 tubules in 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides, TuMAP identified eight image-based morphotypes, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, while IgA nephropathy differed in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes. Area-normalized nuclear density exposed additional within-morphotype differences. TuMAP provides a framework for separating changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.

Title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
Author: Tian Xia
Text_Content: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.

Title: On cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms
Author: Anantajeet Devaraj, Navid Nasr Esfahani
Text_Content: An unconditionally secure $(t, s, v)$-all-or-nothing transform (AONT) is a bijection from $s$ input elements to $s$ output elements over an alphabet of size $v$, such that given any $s - t$ output elements, no information can be obtained about any $t$ input elements. While linear AONTs have been extensively studied, comparatively little is known about the existence of non-linear AONTs. In this paper, we investigate unconditionally secure cryptographically non-linear $(t, s, v)$-AONTs, distinguishing between non-additivity, non-affinity, and cryptographic non-linearity. To achieve this, we first present a computational method for enumerating general AONTs focusing on the case $(t, 3, 3)$-AONTs for $t = 1 and 2$, establishing the existence of non-additive AONTs. We then introduce a general construction of non-additive AONTs from linear ones using coordinate-wise symbol permutations. We measure the non-linearity of the AONT instances generated from this construction, using differential $Δ_F$-uniformity and Walsh magnitude. Finally, we establish theoretical conditions under which $Δ_F$-uniformity is reduced and present statistical results examining the non-linearity of AONTs obtained through our construction.

Title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
Author: Mohammad Mahdi Habibi Bina, Mohammad Reza Daliri
Text_Content: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.

Title: Nearly Optimal Dilation for Non-Uniform k-Center with Constant-Factor Budget Violation
Author: Jannis Blauth, Siri Prüßner
Text_Content: In Non-Uniform $k$-Center, we are given a metric space $(V,d)$ and $L$ levels of balls with prescribed radii $r_1 \ge \ldots \ge r_L$ and nonnegative integer budgets $k_1,\ldots,k_L$. The goal is to place at most $k_\ell$ centers of each level $\ell \in [L]$ in $V$ and minimize the dilation $λ$ such that the corresponding balls of radii $λr_1,\dots,λr_L$ cover $V$. While this problem admits no subexponential approximation factor unless P=NP, the picture changes drastically when additional centers are allowed. An $(α,β)$-bicriteria approximation to Smooth Non-Uniform $k$-Center covers $V$ with dilation $βλ_{\text{opt}}$ such that, for each $\ell \in [L]$, the number of centers of the first $\ell$ levels is at most $α$ times their total budget. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized $(1+\varepsilon,8+\varepsilon)$-approximation and a deterministic $(O_{\varepsilon}(1),2+\varepsilon)$-approximation, both running in polynomial time. Even for classical $k$-Center, obtaining an $(O(1),2-δ)$-approximation is NP-hard for every fixed $δ\in (0,1]$. Thus, our second result almost settles the optimal dilation when a constant-factor violation of the budget is allowed, unless P=NP. We combine a new primal-dual enumeration procedure with a simple bucketing argument that yields a new trade-off between the two approximation factors. It remains open whether there is a polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon,2+\varepsilon)$-bicriteria approximation, which would almost match the classical $2$-approximation for $k$-Center.

Title: Adaptive carrier signal synthesis for frequency-division multiplexed cryogenic detector readout
Author: Timo Muscheid, Benedikt Keppner, Daniel Crovo, Robert Gartmann, Marvin Fuchs, Lukas Scheller, Oliver Sander, Luis E. Ardila-Perez
Text_Content: Frequency-domain multiplexing is a fundamental technology for readout of cryogenic detector arrays on a single transmission line. Synthesizing a large number of static carrier tones for resonator stimulation eventually drives the cryogenic low-noise amplifier beyond its P1dB, introducing detector signal distortion. Scaling array sizes to O(10^6) detector pixels therefore demands minimizing the total power on the transmission line by continuous tracking of the resonances, which requires the readout electronics to be capable of updating the carrier tones dynamically. This work presents an scalable FPGA-based implementation for carrier signal synthesis based on a numerically controlled oscillator and a polyphase filter bank, enabling real-time frequency adaptivity as well as frequency resolution of 4 mHz to precisely tune the operating point, while simultaneously reducing resource usage compared to the current memory-based implementation.

Title: Speed-to-Power Dominates Energy Costs for AI Data Centers: Technoeconomic Analysis of Powering AI in the Continental United States
Author: Alex C. Newkirk, Daniel L. Gerber, Erica R. H. Fuchs, Alex Hubbard, M. Granger Morgan, Arman Shehabi, Sarah J. Smith, Constantine Samaras
Text_Content: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is driving demand for new data centers at large scale and on short deployment timelines. To power them, firms connect to the commercial grid or contract generation directly, but interconnection and gas-turbine delays now incentivize on-site generation. We compare grid-connected and off-grid data center energy infrastructure (AC- and DC-coupled solar-plus-storage, islanded natural gas, and grid interconnection) across the continental U.S. Using an open-source technoeconomic framework built on empirically calibrated AI training loads, climate-driven cooling, stage-by-stage power conversion, and physics-based battery degradation, we model designs providing equivalent energy services. Our central contribution is a speed-adjusted cost of energy that values the compute unlocked by faster construction, making options with different deployment timelines directly comparable on one physically consistent basis. We find DC coupling reduces lifetime energy costs by 18% ($0.09/ kWh) on average versus AC counterparts by eliminating inverters and improving efficiency. Though rarely cheapest on unadjusted energy cost, DC-coupled microgrids' faster deployment makes them the lowest-cost modeled option in 85% of U.S. locations once foregone compute is valued, or 55% under accelerated natural gas timelines. For AI infrastructure, deployment speed rather than unit energy cost determines the economically preferred path to power.

Title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
Author: Hannah Atmer, Yuan Yao, Thiemo Voigt, Stefanos Kaxiras
Text_Content: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

Title: GRID-MRI: Resilience Assessment of Power Systems under Coordinated Cyber-Physical Attacks
Author: Isaac Ortega Romero, Ioannis Zografopoulos
Text_Content: The increasing penetration of inverter-based resources and growing cyber-physical interdependencies expose electrical power systems to disturbances that challenge conventional resilience assessments. Existing approaches often evaluate resilience dimensions independently, overlooking the non-additive effects of coordinated disruptions and the influence of exogenous stressors. To address this gap, this paper proposes a Grid Multidimensional Resilience Index (GRID-MRI) that integrates endogenous disruption severity, coordination effects, and climatic and economic-regulatory conditions. The framework quantifies physical, cyber, and operational degradation, identifies interaction effects through counterfactual (i.e., what-if), simulations of individual and coordinated attacks, and incorporates exogenous stressors as scenario-dependent scaling factors. Its application to a modified IEEE 39-bus system under three escalating cyber-physical attack scenarios, informed by the December 2025 Polish cyberattack incident, reveals that coordinated attacks induce system collapse despite stable individual and additive responses. The corresponding resilience losses are 3.72 and 4.09 times their additive estimates, while GRID-MRI increases from 0.062 to 1.188 and reaches 6.081 under additional exogenous stress. These findings demonstrate the limitations of additive assessments and establish a quantitative basis for distinguishing the dominant mechanisms of multidimensional resilience degradation.

Title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
Author: Alfio Massimiliano Gliozzo, Nandana Mihindukulasooriya, Gaetano Rossiello, Erick Lee, Lisa Amini
Text_Content: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

Title: Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography
Author: Feng Jiang
Text_Content: Provably secure linguistic steganography assumes that the receiver recovers the sender's tokens, but a text channel delivers only text, and ambiguous tokenizations break extraction. Existing fixes change the distribution, synchronize whole pools of tokens at a capacity that collapses with large vocabularies, or track several token histories. We prove that if extraction is exact and error-free across full-support language models, a single-history receiver is confined to a prefix-free candidate set at every step -- even if it reads the entire future text and the sender constrains later steps -- and must therefore give up the stop entropy, the entropy of deciding whether each prefix token ends there. Fixing these stop decisions on the prefix forest with shared randomness yields coin projection: a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, preserves ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key. Across English, Chinese and Japanese, ambiguous text is rare (at most 11 in 1,000 tokens), yet the stop entropy at word and morpheme prefixes takes 7.2-9.0% of the entropy at every step; SyncPool's further loss comes from space and single-byte UTF-8 hubs that merge subtrees while carrying almost no stop uncertainty. Coin projection keeps 91-93% of the string entropy for the coder at every vocabulary size; with the full vocabulary, it turns 2.16-6.85 times as much entropy into message bits as SyncPool and recovers every completed message.

Title: Online Transportation via Shifted Geometric Scales
Author: John Jeang
Text_Content: In the Online Transportation problem, introduced by Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1995), requests arrive sequentially in a metric space and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to one of $m$ facilities with available capacity. The objective is to minimize the total distance between requests and their assigned facilities. The problem generalizes the Online Metric Matching problem, in which each facility has unit capacity, and inherits a $2m-1$ lower bound on the competitive ratio for all deterministic algorithms. For Online Metric Matching, Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1993) and Khuller, Mitchell, and Vazirani (1994) established an optimal deterministic competitive ratio of $2m-1$, attained by the Retrospective (Permutation) algorithm. Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (1998) conjectured that the same ratio is achievable for online transportation. Recently, Seth, Das, and Raghvendra (2026) obtained a competitive ratio of approximately $6.66m-2.89$ using their Robustified Greedy algorithm. We give an algorithm with competitive ratio $ρ(m-1)+1$, where $ρ\approx5.64$. Our algorithm builds on minimum-spanning-tree search techniques developed by Harada and Itoh (2025) and Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, and Uetz (2026), using priority-based virtual depth-first searches over the known facilities. However our algorithm uses a phase to shift the geometric search scales, to decide when to skip certain searches and optimize the thresholds that define what edges to include in a given search.

Title: Development of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence System Based on Scintillating Crystals Read Out with Kinetic Inductance Detectors for BULLKID-DM
Author: T. Lari, G. Spina, A. Acevedo-Rentería, L. E. Ardila-Perez, L. Bandiera, C. Bonomo, M. Calvo, M. Cappelli, R. Caravita, F. Carillo, F. Cescato, U. Chowdhury, D. A. Crovo, A. Cruciani, A. D'Addabbo, M. del Gallo Roccagiovine, M. De Lucia, G. Del Castello, D. Delicato, F. Ferraro, M. Folcarelli, S. Fu, R. Gartmann, M. Grassi, V. Guidi, D. L. Helis, L. Malagutti, A. Mazzolari, A. Monfardini, T. Muscheid, D. Nicolò, F. Paolucci, D. Pasciuto, L. Pesce, C. Puglia, D. Quaranta, C. M. A. Roda, S. Roddaro, M. Romagnoni, G. Signorelli, F. Simon, A. Tartari, E. Vázquez-Jáuregui, K. Zhao, M. Vignati
Text_Content: The BULLKID-DM experiment has been proposed to search for WIMP-like dark matter particles with a mass of 1 GeV or lower and with a WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section down to $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$. To achieve this goal, the experiment utilizes a detector consisting of a stack of 16 silicon wafers instrumented with phonon-mediated superconducting Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs), to be operated at the underground facility of the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy. To reduce the residual background arising from $γ$-rays, neutrons, and muons, a cryogenic active anti-coincidence system (veto) operating at mK temperature, surrounding the main detector, is under development. The veto detector consists of segmented scintillating crystals read out by phonon-mediated KID light detectors. Current status and future developments of the veto system are presented. In particular, we focus on cryogenic tests of both bismuth germanate (BGO) and gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) crystals, which had been previously chosen as veto candidate crystals according to our preliminary studies on the dependence of their optical properties (i.e. light yield and scintillation decay time) on temperature. We finally present the operation and preliminary tests of a two-module veto prototype with multiplexed readout.

Title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
Author: Siu Wun Cheung, Youngsoo Choi
Text_Content: Numerical simulation of transport processes in magnetized plasmas is characterized by extreme anisotropy, where diffusion along magnetic field lines can be many orders of magnitude larger than in the perpendicular direction. This anisotropy leads to thin, steep boundary layers and numerical pollution that standard finite element methods struggle to resolve without prohibitive mesh refinement. In this paper, we introduce the Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method (PU-DDFEM), a data-driven local model reduction approach, for anisotropic diffusion. The method utilizes a bottom-up construction to enable a complete offline-online splitting. We parametrize the local magnetic field and boundary conditions to generate a snapshot space that captures the essential physics of plasma confinement. Dominant modes are extracted via a local spectral problem to identify representative features. These modes are then mapped to the global domain using a partition of unity to form a conforming approximation space. This ensures that the basis functions are fully reusable across different global magnetic configurations, significantly reducing the online computational overhead for large-scale plasma simulations.

Title: Strategic disclosure and epistemic manipulation in extensive games
Author: Sergei Artemov, Benjamin Prud'homme
Text_Content: In many strategic settings, agents can influence opponents by selectively disclosing truthful information about their own future actions. We introduce a game-theoretic framework to model this phenomenon. As a case study, we consider a two-player, alternating-move epistemic game in which Player A evaluates actions under a conservative maximin rule, while Player B-the manipulator-leverages this behavior by strategically revealing commitments. We prove that the manipulator can implement every inducible outcome using at most n disclosures in a binary game of depth 2n with n decisions per player. This establishes a sharp contrast between the game tree's exponential size and the linear amount of information required to control the outcome, highlighting a general mechanism by which limited information can exert disproportionate strategic influence.

Title: List Update with Time Windows and Delays without Batch-Serving
Author: Icey Siyi Ai, Jingwei Li, Clifford Stein
Text_Content: We study list update with time windows and delays when every request requires a separate access. Unlike batch-serving models, serving several requests to one element still incurs one access per request, and each access may change the list for subsequent requests. For time windows of overlap at most $k\ge2$, our deterministic First-Element Removal algorithm is $(3-2/k)$-competitive, hence $3$-competitive in general. Against an oblivious adversary, a randomized adaptation of BIT is $7/4$-competitive on arbitrary $2$-overlap inputs. More generally, on inputs without self-overlap, it is $\left(13/4-9/[2(k+1)]\right)$-competitive for every $k\ge2$. For delays, we give a deterministic $5$-competitive algorithm and a lower bound of $2+\sqrt3$ for deterministic delay-unaware algorithms. Our analyses extend inversion potentials with per-request credits that reconcile different service times and orders.

Title: SALT: State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer for Single-Temporal Cross-Dataset Structural Localization in Remote Sensing
Author: Aggelos Psiris, Georgios Angelidis, Giorgos Sfikas, Maria Vakalopoulou, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos
Text_Content: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/SALT

Title: GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
Author: Rodrigo Labouriau
Text_Content: Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.

Title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
Author: Saleh Ashkboos, Dhruv Desai, Lavinia Ghita
Text_Content: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.

Title: Evaluation of Music Version Retrieval Methods for Setlist Identification in Live Concerts
Author: Andres Ferraro, Albin Correya
Text_Content: Automatic setlist identification aims to identify the songs performed in live concert recordings by matching noisy and variable-quality audio against a database of reference tracks. This task presents challenges beyond conventional music version identification, including substantial arrangement differences, background noise, and the need to process continuous recordings efficiently at large scale. In this work, we evaluate modern music version retrieval methods for setlist identification using the ASID benchmark, comparing the established Re-MOVE system with CLEWS and NAVE, an internal neural audio version embedding model. Our results show that NAVE and CLEWS substantially outperform Re-MOVE. Notably, NAVE uses 256-dimensional embeddings, compared with 1024 dimensions for CLEWS, providing a four-fold reduction in embedding storage while achieving better retrieval performance. We further evaluate music/non-music gating and find modest improvements in detection and temporal coverage, while qualitative analysis suggests that such preprocessing can improve recognition boundaries beyond what the standard ASID metrics capture. Overall, the results demonstrate that segment-level audio embeddings provide a strong basis for scalable setlist identification and that compact representations can achieve strong accuracy under realistic live-concert conditions at much lower storage and serving cost.

Title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
Author: Xinheng Ding, Seyyed Saeid Cheshmi, Ziyang Zhang, Tairan Chen, Wenya Xie, Yu Hou, Rui Zhang, Zirui Liu
Text_Content: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.

Title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
Author: Zaid Abulawi, William Oliveira, Akzhol Almukhametov, Jun Fang, Ling Zou, Rui Hu, Stefano Lorenzi, Yang Liu
Text_Content: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

Title: NonSense: On the (In)security of FPGA Anti-tamper Sensors
Author: Mehmet Ali Cetin, Fatemeh Khojasteh Dana, Saleh Khalaj Monfared, Nima Seyed Aghazadeh, Maryam Saadat Safa, Shahin Tajik
Text_Content: FPGAs are widely used in mission-critical systems, where a successful physical attack can have serious consequences. This makes resilience to such attacks a critical security requirement. To defend against active physical attacks, such as glitching attacks, modern FPGAs rely on on-chip sensors that detect these disturbances and trigger responses, such as key zeroization, before a device is compromised. These sensors are deployed as both hard-IP blocks and soft-IP cores, and their trustworthiness is often taken for granted. In this work, we challenge that assumption and argue that the sensors themselves are a fragile and underexplored attack surface. Drawing on recent results, we show that both the detection and response mechanisms of state-of-the-art sensors can be bypassed without invasive tampering. We further argue that sensor reliability is reduced by factors rarely captured in threat models, including the spatial and frequency-dependent behavior of the system's power delivery network, which can steer a fault to a target while sparing nearby sensors; environmental conditions such as temperature, which shift detection thresholds; and long-term aging, which drifts sensor calibration and may open silent detection gaps. Finally, we propose a set of countermeasures that harden detection and response mechanisms against these effects.

Title: Asymmetric Frequency Conversion and Violation of Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation in Phased Floquet Metasurfaces
Author: Yao-Ting Wang, Emanuele Galiffi, Sander A. Mann, Mauro Antezza, Andrea Alù
Text_Content: We study a system of three closely spaced conducting sheets, whose thermal emission largely violates Kirchhoff's law through nonreciprocal frequency conversion enabled by Floquet phenomena. We leverage surface mode transitions controlled by temporal modulation of one of the metasurfaces, resulting in largely asymmetric frequency conversion. Our findings broaden the capabilities of Floquet metasurfaces for wave conversion and energy manipulation, paving the way towards magnet-free nonreciprocal photonic devices with opportunities for thermal management and efficient photonic refrigeration.

Title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
Author: Hao Li, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Hui En Pang, Kairui Hu, Mingze Sun, Runmao Yao, Xinhao Ji, Xiyuan Zheng, Xuanli Chen, Yalun Dai, Yap Kim Hui, Dingwen Zhang, Yuanyuan Gao, Ziang Cao, Cheng Huang Yean, Jackson Peng, Rui Duan, Yaobo Liu, Zetong Wang, Ziwei Liu
Text_Content: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

Title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
Author: Bowen Wang, Osvaldo Simeone
Text_Content: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

Title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
Author: Stanley Huang, Anthony Baez, Catherine Yeh, Pat Pataranutaporn
Text_Content: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.

Title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
Author: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
Text_Content: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

Title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
Author: Íñigo Zubeldia, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Miles Cranmer
Text_Content: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

Title: Physical Observables and Superselection
Author: Martin Paul Vaughan
Text_Content: It is well-known that a physical state may be represented by a unit vector in a Hilbert space, whilst a physical observable may be represented by a self-adjoint operator on that same space. However, the introduction of a superselection rule on a Hilbert space imposes constraints such that not all self-adjoint operators can represent observables, which has further consequences for the states themselves as well as the physical processes that transform them. In this article, we review the concept of superselection from the view of how such rules would affect what we consider to be physical. Arguments for the existence of a superselection rule due to charge or possibly energy conservation are given and the emergence of effective superselection rules due to decoherence or the lack of a shared reference frame are also discussed.

Title: Finding the Farthest in High Dimensions: Dynamic Diameter and Farthest-Neighbor Search
Author: Mohammad Hajiaghayi, Morteza Monemizadeh
Text_Content: We give faster algorithms for diameter and farthest-neighbor search in high-dimensional Euclidean space. For every fixed $1<c<\sqrt2$, we maintain an actual factor-$c$ diameter pair under arbitrary point insertions and deletions, with worst-case update time $n^{2/c^2-1}\poly(d,\log n)$ and space $n^{2/c^2}\poly(d,\log n)$, suppressing logarithmic dependence on the execution length and failure probability. Here $n$ bounds the number of active points. The update exponent improves Indyk's algorithm~\cite{indyk} (SODA'03) bound from $1/c^2$ to $2/c^2-1$, while the space exponent improves from $1+1/c^2$ to $2/c^2$. At $c=\sqrt{3/2}$, the update exponent decreases from $2/3$ to $1/3$. A separate construction achieves approximation exactly $\sqrt2$ with update time polynomial in $d$ and $\log n$. All these guarantees hold against adaptive updates, even when every previous random choice is exposed. We also improve the time--space tradeoff near linear space. This construction has an always-correct variant with expected amortized update bounds and requires no advance bound on the number of updates. The dynamic structures store a current answer, so reporting its two point identifiers takes constant time. The geometric method also gives static diameter algorithms and a farthest-neighbor structure for a fixed set that answers arbitrary adaptive queries. At approximation $\sqrt2-\varepsilon$, the diameter time is $n^{1+O(\varepsilon)}$, and the query time is $n^{O(\varepsilon)+o(1)}$ with near-linear preprocessing and space, up to polynomial input-parameter factors. On binary points, this improves the $n^{O(\sqrtθ)}$ overhead of the algorithm that Andoni, Jiang, and Zharkov~\cite{ajz2026} (STOC'26) for Hamming approximation $2-θ$ to $n^{O(θ)+o(1)}$.

Title: Irreversible dynamics for ideal fluids on Riemannian manifolds: metriplectic energy-conserving alternatives to Navier-Stokes
Author: Erwin Luesink, Archishman Saha, Tanya Schmah, Cristina Stoica
Text_Content: For modelling dissipative phenomena such as friction, diffusion and viscosity, the Hamiltonian framework has a key limitation: once the Casimir invariants are fixed, Hamiltonian flows preserve phase-space volume, which rules out relaxation to equilibrium. Thus modelling dissipation requires modifying the Hamiltonian structure. Following the metriplectic (equivalently, GENERIC) approach, we add to the Hamiltonian vector field a dissipative term generated by a symmetric bracket, here constructed from a Riemannian metric. The resulting flow conserves the energy, and optionally further invariants, while driving a chosen generalised entropy monotonically, which makes the dynamics irreversible; when the entropy is bounded on energy level sets in the direction in which it is driven, it acts as a Lyapunov functional. We apply this construction to ideal fluids on compact Riemannian manifolds, choosing Casimirs of the Lie-Poisson bracket as entropies. In two dimensions, dissipating enstrophy yields the already-known energy-constrained Navier-Stokes equations, which include a nonlocal term restoring energy balance. In three dimensions, where enstrophy is no longer a Casimir, we derive new irreversible models. For incompressible and compressible fluids carrying an advected scalar, dissipating potential enstrophy or higher potential-vorticity moments gives a nonlinear, anisotropic diffusion that acts to align the gradients of the scalar and of the potential vorticity. For a purely incompressible fluid, taking helicity as the entropy gives a first-order, non-smoothing dissipative term whose stationary states are Beltrami fields.

Title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
Author: Shuhan Li, Huankang Guan, Xintong Guo, Yang Bo, Yuyang He, Dunyuan Xu, Jingyan Chen, Fang Liu, Tsz Kin Wan, Jinpeng Chen, Zhenqi He, Yuxuan Hu, Wenbo Li, Han Gao, Qijun Li, Long Chen, Hongsheng Li, Rui Liu
Text_Content: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

Title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?
Author: Sriom Chakrabarti, Sean Bin Yang, Arijit Khan, Sebastian Link
Text_Content: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization. Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge

Title: Pseudovortex-assisted generation of first-order vector modes
Author: L. Marques Fagundes, P. Schneider Lacerda, T. A. Petry Kock, N. Rubiano da Silva, P. H. Souto Ribeiro, R. Medeiros de Araújo
Text_Content: A practical method of generating first-order vector modes like radially and azimuthally polarized modes is using the so-called vortex waveplates. Shining these plates with Gaussian beams produces parasitic higher-order modes besides the target vector beam.
