Finally, we introduce SparsePack, an efficient protocol for proving the evaluations of sparse, circuit-dependent polynomials, leveraging both packing and batched evaluations. We evaluate the efficiency of our solution on a generic neural network architecture, achieving proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches.

Title: Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR
Author: Harras Mansoor, Muhammad Wisal, Hassan Bhatti, Masood Shakir
Text_Content: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.

Title: CT-SGAL-LIO: Causal Continuous Time Refinement of Discrete LiDAR Inertial Odometry
Author: Nam Tran, Thu Tran, Toan Nguyen, William J Beksi, Tuan Dang
Text_Content: State-of-the-art LiDAR-inertial odometry methods, including those on richer state manifolds, achieve strong global accuracy, yet their pose stream alternates between propagation and correction and can oscillate over short horizons even when globally accurate. Most existing methods follow these approaches: they either modify the filter to enable faster updates or estimate a continuous-time trajectory from raw LiDAR and inertial data. The latter involves extra optimization, delaying state updates and becoming less robust during rapid rotations or accelerations. We propose CT-SGAL-LIO, a continuous-time refinement module that smooths the posterior pose stream of a discrete SGal(3) estimator without modifying the estimator itself. The key novelty is to perform continuous-time trajectory refinement directly on the projected SGal(3) posterior: we fit a cubic trajectory over a bounded window of recent poses and evaluate it at a small fixed lag. This places the query time within the observed interval, so the refined pose is obtained by interpolation rather than extrapolation, while preserving causal operation. CT-SGAL-LIO improves relative trajectory accuracy on 17 sequences from three public benchmarks. Across 17 sequences from GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE, CT-SGAL-LIO improves short-term motion accuracy while largely preserving global accuracy. RTE improves by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and on all seven GEODE sequences, with 9.9-51.1% reductions. A 19.5-min R-Campus run also reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with only a 4.7 mm change in the end-to-start gap. We plan to release our source code and results to support community validation and reproducibility.

Title: Enhancing optomechanical oscillation amplitude and frequency comb bandwidth by intensity-modulated driving
Author: Menno H. Jansen, Ewold Verhagen
Text_Content: Self-sustained oscillations in optomechanical systems are attractive as compact, low-noise sources of GHz signals and optical frequency combs for integrated photonic circuits. For these applications, the achievable oscillation amplitude directly sets clock power and comb bandwidth. This work studies the maximum amplitude that can be reached through combinations of cavity backaction and modulated optical driving, with realistic resources. For an optically driven mechanical resonator, the oscillation amplitude saturates at a level set by the finite cavity bandwidth. We show that modulating the input intensity near the mechanical resonance frequency raises the achievable amplitude toward this limit at equal mean input power and cavity linewidth. We use a cycle-averaged energy-balance analysis to identify the added power that shifts the stable periodic orbit to larger amplitudes. Numerical integration of the full equations of motion confirms the enhancement across two decades of cooperativity and sideband-resolution ratios from 0.1 to 10. The relative increase in amplitude is largest near the self-oscillation threshold and in the sideband-unresolved regime, enabling threshold-free large-amplitude oscillation where backaction alone fails to do so. The enhanced amplitude leads to a larger modulation depth of the optical field, enabling broader frequency combs, with improved stability of the comb spacing. Intensity-modulated driving thus offers power-constrained platforms a simple open-loop route to larger mechanical amplitudes and enhanced comb bandwidth.

Title: CADET: Construction of PCB Routing Instances with Executable Demonstrations
Author: Hyungseok Song, Won-Seok Choi, Seohui Bae, Han-Seul Jeong, Junseok Park, Youngjoon Park, Soonyoung Lee
Text_Content: Printed circuit board (PCB) routing is the stage of physical layout that finds paths connecting the placed pads of each net. Public datasets in this domain are few, and most contain only the final states of routed boards, not demonstrations of the electronic design automation (EDA) engine actions that produce them. To close this gap, we propose CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training), which jointly generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions. The resulting RouteDemos provides 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations (DRVs), together with their demonstrations. Their distributions over 17 statistics resemble those of 142 real reference boards. CADET trains a routing policy on these demonstrations with behavior cloning and fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning (RL). On real test boards, the policy raised the rate of complete DRV-free routing from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline. This rate was comparable to that of the open-source autorouter FreeRouting and exceeded those of the other baselines, including GPT-6 Astra. We release the dataset and its generation code as open source at https://github.com/LGAI-Research/CADET.

Title: Automated PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Scoring with Uncertainty-Guided Triage in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
Author: Kesi Xu, Ayesha Azam, Tanvier Kaur, Monika Kondratowicz, Kinza Asim, Brinder Chohan, Paapa Appiah-Odame, Zhao Chen, David Snead, Nasir Rajpoot
Text_Content: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS) informs immunotherapy selection in non-small cell lung cancer. Near the 1% and 50% cutoffs, the score should also indicate when closer review is warranted. We designed a three-stage framework to follow the sequence of TPS assessment. Stage 1 identifies tumor regions and excludes macrophage-rich patches. Stage 2, a dual-branch cell counting network (D2Count-Net), counts PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative tumor cells in these regions to calculate TPS. Stage 3, TPS-Guard, an uncertainty-guided triage mechanism, reports model uncertainty as the disagreement among independently trained models, refers the most uncertain slides, and flags scores near the 1% or 50% cutoff when model estimates disagree across that cutoff. Flags state the reason for referral or alert the pathologist to possible scoring errors on auto-reported slides. In a retrospective, single-center study, 154 whole-slide images were scored by three pathologists, and the model and each pathologist were compared in turn with the mean of the other two. On the 114 slides unseen in training, model mean absolute error (MAE) was 6.96 percentage points, within the range of the three pathologists (4.24 to 8.29), and model uncertainty correlated with absolute TPS error (Spearman rho = 0.77) and inter-pathologist disagreement (rho = 0.71). After referral of the 15% most uncertain slides, model and pathologist MAE both decreased. Applied without retraining to an external, publicly available dataset, TPS-Guard still directed review to higher-error cases, and referring more uncertain cases raised sensitivity at the 50% cutoff. TPS-Guard provides reasons for reviewing individual automated scores and identifies slides that also produce greater disagreement among pathologists. Prospective reader studies should assess TPS-Guard's effect on TPS reporting.

Title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
Author: Jaemyung Yu, Byeongho Heo, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
Text_Content: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

Title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
Author: Marie Kempkes, Jakob Spiegelberg, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
Text_Content: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

Title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
Author: Joseph G. Bronyah, Nasir U. Eisty
Text_Content: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.

Title: Edge-wise Graph Alignments
Author: Akbar Davoodi, Christoph Flamm, Daniel Merkle, Peter F. Stadler
Text_Content: Pairwise graph ``alignments'', usually defined as maximum common subgraphs, have been considered in many application domains, including the comparison of molecular structures. Most commonly, the problem is formulated as maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS) or maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) problems. Sometimes these formulations are restricted to connected common subgraphs. Common subgraph problems readily generalize to more than two input graphs. However, this concept is fundamentally distinct from the notion of multiple sequence alignments. Abstractly, alignments are defined as super-structures from which the individual input objects are recovered via structure-preserving projections. While the mathematical construction readily applies to common induced subgraphs, it does not fully encompass the common edge subgraph problem, which is the variant more commonly employed in cheminformatics applications. In order to consistently define multiple edge-based alignments of graphs we represent a graph $G$ as E-graph $(E,\mathscr{V})$, where $E$ is the edge set of $G$ and $\mathscr{V}$ is the set of sets of incident edges. This representation implicitly encodes the vertices in terms of edge data. Alignments of E-graphs are themselves E-graphs that contain the input (E-)graphs as subgraphs. Maximum edge subgraphs correspond to maximum induced sub-E-graphs, and they can thus be computed using a slightly modified version of the VF2 algorithm without the need to switch from graphs to line graphs. Furthermore, multiple alignments of (E-)graphs yield a natural definition of a consensus graph that is ``on average'' present in the input without having to be a subgraph of every (and in fact of any) input graph.

Title: TokenStream: Multi-Subject Personalized Video Generation with Token-wise LoRA and Guided Attention
Author: Hung Nguyen, Quang Qui-Vinh Nguyen, Khoi Nguyen
Text_Content: We introduce TokenStream, an optimization-based framework that composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video training dataset or joint optimization of each new subject combination. Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance difficult to separate from static-image bias, while merging independently trained adapters can mix identities. Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, providing a separate adaptation path for each subject. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while retaining personalized values. We also introduce Multi-DB, a 30-subject, 122-prompt benchmark with appearance-free prompts and varied interactions. On Multi-DB at 1.3B, TokenStream improves identity preservation from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.

Title: Chlorophyll-a Fluorescence-Based Optical Temperature Sensor Using Food-Grade Chlorella Extract
Author: Sinei Felix Gonçalves Junior, Giovanna G. S. de Miranda, Leomar S. Marques, Flavio A. M. Marques, Alexandre A. C. Cotta, Jefferson E. Tsuchida, Julio C. Ugucioni, Lidia O. Rosa, Eric Fujiwara, Cristiano M. B. Cordeiro, Jonas H. Osório
Text_Content: This letter reports the development of an optical temperature sensor based on the fluorescence of an extract obtained from \textit{Chlorella}, a unicellular microalga commercially available as food-grade biomass. Using a straightforward ethanolic extraction route, the sensing platform exploits the characteristic emission of chlorophyll-\textit{a} as the optical transducing parameter. The operating principle relies on thermal fluorescence quenching, which promotes a decrease in emission intensity with rising temperature. In the temperature range from $28.6$ to $43.0~^{\circ}\text{C}$, the sensor exhibited a linear response ($R^2 = 0.9963$) with a sensitivity of $(-8.9 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-3}~^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$. Dynamic testing over consecutive heating--cooling cycles confirmed the sensor operation under sub-degree thermal oscillations and enabled the characterization of the system's photobleaching drift ($3.65\%\cdot\text{h}^{-1}$). The results reported herein demonstrate the feasibility of exploiting sustainable, bio-derived microalgal pigments as functional photoactive materials for optical thermometry.

Title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
Author: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter
Text_Content: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

Title: A deterministic theory of kinetic fluctuations in long-range interacting homogeneous systems without collective effects
Author: Anwar El Rhirhayi, Jean-Baptiste Fouvry, Julien Barré
Text_Content: Finite-$N$ fluctuations govern the slow relaxation of long-range interacting systems, yet accessing their full statistics demands huge ensembles of costly simulations. We show that, in homogeneous systems without collective effects, this statistical problem collapses onto just three deterministic kinetic equations. Starting from the Landau-Dean-Kawasaki equation, i.e. the stochastic counterpart of the large deviation principle for the Landau equation, we derive the infinite hierarchy of $n$-point moments of the empirical distribution function at leading order in $1/N$. We prove that it is solved exactly by a quasi-Gaussian closure. The resulting minimal Landau fluctuation hierarchy is formed by the Landau equation, a Lyapunov equation for the two-point moment, and a kinetic equation for the three-point moment. From these three equations, all higher-order moments follow algebraically. The hierarchy exactly preserves the collisional invariants and their fluctuations, and predicts the full probability distribution of observables in the central fluctuation regime. Benchmarked against $N$-body realizations, it reproduces the mean, variance and higher-order moments with an accuracy that improves systematically with $N$. A single deterministic time-integration of three coupled partial differential equations thus replaces large ensembles of simulations, for any large $N$.

Title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search
Author: Jarosław Janas, Paweł Morawiecki, Josef Pieprzyk
Text_Content: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limitations of codebook-based watermarking for short-form attribution.

Title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
Author: Mahesh Madhav
Text_Content: Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges. Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

Title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
Author: Wieger Wesselink, Kees Huizing, Huub van de Wetering
Text_Content: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

Title: Self-consistent thermal-runaway electron equilibria
Author: M. Keu, M. Hole, A. Malaquias
Text_Content: In this work, we develop and solve a self-consistent equilibrium model for plasmas containing thermal and runaway electron (RE) populations, motivated by observations of residual plasma density during alternating-current (AC) transitions in ISTTOK. We adopt an existing monoenergetic, narrow-pitch guiding-center formulation, while retaining a spatially varying toroidal-field function, and show that prescribing the radius-weighted RE density by the orbit label alone conflicts with particle conservation and vector equilibrium wherever the thermal toroidal-field function varies along an occupied drift contour. Both conditions instead require the ratio of RE density to toroidal field to be constant along each drift contour. Taking this ratio as a function of the orbit label gives a compatible closure that relates the equilibrium RE density to a prescribed reference profile. Combined with Grad-Shafranov-Helmholtz thermal free functions, it yields a closed field equation that retains the displacement between drift and magnetic surfaces. At fixed thermal coefficients, we prove existence for every finite reference-profile amplitude under sign and spectral conditions. We also prove local constrained existence and uniqueness near a thermal equilibrium with a nonsingular current-beta response and derive a current-pressure bound. An ISTTOK ramp-down example with a prescribed 20% energetic-current fraction and 2 keV energy gives a magnetic-orbit axis separation of 2.39 mm. The resulting fields and current distributions can serve as initial conditions for studies of electron survival and plasma recovery through AC reversal.

Title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks
Author: Guoliang Weng, Enqi Zhang, Lizhao You, Deqing Wang, Liqun Fu
Text_Content: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.

Title: Optimal Polyomino Fences
Author: Alexis Langlois-Rémillard, Mia N. Müßig, Helmut Podhaisky, Erika Roldan, Günter Rote, Maximilian Brömme, Matthes Norden, Maximilian Prietzel, Daniel Yu, Mykhailo Lyader
Text_Content: The $n$-omino fence problem asks how many cells can be surrounded by placing every $n$-omino exactly once in the grid. We present a new dynamic programming approach for this problem, allowing us to prove optimality for the pentomino and hexomino fence and to classify all possible pentomino orders by optimal area. For the first time we also provide strong heuristic solutions and upper bounds for all fences up to $n = 15$, after which we even approximate the $500$-omino fence with computational experiments. Finally, we generalize the problem to 3D, where we prove optimality for pentacubes and derive heuristic solutions for hexacubes and heptacubes.

Title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
Author: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger
Text_Content: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.

Title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
Author: Paarth Batra, Aryan Keluskar
Text_Content: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

Title: Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems
Author: Hanrui Zhang
Text_Content: We study online selection problems subject to arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, under different arrival orders, with different distributional assumptions. We establish the following bounds: (1) $Θ(\log^2 n / \log \log n)$ for the standard (adversarial-order) prophet problem, (2) $Ω(\log n)$ for the (Bayesian, random-order) prophet secretary problem, and by extension, for the standard (prior-free, random-order) secretary problem, and (3) $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ for the free-order prophet problem. Together with complementary bounds established in prior work, these results pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all these variants of prophet and secretary problems subject to downward-closed constraints. Our results refine and reinforce the big-decisions-first principle by Rubinstein and Singla [2026], establishing a superconstant separation between the random-order and free-order models.

Title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
Author: Xijun Wang, Zhaoyang Liu, Xiang Chen, Howard H. Yang, Chenyuan Feng
Text_Content: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

Title: Topology-Aware Handover Management for Service Continuity in LEO Satellite Networks
Author: Jui-Che Han, Nasir Khan, Siva Satya Sri Ganesh Seeram, Cicek Cavdar
Text_Content: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are expected to play a key role in sixth-generation (6G) non-terrestrial networks. The high mobility of LEO satellites necessitates frequent handovers (HOs), posing challenges to service continuity and availability for user equipment. Conventional methods based on handover margin (HOM) and time-to-trigger (TTT) have limited adaptability to time-varying channel conditions and do not explicitly account for the impact of feeder-link and ground station (GS) connectivity on HO interruption time. To address these limitations, this paper develops a topology-aware HO framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The framework uses reference signal received power (RSRP), satellite--GS associations, remaining visibility time, and elevation angles to determine when to initiate an HO and which satellite to select. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed policy achieves a service availability of 99.32% at a minimum elevation angle of 40 degrees, exceeding that of optimized HOM--TTT (O-HT) and least-delay (LD) satellite selection by 1.67 and 1.41 percentage points, respectively. The policy maintains service availability above 97.52% as the minimum elevation angle increases to 55 degrees, demonstrating its ability to sustain high service availability under stricter elevation constraints.

Title: Informative Path Planning with Gaussian Processes: Error Bounds, Algorithms, and Benchmarks
Author: Kalvik Jakkala, Jennifer Wakulicz, Donald G. Dansereau, Srinivas Akella, Lantao Liu, Jason M. O'Kane
Text_Content: Accurate environmental monitoring relies on Informative Path Planning (IPP) to deploy autonomous systems that maximize information gain. While Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a robust mathematical foundation for modeling the environment, contemporary IPP approaches remain hindered by heuristic operational constraints and the lack of simultaneous theoretical guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. Rather than introducing yet another heuristic, this paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of existing error bounds and algorithms to further develop the mathematical foundation for IPP. By evaluating probabilistic and deterministic bounds on reconstruction error, we establish that predictive variance is the theoretically ideal optimization objective for GP-based IPP. Furthermore, we analyze GreedyCover, a recent approach for optimizing predictive variance, and demonstrate that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms that this approach delivers superior estimation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prominent information-theoretic objectives and optimization methods used in IPP. Finally, this theoretical analysis establishes a rigorous, near-optimal foundation for discrete offline IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints, offering clear and principled guidance for future work in continuous-space and online formulations.

Title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
Author: Boumediene Hamzi, Houman Owhadi
Text_Content: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $κ$ has sharp order $κ^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

Title: Rotationally Symmetric Lattice Boltzmann Pseudopotential Methods for Porous Media Applications
Author: Benjamin Kellers, Arnulf Latz, Timo Danner
Text_Content: Pseudopotential models are a well established approach for multiphase and multicomponent simulations using the lattice Boltzmann method. Although not the most accurate, they are often chosen for ease of implementation and adaptability. A drawback of the models are spurious currents at the interfaces and particularly at solid walls which introduce numerical artifacts. An improved lattice Boltzmann pseudopotential model is presented. The discrete fluid density gradients in the coupling force are computed with rotationally symmetric gradient operators formulated as a convolution. As a result, spurious currents are reduced in settings where solid walls are unaligned with the lattice directions. Additionally, variations of introducing fluid-solid interaction either equally through both fluids or through a single fluid only are compared. Presented model variants are compared using droplets on walls as a common benchmark, analytically solvable capillary rise experiments (Jurin's law), and porous media imbibition as a practical application. Rotationally symmetric operators outperform the classical lattice weights approach in all tests in terms of accuracy, while avoiding extending the lattice to compute higher order gradients. The choice of the fluid-solid interaction variant depends on the problem under consideration and the desired properties of the resulting model.

Title: ACE-CaP-0: Real-World Code-as-Policies in the Era of Experience
Author: ACE-CaP Team, Changxu Wei, Yunpeng Qing, Guozheng Ma, Bowen Liu, Zexin He, Yilun Kong, Haoming Gu, Jingyuan Liu, Tianyu Zhu, Jianfei Wang, Junqiang Kou, Huinan Mo, Hao Lv, Pengbin Li, Yuesong Wang, Bo Li, Huan Zhou, Shunyu Liu, Chunxiao Liu, Bixuan Jin, Shaopeng Yin, Fei Wang, Zhi Hou, Jiaxing Huang, Changqing Zou, Dacheng Tao, Xiaogang Wang
Text_Content: Recent advances in frontier models have pushed the boundaries of agentic robot control, enabling agents to perform complex robotic tasks through reasoning and interaction. However, repeated calls to these models during execution can substantially increase task completion time. Code as Policies (CaP) offers a route for coding agents to acquire physical skills through experience and retain them in executable programs, allowing the reasoning invested in development to be reused across runs. Developing reliable code policies while limiting the cost of physical experimentation remains a central challenge. We investigate human guidance as a source of priors for feasible actions and simulation as an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate policies. Our findings favor robot demonstrations available on request and simulation used selectively during real-world policy refinement. These findings inform ACE-CaP-0, an agentic recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks spanning alignment, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination, the resulting frozen programs achieve 92.1\% success (221/240 trials). Mean execution times across tasks range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. The programs execute with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop. These results highlight CaP's potential to turn experience into reliable, reusable physical skills.

Title: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data
Author: Diyako Ghaderyan, Stefan Werner
Text_Content: Decentralized training of deep learning models keeps training data local and supports on-device learning over networks. In realistic scenarios, heterogeneity across agents' local data poses an optimization challenge and can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs. Building on recent advances in centralized primal averaging, we propose Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer. DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation, and output averaging, while using consecutive mixed iterates to construct a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a convergence bound for DPA and identify conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents for sufficiently many iterations. We also introduce DPA-1G, a variant that uses one communication round per iteration and matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines. Experiments following the GUT decentralized image-classification benchmark show that DPA compares favorably with DSGD, gradient tracking, QG-DSGDm, momentum tracking, and QG-GUTm across datasets, architectures, topologies, and heterogeneity levels, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20. Our code is publicly available.

Title: TRACE: Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis
Author: Wei Wei, Liangze Ke, Tianzhi Tang, Pavan Challa, Tulika Rudra Gupta, Guannan Gong, Satrajit Roychoudhury, Raghav Sundar
Text_Content: External trial evidence can inform oncology trial design, but broad pooling may produce benchmarks poorly aligned with the planned population. We developed TRACE (Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis), combining eligibility screening, Bayesian compatibility assessment using published baseline characteristics, and hierarchical survival modeling. An integrated compatibility score based on the largest standardized difference in jointly reported characteristics identifies compatible external trials. Their reconstructed control-arm survival data are synthesized using a hierarchical beta-Stacy process to generate a predictive survival benchmark. We evaluated TRACE using eleven randomized phase III trials in first-line HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. With KEYNOTE-859 as the target, three external trials were selected. TRACE predicted a control-arm median overall survival of 11.8 months (95% posterior predictive interval, 8.9-15.2), compared with an observed median of 11.8 months (95% confidence interval, 10.9-12.7). In leave-one-trial-out validation, seven targets had compatible external evidence. Predictive intervals contained the observed median for all seven. In comparison, confidence intervals from Kaplan-Meier estimates pooling all other trials' control arms contained it for five. Mean pointwise curve coverage was 92% for TRACE and 59% for pooled Kaplan-Meier. For four targets without compatible external evidence, TRACE returned a weakly informative prior predictive benchmark. TRACE provides a transparent approach to selecting relevant external evidence and generating benchmarks for oncology trial planning.

Title: Raysemble: Metric 3D Bone Reconstruction from a Single X-ray
Author: Xiaoyang Li, Xinghao Yan, Yuan Chai
Text_Content: Raysemble reconstructs eight lumbar and pelvic bones from a single X-ray by separating shape and placement. Each 3D query samples regional and global features at its image projection. A shared decoder predicts normalized bone shapes. Predicted depth and camera geometry determine 3D centers and scales for resampling these shapes onto a common grid in millimeters. Evaluation uses 23 held-out patients with 43 CT scans, each generating one simulated anteroposterior radiograph. Without rigid alignment to CT,Raysemble leads 15 evaluated methods, averaging 65.24% Dice, 9.09 mm HD95, and 3.32 mm ASSD over three random seeds. With identical inputs, it improves Dice over VolumeNeRF by 5.86 percentage points.

Title: Inverse Design of an On-chip Phase-Change Switch Composed of Sparse Heterogeneous Metasurfaces
Author: Sanaz Zarei
Text_Content: Photonic switches are exploited for optical signal routing and control within optical communication systems. The integration of phase change materials with silicon photonic switches overcomes the drawbacks of the state-of-the-art photonic switches based on electro-optic and thermo-optic effects. In this work, a 1x2 on-chip switch with a footprint of 6.3umx31um based on on-chip one-dimensional metasurfaces is inverse-designed. The on-chip metasurfaces are heterogeneous, which their meta-atoms can be composed of either SiO2 or the phase-change material Sb2Se3. This helps to the realization of higher extinction ratio between the switch outputs, especially at the amorphous state which has a small refractive index contrast to that of the silicon. To benefit from structural, fabrication and switching simplicity, sparse parameterization is followed in the inverse design of the switch using ternary search (TS) and particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithms.

Title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning
Author: Deyao Hong, Jiayi Jiang, Yuchun Chen, Yixuan Shi, Wenyi Li, Zheng Jiang, Chengxing Xie, Mingyu Su, Qingle Liu, Mingju Gao, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Calvin Xiao, Kaisen Yang, Huan-ang Gao
Text_Content: While language-model agents excel at long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, this success relies on two conditions: explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. However, neither condition holds in real-world problems where critical information exists only in images, leaving it unclear whether long-horizon capability transfers from text to visual reasoning. In such visual settings, because rules and clues resist text transcription and lack test-case feedback, agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations, and autonomously cross-check clues. Despite this challenge, existing evaluations fail to capture such capability: visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, whereas agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that permit trial-and-error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual Cipher Bench, a collection of 40 original visual puzzles across four categories: spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle provides only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, requiring agents to discover the underlying solving mechanism entirely from the images. Across 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves only 26.7% accuracy, while five of the eight models score below 1%. Yet on a ten-task subset, providing a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 7.8% to 55.6%. This sharp contrast shows that the primary bottleneck of current agents lies not in executing multi-step plans, but in autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. Visual Cipher Bench thus provides a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents.

Title: Complex nematic dynamics driven by steady Kolmogorov flows
Author: Rahil N Valani, Sumesh P Thampi, Julia M Yeomans
Text_Content: Complex nematohydrodynamics, including irregular defect dynamics, is commonly associated with time-dependent flows, most notably in active turbulence. Here we consider a simple model of a planar nematic subjected to a temporally steady but spatially varying flow and investigate the onset of time-dependent dynamics. Subjecting a passive nematic to steady Kolmogorov flow, while eliminating velocity fluctuations and hydrodynamic feedback, we find that increasing the flow strength drives a transition from stationary to periodic and, at stronger forcing, irregular spatiotemporal dynamics. The time-dependent states involve repeated local suppression of nematic order and director reorganisation, arising from the competition between spatially varying shear and nematic relaxation. Bifurcation and phase-space analyses characterise this progression, while reduced-order models identify the dynamical origins. A two-mode model captures the onset of periodic motion through a saddle-node infinite-period bifurcation. A five-mode Galerkin truncation further recovers the progression from stationary to periodic and irregular dynamics. These results allow us to explain how a fixed, spatially heterogeneous velocity field can generate temporal complexity through the nonlinear dynamics of nematic order alone.

Title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
Author: Pedro Augusto Londe Ribeiro, Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Joberto S. B. Martins, Tereza C. Carvalho, Flávio de Oliveira Silva
Text_Content: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.

Title: Ultracompact and Nonvolatile On-chip Switch Based on DBS and PSO Algorithms
Author: Sanaz Zarei
Text_Content: A 1x2 photonic switch based on silicon-on-insulator (SOI)-Sb2Se3 hybrid platform is inverse-designed using direct binary search (DBS) and particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithms. The nonvolatile on-chip switch is designed to consist of minimum switchable phase-change units and operates based on the en-masse switching of all Sb2Se3 cells from crystalline to amorphous and vice-versa. The device has a small footprint of only 6.3umx31um. At the wavelength of 1550nm, it exhibits an insertion loss of less than 0.96dB, and its crosstalk is measured to be less than -12dB within the three-dimensional (3D) finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations.

Title: Constrained intersection representations and forbidden patterns
Author: Laurent Feuilloley, Michel Habib, Amalia Sorondo
Text_Content: We study the interplay between two types of graph classes: the ones defined by intersections of geometric objects and the ones defined by the absence of a substructure. More precisely, we study intersection graphs that are grounded, that is, the objects lie above a horizontal line that they touch, and ordered graphs with forbidden patterns, that is, ordered graphs that avoid a set of ordered induced subgraphs. These two approaches are fundamentally different, but it is known that several interesting graph classes have both types of characterizations, and we aim to understand whether this is a general phenomenon. Our contributions are the following. First, we identify a family of patterns on four vertices and a natural hierarchy of intersection graphs of strings whose classes are nicely interleaved. This raises hopes to prove connections between the two perspectives. Second, we dampen these hopes by proving that a class of (ordered) intersection graphs that we study cannot be characterized by a finite set of forbidden patterns. Third, we show a dual impossibility result: there exists a pattern-defined class of our hierarchy that admits no intersection representation, if we require this representation to be closed under natural operations such as translation and scaling. However, it turns out that if we allow slightly more exotic intersection representations, then we can find one for this pattern-defined class.

Title: Impact of edge-localized resonant magnetic perturbation on L-H transition in the KSTAR tokamak
Author: Y. Zhang, M. Jiang, K. X. Han, W. H. Ko, S. M. Yang, J. D. Hu, Z. B. Guo, M. J. Choi, J. W. Juhn, J. Lee, J. H. Lee, Y. H. Lee, Y. F. Liu, X. B. Li, Y. R. Zhu, G. Q. Dong, G. Z. Hao
Text_Content: The impact of edge-localized resonant magnetic perturbation (ERMP) on the low-to-high (L-H) confinement mode transition is investigated through dedicated experiments on the KSTAR tokamak with tungsten divertor and numerical simulations with a one-dimensional (1D) reduced transport model. Experimentally, under matched conditions, the ERMP inhibits the L-H transition, whereas the reference discharge without ERMP enters H-mode. The ERMP enhances edge electron temperature fluctuations and the turbulence decorrelation rate, and flattens the toroidal rotation, reducing the edge $E\times B$ velocity shear below the threshold required for turbulence suppression. An extended 1D predator-prey model, which incorporates toroidal flow evolution and realistic radial profile of the magnetic perturbation due to plasma response field, reproduces the experimental trends of enhanced turbulence, reduced ExB flow shear, and inhibited L-H transition. These findings contribute to a better understanding of how ERMP affects L-H transition dynamics in tungsten divertor environments and offer a valuable reference for the application of ERMP in current and future fusion devices.

Title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
Author: Qin Xin
Text_Content: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $Δ_0$ suffice for a $15(Δ_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $Θ(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(Δ_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((Δ_0+1)(d+\log(k/η)))$ slots with failure probability at most $η$; for fixed $Δ_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/η))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

Title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
Author: Aarne Talman, Stergios Chatzikyriakidis
Text_Content: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

Title: Functional Regression with Interacting Latent Mean and Variance Processes
Author: Ching-Chia Chou, Jeng-Min Chiou
Text_Content: In many applications, variability itself carries important predictive information beyond the mean, and its association with an outcome may further depend on the underlying mean trajectory. However, existing functional regression approaches primarily rely on mean-based representations of functional predictors, while variability is often ignored or reduced to scalar summaries. We propose a functional regression framework that incorporates latent mean and variance processes as predictors, together with their mean-variance interaction, allowing the predictive contribution of variability to depend on the underlying mean trajectory. We establish consistency and convergence rates for the estimated coefficient functions and interaction surface, accounting for reconstruction errors, increasing observation frequency, and diverging truncation dimensions without requiring independence between the latent processes. Applications to real data demonstrate substantial gains in predictive accuracy from incorporating the variance process, with the proposed approach outperforming competing functional regression methods in the Tecator application and revealing localized mean-variance interaction patterns.

Title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
Author: Sheng Tang, Shengzhe Wei, Tiancheng Chen, Wenhua Jin, Xinyang Lu, Tinghao Jiang, Shuoxuan Feng, Yupeng Liu, Yu Zhang, Xingshuo Chang, Keren Zhou, Yuhan Xiong, Jiahao Li, Haoming Liu, Jituo Tian, Hui Liang, Chaoqun Tang, Feng Tian, Wentao Ouyang, Kaojin Zhu, Xiaolin Chai, Peihuang Fu, Miao Zheng, Yunbo Hu, Feixue Cai, Zizhen Zou, Weigang Wang, Yexuan Yang, Haoyu Feng, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
Text_Content: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

Title: An upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron
Author: A. Yu. Chirkov, S. I. Veselov, D. V. Gribanov, D. S. Malyshev, N. Yu. Zolotykh
Text_Content: We establish the first nontrivial upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron, resolving a long-standing open question. For an $n$-dimensional corner polyhedron associated with an integer lattice of determinant $δ$, the number of edges is at most $$ O\left(n6^n \cdot \bigl(1+\log_2(2δ)\bigr)^{2n-3}\right). $$ This improves the standard bound obtained by counting pairs of vertices, reducing the logarithmic exponent from $(2n-2)$ to $(2n-3)$.

Title: The landscape of quantum technology companies in 2026
Author: Zeki Can Seskir, Orcun Kocak, Arsev Umur Aydinoglu
Text_Content: We update our 2022 mapping of 441 quantum technology (QT) companies and examine how the industry has developed. The principal dataset now includes 1,092 companies founded with a QT focus, of which 935 remain active. Public sources and archived company websites provide evidence on company formation, technology fields and geography, alongside acquisitions, closures, valuations and involvement in artificial intelligence, defence and space. Company formation continued beyond the apparent 2018 peak in the earlier study. Computing software and applications remain the largest field, with suppliers and supporting businesses accounting for almost a third of active companies. Countries with similar company totals can have different technological profiles, and regional comparisons reveal concentrations obscured by country rankings. The first companies generally preceded the selected national policy milestones. Supporting businesses usually followed technical companies in the same jurisdiction. AI is more prevalent than defence in current company activities, while defence shows the larger increase from the earliest assessed evidence. Space relevance is documented for more than a quarter of active companies, often alongside defence involvement.

Title: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring
Author: Huiling Xie, Zitan Chen
Text_Content: For any fixed integers $q\ge2$ and $t\ge1$, we construct explicit $q$-ary codes of length $n$ that correct any combination of at most $t$ insertions, deletions, and substitutions, with redundancy at most $2t\log_q n+O_{q,t}(\log\log n)$ $q$-ary symbols. This matches the leading redundancy term of Levenshtein's classical existential bound. Building on the standard graph-coloring approach, we use a prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph to assign multiple colors to each $q$-ary word of length $m<n$. Appending a short, edit-protected representation of an assigned color to the length-$m$ word yields a length-$n$ codeword. The choice among the assigned colors carries additional message information, thereby reducing the redundancy. The construction admits deterministic encoding and decoding in $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{6t+2})$ and $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{7t+2})$ time, respectively.

Title: Earlier citation practices are linked to signs of artificial intelligence use in scientific writing
Author: Hongkan Chen, Yongyuan He, Qingshan Zhou, Yi Bu
Text_Content: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more common in scientific writing, some authors show fewer signs of AI assistance than expected across successive periods. We analysed OpenAlex publication histories for 71,133 authors with at least one eligible first-authored English-language publication each year from 2023 through September 2026. Using abstract-based writing scores, we defined resistance as the predicted minus observed share of abstracts classified as AI-assisted. Positive scores indicate fewer such abstracts than expected. Early resistance was positively associated with later resistance, although the share with positive scores fell. Environmental characteristics contributed more than individual characteristics to predicting later scores, although overall predictive power was low. Having a collaborator with a non-positive early score was associated with lower subsequent resistance. Authors with positive mean scores in both 2023-2024 and 2025-2026 cited older work, drew on fewer subfields and more often cited sources they had used before than authors with non-positive mean scores in both periods. These differences were evident before 2023. The adjusted gap in reference reuse rose from 3.24 percentage points before 2023 to 7.95 in 2025-2026. The findings link variation in signs of AI assistance to earlier differences in how scientists used prior work.

Title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
Author: Sofia Baiocco, Gianluca Bonifazi, Christopher Buratti, Michele Marchetti, Camilla Mazzoli, Federica Parlapiano, Giulia Quaglieri, Davide Traini, Domenico Ursino, Luca Virgili
Text_Content: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

Title: A Class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions on $SE_n(3)$ for Motion Estimation
Author: Shijie Wang, Haichao Gui, Rui Zhong
Text_Content: This paper proposes a novel class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions (BCDs) on extended special Euclidean groups SE_n(3) for global motion uncertainty representation and estimation. BCDs are constructed by restricting matrix Gaussian distributions on ambient Euclidean space to SE_n(3), avoiding singularity of local coordinates. The unique feature of BCDs is their conjugacy to a broad class of sampling distributions arising in motion estimation, enabling exact closed-form Bayesian inference. Optimal estimation with respect to BCDs is further investigated for implementing motion estimation. Two means are extracted as random state estimates, which maximize probability and minimize mean squared error, respectively. Moreover, within the BCD class, moment matching is shown to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and maximum likelihood estimation is also derived, which provide analytical methods to approximate underlying distributions with the optimality guarantee. As an application, a Bayesian estimator for pose and velocity estimation of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is developed within an assumed density filtering architecture. The propagation and estimate extraction leverage the optimal estimation related to BCDs, and the landmark measurements are exactly fused with the BCD prior in closed form due to the conjugacy. Numerical simulations of a UAV flight indicate the advantages of BCD-based estimators over two classic Kalman filters on Lie groups with various initial uncertainties and measurement noise.

Title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
Author: Mariya
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tested on medical exam questions, but accuracy alone does not show when an answer can be trusted. I study the calibration and uncertainty of two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat (both run in 4-bit precision), on 2,816 English multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA and 4,927 Arabic multiple-choice questions from MedAraBench. Accuracy was 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais. Raw option probabilities were overconfident in all four settings (expected calibration error 0.242 to 0.486), and a single temperature parameter removed 82% to 93% of that error. Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty.

Title: Canonical Truncation for Mixed-Integer and Combinatorial n-Fold Optimization
Author: Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, Björn Schumacher
Text_Content: We consider a special block-structured integer program with $n$ blocks. Every block has a prescribed number of vectors that need to be selected while minimizing the objective $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$, where $c$ is a rational cost vector, $A$ is an integral matrix with $d$ rows, and $g \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to \mathbb{Q}\cup \{+\infty\}$ is an arbitrary function. We access $g$ via an oracle that minimizes $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$ when all but $O(d)$ variables are fixed. Our algorithm runs in time $(ndΔ)^{O(d)}(Q + \text{poly}(|I|))$ where $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of an entry in $A$, $Q$ is the necessary time to evaluate the oracle for $g$ and $|I|$ is the size of the input. This model is a variation of the model studied by Dadush et al.~[IPCO 23]. Their model has only a single block but individual upper and lower bounds on the variables instead of prescribed block sums. For their model they present an algorithm with running time $t^d(dΔ)^{O(d^2)}Q$ where $t$ is the number of variables. We use our algorithm to solve mixed-integer linear programs with no upper bounds on the variables, a linear objective, and arbitrarily many constraints involving only fractional variables in time $(mΔ)^{O(m)}\text{poly}(|I|)$, where $m$ is the number of constraints involving integral variables and $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of coefficients of integral variables. This improves the dependence on $m$ in the exponent to asymptotically match the dependency in the integer setting. Further, we use our algorithm to generalize the parameterized algorithm for scheduling on uniformly related machines by Rohwedder~[ICALP 25] to obtain an algorithm for multiple knapsack with running time $w_{\max}^{O(d)}\text{poly}(|I|)$ where $w_{\max}$ is the maximum weight of an item and $d$ the number of different weights.

Title: Signed Dyadic Path Encoding for Efficient Non-Interactive Private Decision Tree Evaluation over TFHE
Author: Xintong Song, Yiqiang Zhao, Qizhi Zhang, Yao Li, Jiaji He, Fei Zhao
Text_Content: Private decision-tree evaluation lets a server classify a client's encrypted query without learning the input. In the non-interactive, path-based setting over TFHE, the server returns a single encrypted prediction by aggregating per-path comparison outcomes, and the standard per-leaf formulation pays one programmable bootstrap (PBS) per leaf, which dominates the cost. We propose a signed dyadic path-sum encoding that nearly halves this cost: each internal node receives a signed dyadic label so that every root-to-leaf path accumulates a distinct integer sum, which lets the two children of a leaf-parent be packed into a single test polynomial and resolved by one PBS, reducing the PBS count from the number of leaves to the number of leaf-parents. We formalize the distinct-sum property and prove that the dyadic labeling is the range-minimal encoding satisfying it, and its half-symmetric signed form is magnitude-optimal, tightening the comparison-stage noise bound at fixed parameters. We derive the two conditions under which the encrypted evaluation returns the exact prediction and instantiate parameters with per-inference failure below $2^{-64}$ at 128-bit security. We show that the ring degree grows linearly with the consumed plaintext range, which confines the profitable regime to depths $\leq 4$, where our method stays faster even when each scheme runs at its own cost-optimal parameters. We further extend the encoding to gradient-boosted ensembles. On standard UCI benchmarks at depths 1-4, our method reduces single-tree latency by $1.51\times$-$1.92\times$ and ensemble latency by $2\times$, without accuracy loss, while preserving the compact, non-interactive response.

Title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
Author: Tiandong Wang
Text_Content: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks.
