Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

Title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
Author: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis
Text_Content: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.

Title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms
Author: Seungwoo Han, Gil Hong, Jewan Kim, Jeuk Yu, Sangjun Lee, Byeongok Cho, Jusung Jeon
Text_Content: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli naïve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.

Title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls
Author: Divyanshu Goyal, Gabriel Ruiz, Amir Meisami
Text_Content: Photo retouching models are trained on pairs of original and retouched photographs, usually edited by experts. Expert edits are costly, so the two main public sets, FiveK and PPR10K, hold only 16,161 originals. Good photographs on their own are far easier to find: commercial stock collections and free ones such as Pixabay and Unsplash hold millions. We learn retouching from them alone: we damage each photograph the way a camera or a careless edit would, which gives a worse and a better version of the same photograph. From these pairs, our model, ATune, learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise a photograph's quality. The edit is declarative: ATune sets target values for the attributes, and a simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box photo editor until the photograph reaches them. Every edit is a list of slider values a person can read and adjust. The same model can drive any editor that makes those changes; we test RawTherapee and darktable. We train on 10M photographs from a commercial stock collection and test on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ. Nine quality judges score every edit, and in a user study 157 human raters made 9,253 choices between our edit and another method's edit of the same photograph. When Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra edit the same photographs in the same editor, raters prefer our edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rate them even with Claude's (50.5%). We also compare with supervised retouchers on their home ground: NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, each trained on that set's own expert edits. Raters chose our edits in 46.3% of those comparisons. ATune, a 54M-parameter model trained without a single expert edit, now matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders.

Title: Axial von Mises Framework for Tensor-Dependent Second-Harmonic Generation
Author: Sui Ip Ng, Yi-Ping Ho, Ken-Tye Yong
Text_Content: We derive closed-form relations between projected fibril-axis statistics and tensor-dependent second-harmonic generation (SHG) harmonics using a single axial von Mises population. Under coherent emission within domains and detected intensity addition across domains, each angular harmonic factors into a local tensor coefficient and an axial circular moment. Parallel-analyzer detection contains second, fourth and sixth harmonics; ideal equal-weight analyzer-free detection contains second and fourth harmonics. The resulting formulas identify geometry-specific harmonic zeros, sensitivity loss and ambiguous inversion of a secondary fixed-angle ratio. In particular, the analyzer-free fourth-harmonic zero at $ρ=1/3$ does not imply loss of all orientation sensitivity. Prepared-cornea forward/reverse recordings illustrate extraction of empirical analyzer-free harmonics. In the bundle ROI, second harmonics are resolved in both sweeps, while their normalized amplitudes differ and fourth harmonics remain unresolved. An exploratory central ROI from the same recordings yields a different forward/reverse profile. Within the same operator-identified tissue, low-signal space coverage and apparent fibre alignment vary slightly across recordings. These observations support angular-measurement feasibility while leaving quantitative normalized-shape agreement unestablished. The thermal extension illustrates consequences of assumed kinetics rather than calibrated tissue trajectories. The contribution is an analytical interpretation of SHG harmonics with explicit conditions for physical inference; the measurements do not establish absolute susceptibility ratio $ρ$, axial concentration $κ$, or experimental separation of thermal disorder from degradation.

Title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
Author: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Daksh Maan, Avinash Benki, Parijat Chatterjee, Pasunuti Prasanjith, Purusharth Malik
Text_Content: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.

Title: Testing Conditional Mean Independence
Author: Chung Eun Lee, Xianyang Zhang
Text_Content: This article introduces a novel nonparametric test for conditional mean independence, which formally evaluates whether a random vector X has an additional impact on the mean regression function of a response Y when a conditioning random vector Z is already included. By framing the problem as classical partial effect testing, our approach goes beyond traditional parametric models to provide a highly general and flexible framework. The test statistic is constructed using martingale difference divergence (MDD) after neutralizing the effect of Z on Y via a sieve approximation. The population residual MDD characterizes conditional mean independence under suitable moment conditions. We present a theoretical framework for the test under both a fixed number of basis functions and a growing sieve dimension. We derive the nonstandard and non-pivotal asymptotic null distributions in both regimes. To facilitate practical implementation, we propose a wild bootstrap procedure to approximate these limiting distributions and establish its asymptotic consistency. To establish the fundamental properties required for the test to be widely useful, we conduct a power analysis, demonstrating the test's consistency under fixed alternatives and establishing its asymptotic power against local alternatives. The practical utility and finite-sample performance of the proposed test are examined through simulation studies and an exploratory application to a real-world variable selection problem in regression modeling. The code for the proposed test and numerical simulations can be found at: https://github.com/leece087/Conditional-Mean-Independence-Test.

Title: Disentangled Embedding Optimization for Diffusion-Based Dataset Distillation
Author: Hongcheng Li, Yucan Zhou, Yibin Wang, Xiaoyan Gu, Bo Li, Weiping Wang
Text_Content: Dataset distillation aims to compress large-scale datasets into compact synthetic subsets that enable efficient model training with comparable performance to the original data. Recent advances show that diffusion models are highly effective for this task due to their strong generative capability. Existing diffusion-based approaches typically perform class-wise clustering and use the obtained cluster prototypes as diffusion inputs to generate distilled samples. However, the uniformly distributed original samples in a category inevitably lead to entanglement near cluster boundaries, pulling the cluster prototypes closer and reducing the inter-cluster separation. Consequently, the diffusion model receives overly similar latent inputs, resulting in synthetic data with limited diversity. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO), a simple yet effective framework that replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. These embeddings are optimized to match the Gaussian statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of the original data distribution, while a diversity regularizer is designed to encourage separation among these embeddings to improve the intra-class variability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DEO can generate more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior generalization across multiple datasets.

Title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
Author: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, Zhuoshi Tong, Haisen Liao, Sicheng Zhou
Text_Content: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

Title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
Author: BWM Team
Text_Content: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

Title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
Author: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
Text_Content: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

Title: A Coupled Control Barrier Function Approach to Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Conflict Resolution
Author: Gary Rostomyan, Ketan Savla, Petros A. Ioannou
Text_Content: Many robotic applications involve scenarios where multiple robots interact and the decisions of one robot influence the behavior of others. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based feedback controller for multi-robot conflict resolution with input constraints. Safety is enforced using coupled Control Barrier Function (CBF), while a yielding matrix encodes how robots influence each other. Unlike existing methods with fixed or hard priorities, the proposed framework enables yielding preferences while guaranteeing deadlock-free operation by design. Sufficient conditions are established for the controller to be locally Lipschitz. The optimal CBF sign- indefinite slack is shown to admit a finite uniform bound, which is compensated through an enlarged CBF safety margin to obtain a forward invariant set contained within the desired safe set. The analysis also identifies an irreducible slack component due to finite maximum deceleration that cannot be eliminated by increasing the slack penalty. Finally, sufficient conditions on the yielding matrix and nominal controller are derived to exclude deadlock states. Simulations demonstrate adaptive coordination across yielding preferences and robustness to robot failures.

Title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
Author: Zhiyu Hou, Wen-Jie Shu, Harold Haodong Chen, Weilin Ruan, Chenfei Liao, Liuzhou Zhang, Disen Lan, Xiaogang Xu, Qi Chen, Ser-Nam Lim
Text_Content: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

Title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
Author: Mohanned Ahmed
Text_Content: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.

Title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
Author: Sahit Chintalapudi, Xiaoyan Wang, Aryan Zoroufi, Aditya Agarwal, Nancy Kanwisher, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
Text_Content: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.

Title: SPEM: Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling for LiDAR Point Cloud Compression
Author: Bojun Liu, Yangzhi Ma, Jie Li, Dong Liu, Li Li
Text_Content: LiDAR point clouds exhibit scan-induced spatial regularities that are informative for geometry compression. Existing scan-aware approaches often exploit these regularities by transforming coded geometry into spherical or beam-aligned coordinate systems. However, this couples acquisition priors with geometry representation, altering spatial partitioning and quantization, and potentially preventing exact recovery of the original Cartesian geometry. We argue that acquisition priors should guide probability modeling rather than dictate the coding representation. We propose SPEM, a Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling framework that exploits LiDAR scanning regularities within the entropy model without requiring coordinate transformation. We introduce a multi-frequency spherical rotary positional encoding that captures scan-aligned spatial relationships in both backbone self-attention and decoded-context retrieval. Building upon this encoding, we develop a decoded-memory autoregressive predictor that efficiently exploits previously decoded occupancy information through reusable key/value caches. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both lossy and lossless LiDAR geometry compression, highlighting the effectiveness of scan-prior modeling across different coordinate representations.

Title: One Fuzzer, Many Reasoners: Adaptive Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzing with Reliability-Calibrated and Context-Gated Guidance
Author: Jinghao Wen, Xianglong Yu, Shaohuang Wang, Xun Jiao
Text_Content: Neural-symbolic AI (NSAI) combines learned perception with programs, constraints, and compositional reasoning, but remains difficult to test because small semantics-preserving changes can alter grounded symbols and trigger discontinuous reasoning failures. Existing neural fuzzers mainly rely on neural coverage or representation-space feedback and do not provide a common testing interface for heterogeneous NSAI systems. We introduce NSAI-Fuzz, a unified semantics-aware fuzzing framework that separates task-specific valid mutation from architecture-neutral guided search and represents each candidate using five availability-aware, rank-normalized risk signals: boundary pressure, grounding uncertainty, representation drift, constraint violation, and archive novelty. We further propose Reliability-Calibrated Weighting (RCW), which learns dataset-model-level signal allocations from calibrated reliability, and Contextual Signal Gating (CSG), which adapts signal weights to the current candidate pool. We evaluate four NSAI systems across four reasoning tasks, nine compatible dataset-model cells, 20 policies, and 1,800 on-policy runs. Fixed five-signal guidance outperforms Random and Uniform in every cell, while RCW and CSG further improve over Fixed in all nine cells. Under matched mutation and query budgets, RCW and CSG achieve 16.17% and 16.06% aggregate failure discovery, compared with 6.06% for the strongest neural-fuzzing baseline. Wall-clock evaluation further shows that TensorFuzz requires 1.11x the runtime of RCW while achieving only 0.45x its failure throughput. These results show that effective and efficient fuzzing of heterogeneous NSAI systems benefits from a common neural-symbolic risk interface with adaptive signal allocation.

Title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
Author: Jiaye Chen, Rui Qiu, Zhou Yu
Text_Content: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

Title: Core nonemptiness for $2/3$-convex games
Author: Keisuke Bando, Toshiyuki Hirai, Kenzo Imamura, Ryuhei Mizutani
Text_Content: We study the core of $2/3$-convex games, a class of transferable-utility (TU) games that generalizes convex games, which requires at least two of any three distinct coalitions satisfy the supermodular inequality. We show that every $2/3$-convex game admits a marginal worth vector in the core, and hence has a nonempty core. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time algorithm for finding such a core allocation. We also show that $2/3$-convexity does not imply permutational convexity in general, while the implication holds under an additional superadditivity condition on pairs of singletons. As an application, we introduce a TU model motivated by the OSCE's consensus-minus-two procedure and show that the resulting game is $2/3$-convex but need not be convex.

Title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
Author: Zixu Wang, Yu Zhao, Xing Zheng, Bingbing Xu, Tian Xueyun, JiaTang Luo, Weiqiang Wang, Bowen Song, Huawei Shen, Xueqi Cheng
Text_Content: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.

Title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
Author: Zihan Pan, Jinghan Wang, Hang Li, Feng Cheng, Tianchen Liu, Gaoliang Peng
Text_Content: Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar-inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird's-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54-2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at: https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.

Title: An Agentic Python Framework for LLM-Driven UVM Testbench Synthesis with Closed-Loop Compiler Feedback
Author: Vikash Kumar
Text_Content: Protocol bridge verification is a persistent bottleneck in SoC development: for every new bridge instance, engineers hand-craft a full UVM testbench from scratch, consuming 40--100 engineering hours of bring-up effort. We present an agentic Python framework that generates complete, protocol-aware UVM testbenches for arbitrary IP and subsystem configurations from a structured Verification Manifest---a JSON specification encoding interface topology, protocol semantics, and coverage intent. The framework employs a dual closed-loop architecture: an inner compiler feedback loop that injects categorised UVM diagnostics rather than raw tool output, and an outer coverage loop driven by intent-gap analysis against the Manifest. Validated on the AMBA AHB-to-APB bridge---a representative production protocol bridge with a 7-state control FSM, two-phase APB handshake, and non-trivial burst serialisation logic---the framework achieves 96.8% functional coverage, a $4.7\times$ bring-up speedup, and a Protocol Verification Completeness score of 0.87, with only 2.1% of the generated 4,623-line testbench requiring human correction. The generated scoreboard independently identified a critical RTL functional fault that the manual baseline missed entirely. Generalisation across four protocol families confirms that speedup increases with protocol complexity, ranging from $3.1\times$ (APB Subordinate) to $6.1\times$ (CHI Subordinate).

Title: An Extensive Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sentiment Analysis: Insights from Amazon Customer Reviews
Author: Muhammed Ihsan Corak, Cuiyuan Wang, Xiaowen Zhang
Text_Content: The rapid growth of user-generated text on online platforms creates opportunities for understanding customer opinion and supporting data-driven decisions. This study compares five traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Classifier, and Multinomial Naive Bayes) and six deep learning architectures (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, RNN, Attention, and FastText) for three-class sentiment classification of 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. Machine learning models used Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF features limited to 5,000 terms; deep learning models used learned embeddings over a 20,000-word vocabulary. Models were evaluated on the original imbalanced data and on a random-oversampled balanced set of 1,070,469 reviews, using accuracy, macro and per-class precision, recall, and F1-score, and training time. On the balanced set, Random Forest with BoW achieved 99\% accuracy and the Attention model achieved 98.7\%. Linear SVC reached 89\% accuracy in 1 min 15 s, and Logistic Regression reached 90\% in 3 min 37 s. On the imbalanced set, the Attention model achieved 97.8\% accuracy, and FastText achieved 95.3\% in 3 min 26 s, while the RNN reached 91.9\% with a neutral-class F1-score of 0.08. Deep learning models were more stable across class distributions, whereas the best classical model depended on balancing. We also report a user-facing application that applies the trained Random Forest and Attention models to new review text. Because the labels are derived from star ratings, the results measure agreement with rating-derived sentiment classes rather than annotated sentiment; the dataset is a single source, and the findings should be read with that limitation in mind.

Title: Proliferating against the current: how multistep branching nucleation can sort microtubule polarity in the spindle
Author: Ido Lavi, Sebastian Fürthauer, Daniel J. Needleman, Michael J. Shelley
Text_Content: The spindle, which segregates chromosomes during cell division, is a paradigm of cytoskeletal self-organization: a highly ordered structure that persists for hours is assembled from dynamic microtubules that branch, grow, slide, and turn over within tens of seconds. Its microtubules point inward, with minus ends clustered at the poles and plus ends extending toward the chromosomes at the center of the structure. In large meiotic spindles this arrangement is puzzling, since microtubules nucleate near the chromosomes and grow at their plus ends much faster than motors slide them backward. One would therefore expect the plus ends, rather than the minus ends, to radiate outward. Here, we propose a resolution to this seeming paradox through a kinetic model that integrates the core filament-level processes. When branching complexes assemble with a sufficient delay, for instance through several sequential rate-limiting steps, they accumulate on old microtubule lattice sites near the backward-sliding minus ends of mother microtubules. Each generation is then born farther back than the last, so the self-renewing population drifts toward the minus ends even though each filament's center advances toward its plus end. For the sliding and growth velocities measured in Xenopus egg extract spindles, a multistep mechanism requires at least four rate-limiting steps. The kinetic theory has a surprisingly amenable structure: the filament length configuration variable can be eliminated exactly, yielding a finite space-time hierarchy, and the direction of population drift follows from a general criterion comparing the mean lattice age at branching sites with the ratio of plus-end advance to sliding speed.

Title: "We Are the Dirty Hands": Reimagining an Ambient Intelligence Care System with Professional Caregivers
Author: Andrea Green, Jane L. E, Sneha Jain, Parker Ruth, Matthew Jörke, Sarah L. Billington, James Landay, Andrea Cuadra
Text_Content: While ambient assisted living (AAL) sensing systems offer promise for aging in place, their impacts on professional caregivers are overlooked. We conducted two collective speculation workshops (N=24) with personal health aides (PHAs, n=18) and certified nursing assistants (CNAs, n=6) to examine the ethical implications and value tensions of a care system with ambient intelligence (CSAI), our conceptualization of an AAL. Participants anticipated different implications across care roles and settings. PHAs anticipated additional responsibilities from CSAI, including learning how it operates and supporting older adults in its use. CNAs, who had greater access to workplace resources and protections, similarly noted that CSAI could create additional work. Participants also identified tensions around visibility, as sensing could support caregivers by documenting difficult working conditions while simultaneously making their behavior more vulnerable to misinterpretation. Through their modifications and surfaced discussions, we propose design guidelines for AAL systems, such as integrating context-aware sensing.

Title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
Author: Sajjad Arzemanzadeh, Karol Miller, Ron Kikinis, Adam Wittek
Text_Content: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.

Title: GA-HEL: A Knowledge-Driven Expert System for Open-Set, Granularity-Aware Hierarchical Event Linking in Social Media
Author: Shengqi Zhou, Zhigang Liu, Wenxiang Zhu, Zhentao Cang
Text_Content: Social-media event intelligence requires a system to determine whether a post belongs to a registered event space, identify the supported hierarchy path, and stop at the deepest level warranted by the evidence. We formulate this requirement as open-set hierarchical event linking over frozen Storyline--Episode--Atomic Event Cards. GA-HEL implements a three-stage, knowledge-driven expert-system funnel: open-set scope control limits candidate exposure before hierarchical reasoning, hierarchy-aware decoders select a supported path and depth, and deterministic legal-path validation checks each record before database-compatible use. A 200-post Pilot supports task and mechanism development, while a separately annotated 497-post Expansion set evaluates transfer across four held-out Storylines and a hard-negative pool. Method implementations, prompts, Event Cards, candidate order, and six systems' predictions were frozen before Expansion Gold annotation. The resulting evaluation combines end-to-end hierarchical matching, open-set rejection, structural validation, ablation, cross-Storyline analysis, and an independent expert reannotation of a fixed audited subset. GA-HEL remains competitive with strong global full-card reasoning while providing explicit scope control and hierarchy-valid structured records. Error analysis identifies unsupported descent from Episode-level evidence to Atomic Events as the dominant remaining challenge. The task definition, frozen resource, and auditable protocol provide a reproducible foundation for scope-aware event intelligence. Code, Event Cards, labels, frozen predictions, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/SHbiao/GAHEL_release.

Title: Weak Composition Theorems for Randomized Communication
Author: Pachara Sawettamalya
Text_Content: We present two results towards the randomized communication complexity of composed functions. Our contributions include: - \textbf{Lifting-by-Influence.} For any binary function $f$ and any outer gadget $g:\{0,1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we show that up to additive terms, computing $g \circ f^n$ information-theoretically requires solving at least $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ instances of $f$, where $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ denotes the total influence of $g$. To our knowledge, this is the first composition lower bound for randomized communication that applies to \emph{every} choice of $f$ and $g$. - \textbf{Symmetric Composition.} When $g$ is a symmetric function with a value transition at Hamming weight $d$, we strengthen the number of required instances to $\min\{d,n+1-d\}$. As an implication, this recovers the previously known direct-sum theorem, XOR lemma, and majority lemma. Our proofs develop novel and distinctive usages of the classical \emph{input embedding} argument of Barak, Braverman, Chen, and Rao (SICOMP 2013). As an additional ingredient, we introduce a new public sampling framework that avoids auxiliary communication during the recovery phase of the protocol, ultimately reducing the extra cost from $O(n)$ bits of information to just $O(1)$.

Title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
Author: Ali Tajfar, Behnam Tajfar
Text_Content: Interpretability tools increasingly support safety claims, such as that a sparse dictionary has recovered most of a model's features. Such claims rest on measurements with arbitrary thresholds, and small changes to the model weights, a different training seed or a different threshold can reverse them. We study two widely used measurements in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth: the feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate (FRR) with a cosine threshold. We characterize exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous and replace it with a regularized (ridge) version with sharp stability bounds: the ridge leverage score changes by at most $3\sqrt{3}/(8\sqrtλ)$ times the operator-norm change of the weights, and this constant cannot be improved; for the regularized dimensionality the stability constant grows like $ρ/4$ in the scale $ρ=R/\sqrtλ$, with explicit upper and lower bounds. We also prove certificates stating when a claim "feature $i$ is recovered" must survive a given change of the dictionary. The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries; at the standard threshold, whether a feature counts as recovered changed with the training seed for 55 percent of features. Experiments use toy models only. The proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents directed by the authors and checked by an independent blind AI reviewer and by numerical tests; the authors take full responsibility for the content.

Title: SBA: A Practical Memory Performance Denial-of-Service Attack
Author: Amin Mamandipoor, Connor Rudy Sullivan, Cole Ridge Strickler, Mohammad Alian, Heechul Yun
Text_Content: Modern cloud platforms use memory bandwidth regulation to isolate co-located workloads, implicitly assuming that high aggregate bandwidth consumption implies high interference. We show that this assumption is fundamentally flawed. We present the Single-Bank Attack (SBA), a practical memory denial-of-service attack that induces extreme cross-core slowdowns---over three orders of magnitude on memory-intensive victims (e.g., LLM decode)---while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth. SBA exploits the gap between peak and worst-case DRAM throughput by concentrating memory write operations on a single bank, forcing persistent row conflicts and frequent write draining, thereby collapsing the memory service rate. Across Intel and AMD systems, including DDR5- and HBM2E-based platforms, SBA consistently causes orders-of-magnitude slowdowns under realistic multi-tenant settings, revealing a fundamental limitation of bandwidth-centric memory isolation. We further show that this localized contention propagates system-wide: single-bank congestion saturates memory controller queues and induces back-pressure into shared cache and coherence structures, ultimately throttling memory request injection across cores. Consequently, severe interference can arise even at low aggregate bandwidth, evading existing bandwidth-based QoS mechanisms such as Intel RDT MBA. To address this limitation, we propose IQ-MemGuard, a lightweight, software-based memory bandwidth regulator that detects sustained contention using microarchitectural signals and selectively throttles pathological request injection. Our implementation on an Intel platform effectively mitigates SBA, whereas Intel's hardware QoS mechanism fails completely.

Title: PERA: Plug-in Experts for Robotic Actions in Continual Whole-Body Control
Author: Shangchao Hu, Yadan Sun, Xibo Yu, Wei Huang
Text_Content: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.

Title: Flow-CAD: Flow Matching for Contextual Anomaly Detection and Explanation in Tabular Data
Author: Zhong Li, Qi Huang, Yuhang Wang, Yang Cao, Thomas Bäck, Niki van Stein, Matthijs van Leeuwen, Lincen Yang
Text_Content: Contextual anomaly detection in tabular data aims to identify objects whose behavior is unexpected under their contextual conditions. In data-engineering pipelines, this task screens table rows whose measurements violate context-dependent integrity relationships. Most existing approaches rely on either shallow conditional models with limited distributional expressiveness or localized estimators that require per-context modeling, making it difficult to capture complex conditional relationships and scale to high-dimensional settings. We propose Flow-CAD, a new framework for contextual anomaly detection based on Flow Matching. Flow-CAD learns a single global and amortized conditional generative model that flexibly represents behavioral distributions conditioned on context, without assuming simple parametric forms or retraining local models. To enable robust and interpretable anomaly scoring, we introduce a scale-normalized and truncated residual energy derived from the learned conditional flow, which stabilizes anomaly scores, mitigates domination by extreme deviations, and supports feature-wise attribution. We further provide theoretical insights showing that the proposed residual-based anomaly score is stable under velocity estimation error, and that its Monte Carlo estimator satisfies concentration bounds. Experiments on 20 benchmark datasets with 13 competitors demonstrate that Flow-CAD has the best average rank for PR AUC, ROC AUC, and P@n, highlighting its effectiveness and practicality for contextual anomaly detection in tabular data. We provide the source code at https://github.com/ZhongLIFR/FlowCAD.

Title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
Author: Hongyu Li, Zhan Yu, Zhe Zhao, Kimmo Yan, Xiong Kuang, Renfen Hu
Text_Content: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.

Title: Same-State Pairs Make One JEPA Proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis Vacuous
Author: Xin Li
Text_Content: In a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), the JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) assumes that every observation determines the world state and that a spectral gap makes minimizers unique up to rotation. Under the hard-whitening population objective, same-state positive pairs make the induced world kernel the identity: every centered whitened state function is a global minimizer, and, when $d_z-1\ge 2k$, two minimizers can have best-rotation squared residual $2k$. The uniqueness claim is conditional; for $k<d_z-1$, where $d_z$ is the number of world states, this limit makes its premise unsatisfiable, so the claim has no content there. The experiments that motivate it leave the assumption: a caption sees only part of an image, and the paper states no experiment meets its hypotheses exactly. The theorem does not reach those experiments, and for $k<d_z-1$ its idealized same-state limit is vacuous. One of the paper's four quantitative results survives: a gap-free lower bound. Its bound vanishes only at perfect scene-explained fraction; it bounds alignment error but cannot certify good-view alignment. A canonical frame is determined only up to a rotation and a latent permutation. Paired samples fix the relative frame at effective rank $k$; a global rotation remains. Component semantics fix the relative permutation only up to signs; value anchors fix it once the mixing frame is pinned. A resource--gauge ledger records which resource fixes which gauge.

Title: Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work
Author: Hongjin Kim, Igjae Kim, Kwanghoon Choi, Minho Ha, Jaehyuk Huh
Text_Content: When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on demand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5-11% of it is spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation, memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs again even though the outcome is identical across servers or independent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1-5.2x on servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

Title: Concatenated Codes with One Inner Code: Low-Rate Gilbert-Varshamov Asymptotics from Algebraic-Geometric Codes
Author: Yota Maeda, Ruho Kondo
Text_Content: Constructing codes that attain the Gilbert-Varshamov (GV) bound while admitting efficient encoding and decoding is a fundamental problem in coding theory. We study concatenated codes that reuse a single binary inner code across all outer coordinates. To exploit existing encoding and decoding algorithms, we restrict the outer codes to random subcodes of scaled copies of prescribed algebraic codes and investigate their minimum distance. Our first contribution is a general upper bound on the minimum-distance failure probability that separates two terms controlled by the inner code's bias moments and the dual weight distribution of the prescribed code, together with sufficient conditions for exponential decay. Our second contribution is a concrete construction satisfying these conditions using algebraic-geometric codes from the Garcia-Stichtenoth tower. For every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, we construct a family of random binary codes $C_m$ whose rates approach $\varepsilon^2$ and satisfy \[ \Pr\left[δ(C_m)\geq\frac12-\sqrt{\frac{\ln 2}{2}}\left(\varepsilon+\frac{\varepsilon^3}{2}\right)\right]\geq 1-2^{-c\varepsilon^4N_m}, \] for all sufficiently large $m$, where $N_m$ is the block length and $c>0$ is independent of $\varepsilon$ and $m$. Thus, the distance guarantee matches the leading coefficient of the GV bound at low rates. For each fixed $\varepsilon$, the construction uses a single inner encoding map throughout the family and admits polynomial-time encoding and unique decoding within a guaranteed radius. This answers the question of Doron, Mosheiff, and Wootters for subcodes of scaled algebraic geometry codes at low rates.

Title: A One-Sided Sublinear-Query Tester for Bounded-Degree 2SAT
Author: Yuichi Yoshida
Text_Content: We give a one-sided tester for satisfiability of 2CNF formulas in the bounded-degree model. For every degree bound $Δ$, distance parameter $\varepsilon>0$, and $ν\in(0,1/2)$, its query complexity on $n$-variable formulas is $\widetilde O_{\varepsilon,Δ,ν}(n^{1/2+ν})$.

Title: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing
Author: Shinichi Arimura, Yuchen Li, Julian Togelius
Text_Content: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes---runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.

Title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
Author: Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Ting-Yao Hu, Sanjoy Chowdhury, Oncel Tuzel, Raviteja Vemulapalli
Text_Content: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

Title: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance
Author: Snehalkumar `Neil' S. Gaikwad, Punya Aragula, Shiva Kruthi Palpanoori, Pratik Patekar
Text_Content: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.

Title: Self-Supervised Attention-Based Virtual Metrology for CMP MRR Prediction
Author: Jonathan Adam Rico, Nagarajan Raghavan, Senthilnath Jayavelu
Text_Content: Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) is a critical semiconductor manufacturing process where material removal rate (MRR) is a key metric for process monitoring and advanced process control (APC). Virtual metrology enables MRR estimation from process time series signals, supporting run-to-run(R2R) control and process optimization while reducing reliance on physical metrology. Existing approaches typically rely on simplified linear assumptions or require handcrafted feature engineering. In this paper, we propose Global Regression Pretraining(GREP), a self-supervised, attention-based framework for CMP MRR prediction. GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation. The framework is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under three conditions: limited labeled data, sensor noise, and temporal process drift. Experiments on the PHM 2016 CMP dataset demonstrate competitive performance under limited labeled-data conditions, with improvements in selected cases and performance largely comparable to the baseline across different labeled-data fractions. Both models exhibit relatively small changes in prediction error with increasing noise, while GREP achieves a 17.0% RMSE reduction in the final temporal interval.

Title: MRxD: A Usage-Pattern Framework for Mixed-Reality Cross-Device Interaction
Author: Yang Zhan, Yuxuan Huang, Yuchen Cai, Yichen Andy Yu, Xiaoran Yang, Ye Yuan, Qiao Jin
Text_Content: Mixed reality (MR) cross-device experiences often combine MR headsets with non-immersive devices such as laptops, tablets, and phones. Yet such cross-device design remains challenging because users must coordinate workflows across heterogeneous devices with different roles. This motivates our focus on usage patterns: recurrent ways in which people distribute and coordinate work across devices. Through a systematic analysis of 238 MR cross-device papers, we developed MRxD, a usage-pattern framework organized around three dimensions: user attention, task relatedness, and cognitive symmetry. Using these dimensions, we identified six usage patterns and synthesized the design strategies commonly used within each pattern. We further investigated the framework's application in design practice through a workshop (n=6) and the results suggest that MRxD can guide pattern-based design exploration and identify blind spots. We further discuss how usage patterns may shift or combine, and outline research gaps and design implications for future MR cross-device systems.

Title: Feature-Aware Edge Sampling for Approximate One-Step Laplacian Propagation
Author: Jonathan Z. Sun, Zheng Wang, Kebin Xu
Text_Content: This paper studies how to approximate one-step combinatorial Laplacian messages in graph neural networks using edge sampling. We propose a spanning tree based hybrid sampler that combines feature-conditioned message scores and effective-resistance leverage scores, derive the expected one-step message error and obtain the optimal sampling probabilities and error frontier for a given expected edge budget. Preliminary experiments on synthetic community graphs show that message error decreases, while classification accuracy increases slightly, as the edge budget grows, and performance of the hybrid sampler is in between of optimal selection uniform random sampling. We leave multi-step propagation and evaluation on larger and real graphs for future work.

Title: Exact and Approximation Algorithms for Computing Smallest SESs and BMSs
Author: Hiroki Shibata, Hideo Bannai
Text_Content: Compression schemes represent repetitive strings compactly by using repeated substrings. Computing the minimum size of a representation of a given input string is important for compression and for understanding relationships between compression schemes, although this task is NP-hard for several schemes. In this paper, we introduce exact and approximation algorithms for finding smallest substring equation systems (SESs) and bidirectional macro schemes (BMSs). Specifically, for an input string of length $n$, we give deterministic and randomized algorithms for computing a smallest SES using $O^*(4^n)$ and $O^*(2^n)$ time and space, respectively. We also give a deterministic algorithm for computing a smallest BMS using $O^*(2^n)$ time and space. We further give deterministic and randomized $(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest SESs using $O^*(4^{e^{-α}n})$ and $O^*(2^{e^{-α}n})$ time and space, respectively, for every $α\ge 0$. A conversion from SESs to BMSs gives $4(1+α)$-approximation algorithms for smallest BMSs with the same time and space bounds. All time bounds hold in the worst case, and the randomized algorithms return correct answers with high probability. Our algorithms adapt several approaches to exact and approximation algorithms for combinatorial problems, such as dynamic programming over determinant expansions and a greedy algorithm for monotone submodular functions.

Title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking
Author: Jianan Wei, Qiang Zhang, Hao Sun, Yi Yang, Wenguan Wang
Text_Content: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

Title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
Author: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna Bößendörfer, Mirko Mählisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
Text_Content: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.

Title: From Tokens to Behaviors: Rethinking Generative Recommendation for User Trajectory Prediction
Author: Jiaqi Wang, Hanchen Yang, Hengyu Zhang, Hongxu Ma, Wenqi Rao, Hongyang Wang, Zhongbo Sun, Renliang Qian, Weixin Chen, Wengen Li, Jihong Guan, Shuigeng Zhou, Qingpeng Cai, Peng Jiang, Hong Cheng
Text_Content: User behavior trajectory prediction (UBTP) aims to capture how a user's needs evolve over time by predicting the sequence of future interactions from that user's interaction history. Recent generative recommendation (GR) methods address this task through autoregressive generation of semantic IDs (SIDs). However, serial SID decoding couples token generation with behavior state transitions and requires multiple dependent steps per interaction. Discrete item feedback overlooks predictive uncertainty, and teacher-forced training leaves a training-inference gap in trajectory generation. To address these limitations, we propose TraGR, a behavior-aware generative recommendation framework that aligns generation, feedback, and learning with successive user behaviors. Its behavior-level architecture predicts SID tokens in parallel within each interaction and models behavioral transitions through recurrent state updates, with joint SID and item-level supervision. Probability feedback combines the selected behavior with a probability-weighted summary of alternatives to guide subsequent predictions. Relation-aware trajectory learning incorporates collaborative transition signals and later credit assignment into training on model-generated trajectories. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that TraGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across different prediction horizons. Code: https://github.com/CalmaQi/GR4UBT.

Title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
Author: Weimin Fu, Minghao Shao, Zeng Wang, Qiying Li, Yuntao Liu, Johann Knechtel, Ozgur Sinanoglu, Muhammad Shafique, Ramesh Karri, Xiaolong Guo
Text_Content: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.

Title: Accelerating Distributed Variational Quantum Computing over Wireless Networks with Incentive Mechanism Design
Author: Shaba Shaon, Dinh C. Nguyen, Octavia Dobre
Text_Content: Distributed variational quantum computing (DVQC) appears as the emerging paradigm to address the limitations of near-term quantum devices by decomposing large parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) into smaller subcircuits executed across multiple quantum processors. In this context, how to incentivize quantum processors to participate actively is crucial for accelerating DVQC, yet remains largely unexplored in the literature. To address this significant gap, we propose a novel two-stage incentive framework for wireless DVQC. In the first stage, we minimize processor-side energy cost via a joint optimization of subcircuit parameters, number of noise measurements, and transmit power, efficiently solved using block coordinate descent (BCD) and successive convex approximation (SCA). In the second stage, we maximize aggregator-side system utility by selecting an optimal subset of processors based on their optimized energy costs derived from the first stage, formulating a non-convex combinatorial selection problem addressed using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Extensive numerical experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our DVQC framework achieves training and testing performance comparable to centralized quantum computing in terms of accuracy and loss, with similar convergence behavior on MNIST and slightly slower initial convergence on CIFAR-10. Moreover, our optimization approach consistently outperforms baseline schemes in energy efficiency and system utility, revealing a strong synergy between processor-level energy minimization and incentive-driven processor selection, where reduced energy costs directly enhances a processor's likelihood of selection and contributes to higher overall system utility.

Title: Bounded Metrics for Probability Measures on the Sphere
Author: Kisung You
Text_Content: Directional distributions can have the same normalized mean direction while differing substantially in shape. Comparing them requires a distance whose response to geometric displacement and probability overlap matches the statistical question. We examine ten bounded metrics or metric families for probability measures on the sphere, scaling each to have maximum value one, covering transport, sliced transport, kernel and energy distances, and comparisons based on probability mass. We explain which metrics describe weak convergence, which admit Hilbert-space norm representations, and which pairs attain the maximum distance. Examples and counterexamples show how these distinctions affect empirical comparisons and numerical approximations. A summary table and relationship diagram support the choice of a distance. The discussion separates exact metrics from finite representations, unbiased estimators, and regularized transport costs.

Title: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures
Author: Tom Slooff, Anthony Etim, Jiaqi Yu, Francesco Regazzoni, Jakub Szefer
Text_Content: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this work evaluates an online traffic light controller in a microscopic traffic simulator, where a single injected infinite value degrades accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x while corrupting under 4% of the Q-table, and where triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in our tests, although glitching could still halt the device. Altogether, this work provides a basis for understanding and securing RL deployments against fault injection attacks.

Title: HyperPage: Learned Page Layouts for Disk-Resident Graph Vector Indexes
Author: Xinyu Zhang, Jingze Li, Baihua Zheng, Weiwei Sun
Text_Content: Disk-resident graph indexes such as DiskANN store each vector with its graph edges as one record on SSD pages.
