A search needs the page of every record it expands, so its page reads depend on the page layout, that is, which records share a page. Search agents trained with reinforcement learning query one such index run after run, and every graph traversal can be logged with the records it expands. We therefore use the logs of a finished run to lay out the index for a declared memory budget, so later runs read fewer pages. In contrast, existing layouts such as Starling and MARGO are computed from the graph and vectors and use no logs. Learning a layout from logs is challenging, because the logs must stay valid under every layout, the saving depends on what the budget caches, and the best layout is NP-hard to find. Our key observation is that DiskANN-style search routes on in-memory codes and the records it expands, never on their page-mates. As a result, the logged traversals price every layout by replay, and cached records add no page reads. Accordingly, we propose HyperPage, which first builds layouts for the declared budget on the logged traversals of uncached records. It then selects one layout, together with the budget split between hot records and a page cache, by replaying validation steps. In addition, a Lagrangian lower bound shows how far a layout may be from the optimum. We learn from one Search-R1 agent run and test on a later run with a different reward, over 1M and 21M passages. Across seven cache budgets, HyperPage reads 5.2% to 21.2% fewer pages than MARGO, and no compared layout reads fewer. The advantage is largest when the cache is small. For example, at 1% of the 1M index, MARGO needs nearly 3 times the budget to read as few pages. On the 21M index, HyperPage also cuts search time per step by up to 10.4%. The saving holds for a second agent model and a second corpus.

Title: Calibrated Early Termination with Bounded Optimality Gaps for Constrained Vector Search
Author: Xinyu Zhang, Jingze Li, Baihua Zheng, Weiwei Sun
Text_Content: Vector search over learned embeddings is the retrieval layer of recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation, and many applications cap how many answer items one category may contribute. Graph indexes answer a query by best-first traversal, and where it stops determines its cost and whether its answer is exact. We study early termination for such constrained $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) queries, with plain $k$-NN as a special case, and seek the cheapest stopping rule whose answer is exact with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Learned early-termination methods instead target average recall, which does not guarantee exact answers. Multiple testing can calibrate any parameterized stopping rule to our target, but it cannot tell how much a better rule with the same risk and observations would save. Answering this needs a lower bound on the optimum of a rule family too large to enumerate, valid for the query population. Our key idea is to declare the observations a rule may use and to consider every rule monotone in them. Risk-constrained stopping then becomes a linear program over an order polytope, whose Lagrangian minimizers form a nested chain of staircase rules computed exactly by dynamic programming. Fixed-sequence binomial tests along this chain calibrate our rule, CaST, whose failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-δ$. Lagrangian weak duality bounds the optimum of the declared class from below at all risk levels at once, without a union bound over the rules. On two datasets of one million items each, CaST replayed on logged searches costs at most 1.132 times the class optimum for risk levels from 0.03 to 0.10, at 95% joint confidence per setting. Larger savings thus need a rule outside the class. At a common risk target on held-out queries, CaST is faster than every other calibrated rule we time, which take 4.8% to 45.5% more mean time.

Title: Humidity-modulated Ostwald Step Rule in $\rm FAPbI_3$ Martensitic Transitions
Author: Ping Tuo, Ju Li
Text_Content: Experimental observations reveal a dual role of moisture in $\rm FAPbI_3$ phase transitions. During fabrication at high temperatures, humidity improves the quality of the perovskite ($α$ phase) films, whereas at low service temperatures, humidity accelerates degradation of the photoactive $α$ phase into the photo-inactive hexagonal $δ$ phase. Despite extensive experimental evidence, the microscopic mechanisms by which moisture modulates phase stability and transition pathways remain unknown. Here, using large-scale atomistic simulations powered by an ab initio machine-learned potential, we reproduce the experimentally observed increase in the $δ$-to-$α$ transition temperature under increased humidity. Our simulations reveal a layered metastable intermediate along the Burgers transition pathway that exhibits a strong affinity for water. The competing water uptake of this intermediate and the $δ$ phase governs the humidity dependence of transition kinetics. These findings elucidate the dual role of moisture in perovskite phase transitions and demonstrate how environmental species can stabilize metastable intermediates and reshape transition pathways, providing an environment-dependent perspective on Ostwald's step rule.

Title: Two-Stage Secret Sharing
Author: Mizuki Murata, Mamoru Shibata
Text_Content: We give an information-theoretic formulation of two-stage secret sharing for situations in which secret information becomes available progressively. In the proposed model, shares for an initial part of the secret are distributed before the remaining part becomes available, and additional shares are distributed to new participants after the remaining part becomes available, without updating the shares already distributed and without using any additional information other than shares. To characterize this setting, we propose the notion of a two-stage access structure and provide its characterization. We further quantify the amount of information about the first-stage secret that the dealer must retain between the two distribution stages, derive a universal lower bound, and present a construction that achieves this bound for every two-stage access structure. We also position advance sharing as a special case of the proposed model and give its characterization and a related construction in classical information-theoretic secret sharing.

Title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
Author: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Valeriia Oliferuk, Vladyslav Babenko, Danylo Kovalchuk, Dmytro Kostetskyi
Text_Content: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.

Title: Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers
Author: Nilava Metya, Oscar Leong, Yong Sheng Soh
Text_Content: We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions. To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

Title: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models
Author: Fariz Zeynalov, Razim Mammadli
Text_Content: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, ignoring behavioral patterns that emerge across sequences of messages from the same sender. We study outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, where the goal is to predict at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam. Using a proprietary production database of 43,741 outbound SMS messages with UTC transmission timestamps and carrier delivery statuses, we report three sets of results. On an 8,749-message held-out test set, a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. A deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382, and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate, class-balanced 20,000-message production evaluation set; these results are not directly comparable with the held-out test results. We also describe TemporalBertSpam, an architecture that encodes each sender's message history with a causal Transformer, and outline the same-split evaluation needed to measure its contribution.

Title: Individually Fair Facility Location
Author: Rajni Dabas, Samir Khuller, Milind Maiti
Text_Content: We study individually fair facility location, where each client must connect to an open facility within a prescribed radius and the objective is to minimize total opening and connection cost. We show that preserving the radii changes the approximability of metric facility location fundamentally. For every fixed radius violation below three, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves a sublogarithmic cost factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. The hardness holds with uniform opening costs and uniform radii. It contradicts the strict-fairness constant-factor guarantee recently claimed by Liu, Xu, and Zhang [Theory of Computing Systems, Vol. 70 (2026)]. We then establish a positive result for arbitrary client radii. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that has cost at most $1.725$ times the strictly fair optimum and serves every client within three times its fair radius (in the Appendix we show how this can be de-randomized). We use the approach of Byrka, Srinivasan and Swamy [IPCO 2010]. The facility-location radius factor three is therefore optimal among deterministic polynomial-time algorithms with constant cost factor, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Experiments on real-world data indicate that the worst case radius bound is rarely realized in practice: the algorithm serves over 99.8% of clients within their stated radius, and never beyond 1.5 times it. Our code is available at https://github.com/milindmaiti/IFFL_Implementation.

Title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
Author: David Hyland-Wood, Rob Ewin
Text_Content: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.

Title: Split-and-scale Latent 3D Representations
Author: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
Text_Content: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.

Title: Integrated optical isolators enabled by 2D semiconductors via spin-momentum locking
Author: Fernando Martín-Romero, Víctor J. Gómez, Alberto G. Curto
Text_Content: Integrated optical isolators based on spin-momentum locking hold great potential for protecting photonic integrated circuits from unwanted reflections. Currently, the most common implementations are magneto-optical isolators that require an externally applied magnetic field. Nevertheless, a wide range of nonreciprocal effects remains to be exploited in alternative material platforms. Although the majority of these effects induce changes to the propagation of light as a function of its polarization, they can be directly connected to the propagation direction through spin-momentum locking. We employ a computational approach to investigate various designs of integrated isolators based on nonreciprocal 2D semiconductors, studying the influence of their geometry and optical properties on the device performance. Additionally, we propose a novel concept for an all-optical isolator based on spin-valley polarization and optically tunable magnetism in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers. Our results establish 2D semiconductors as an advanced platform for integrated nonreciprocal devices, enabling functionalities that are difficult to achieve with conventional magneto-optical materials like all-optical operation.

Title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
Author: Junru Zhu
Text_Content: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

Title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
Author: Fady Copty, Neta Haiby, Max Braitmaiere, Julia Korsunsky
Text_Content: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.

Title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
Author: Anuj Chaudhri
Text_Content: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

Title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
Author: Vahid Haratian, Vahid Ansari, Mohammadhossein Malmir, Alois Knoll
Text_Content: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

Title: ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests
Author: Vahid Haratian, Atakan Akar, Eray Tüzün
Text_Content: Modern software development relies on pull requests (PRs) that introduce small, targeted code changes. Once merged, these changes should be protected by focused tests that exercise the behavior the PR introduces, yet developers often submit PRs without such tests, leaving the new behavior unguarded against future regressions. Most test generation techniques target entire software units and optimize objectives such as code coverage rather than the behavior a change introduces, and prior diff-aware approaches have had limited success in capturing it. We propose ADAPT (Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing), a regression test generation approach that uses an autonomous coding agent to produce change-focused tests for PRs. Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between the base and head versions to identify the modified functions and their context, then plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool runs each candidate on both versions and, after F2P success, reports which executable changed lines remain uncovered; guided by this feedback, the agent iteratively refines its tests. We evaluate ADAPT on the same 426 real-world PRs used by the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with GPT-4o and GPT-5-mini. ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426), compared with BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs, compared with 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost. A manual evaluation confirms that the F2P-valid tests target each PR's intended change, with mean scores of up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability, often covering behavior beyond the developer-written tests.

Title: Harnessing Environmental Scatterers for Endogenous Target Covertness in 6G ISAC: A New Paradigm for Sensing Security
Author: Yifan Zhang, Boxuan Xie, Mingyang Yang, Ying Liu, Riku Jäntti, Zan Li
Text_Content: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a cornerstone of 6G networks, enabling simultaneous data transmission and environmental perception. However, the ubiquitous radiation of sensing waveforms introduces a critical security vulnerability where the physical existence and characteristics of targets are continuously exposed to unauthorized wardens. Meanwhile, existing sensing-secure methods primarily focus on degrading a target warden's parameter-estimation accuracy, yet they fail to prevent wardens from detecting the target's physical presence. In this article, we first analyze sensing security threats in ISAC systems and survey existing sensing-secure methods. To address the critical gap, we propose a novel security paradigm termed endogenous target covertness. By intentionally harnessing environmental scatterers, such as known objects, ambient backscatter devices, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), as ghost targets, the proposed scheme ensures a low probability that the warden detects the true target for the true target at the warden. This deliberately renders the true target's existence indistinguishable to the warden, while the legitimate base station can extract the true target's response using prior knowledge of the scatterers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme through a case study, proving that absolute target covertness can be achieved without consuming dedicated jamming power. Finally, we outline key open challenges and promising research directions to realize truly secure, ubiquitous sensing in future ISAC ecosystems.

Title: How Do People Debug Complex SQL Queries With LLMs? A Qualitative Study
Author: Nicole Sullivan, Ella Cao, Leilani Battle, Magdalena Balazinska
Text_Content: While LLMs are increasingly used in various contexts, we lack a fundamental understanding of how they impact SQL query debugging. In response, we conducted a user study with 16 participants of varying SQL expertise, examining how they debug complex SQL queries with and without LLM support. Initial benchmarking indicated that our selected models are already capable SQL debuggers. Qualitative analyses of our study data revealed that while participants trusted the LLM, they varied widely in how and whether they delegated debugging tasks to the LLMs, which we characterized through a new three-state model of participants' SQL reasoning processes. Additionally, participants enforced specific collaborative roles for the LLM such as TA or sounding board, which participants controlled by withholding context from the LLM. These findings suggest that LLM-based tools could enable preset role selection, broader context management, and flexible automation features, including low automation options, to support SQL debugging moving forward.

Title: Trained on What Screen Readers Cannot Read: Accessibility Debt in the GUI Corpora Behind Computer-Use Agents
Author: Obada Kraishan, Kulsawasd Jitkajornwanich
Text_Content: Computer-use agents learn to operate mobile interfaces from corpora of captured screens and accessibility trees. The same trees are what a screen reader consumes, so an agent trained on them inherits whatever labelling gaps the underlying applications carry. This paper measures one of those gaps, content-description coverage, in two Android corpora: Rico, collected in 2017, and AndroidControl, collected in 2024. Across 17,373,614 interface elements, 17.74% of the Rico elements that need a content description under our coding rule carry one, against 57.27% in AndroidControl. The difference of 39.5 percentage points holds under five alternative coding rules and when whole apps are resampled. It describes two datasets that also differ in app selection, capture method and platform version; it does not measure change over time. Input controls are the least labelled role in both corpora (2.20% and 27.21%, or 30.99% in AndroidControl if hint text counts as a name). Descriptions in the older corpus are also five times more likely to be placeholders (10.25% against 1.95%), so the difference is not an artefact of developers typing filler. Resolving 26,205 task actions to the elements they touched shows that, among tappable graphics with no text, demonstrations operate elements described 9.0 points more often than the others on the screens they visit, about 3.5 points of it from the choice of element within a screen. That is a selection effect inside the benchmark. A two-coder reliability check (kappa = 0.91 and 0.96) and the full pipeline accompany the paper.

Title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning
Author: Jessica Lundin, Katherine Rosenfeld, David Adelani, Geoffrey Mosoti Nyakiongora, Halfan Ngowo, Sloan Coffin, Ralph Abboud, Guillaume Chabot-Couture
Text_Content: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.

Title: Low Probability of Target Detection in Wireless Sensing by Harnessing Reconfigurable-antenna based Reflectors
Author: Yifan Zhang, Zhentian Zhang, Jantti Riku, Yichuan Wang, Xingwang Li, Tuo Wu
Text_Content: In this paper, we introduce low probability of target detection (LPTD) as a new security objective for wireless sensing systems, where the existence of a target is concealed from passive wardens. Unlike conventional communication security and covert communication, LPTD aims to protect the sensed target itself from malicious detection, rather than concealing transmitted signals or communication activities. Specifically, we propose a reconfigurable-antenna-based reflector-assisted target covertness scheme, where passive reflectors deployed around the target are harnessed as artificial scattering sources to confuse the warden. By adjusting their reflection coefficients, these reflectors reshape the local scattering environment and mask the target-induced echo. We then analyze the warden's optimal detection strategy and derive the false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, followed by a closed-form expression for its minimum total detection error probability. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that sufficient cooperation among reflectors can increase the warden's minimum total detection error probability to approximately 0.94--0.96, making target detection close to random guessing.

Title: Is generative AI really changing public sector work? Evidence from a multi-country survey
Author: Saba Esnaashari, Tvesha Sippy, Youmna Hashem, Sukankana Chakraborty, Jonathan Bright
Text_Content: Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform how public services are delivered, with important implications for public service productivity. But how widely is the technology actually being used - and is it making any difference? Our survey of 3,362 public sector workers across the UK, the USA, South Africa and the EU finds widespread use of AI in every region. Our findings suggest that this spread is being driven by bottom-up individual adoption rather than top-down institutional adoption. In the EU, for example, 65\% of respondents use AI, while only 19\% say their organisation has formally adopted it. Most users are positive about its effects, with 79\% saying AI has improved their productivity. However, only 29\% say it has increased what is expected of them at work, raising questions about how truly transformative the technology is so far. Across regions, South Africa is a clear outlier, with the highest levels of use, organisational adoption, optimism and awareness of guidelines.

Title: Hiding a Gap Does Not Close It: The Price of Removing the Mean Group Contrast from Learned Models of Learning Dynamics
Author: Sosthène Bidojesussi Hounzinhin, Ahmed Ratnani, Abdeladim El Akri
Text_Content: Adaptive tutors use models learned from student data, and a common fairness remedy erases the group signal from these models. We turn the cost of this remedy into an audit tool. Building on mean-parity regression, we give the minimum extra error, relative to the best predictor, of removing the mean group contrast from a predictor that cannot use the group, $p_0p_1Δ^2/R^2$, and the exact cost of any correction built from an estimated group model, which, for the best predictor, is never below this minimum. A three-stage audit (fit on training units, announce the cost on validation units, test on independent units) estimates this cost before the correction is used. In a controlled study, the price can be large even when the state predicts the group poorly. On three real data sets, erasing the group from a learned model of learning dynamics predicts almost no gap where one is observed. In a selected knowledge-tracing network, erasing the hidden state leaves most of the gap; a correction of the prediction removes it at an extra Brier score of 0.021 on average. On Eedi, with the network selected on separate units, the audit accepted the announced cost in all five splits, the measured cost fell inside the announced interval in all five, and the gap reduction transferred to new classes in four; on new ASSISTments schools the audit abstains. In a tutoring simulator, the objective and the help budget matter more than the erasure, and floors on each group's knowledge separate narrowing a gap from levelling down. Hiding a gap in a model does not close it.

Title: CupOFMoCA: Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly
Author: Ruoxi Rosie Zhang, Ziang Li, Jiatao Gu, Pranam Chatterjee
Text_Content: Molecular conjugates, including PROTACs and peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs), derive their function from the joint behavior of multiple coupled components, yet most generative approaches design these components independently and combine them only after generation. Such staged pipelines ignore cross-component dependencies and often produce conjugates that are chemically invalid, fall outside empirical conjugate distributions, or lose function upon assembly. In this work, we introduce Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly (CupOFMoCA), a discrete generative method that enforces cross-component chemical constraints during conjugate generation. CupOFMoCA restricts guided updates to chemically feasible conjugate states and reweights local transitions using molecular design objectives. Across three PDC systems, coupled generation achieved 100% conjugation validity among valid peptides and increased valid yield over matched post-hoc filtering, with comparable predicted binding scores across the full valid sets. In three-seed evaluations of three PROTAC systems, CupOFMoCA achieved the highest assembly validity on two systems and generated more assembly-valid molecules per second than the evaluated baselines. We further evaluated the generated PROTACs with post-hoc DegradeMaster scoring and explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, supporting their predicted activity and conformational properties. Together, these results establish CupOFMoCA as an efficient generator of molecular conjugates, supporting therapeutic development via coordinated control of assembly and molecular properties.

Title: VISTA: View-Independent micro-Doppler Reconstruction with Multistatic ISAC
Author: Jacopo Pegoraro, Marco Canil, Aurora Peloso, Jesus O. Lacruz, Xitao Gong, Richard A. Stirling-Gallacher, Michele Rossi, Joerg Widmer
Text_Content: The micro-Doppler (uD) spectrum provides detailed characteristics of target movement, making it highly valuable for applications such as target classification and human activity recognition. However, traditional Integrated Sensing And Communication (ISAC) systems are highly view-dependent and limited by blind spots and angle dependencies. Existing approaches rely on either configuration-specific solutions or data-driven models. The former results in poor generalization when device deployments or target orientations change, while the latter requires acquiring extensive multi-view datasets, which is time-consuming and not always feasible. To address these limitations, in this work we propose VISTA, a novel method for reconstructing the uD spectrogram in an absolute coordinate frame, yielding view-independent Doppler features that are invariant to the spatial distribution of ISAC nodes. We formulate the uD estimation as a sparse reconstruction problem that jointly leverages measurements from all ISAC receivers. This is solved using a modified Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) algorithm, which iteratively alternates between jointly selecting candidate velocity vectors across all receivers (RXs) and independently estimating the complex channel gain amplitudes for each RX. Our results show that, provided sufficient spatial diversity, VISTA successfully reconstructs the targets' absolute uD spectrograms with a median error \leq 0.69 m/s for speeds \leq 15 m/s.

Title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
Author: Kaixuan Ji, Quanquan Gu
Text_Content: We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $Ω(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $Ω(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

Title: The Ultimate Karp-Lipton Collapse
Author: Edward A. Hirsch, Ilya Volkovich
Text_Content: Karp and Lipton proved that if $NP\subseteq P/poly$, then $PH$ collapses. A long line of work pushed the collapse to smaller classes. In particular, Chakaravarthy and Roy obtained two such collapses, to (apparently) incomparable classes $O_2^P$ and $P^{prMA}$. We united them earlier by a collapse to the input-oblivious version $P^{prOMA}$ of $P^{prMA}$, which is contained in both; and, jointly with Williams, to a slightly smaller class. Two other deepest known collapses are to $ZPP^{ONP}$ (following from Köbler and Watanabe) and to $OL_2^P$ (proved in this paper). We unite the three collapses by a collapse to a class contained in all of them. We use a three-stage computational model OGTD (oblivious generator-tester-decoder): a polynomial-time generator with an oracle computes an advice string from $1^n$, a tester certifies it, and a polynomial-time decoder uses it (it is the only one that sees the actual input). Let $OM$ be the class of OGTD languages defined by a restricted version of $prOMA$ as the generator's oracle, by a co-$ONP$ tester, and a $P$ decoder. We show that it is contained in the three collapse classes above and prove that $PH$ collapses to $OM$ under $NP\subseteq P/poly$. The collapse also holds for an unambiguous version of $OM$. All these input-oblivious collapse classes lie in $P^{prSBP}$, and so do even the non-input-oblivious versions $P^{prMA}$, $L_2^P$ and $S_2^P$: we prove that $P^{prS_2^P}\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. This strengthens the containment $S_2^P\subseteq P^{prAM}$ of Chakaravarthy and Roy and our earlier containment $L_2^P\subseteq P^{prSBP}$. The proof unites the Goldreich-Wigderson-type procedure of Chakaravarthy and Roy with our earlier approximate-counting technique. Its input-oblivious counterpart concerns $O_2^P$, the first collapse class of Chakaravarthy and Roy: every language in $O_2^P$ has polynomial-size circuits constructible in $FP^{prSBP}$.

Title: Optical symmetry breaking for single-image field reconstruction
Author: Egor Manuylovich
Text_Content: Light carries information in both amplitude and phase, although cameras record only intensity. Reconstructing the optical field is at the heart of wavefront sensing, microscopy and coherent communications. Existing methods often rely on multiple measurements or iterative phase retrieval. In fields described by known spatial modes, intensity is determined by pairwise products of their complex coefficients. Yet optical symmetries can make these products indistinguishable, leaving different fields with nearly identical images. Here, we show that engineering the optical measurement to break these symmetries enables direct reconstruction of the complex field from a single intensity image. We optimise a phase mask followed by propagation to separate pairwise modal signatures while retaining light on the detector. A calibrated linear inverse and rank-one projection then recover modal amplitudes and relative phases without iterative phase retrieval. In simulations, optimised masks satisfy conditioning and light-capture requirements unmet by random masks. Experiments reconstruct 42-mode fibre fields using either a spatial light modulator or a passive diffuser, with median complex-field errors of 9.1% and 4.6%, respectively, against holographic references. This extends an earlier five-mode experimental demonstration of fast intensity-only modal decomposition. Per-frame computation takes 2.1 ms, and batched throughput exceeds 4,000 frames per second. These results establish measurement-space symmetry breaking as a route to rapid single-image optical field reconstruction.

Title: Measuring Preferred Representation in AI-generated Images with Community Scorers
Author: Melanie F. Pradier, Camilla Longden, Anja Thieme, Rita F. Marques, Nari Johnson, Sidhika Balachandar, Xinnuo Xu, Linda Y. Wen, Martin Grayson, Katja Hofmann, Cecily Morrison, Daniela Massiceti
Text_Content: AI-generated images often misrepresent historically marginalised communities, with real-world consequences beyond the images themselves. However, conventional metrics fail to measure how communities want to be represented in AI-generated images. To address this, we introduce the concept of preferred representation. Building on previous work, we propose a measurement instrument that operationalises this concept through a Community Scorer - a model that evaluates a specific community's preferred representation in AI-generated images. We interrogate the validity of Community Scorers on three diverse disability communities that span the Global North and South. The results show that Community Scorers align significantly better with community ratings compared to other widely used text-to-image metrics. We then demonstrate the usefulness of these scorers in a downstream content filtering task. We release the Community Preference Dataset to enable others to optimise how Community Scorers can be scaled for culturally specific evaluation of AI-generated visual media.

Title: Multi-UTE Myelin Fraction Mapping: Repeatability and Cross-Field-Strength Reproducibility at 1.5T and 3T
Author: Nan Yin, Marco Reisert, Theo Demerath, Shuai Liu, Alexander Rau, Uzay Emir, Horst Urbach, Michael Bock, Ali Caglar Özen
Text_Content: Purpose: To evaluate the repeatability and cross-field-strength reproducibility (1.5T vs 3T) of in vivo cerebral myelin fraction (MF) mapping with multi-contrast dual-resolution 3D UTE (multi-UTE), and to compare it with magnetization transfer (MT)-based methods. Methods: MT methods provide an indirect myelin-sensitive measure derived from magnetization exchange between macromolecular and free-water proton pools, whereas multi-UTE targets the ultrashort-T2* signal components. In five healthy volunteers, multi-UTE and MT-based measurements were performed at 1.5T and 3T, and the calculated MF maps were compared with magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) and magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) maps. Two volunteers underwent repeated multi-UTE measurements within and between days. Field-strength reproducibility and test-retest repeatability were evaluated using linear regression, Bland-Altman analysis, concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results: Multi-UTE enabled simultaneous acquisition of quantitative and high-resolution structural images at both 1.5T and 3T. MF repeatability was high at 3T (ICC = 0.94-0.96) and more variable at 1.5T (0,64-0.96). Across field strengths, MF and MTsat showed comparable reproducibility (CCC 0.70 vs 0.60) with small median absolute differences (8.8% vs 8.9%). MTsat showed tighter correlation (R2 = 0.77 vs 0.68), while MF showed a wider inter-regional dynamic range. MTR differed strongly between field strengths (CCC = 0.06). Conclusion: Multi-UTE MF, obtained without B1 or T1 mapping and alongside a high-resolution structural image, achieves cross-field reproducibility comparable to, but not exceeding, MTsat. Lower SNR at 1.5T and unmodelled T1 weighting may have contributed to residual field dependence.

Title: One Future Fits All: Text-to-image AI and the Narrowing of Global Imagination
Author: Stephanie Diepeveen, Somnath Batabyal, Edward Ademolu, Peter Chonka, Gabriele de Seta, Iginio Gagliardone, Elisabeth Gunawan, Fabio Gygi, Yidnekachew Haile, Yenn Lee, Chipo Mapondera, Craig Ryder, Matti Pohjonen, Michiel Baas
Text_Content: Persistence of algorithmic bias is well established in scholarship, reflecting, reproducing and reshaping inequalities and injustices. Yet, as technology changes, we cannot assume that inequalities will be reproduced in the same or similar forms. This article explores the reproduction of bias in text-to-image generative AI, looking at the tool, Microsoft Bing Create, based on DALL E 3. It draws on results of a collaborative exploratory study of 907 image-based outputs of text-to-image generation in 15 languages and concerning 12 countries. We utilise the notion of synthetic probes (de Seta, 2024) to iteratively explore correlations of inputs and outputs within the context of place, language and power. We find striking simplicity in the scope of possibilities through which Bing Create considers the current and future city. Stripping out (explicit) indications of conflict, poverty and politics, we are left with images whose localised diversity harkens back to versions of Orientalist imaginaries. Images of the future emerge as one civilising mission or modernisation narrative, with all places headed to one future of hovercrafts, urban gardens and solar panels, encased in a composition of shades of blue and green. We argue that the visual outputs of this generative AI tool reflect and reproduce a simple but pervasive and persistent colonial/developmental worldview. We explore explanations for this emergent narrative and its implications, suggesting the threat of generative AI is not in its complexity or intelligence, but rather its banality. With this, we propose banality not as mere repetition, but the systematic narrowing of representational possibility: a convergence on tourist-friendly, depoliticised, development-saturated visual grammars that smooth contradiction and foreclose plural futurisms.

Title: Subsurface schematisation from sparse CPT data using the tabular foundation model TabPFN
Author: Taiga Saito, Fabian Campos Montero, Bruno Zuada Coelho, Ana Martins Teixeira, Stephen Wu, Timo Schweckendiek, Yu Otake
Text_Content: Subsurface schematisation supports geotechnical decisions but remains challenging because sparse site-investigation data leave substantial gaps in information about ground conditions. This study explores TabPFN, a foundation model pretrained on general synthetic tabular data, for this task. Using only grid coordinates and soil behaviour type index observations from sparse cone penetration tests (CPTs), we first reconstruct two-dimensional sections without geotechnical fine-tuning or predefined layer boundaries. We evaluate the approach on synthetic sections and at two field sites in the Netherlands, comparing it with SchemaGAN, a conditional generative adversarial network trained on synthetic geotechnical sections, and with reference interpolation methods. In the baseline comparisons, TabPFN achieved mean errors close to SchemaGAN's on synthetic sections and lower mean errors at both field sites. On synthetic sections, TabPFN's mean absolute error decreased at each tested increase in CPT count, and, under the baseline input setting, its pointwise prediction intervals had mean coverage close to nominal levels. Subsequent fine-tuning on the synthetic sections used to train SchemaGAN improved synthetic test accuracy but increased mean errors at both field sites. These findings indicate that general-purpose tabular foundation models offer a promising route for updating subsurface predictions from sparse and evolving site-investigation data without retraining.

Title: Tendex Lines and Short-Time Deformation: The Geometry of Lunar Tides
Author: F. J. Beron-Vera
Text_Content: Tendex lines and the stretchlines and squeezelines of Lagrangian coherent structure theory share a geometric construction: they integrate eigenvector fields of symmetric tensors. We connect their dynamical interpretations through the short-time deformation of particles released with zero initial velocity relative to a freely falling reference in an autonomous gravitational field. The leading departure of the Cauchy--Green tensor from the identity is quadratic in time and equals the tidal tensor multiplied by the squared observation time. The tidal tensorlines therefore give the limiting principal stretching and squeezing directions. For the planar lunar field, these tensorlines are radial lines and concentric circles centered on the Moon. The same tidal tensor defines a Lorentzian metric whose null directions have no quadratic change in line-element length. Its null geodesics are logarithmic spirals, describing the short-time limit of finite-time unit-stretch geometry. Near Earth, the principal tensorlines clarify the two outward tidal tendencies, while the null directions distinguish vanishing leading extension from vanishing relative acceleration.

Title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
Author: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang
Text_Content: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

Title: TGen-SQD: Physics-Informed Transferable Configuration Generator for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
Author: Niloy Deb Roy Mishu, Lei Jiang, Mohsen Heidari, Ruizhe Zhang, Fan Chen
Text_Content: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) avoids iterative variational circuit optimization, but its accuracy and cost depend on selecting a compact determinant subspace that captures the ground state. Existing machine-learning selectors use task-specific physical cues and typically retrain for each Hamiltonian. We introduce TGen-SQD, a physics-informed generator jointly trained across multiple Hamiltonians. It learns from configuration-interaction-weighted data and uses orbital- and system-level descriptors to guide generation. After training, its weights remain frozen for inference on seen and zero-shot geometries. On a 20-qubit H10 chain, TGen-SQD achieves mean energy errors of 40.18 +/- 1.52 and 43.97 +/- 1.20 mHa on seen and unseen geometries, respectively, 12.7% and 11.7% lower than the state-of-the-art PIGen-SQD baseline under matched shot and proposal budgets.

Title: An EPTAS for Max-Cut on Interval Graphs
Author: Hani Ahmadzadeh, Morteza Alimi
Text_Content: Max-Cut was shown NP-hard on interval graphs by Adhikary, Bose, Mukherjee, and Roy (SoCG 2021). The best previously known approximation ratio for this class, due to Ahn, DeHaan, Kim, and Lee (APPROX 2025), exceeded the Goemans--Williamson ratio of about $0.878$ by only $10^{-34}$. We give a deterministic efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS): for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate cut of an unweighted $n$-vertex interval graph can be found in time $2^{O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^3(2/\varepsilon))}n^2$. The same guarantee and running time hold for Max-Bisection. An FPTAS is impossible unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Our algorithm rests on a structural theorem: every interval graph with $m$ edges can be turned into an interval graph of clique-width $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(2/\varepsilon))$ by deleting at most $\varepsilon m$ edges. The construction combines endpoint-rank coordinates, length-dependent rounding, and a shifted dyadic hierarchy. Intervals intersecting cell boundaries at their own scales are isolated at small total edge cost; the interactions of remaining long intervals with smaller subproblems can be summarized by counts. The structural theorem also yields a randomized EPTAS via Lampis's scheme for bounded clique-width; our direct dynamic program is deterministic and handles Max-Bisection. Finally, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is NP-hard to approximate Max-Cut within $84/85+\varepsilon$ on unweighted chordal graphs, which contain interval graphs. Thus an approximation scheme for Max-Cut on chordal graphs would imply $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$.

Title: Agentic Computational Algebra
Author: Ryan A. Anderson, Matthew Trager, Ben Bowman, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
Text_Content: We explore the use of AI agents for solving computational problems in algebra. For the problems we consider, the main challenge is not correctness but \emph{time}: general-purpose algorithms are guaranteed to provide correct solutions but can be prohibitively slow, while reformulations that exploit special structure often allow solving a problem much faster. We propose to use this setting to evaluate how effectively agents discover and exploit structure within and across tasks to reduce computational costs. More broadly, computational algebra supplies infinitely many problems with independently verifiable answers and systematically controllable structure and difficulty. To illustrate these possibilities, we use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances using persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known problem family. Our experiments show that (i) agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can sometimes outweigh computational savings; (ii) memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies; (iii) compilation produces faster reusable solvers but at substantial upfront cost. Overall, computational algebra offers concrete, measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure.

Title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers
Author: Xuan Luo, Zhiyuan Wang, Hanzhong Cao, Xifeng Yan
Text_Content: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.

Title: Mapping the High-Field Response of Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
Author: Harshit Agarwal, Yueh-Chun Wu, Katyayani Seal, Niels Noordzij, Andreas Fognini, Ronan Gourgues, Gábor B. Halász, Benjamin J. Lawrie, Nirjhar Sarkar
Text_Content: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) are increasingly being integrated into cryogenic quantum-sensing platforms that operate in large magnetic fields. Here, the high-field limits of these measurements were probed by characterizing the dark count response of a NbTiN SNSPD at up to 14~T using in situ control of the detector orientation and benchmarking that performance against normal detector operation in smaller magnetic fields. The detector performance is strongly anisotropic: perpendicular magnetic fields rapidly reduce the usable bias-current range, whereas near-parallel alignment enables operation at substantially larger total fields, with a finite operating margin retained to 12~T and measurable dark-count response at the 14~T field limit. The angular dependence is governed predominantly by the perpendicular component of the magnetic field, consistent with vortex-mediated suppression of the superconducting current scale. The same field-dependent current scale also determines the electrical pulse amplitude, linking high-field detector operation directly to readout performance. These results establish a practical route for deploying SNSPDs in multi-tesla quantum-sensing and high-field cryogenic experiments.

Title: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
Author: Mohammad Omar Khursheed, Thomas Morris, Fabien Roger
Text_Content: Developers train models to follow a consistent character using methods like Model Spec Midtraining (Li et al., 2026), which have been hypothesized to make alignment more robust and generalize broadly. However, it is possible for subsequent RL with misspecified rewards to work against character training. In this work, we apply character training to teach gpt-oss-20b a semi-realistic constitution and study how it interacts with two types of RL that reward breaking the constitution's rules (opposing RL): answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems, and reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower than gpt-oss-20b to answer harmful requests. Character-trained models also display more motivated reasoning on harmful answers than gpt-oss-20b, and hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. Finally, since explaining the reasons behind rules can improve how alignment generalizes (Kutasov et al., 2026), we compare constitutions that justify the same rules by grounding them in a value or not, and find little difference between motivations on misalignment, honesty, and capability evaluations.

Title: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
Author: Joonas Pääkkönen
Text_Content: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised and their minimal cost is determined. The entire cost-vulnerability frontier is then determined for every bias. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric; they do not constitute a cryptographic masking scheme.

Title: Tokenized Reward Systems for Federated Learning: The Privacy vs. Fairness Tradeoff
Author: Andreas Sendros, Nikolaos Pavlidis, Vasilios Perifanis, Pavlos S. Efraimidis
Text_Content: Federated learning (FL) systems increasingly rely on blockchain based reward mechanisms to incentivize participation while preserving data privacy. We design and empirically evaluate two complementary Solidity smart contracts for FL reward distribution: the first one that allocates rewards proportionally to a publicly disclosed quality score, and a privacy preserving variant that hides individual quality scores behind a zero-knowledge (ZK) proof of a threshold condition. Both contracts mint a non transferable, use-and-burn token maintaining a trustless incentive structure. We evaluate the two designs through MNIST training with adversarial behavior, including Sybil attacks, zero gradient and random noise, across three independent random seeds. Our results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness. The privacy preserving architecture strictly degrades system robustness, doubling the adversary's average reward capture while introducing severe outcome variance. This vulnerability is driven by a structural self-inclusion bias within cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates naturally diminish, rendering them statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise. Adversaries exploit this dynamic to systematically breach the ZK threshold, triggering a late stage failure cascade that culminates in absolute adversary monopoly over the reward pool and the total exclusion of honest contributors. Alongside a closed-form theorem formalizing this privacy--Sybil resistance tradeoff, we map strict mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, explicitly incorporating the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per transaction gas cap. Ultimately, while cryptographically secure, static threshold ZK gates fail as incentive layer fairness mechanisms under realistic FL convergence dynamics on standard benchmarks.

Title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
Author: Haoyi Qiu, Akshat Agarwal
Text_Content: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.

Title: Vocabulary-Free Next-Event Prediction on Temporal Graphs
Author: Zhishang Luo, Venu Madhav Tammali, Amila Weerasinghe, Osso Vahabzadeh, Olcay Boz, Xue Hao, Yusu Wang
Text_Content: Autoregressive transformer training through next-token prediction has driven remarkable advances in language modeling and has become increasingly effective for time-series modeling. Yet its success in temporal graph learning remains limited, and most temporal link-prediction methods are discriminative rather than autoregressive. While temporal graphs can have a natural serialization through chronological ordering edges, they lack an obvious graph-independent tokenization: existing node tokenization often uses a vocabulary that grows with the number of nodes, limiting scalability and cross-graph training. We propose GTGT, Generative Temporal Graph Transformer, a simple yet powerful vocabulary-free framework for self-supervised next-event prediction on temporal graphs. It predicts events for observed destinations, behavioral descriptors for novel destinations, and time gaps before new event. These targets have shared meanings across graphs, allowing one transformer to train across disjoint node sets without node-specific learned parameters. Local node identifiers let attention capture graph structure: Theoretically, we can show that our transformer-based model has the capacity for time-respecting message passing mechanisms. On Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB), our GTGT not only achieves comparable or better link-prediction performance than established baselines, but also has much lower training cost. These results open the door to temporal graph pretraining for forecasting and other downstream tasks, providing a concrete step toward temporal graph foundation models.

Title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models
Author: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
Text_Content: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $κ= 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($κ= 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($κ= 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.

Title: REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
Author: Minghao Li, Nick Koudas, Raghav Mittal
Text_Content: Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled. Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

Title: Human Capital in Context: What Employment Survival Reveals About Worker-Firm Match
Author: Jung Ho Choi, Mario Milone
Text_Content: There is no best worker in general, only a best worker for a particular firm. We develop a measure of worker-firm match quality that treats fit as a property of the pair, learned from the survival of employment relationships. A two-tower neural network embeds workers, from their career histories and current positions, and firms, from their characteristics and business descriptions, into a common space, and match quality is the cosine similarity of the two vectors. The measure takes its functional form from the skill-weights model of firm-specific human capital, and its only estimated objective, a separation hazard, from the view of the job match as an experience good. Estimated on more than a billion person-periods covering 101 million workers and 8.4 million firms, a 0.1 increase in match quality lowers the odds of separation by 48%. About a quarter of the variance of match quality is specific to the worker-firm pair, which worker-, firm-, and occupation-level measures set to zero by construction. Workers earn more when better matched, especially early in a relationship, and firms whose workforces score higher grow faster, become more profitable, and are issued more, and more valuable, patents over the next five years than their industry peers. Because it scores pairs that never formed, the measure also predicts where movers go, and acquirers record a larger share of the price as goodwill when the target's workers would fit the acquirer better than they fit the target.

Title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
Author: Fabrizia Giulia Garavaglia, Marco Giunti
Text_Content: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

Title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
Author: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
Text_Content: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding.
