Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.

Title: Koopman Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
Author: Wenjian Hao, Paulo C. Heredia, Shaoshuai Mou
Text_Content: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig.1.

Title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Lifted Bellman Linear Programming
Author: Jongchan Park, Hyukjun Yang, Narim Jeong, Donghwan Lee
Text_Content: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $ρ$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.

Title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
Author: Gabriel Maresch, Erik Schulze, Jnan Yalla
Text_Content: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

Title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
Author: Christoph Jahn, Delvin Bacho, Urs Waldmann, Bastian Goldluecke
Text_Content: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

Title: Cross-Border Fulfillment Center Selection via Doubly Robust Estimation and Linear Programming
Author: Kriti Mahajan, Patrick Bloebaum
Text_Content: We introduce the cross-border (XB) fulfillment center (FC) Selection Model: a multi-stage optimization framework combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to select optimal source FCs. For each source-destination shipping arc, the objective is to choose a subset of source-country FCs that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. We evaluate the model on three production-scale international shipping corridors for a large e-commerce company using 12 months of shipment data, employing both aggregate offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching. Across all shipping corridors, the XB FC Selection Model achieves 8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost relative to human expert-defined FC selection policies, with up to 6.5 percentage-point improvements in 5/5 target compliance (5 days, $5 USD). Pareto analysis shows the model consistently dominates single-objective ranking strategies and unconstrained LP on the efficiency-reallocation frontier, with all results statistically significant.

Title: BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification under Unknown Distributions
Author: Shenxi Liu, Yiwei Li, Mingyang Zhao, Yuhang Tian, Kan Li
Text_Content: Repeated sampling with majority selection is an effective means of enforcing self-consistency in large language models. Recently, a variant has also been introduced that terminates early to save costs when the output distribution is favorable. But it still cannot yield a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. For this issue, we formalize this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a budget and a target error rate, and propose BARS, a sequential rule certifying the top-two gap and returning an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, and it tells practitioners when to widen the budget or switch models. A certified mode carries proven bounds on the joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while a practical mode, used in our experiments, replaces them with empirical calibration. On synthetic instances drawn from known distributions over thousands of seeds, the difficulty-driven behavior is recovered and the price of the certified mode is measured.On GSM8K the practical mode draws 22.3\% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling over the same pool, refused questions included, at the cost of declining 18.8\% of the questions. On MATH, it greatly improves the accuracy of its output answers into 82.5\% at the cost of honestly refusing to answer half of the difficult questions that the model itself is unable to solve.

Title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
Author: Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
Text_Content: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

Title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete
Author: Leon Riccius, Iuri B. C. M. Rocha, Erik Schlangen, Frans P. van der Meer
Text_Content: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 μm to 80 μm commonly assumed in the literature.

Title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
Author: Junaid Akram, Ali Hassan, Danish Vasan
Text_Content: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.

Title: Nonadaptive One-Sided Testing of Binary Rank
Author: Nader H. Bshouty
Text_Content: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition its one-entries. We study entry-query testing of binary rank at most $d$, with one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. We give a tester using $\tilde O(d^4/ε^2)$ queries, independent of the matrix dimensions and a general lower bound of $\tilde Ω(d^{3/2}/ε)$.

Title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
Author: Scott Weady
Text_Content: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.

Title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
Author: Lucas Fourel, Paul Devianne, Marine Debouvry, Tristan Destruhaut, Russell Gunn, Ashwini Gupta, Lori Graham-Brady, Jean-François Molinari
Text_Content: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

Title: Uneven Self-Reported AI Use: An Embedded Case Study Across Eleven Teams in a Software Organization
Author: Daniele Veri'
Text_Content: This paper presents a descriptive, embedded single-case study examining self-reported AI use within a software organization. The study draws on 98 structured interview records collected across 11 teams, using ten standardized team-level instruments (n = 65) and one instrument with distinct response anchors (n = 33). Among respondents assessed using standardized instruments, 36 of 65 (55.4%) reported AI-use frequency scores of 4 or 5 on a five-point scale. Team-level proportions varied from 20.0% (1/5) to 71.4% (5/7). A record-level cross-tabulation revealed limited awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies across both frequency groups: 86.1% (31/36) of respondents scoring 4-5 and 96.6% (28/29) of those scoring 0-3 reported either no policy awareness or uncertainty about policy details. In the group assessed using the distinct instrument, 31 of 33 respondents (93.9%) scored 4 or 5. Although the pooled proportion reached 68.4% (67/98), differences in response anchors limit direct comparability, making the standardized-instrument results the primary analytical reference. Interviewer-recorded observations provide qualitative context on reported practices and constraints but do not support estimates of their prevalence or causal explanations for differences in AI-use frequency. The findings characterize AI-use patterns and policy awareness within the interviewed sample, without supporting inferences about organization-wide adoption, policy compliance, or the effectiveness of AI use. The study contributes an empirically grounded organizational case and an explicit account of the methodological boundaries of cross-team comparisons using heterogeneous interview instruments.

Title: Unipolar Neuron Networks Trained by Recirculation for Reward-Based Continual Learning
Author: Florin Leon
Text_Content: Unipolar neurons are the predominant type of nerve cell in the octopus and in most other invertebrates. A single neurite (a fiber extending from the cell body) branches into a tree that carries both input and output synapses. The branches send graded local outputs to nearby cells, and one site on the main neurite sends a global output to distant targets. This paper proposes a network of such neurons and a learning rule for it. Each neuron is modeled as a tree of passive segments, whose activations are computed exactly as the steady state of a linear system. The network learns from reward alone, with a rule called recirculation. After each forward pass, a second pass sends requested changes of the outputs back through the same connections. Each synapse then adjusts its weight using only quantities available at its own location. Because the system of each neuron is symmetric, this update closely follows the gradient of the error in the predicted reward. Two mechanisms limit forgetting when tasks are learned in sequence: a task code inhibits a different subset of branches in each task, while consolidation lowers the learning rate of synapses that changed strongly in the recent past. The model is evaluated on a sequence of MNIST and Iris tasks. The network maintains high accuracy with low forgetting, whereas gradient-based training of the same network forgets earlier tasks almost completely.

Title: Where are the shortest-path nodes in spatial networks?
Author: Xinhan Liu, Robert Kooij, Piet Van Mieghem
Text_Content: To predict the spatial distribution of shortest-path nodes, we propose a Gaussian estimate of the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$, the probability that a node $w$ lies on a shortest path between a source $u$ and a destination $v$. According to the Gaussian estimate, three variables affect the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$ and combine into one variable, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$. In our simulations of hard and soft random geometric graphs in Euclidean, hyperbolic and spherical space, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$ alone approximately determines how fast the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$ decreases as the node $w$ moves away from the geodesic between the source $u$ and the destination $v$. We find and explain that, when the hopcount variance $σ^2(H_{uv})$ is very small, the shortest-path nodes have a discrete spatial distribution, a quantized distribution of shortest-path nodes. We further extend the study to spatially inhomogeneous networks, for which we propose a method to find the shortest-path nodes.

Title: Limits of Cell Sensing in Observer-Absorber Assemblies
Author: Julius B. Kirkegaard, Albert Alonso, Robert G. Endres
Text_Content: Absorption improves concentration sensing for an isolated cell by suppressing rebinding correlations. We study how that local advantage competes with collective depletion in assemblies of cells coupled through the shared diffusion field. We introduce an observer--absorber model for permeant ligands sensed and consumed intracellularly with finite volumetric uptake rate $κ$ that continuously interpolates between Berg--Purcell monitoring and perfect absorption. For a single spherical cell, monitoring correlations, uptake statistics and optimal joint estimator are obtained analytically, and we characterize the transition between using observer and absorber information for sensing. In this case, all sensing strategies improve monotonically with $κ$. For arbitrary cell assemblies, we show that the long-time sensing problem can be reduced to solving for just two steady-state quantities for each cell: the mean internal concentration $\Cbar$ and its local sensitivity $\Tbar=-\partial_κ\log\Cbar$. In multicellular systems, uptake shortens rebinding memory, but it also depletes the signal available to neighbors. We reveal geometry-dependent optima for absorption rates, with Pareto fronts arising from competing objectives, as well as pure observing, pure absorbing, and partially absorbing regimes.

Title: From Search to Decision: How Post-Training Shapes Information-Seeking Capabilities in Large Language Models
Author: Haohang Huang, Xuan Lu, Mingjin Kuai, Yuxuan Zhang, Wei Ji, Haiyang Zhang
Text_Content: Information seeking in large language model (LLM) systems increasingly involves decisions about when to acquire information, where to search, and how to evaluate and use evidence. Recent post-training methods have improved several such behaviors, but their objectives and evaluations span different tasks and system settings. This paper organizes research around six interrelated information-seeking capabilities and examines the learning signals, optimization methods, update loci, and credit-assignment mechanisms used to develop them. We synthesize empirical progress in targeted behaviors, end-to-end performance, search control, and generalization. Existing studies report gains in retrieval routing, query refinement, multi-tool exploration, evidence-grounded reasoning, and resource-aware search, although the scope of behavioral evidence varies across capabilities. We identify open challenges in estimating prospective retrieval utility, coordinating information-seeking decisions, and adapting to unfamiliar retrieval environments, and discuss evaluation practices for interpreting future progress.

Title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
Author: Zhicheng Zhang, Mingsheng Ying, Lirong Xia
Text_Content: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

Title: Energetic costs of reaching the physical limits of sensing
Author: Albert Alonso, Julius B. Kirkegaard, Robert G. Endres
Text_Content: Cells sense chemical gradients by absorbing ligand molecules, a nonequilibrium process that necessarily produces entropy. But how many molecules must a cell absorb, and therefore energy dissipate, to approach the physical limits of sensing? We derive closed-form expressions relating gradient sensing uncertainty to the number of absorbed molecules, which we link to entropy production. Unlike concentration sensing, which depends only on the total count, gradient sensing must resolve the angular asymmetry of the absorbed flux, adding a bounded dipole-contrast factor set by how strongly the cell absorbs. In the strong-signal regime, cells approach peak chemotactic alignment while absorbing a small fraction of the diffusion-limited uptake, with the required number of uptake events set by the relative concentration change across the cell. Re-analysis of Dictyostelium chemotaxis places the cell at 0.25% of that limit with a minor metabolic load, suggesting that sensing is limited by counting noise rather than by energetic cost.

Title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models
Author: Yuhong Wang, Yujun Cai, Lei Feng, Songze Li
Text_Content: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.

Title: Deviation-Aware Pretraining for Cardiovascular Disease Detection from Electrocardiograms
Author: Siyuan Yan, Haibo Zheng, Feng Lu, Wei Li
Text_Content: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are critical for cardiovascular disease (CVD) detection. Most current deep learning models rely on supervised, task-specific training, which limits their ability to generalize across diseases, patient populations, and acquisition settings. This paper presents a self-supervised ECG feature extraction framework that learns from nearly one million unlabeled 12-lead ECG recordings. The framework includes two modules: Deviation Localization Embedding (DLE), which detects waveform-level deviations from normal patterns, and Association Reconstruction Embedding (ARE), which models cross-lead associations through deviation-guided reconstruction to capture abnormal patterns expressed across multiple leads. These modules enable the framework to capture subtle deviation-related patterns and their cross-lead context. The framework achieves up to 6.5% AUROC and 12.8% F1 improvements over prior methods on multiple public datasets, even without additional fine-tuning the pretrained feature extractor. Embedding visualizations show that the learned features support meaningful disease grouping and anomaly identification. The approach reduces the need for labeled data and can support clinicians in diverse healthcare settings. The framework has potential to improve early detection and monitoring of cardiovascular diseases, contributing to more accessible and equitable heart care.

Title: HaiRuo: Forecasting Ocean Eddies as Fields and Objects with a Satellite-Altimetry Foundation Model
Author: Xukun Qin, Haochen Sun, Yuyang Tian, Ge Chen
Text_Content: Mesoscale eddies carry most of the ocean's kinetic energy and move heat, salt and nutrients across basins, yet where an eddy will be two weeks ahead is still read off ocean models with post-hoc tracking heuristics. We introduce HaiRuo, which forecasts eddies as fields and as objects at once: from 30 days of satellite sea-level maps, one forward pass returns 15 days of sea level and geostrophic velocity, daily eddy masks and the trajectory of every eddy alive today. HaiRuo pairs two components with a clear division of labour: (1) HaiRuo-1B, an open-weight 1.05-billion-parameter foundation model pretrained without labels on 24 years of global satellite-altimetry observations, which supplies the 15-day physical fields and masks (+0.14 field skill and +1.1 mIoU points under the same decoder) and further lowers 15-day centre error by 1.2 km frozen (1.35 km over training from scratch); and (2) XuanJi, a Lagrangian object decoder that samples the evolving forecast in each eddy's co-moving polar frame and refines the 15-day path across three look-ahead rounds, removing 2.5 km on HaiRuo-1B (2.9 km with joint fine-tuning) and 2.5-3.3 km via its object attention across six published backbones. Under one pre-registered global evaluation over the whole ocean, HaiRuo improves on fourteen methods on every endpoint (25.2 vs. 30.6 km 15-day centre error, -18%), holding its margin outside the labelled regions and through both phases of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), while reproducing westward drift, 50-60 deg S eastward reversal and poleward cyclone-anticyclone deflection. Over ten days through one fixed tracker, HaiRuo's forecast field cuts the eddy-centre error of WenHai and XiHe by 37-43% (-2.8 km vs. day 0 while they degrade +4.3-8.7 km), and its object trajectories cut pipeline error by 77-78% globally. Open-weight checkpoints, code and project page: https://github.com/xkqin/HaiRuo

Title: Sim(3)-TurboReg: Robust and Efficient Scale-Aware Registration via Tri-Scale Consistency
Author: Zijun Zhou, Shaocheng Yan, Zhenjun Zhao, Yutong Hu, Ke Yang, Yingdong Gu, Pengcheng Shi, Jiayuan Li
Text_Content: Feed-forward 3D foundation models recover geometry at high fidelity, yet inference memory constraints keep them from processing long sequences natively. Current streaming systems work around this limit with sliding-window chunking, which introduces severe monocular scale ambiguity. Resolving this ambiguity requires Sim(3) registration that stays accurate and efficient under outlier contamination. We introduce Sim(3)-TurboReg, which reformulates the compatibility graph construction of TurboReg by replacing absolute distance constraints with a strict Tri-Scale Consistency (TSC) criterion. Our analysis shows that TSC suppresses both mismatching and coordinate-distortion outliers. We integrate the resulting solver into existing streaming systems and obtain high-fidelity, kilometer-scale reconstruction for feed-forward models. On controlled unknown-scale registration at 90% outliers, ours matches RANSAC accuracy with 92.5% lower median latency. In DA3-Streaming on KITTI, ours improves mean ATE RMSE by 22.2% and reduces mean end-to-end time by 16.6%. Code: https://github.com/ivan-zzj/Sim3-TurboReg

Title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
Author: David Dembinsky, Adriano Lucieri, Andreas Dengel
Text_Content: Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) promises models that are not only accurate but also rely on task-relevant evidence. However, whether improved agreement between model explanations and human-provided rationales also implies a changed decision strategy remains unclear. We study this tension under controlled synthetic shortcut introduction using a constructed shortcut dataset. Inspired by real-world applications, our benchmark covers shortcuts of different kinds, including localized, background-based, and global cues. This allows us to evaluate whether different EGL objectives produce behavioral changesand explanatory changes. Across these axes, we find that the effects of EGL are strongly objective-specific. Rationale-based data augmentation provides the clearest robustness gains when shortcut evidence can be separated from task-relevant foreground information, reaching average accuracy improvements of up to +4.8 percentage points (pp) together with increased foreground reliance. Attribution-constraining objectives primarily improve explanation plausibility, increasing Importance Mass by up to +14 pp on average, but provide weaker and less consistent behavioral correction, with average accuracy gains of at most +1.6 pp. Moreover, neither improved robustness nor improved plausibility reliably implies higher perturbation-based fidelity. Overall, our results show that EGL can be useful, but its success cannot be inferred from rationale agreement alone and should instead be evaluated along complementary behavioral and explanation-level axes. We publicly release all experimental results to enable further analysis (https://right-for-wrong-reasons.dfki.de/).

Title: Exponential Control of Adiabatic Time Reflection by Complex-Time Singularities
Author: Shiyue Deng, Qian Niu
Text_Content: Nearly identical temporal switching profiles can produce very different reflections even when both have small local adiabatic measures. In a lossless dielectric, we obtain this difference by adding a weak feature that changes the complex-time singularities while preserving monotonicity, endpoints, and central slope. A perturbation bounded by $0.6\%$ of the total inverse-permittivity change raises the reflected mode amplitude from $8.02\times10^{-10}$ to $1.28\times10^{-3}$. The complex action and pole residue predict this amplitude to within $0.32\%$. Within this waveform family, deviation and monotonicity constraints select three design regimes. At fixed deviation bound, reoptimization keeps the central feature's time scale comparable to the inverse incident angular frequency. The optimal amplitude is then proportional to $1/T$ as the switching time $T$ tends to infinity. Stretching a fixed profile gives exponential suppression. Full-wave Maxwell simulations resolve the backward packet, and filtering calculations quantify its sensitivity to modulation bandwidth.

Title: Continuous 3D Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction via Histology-Informed Implicit Neural Representations
Author: Kaito Shiku, Ryoma Bise, Ahtisham Fazeel Abbasi, Yuichiro Iwashita, Shumpei Takezaki, Andreas Dengel, Muhammad Nabeel Asim
Text_Content: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) enables the analysis of gene-expression patterns across tissue depths. However, 3D ST measurements are acquired from discrete 2D tissue sections, which are often sparsely sampled due to high acquisition costs. To address this limitation, we propose a histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (HIM-INR) for continuous 3D gene-expression reconstruction from sparse ST observations. HIM-INR jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations using an INR with a shared backbone, leveraging densely sampled histological images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, HIM-INR predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without requiring histological images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as the number of missing ST sections increases.

Title: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Pooling-Induced Substructures
Author: Luca Sbicego, Xiaowen Dong, Dorina Thanou
Text_Content: Hierarchical graph-level tasks that require reasoning over substructures that extend beyond local neighborhoods are posing challenges for standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). While graph pooling aims to address this by coarsening graphs into hierarchical representations, existing methods often fail to explicitly preserve the substructures they induce, leading to inconsistent empirical performance. Moreover, evaluating such approaches remains challenging due to the lack of benchmarks with explicit hierarchical structure. We propose Pooled-Substructure-Aware GNNs, an approach to graph pooling that explicitly preserves and processes substructures uncovered by structure-based pooling schemes. We show that this design enhances the expressive power of pooling-based GNNs in the sense of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. To enable principled evaluation, we introduce two new synthetic datasets with controllable hierarchical structure and propose a metric to characterize the prevalence of hierarchical patterns in real-world graph-level benchmarks. On tasks with relevant hierarchical structure, our approach outperforms matched pooling baselines, while remaining competitive on structurally simpler benchmarks. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/lsbicego/PSA-GNN/.

Title: Asymptotically good codes from Siegel modular varieties
Author: Yota Maeda
Text_Content: We construct asymptotically good codes by evaluating Siegel modular forms at superspecial points on congruence towers of Siegel modular varieties. For every genus $g\ge2$ and every fixed weight $w\ge g+1$, the construction gives such a family in sufficiently large characteristic, over a finite field which is independent of the level of the tower. The towers can be chosen so that this field is $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$. We give an explicit lower bound for the asymptotic rate. The lower bound for the relative minimum distance follows from the Pieri formula on the space of flags in the Hodge bundle and an intersection argument along its strata. We also prove that, for $p\ge5$ and $0\le w\le p+1$, the kernel of evaluation in every genus consists precisely of the multiples of the ordinary Hasse invariant. For $g=2,3$, the geometry of the supersingular locus gives explicit bounds for the relative minimum distance and recovery sets whose sizes are bounded independently of the level.

Title: CroCoMAE: Cross-modal self-supervised collaborative representation learning for SAR-optical remote sensing data
Author: Vito Recchia, Giuseppe Guarino, Cássio Fraga Dantas, Giuseppina Andresini, Annalisa Appice, Dino Ienco
Text_Content: Remote sensing increasingly captures the Earth's surface through complementary sensors such as SAR and optical, yet ground-truth annotations remain scarce, limiting supervised approaches. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses the label scarcity, and cross-modal SSL further exploits the complementarity between co-located sensors, but existing cross-modal frameworks align modalities mostly through global image-level representations or treat them as largely redundant, leaving their fine-grained complementary structure underexploited. We propose CroCoMAE, a cross-modal SSL framework for SAR-optical remote sensing that unifies contrastive learning and masked image modeling within a ViT-based architecture, operating at two complementary levels. At the image level, an intra-modality contrastive loss on the class token yields globally discriminative, augmentation-invariant representations. At the patch level, masked image modeling drives fine-grained per-modality representations, while a cross-modal contrastive objective aligns a shared subspace across SAR and optical patch tokens, leaving the complementary subspace unconstrained to retain modality-specific information. On two SAR-optical benchmarks covering scene classification and semantic segmentation, CroCoMAE improves over uni-modal SSL baselines and outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal frameworks in most configurations, with gains in both single-modality and multi-modal evaluation across varying label regimes and the largest improvements on semantic segmentation.

Title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
Author: Federico Ravenda, Mirko Cesarini, Daniele Montagnani, Volodymyr Karpenko, Antonietta Mira, Andrea Raballo
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

Title: Criticality-Aware RAN Function Placement for Robust 6G Networks
Author: Gabriel M. Almeida, Joao F. Santos, Walid Saad, Nicola Marchetti, Kleber V. Cardoso
Text_Content: The disaggregation of base stations into radio access network (RAN) functions introduces new vulnerabilities to mobile networks, as disruptions in cloud locations can interrupt multiple RAN functions and trigger cascading failures, leading to widespread outages. In this paper, we propose a criticality-aware RAN function placement solution to improve the robustness of disaggregated mobile networks against random failures and targeted attacks. Our solution optimizes the placement of centralized units (CUs) and distributed units (DUs) across cloud locations to reduce functional dependencies and limit the criticality of cloud locations, while preserving the cost benefits of RAN function centralization. We formulate the placement as an optimization model that jointly minimizes functional dependency and placement cost, subject to criticality constraints, as well as computing and transport requirements. We numerically evaluated our approach on a real-world mobile network topology across multiple disruption scenarios and demonstrated that our solution improves robustness, yielding up to 75% more operational radio units (RUs) after disruptions than existing approaches.

Title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases
Author: Dominika Maslarova, Mattys Pouyez, Patrik Jansson, Jan Vabek, Robin Weissenbilder, Linus Hagedorn, Anne L'Huillier, Tünde Fülöp
Text_Content: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.

Title: TAMEing the Open-World Personalization: Towards Open-Set Personalized MLLM Assistant
Author: Rongpei Hong, Jian Lang, Ting Zhong, Fan Zhou
Text_Content: Personalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as intelligent assistants has recently emerged as an active research topic, where an MLLM is expected to go beyond generic, one-size-fits-all replies, and instead generate responses grounded in user-specific objects, entities, and concepts encountered during interactions. Nevertheless, existing studies mainly focus on personalizing MLLMs on a static, predefined set of personalized concepts and require users to manually and frequently extend this set to accommodate newly emerging concepts, which is infeasible in dynamic-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we recast conventional MLLM personalization as an Open-Set problem, and propose TAME-O, the first long-context open-set personalized MLLM assistant. Specifically, TAME-O introduces a training-free, plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill (CR Skill). It enables the assistant to automatically unlock novel concepts during prolonged human-MLLM interactions while preventing confusion with previously unlocked ones, allowing the MLLM to continually grasp more and more concepts and progressively refine the modeling of known ones. Extensive experiments under the open-set personalization setting underscore the efficacy of our method.

Title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
Author: Patricio M. Vera
Text_Content: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? First, we reanalyzed trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018), computing each test image's distance to the examples shown in the space of a frozen self-supervised visual encoder (DINOv2). Distance was associated with extension (log odds -3.23 per standard deviation; 520 people), and an exploratory post hoc analysis suggested that this association persisted within the taught domain after controlling for taxonomic level and teaching condition. Example composition also mattered: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. Second, in an artificial learner using the same encoder, words joining two categories were learned less accurately the farther apart the categories were (84.7%, 65.4%, and 53.0% naming accuracy for near, mid, and far pairs). The encoder's distances correlated with human similarity and confusability measures from three datasets (rho = .501-.795), but this representational alignment did not translate into conclusive evidence that human-derived distances predict learner difficulty, and a second encoder trained on one child's experience reproduced the tier ordering but not the pair-level effect. The secondary human data were analyzed under an internal plan fixed before the confirmatory analyses (not externally preregistered). Visual similarity accounts for part of how generalization is organized in both systems, while the composition of examples contributes what the distance we used does not capture.

Title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
Author: Qinfeng Zhu, Weiguang Zhao, Ke Sun, Xihao Guo, Yunxi Jiang, Rui Zhang, Lei Fan, Kaizhu Huang
Text_Content: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.

Title: Looking One Step Ahead: An Anticipation-guided Agent for Object State Readout in Videos
Author: Yuanhe Tian, Yan Song
Text_Content: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

Title: SGAA: Independent active alignment of optical subgroups with uncompensated aberrations
Author: Le Dai, Zhenyao Zheng, Wenyong Li, Yuhan Bao, Weijian Hu, Kailun Yang, Kaiwei Wang
Text_Content: Uncompensated subgroup aberrations complicate subgroup-level active alignment (AA), as local image-quality extrema do not directly indicate the target alignment state. We propose SGAA, an image-learning-based method for independent active alignment of optical subgroups. Multi-field point spread functions (PSFs) from a dedicated test configuration characterize misalignment, while golden-sample reference calibration and unified regression predict adjustments toward a common optical target across toleranced specimens. In simulations with tolerances, one step reduced the mean differential wavefront RMS from $0.0592λ$ to $0.0086λ$, an 85.4% reduction. In alignment experiments on 100 production subgroups, SGAA increased the mean full-lens weighted modulation transfer function (WMTF) at 30, 50, and 80 lp/mm by 0.073, 0.065, and 0.040, respectively, relative to industrial MTF-based scanning. The 8 MP acceptance yield increased by 29.2 percentage points, and mean alignment time decreased from 43 s to 3.1 s. SGAA thus translates independent subgroup reference-state restoration into gains in full-lens imaging, acceptance yield, and alignment speed.

Title: Model-Free Runtime Measurement of Task-Relevant Information
Author: Dimitris Panagopoulos, Adolfo Perrusquía, Yang Xing, Weisi Guo
Text_Content: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly. Consequently, such systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model free architecture that evaluates ongoing information acquisition from observable evidence relative to declared task requirements. Specifically, a domain interface maps raw observations into task resolution coordinates and normalized comparative representations, which are processed by a fixed causal monitor. This monitor emits two continuous real time signals that quantify (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction generated when recurrent evidence yields negligible informational gain. We evaluated a single, unadjusted monitor configuration across eight diverse domains including search and rescue dialogue, spatial grid exploration, hierarchical capability acquisition, continuous robotic manipulation, and probabilistic intent estimation. We show that across these domains the friction channel distinguished unproductive stagnation from purposeful exploration prior to task completion, while remaining muted during post completion activity. Furthermore, in closed loop reinforcement learning experiments under early termination constraints, we demonstrate that penalizing informational friction allowed agents to sustain high mission success, whereas unpenalized policies and baselines with matched operational costs failed to complete required tasks.

Title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
Author: Martim Afonso, Inês Lynce, Maurizio Morisio, João F. Ferreira
Text_Content: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

Title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
Author: Calum S. Skene, Jeffrey S. Oishi, Keaton J. Burns, Moritz Linkmann, Geoffrey M. Vasil, Alexander Morozov
Text_Content: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.

Title: Mobility-Aware Task Offloading in Mobile Edge Computing-Empowered Space-Air-Ground Integrated Internet-of-Things Networks
Author: Minghao Sun, Jinghuai Xiong, Xiaoli Chu, Zitian Zhang
Text_Content: Mobile edge computing (MEC)-empowered spaceair-ground integrated Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks (SAGIINs) provide a promising solution for computation-intensive tasks generated by mobile IoT devices (IDs). However, task offloading in SAGIINs is challenging due to time-varying IDto-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) channels, intermittent LEO satellite service availability, and the coupling among UAV trajectory, communication, computation, and energy decisions. This paper investigates an energy-efficient task offloading and UAV trajectory planning problem in an MEC-empowered SAGIIN, where one UAV acts as both an aerial relay and an MEC server, and multiple LEO satellites provide supplementary computing resources. The UAV trajectory planning, task splitting, and computing resource allocation are jointly optimized to minimize the total system energy consumption under task completion, communication, computation, flight region, and satellite service window constraints. The resulting non-convex problem is decomposed into a UAV trajectory planning subproblem and a task splitting and computing resource allocation subproblem. To solve the former, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-assisted large language model (LLM)-enhanced deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm, termed RLD, is proposed. The latter is shown to be convex and can be solved by using CVXPY for a given UAV trajectory. A weighted retrieval score is further designed to balance ID mobility-pattern similarity and historical UAV trajectory energy performance. Simulation results show that RLD completes all computational tasks in previously unseen test scenarios while consuming less total energy than the benchmark algorithms.

Title: Particle-hole asymmetry and a fluctuating pair-density-wave state in a lightly doped Mott insulator on the square lattice
Author: Hao-Xin Wang, Zheng-Yuan Yue, Wen-Yuan Liu, Zheng-Cheng Gu
Text_Content: Whether a lightly doped Mott insulator on the square lattice supports robust $d$-wave superconductivity remains a central question in strongly correlated physics and in the microscopic theory of cuprate superconductivity. Experiments and numerical studies reveal a pronounced particle-hole asymmetry, pointing to a delicate competition among $d$-wave superconductivity, pair-density wave (PDW), stripe, charge-density wave (CDW), and antiferromagnetic correlations. Here we combine large-scale DMRG and finite-size PEPS to study the square-lattice $t$-$J$ model at low doping, $δ\leq 0.1$, while tuning the next-nearest-neighbor hopping $t'$ from the electron-like ($t'>0$) to the hole-like ($t'<0$) regime. The electron-like side supports robust, nearly uniform $d$-wave pairing, whereas decreasing $t'$ induces a period-two plaquette modulation and ultimately produces, on the hole-like side, a charge-dominated state with a strongly suppressed static pairing amplitude. DMRG calculations on open strips and squares, together with PEPS calculations on open squares up to $16\times16$ sites, support this evolution. On squares with $C_4$-symmetric Hamiltonians, both methods find that the pair correlations of the hole-like state select the plaquette momenta $(π,0)$ and $(0,π)$ and decay within a few lattice spacings, while the dominant charge-density modulation forms a bidirectional checkerboard whose period extrapolates to about $4a_0$, close to that observed in lightly doped Bi-2201. These observations establish a fluctuating plaquette PDW in the lightly doped hole-like regime, in which local pairs carry finite momentum but lack phase coherence. Our results firmly establish particle-hole asymmetry as a central organizing principle for competing pairing tendencies in the lightly doped $t$-$J$ model.

Title: Sckwoky at SHROOM-Visions: Character-Level Hallucination-Span Detection in Image-Conditioned VLMs via Dual-Prompted LoRA Decoders
Author: Mikhail Kulakov, Ruslan Solikhov, Ivan Bondarenko
Text_Content: We present our system for the SHROOM-visions 2026 shared task on character-level hallucination span detection in image-conditioned vision-language model (VLM) responses, evaluated across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. The detector is built on a frozen Gemma-4-12B-it backbone with trainable LoRA adapters (approximately 10.7M parameters). Because the backbone is a causal decoder, hidden states read from a single copy of an answer cannot attend to subsequent tokens; we therefore repeat the candidate answer within one prompt and extract features from its second occurrence, giving every position approximate bidirectional context in a single non-autoregressive pass. A character-level locator combines intermediate hidden states to predict hallucination probabilities, BIO boundaries, and a response-level abstention score, while separate language-specific classifiers assign one of five hallucination types to each predicted span. On the closed test set, our system reaches a macro-averaged character IoU of 0.4404, more than doubling the official baseline (0.1854), and ranks 5th-6th on IoU across the four languages. On the English tuning split, controlled ablations attribute a gain to the repeated answer that is comparable to that of LoRA adaptation (its held-out gain is smaller and concentrated on hallucinated answers), and they show that the detector relies on the image-answer pairing: shuffling images across examples drives IoU down to the level of the predict-nothing floor or below it in every language. In deployments where the same Gemma-4-12B-it model also generates answers, its base weights can be reused, making the approach practical for local question-answering systems that cannot run a separate verifier.

Title: Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic: Adaptive Switching Costs for Robust Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
Author: Khaled Ammoura, Aya Kayal, Naseem Daher
Text_Content: Deliberation costs are commonly used in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to prevent options from collapsing to primitive actions. Existing approaches rely on fixed penalties or duration-based adaptations, both of which are indirect proxies for an option's utility. This paper argues that option persistence should instead depend on the opportunity cost of abandoning the current behavior. We propose the Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic ($OC^2$) framework, which defines a state-dependent deliberation cost using the positive value gap between the active option and its best alternative. This encourages persistence when the current option is clearly preferable and allows rapid switching when a better option emerges. We show that directly learning such costs leads to a degenerate zero-cost solution and introduces an auxiliary objective that aligns the learned cost with the value-gap target. The approach is evaluated in Four Rooms and Pinball domains under stationary, goal-shift, and geometry-shift conditions. In the Pinball goal-shift task, the $OC^2$ framework achieves a 52\% first-ten-episode success rate compared with 18\% for a fixed-cost baseline. The results suggest that opportunity-cost-based persistence improves adaptation in non-stationary environments.

Title: CUVE: Making Supervised Classification more Accessible through Visualization
Author: Sanchitha Kuppusami, Xiyao Wang, Miguel Nacenta
Text_Content: We present CUVE, an interface that enables people to build classifiers by generating visualizations that are interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms (the Visualization as Intermediate Representation approach). This UI enables users to create supervised classifiers and to visually investigate how to improve them and how they carry out their function. A preliminary study investigates the usability of our prototype and compares it with a traditional text-based programming interface.

Title: A Kato-Type Criterion for Vanishing Viscosity and Magnetic Diffusivity Limits for Compressible Magnetohydrodynamics
Author: Siran Li, Tong Tang, Yuanjing Tang
Text_Content: In this paper, we investigate the vanishing viscosity and magnetic diffusivity limits for the compressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations on a smooth bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Under the assumptions of interior regularity and uniform local boundedness near the boundary, we establish a Kato-type criterion under which finite energy weak solutions to the dissipative MHD system converge to weak solutions to the ideal MHD system as the viscosity and magnetic resistivity coefficients decrease to zero. In particular, under such criterion, the anomalous energy dissipation in the vanishing viscosity and diffusivity limits for MHD is precluded.

Title: Modelling velocity gradient invariants in turbulence with Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble
Author: Zhi Zheng, Weiyu Shen, Jin-Han Xie, Yue Yang
Text_Content: We investigate the joint probability density function $P(Q,R)$ of invariants $Q$ and $R$ of the velocity gradient tensor in the synthetic turbulent field formed from the Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble, which is referred to as the woven Lundgren turbulence (WLT). The WLT inherently captures non-Gaussian vorticity correlations and multiscale interactions, which are essential for reproducing $P(Q,R)$ observed in homogeneous isotropic turbulence. By analyzing the contributions of stretching, winding and dissipation processes in WLT, we demonstrate that the $Q$-$R$ diagram can be divided into three distinct physical regions: a head region dominated by stretching, a body region dominated by spiral vortex arms, and a tail region dominated by dissipation. We systematically vary three key parameters in WLT, the background strain rate, the cutoff age of spiral vortices and the viscous decay factor, and monitor the evolution of $P(Q,R)$ in different topological regions. It is revealed that increasing the stretching rate broadens the head region, larger cutoff ages enhance the inclination of the body region, and reducing viscous factors extends the tail region, thereby mimicking the effects of strain self-amplification and vortex stretching across scales. Based on WLT statistics, we establish and validate an explicit model of $P(Q,R)$ consisting of the stretching, spiral and dissipation contributions. Thus, the WLT provides a physically interpretable framework for understanding the relation between local geometry and global statistics of turbulence.

Title: Wave-Domain Semantic ISAC: Holographic Surfaces as Analog Semantic Encoders for Integrated TN-NTN
Author: Shadi Danesh, Pooria Salami, Hesaam Zaravashan, Abdulkadir Köse, Ayhan Akbas, Chuan Heng Foh, Mohsen Khalily
Text_Content: Semantic communication, near-field operation, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) are often considered separately in terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks (TN--NTN). We show how a large electromagnetic aperture can connect them. \textcolor{black}{Nonlocal metasurfaces and holographic apertures act on the spatial spectrum of an incident field and can execute linear projections, which form an early stage of semantic feature extraction, directly in the wave domain before digitisation, thereby reducing the corresponding digital processing burden.} Near-field focusing also provides position-dependent sensing features, allowing the aperture to serve as an analog semantic-ISAC front end on resource-constrained aerial and satellite platforms. We describe the underlying physics, the co-design of constrained analog projections with lightweight digital decoders, and a case study in which a data-adaptive projection outperforms a fully digital baseline in the simulated energy-limited regime while transmitting four times fewer coefficients and using 11.4 times fewer decoder MACs. Finally, we identify relevant 3GPP, ITU-R, and ETSI activities and the remaining standardisation gaps.

Title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
Author: Mohammad Mahdi Dehshibi, Tomás Martínez Cortés, Amar D'Adamo, Daniel de la Prida, Luis-Antonio Azpicueta-Ruíz, Laia Turmo Vidal, Marte Roel Lesur, Joaquín R. Díaz-Durán, Alexander Väljamäe, Angel Sánchez, Temitayo Olugbade, Nadia Bianchi-Berthouze, Fernando Díaz-de-María, Ana Tajadura-Jiménez
Text_Content: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

Title: DexSeed: Expanding Human Hand-Object Interactions into Robot Demonstrations for Dexterous Policy Learning
Author: Huaijin Pi, Zehong Shen, Yong Wang, Kechun Xu, Changpeng Wang, Dingkun Wei, Xueyang Wang, Wenjia Wang, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Taku Komura
Text_Content: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.

Title: Classical Tensor Codes and Quantum Tanner Codes Achieve Capacity on Erasure Channels
Author: Henry D. Pfister, Oscar Sprumont, Gilles Zémor
Text_Content: We show that on the classical erasure channel, the tensor product of two capacity-achieving code families is itself capacity-achieving under mild conditions. We also prove that duals of tensor products of independent uniform random binary linear codes achieve erasure capacity. Using these local codes, for every erasure probability $ρ\in(0,1/2)$ and every rate gap $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain a family of binary quantum Tanner codes of rate at least $1-2ρ-\varepsilon$. For fixed $ρ$ and $\varepsilon$, these codes have bounded check weights, minimum distance growing linearly with the blocklength, and a linear-time erasure decoder whose decoding error decays exponentially with the blocklength.

Title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
Author: Tomer Solberg
Text_Content: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU.
