We develop VIRIS-3D-L by extending the airborne transmission model in VIRIS (a reaction-diffusion equation) to three dimensions (3D) and replacing global removal with a Robin boundary condition representing localised removal due to surface deposition. We compare VIRIS and VIRIS-3D-L across three single-storey buildings with increasing architectural and people-movement complexity: a courtroom, a care home, and a supermarket. We find that VIRIS underestimates the disease transmission rate and infection risks for individuals by up to 50% relative to VIRIS-3D-L in all three buildings. However, VIRIS-3D-L requires, on average, four times the computation time of VIRIS, mainly because it extends the computational domain from a 2D surface to a 3D volume. Overall, VIRIS-3D-L provides a more realistic modelling of airborne transmission than VIRIS and is particularly suited to settings with variations in people and furniture heights and frequent 3D movement. For simpler single-storey buildings, VIRIS is suitable because of its lower computational cost.

Title: AHEADance: Anticipatory Humanoid Dance from Streaming Audio
Author: Tianhu Peng, Yukun Wang, Lingfan Bao, Yiyang Jia, Chengxu Zhou
Text_Content: A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance

Title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
Author: Alexandros Hollender, Sonja Kraiczy
Text_Content: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.

Title: Ender: Visual Scaffolding for Geometric Proof Comprehension
Author: Hwei-Shin Harriman, Yuchen Jin, Dominik Moritz, Joshua Sunshine
Text_Content: Geometric proof is a foundational but notoriously difficult topic in secondary mathematics, primarily due to the high cognitive load required to integrate visual diagrams with logical text. As proofs evolve, tracking the initial givens and an expanding set of derived truths can easily overwhelm working memory. While established scaffolding techniques are often visual and diagram-based, current digital learning environments mostly rely on static, text-heavy interfaces that force students to manage these complex mental models on their own. This paper introduces Ender, an interactive rendering system designed to visualize the logical status of two-column proofs. Ender's design is grounded in four literature-derived requirements: (1) diagram annotation, (2) structural tracing, (3) support for partial or incorrect work, and (4) synchronization between the diagram and text. To evaluate the system, we conducted a between-subjects, think-aloud experiment with 12 secondary school students in the United States, comparing Ender against a traditional digital proof interface. Our results indicate that students using Ender performed significantly better on proof comprehension tasks--specifically in identifying and correcting logical errors. These findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding may ease the working memory burden of digital interfaces, offering a promising building block for future AI-based proof tutoring systems.

Title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
Author: Tomas Perez-Acle
Text_Content: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.

Title: Mapping Instructors' Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
Author: Iman Mohammadi, Ali Keramati, Sina Rismanchian
Text_Content: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of large language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students' academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with Generative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers' motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration.

Title: A Technique to Model Product Information and User Reviews (MPIUR)
Author: Emna Belguith, Fajrian Yunus, Talel Abdessalem
Text_Content: Modern e-commerce platforms naturally provide three complementary modalities: textual item descriptions, item images, and user reviews. However, existing multimodal recommendation methods often omit reviews or do not integrate all three modalities within a unified framework. In this paper, we propose MPIUR, a multimodal graph-based recommendation model that encodes reviews in heterogeneous graphs, aligns image and text representations, and adapts collaborative--semantic alignment to item interaction density. Experiments on the Amazon Reviews 2023 Musical Instruments and Baby categories show that MPIUR achieves the best global nDCG@10 and Recall@10 among the evaluated methods on both datasets. It also obtains the best nDCG@10 and Recall@10 on sparse items, indicating that jointly exploiting reviews and multimodal item content is particularly useful when interaction histories are limited.

Title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
Author: Ruifeng Cao, Xidan Song
Text_Content: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

Title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
Author: Fedor Buzaev, Dmitry Efremenko, Daria Pugacheva, Fedor Ratnikov, Egor Bugaev, Vladimir Gordin, Denis Derkach
Text_Content: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

Title: Understanding Students' Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis
Author: Iman Mohammadi, Sina Rismanchian, Ali Keramati, Shayan Salehi
Text_Content: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty.

Title: When Are Predictions Enough? An Evaluation Protocol for Frozen Expert Composition
Author: Alessandro Pereira, Keith J Ransom, Lewis Mitchell
Text_Content: Practitioners often combine independently trained models while keeping their weights frozen. These experts are commonly combined through their final predictions, although their internal features may retain useful information that those predictions omit. We ask when combining features improves on combining predictions, and how to make that comparison fair. We introduce a reusable evaluation protocol, apply it to 21 frozen deepfake detectors from DF40 (Yan et al., 2024), and audit how evaluation choices change the conclusions. The protocol uses strong prediction baselines, compares simple and larger feature combiners, varies architecture and training data separately, and reports results by held-out generator with train/test overlap controls. Under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, logistic regression on the features of six architecture-diverse experts improves macro AUROC by 0.081 over the best tested prediction combiner in each fold, with gains on seven of eight generators. The larger network shows no clear improvement over the linear model (approximately 3.5M versus 10K parameters), suggesting that access to richer information matters more than additional combiner capacity on this pool. Features may help when they retain information that the predictions omit and that transfers to new generators. Predictions may be enough when the strongest prediction baseline already performs well, while neither approach reliably compensates for poor expert transfer. Weakening prediction baselines on the overlap-affected standard split inflates the apparent feature advantage by up to 0.172 AUROC. Overlap-aware evaluation also changes the estimated gain, though the contrast does not isolate overlap. Results by generator and expert pool show where the advantage holds, weakens, or reverses. Without these controls, the same benchmark can support different conclusions.

Title: DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents
Author: Hao Zhao, Minghao Lin
Text_Content: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held-out counterexamples. Two security experts manually verified task ground truth over a two-week period; stage labels remain LLM-generated. The concentration analysis describes task structure and audited outcomes, not an identified internal mechanism.

Title: Closed-Form Gaussian Information Projection for Embedded Simplices and Simplicial Mixtures
Author: Ali Darijani, Emadedin Soufian, Jürgen Beyerer
Text_Content: We study Gaussian approximation of Dirichlet--Gaussian probability density functions on embedded simplices. We derive the unique information projection onto the family of nondegenerate ambient Gaussian probability density functions, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal Gaussian and the minimum divergence for arbitrary positive Dirichlet parameters. The minimum divergence depends only on the intrinsic simplex dimension and Dirichlet parameters, is invariant up to an affine isomorphism, independent of the ambient dimension, and independent of the normal covariance. Furthermore, by joint convexity of Kullback--Leibler divergence, we establish explicit intrinsic dimension-dependent sharp upper bounds for finite Gaussian Mixture with shared component weights. For uniform probability density functions, these bounds reduce to dimension-dependent constants. The results provide closed-form Gaussian Mixture constructions and rigorous approximation guarantees for probability density functions associated with embedded simplicial complexes. A numerical example on a circular curve illustrates the theoretical results and their connections to geometric Gaussian Mixture representations.

Title: Multi-Stage Phase-Aware Self-Supervised Reconstruction for Multi-Echo Gradient-Echo MRI
Author: Juan Liu, Nian Wang
Text_Content: Purpose: To develop a phase-aware self-supervised framework for accelerated high-resolution multi-echo gradient-echo (mGRE) MRI that preserves anatomical detail and complex echo information for quantitative mapping. Methods: We developed multi-stage phase-aware self-supervised reconstruction (MSPR-GRE), integrating progressive k-space expansion with phase estimation and refinement. Sequential unrolled networks reconstruct complex multi-echo images and update echo-dependent phase priors. A relaxation-informed temporal subspace is used for acquisitions with at least four echoes, while shorter echo trains are reconstructed in the image domain. Training uses held-out acquired k-space samples without fully sampled targets. Evaluation included 9.4 T ex vivo mouse-brain data 30um eight-echo and 18um dual-echo) and retrospectively undersampled 7 T AHEAD human-brain data, with supervised ablations. Results:MSPR-GRE reduced artifacts in regions of rapid phase variation and preserved fine mouse-brain anatomy. Across five AHEAD test datasets at R = 4, 8, and 12, it generally improved magnitude-image, T2* map, and QSM metrics, particularly at higher acceleration. At R = 12, fourth-echo magnitude NRMSE was 12.09$\pm$0.60% versus 21.55$\pm$1.12% for SSDU. Ablations indicated benefits of phase refinement, while supervised experiments supported multi-stage phase-aware reconstruction. Conclusion: MSPR-GRE improves accelerated mGRE reconstruction and quantitative-map agreement without fully sampled training targets. Further validation of generalizability and phase-estimation accuracy is needed.

Title: Optically modulated field-dependent electrical response in a non-collinear antiferromagnet/ferromagnet heterostructure
Author: Adrielson Dias, André José, José Lucas, Rodrigo Cristian, José Holanda
Text_Content: The interplay among optical, electrical, and magnetic stimuli offers opportunities to control the functional response of spintronic heterostructures. Here, we investigate the field-dependent electrical response of MgO/IrMn$_3$/Py/Au under radio-frequency (RF) excitation, white-light illumination, and direct-current (DC) bias. Under a 20 MHz RF signal with a nominal power of 2 W, the measured voltage in the dark remains at several tens of nanovolts. Upon illumination with approximately 1 W of white light, a pronounced field-dependent feature emerges around 315--320 Oe, reaching 0.9--1.0 $μ$V. The illumination-associated differential voltage is approximately 0.95 $μ$V. A DC current of 1 mA produces a response of approximately 1 $μ$V, while the simultaneous application of RF, DC, and optical excitation increases the voltage to approximately 1.8 $μ$V. Magnetic characterization reveals exchange bias with a blocking temperature near 380 K, while electrical resistance measurements show a pronounced dependence on magnetic-field orientation, consistent with the anisotropic response of the heterostructure. These results demonstrate that the field-dependent electrical response can be modulated through combined optical and electrical excitation, involving magneto-optical interactions and spin-dependent transport phenomena, potentially including spin Hall-related contributions and the magnetic spin Hall effect. This work provides insights into coupled optical, electrical, and magnetic-field effects in heterostructures based on non-collinear antiferromagnets and ferromagnetic layers.

Title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
Author: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
Text_Content: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

Title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
Author: Sawyer Dobson, Zhenghan Wang
Text_Content: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

Title: Advancing Mass-Conserving Deep Learning for Distributed Hydrologic Modeling: A Case Study in a Snow-Dominated Watershed
Author: Yihan Wang, Lujun Zhang, N. Benjamin Erichson, Yang Hong, Tiantian Yang
Text_Content: Recent progress in physics-aware deep learning (DL) has embedded mass conservation within Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for hydrologic modeling, improving physical consistency and enabling diagnostics of internal states. However, existing mass-conserving neural networks are primarily developed in lumped formulations. Consequently, previous studies provide only fragmented and often indirect evidence of when and why imposed physical constraints may lead to unrealistic hydrologic behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Physics-Enhanced Conservation-Augmented Net (PECAN), a mass-conserving convolutional LSTM-based framework for distributed hydrologic modeling and diagnosing structural limitations of physics-aware DL models. PECAN is implemented in two variants: (1) PECAN-MC with a strict precipitation-based conservation constraint and (2) PECAN-MCR with a relaxed conservation constraint allowing additional water inputs beyond precipitation. Both variants are trained solely on gauge streamflow and evaluated in a snow-dominated watershed in Colorado. We benchmark PECAN against lumped DL baselines and the distributed process-based Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model. Results show that PECAN achieves competitive outlet streamflow simulation accuracy while producing spatially explicit latent states for interpretation. Comparisons with reference soil moisture indicate that PECAN cell states resemble meaningful temporal soil moisture dynamics. However, analyses also reveal that PECAN misrepresents snow processes by prematurely removing winter snow water storage from the system rather than retaining it for spring release. PECAN demonstrates accurate streamflow simulation at gauges and shows diagnostic potential to expose structural limitations in hydrologic process representation, thereby informing future physics-aware neural network development for hydrology.

Title: PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots
Author: Shaohong Zhong, Marco Pontin, Perla Maiolino
Text_Content: Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives. However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently. A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation. Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation. Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines. Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks.

Title: Early Rug Pull Detection on Solana
Author: Saba Heydaridoost, Kasra Kashani, Mohammad Mowlavi Sorond, Behnam Bahrak
Text_Content: Web3 platforms that help users discover and trade newly launched crypto tokens, including launchpads, decentralized-exchange (DEX) interfaces, wallets, and token-analytics sites, must assess tokens before their legitimacy is clear. On Solana, where token creation is inexpensive and tokens use standard programs rather than custom per-token smart contracts, rug pulls can unfold within minutes. Effective warnings must therefore rely on limited histories. Although graph neural networks (GNNs) have improved rug-pull detection on EVM chains, it remains unclear whether transfer structure adds predictive value over non-graph models at minute-scale decision points, and how that value changes as history accumulates. We study 2,700 tokens sampled from SolRPDS, collecting one-minute market histories from Birdeye and token transfers from Solana RPC. We define a rug pull operationally by requiring a liquidity drain, price collapse, and persistent liquidity depletion over a nominal 24-hour period after token creation. All features use only information available at or before each prediction cutoff. We evaluate observation windows of 12.5, 35.5, and 93 minutes, selected in advance from the published lifespan distribution of Solana rug pulls, and represent each token as a temporal transfer graph. Within the first 12.5 minutes, rug-pull and non-rug graphs already differ in size, density, reciprocity, and receiver-side centralization. We compare GNNs against matched non-graph models using the same token-level and graph-summary features on identical samples. A fixed panel of tokens observed in all three windows further isolates the effect of longer observation from changes in token population. Our findings inform the design of early-warning mechanisms for newly launched Solana tokens in Web3 interfaces.

Title: Universal spectral shapes of nonlinear light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings
Author: Aleksei Zheltikov
Text_Content: Operating within the framework of the collisionless Boltzmann equation, we identify universal spectral profiles inherent in stimulated and coherent light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings and derive physically intuitive solutions for such spectral shapes, expressing them in a manifestly causal closed form that satisfies the Kramers - Kronig relations and fulfills the fluctuation - dissipation theorem. Benchmarking against gold-standard experiments on dilute-gas stimulated light scattering verifies a high descriptive and explanatory power of these solutions and demonstrates their ability to isolate universality motifs in nonlinear scattering spectra as the key to fully understanding the physics behind dilute-gas nonlinear light scattering. As one of important outcomes, such analysis reveals the physical content of the bandwidth of dilute-gas nonlinear scattering spectra as an expression and a quantifier of the phase-mixing time, i.e., the time required for free-streaming gas particles with a mean thermal velocity to traverse the distance equal to the spacing of the laser-driven density grating.

Title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
Author: Bogdan Mamaev, Qizhou Wang, Christopher Leckie, Matteo Vergani
Text_Content: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

Title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
Author: Gokul Bhusal, Delanna Do, Ekaterina Merkurjev, Kevin Miller, Stephan Wojtowytsch
Text_Content: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

Title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
Author: Daoan Zhang, Qinbo Bai, Dehai Min, Xingyu Mu, Ziyi Chen, Jianing Yin
Text_Content: The effectiveness of a self-improving system relies heavily on the quality of its verifier, which judges the outcome of each improvement round. However, the verifiers of most tasks are written by hand, which is expensive and does not scale to tasks that come without one. We propose Veritas, a harness that generates verifiers automatically. Unlike general-purpose agent harnesses, Veritas adds three mechanisms for verifier generation: an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles, partly refined by a self-improvement loop. We evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution, whose official verifiers we first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses. With the model fixed, the verifiers Veritas generates agree better with the official verdicts than those of seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks. On the two pairwise benchmarks they are at or near the best. They also agree better than those of the vendor's own harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms also improve 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs scored by execution across three harnesses.

Title: Disentangling Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding in Vision-Language Models
Author: Zhaoyi Liu, Haichuan Zhang, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Bowei Tian, Wanghao Ye, Yufan Zhang, Ang Li
Text_Content: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.

Title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
Author: Shu Jiang, Graham A. Colditz
Text_Content: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.

Title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
Author: Katarzyna, Swirydowicz, Nicholas Malaya, Noah Wolfe, Paul Bauman, Pieter Ghysels, Jonathan Belof
Text_Content: A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most HPC workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates some of those claims and explores the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads, across a variety of common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy requirements of these workloads. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations of these approaches. These results indicate that Ozaki emulation should not be evaluated as a general replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-shaped. Our analysis indicates this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Furthermore, even in this favorable regime, standalone GEMM speedup is not enough to accelerate (or avoid performance regression) for the application: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale. This paper characterizes those boundaries empirically. Furthermore, we show that dense GEMM accounts for only a small fraction of FP64 computation across HPC workloads, leaving most application-level FP64 work beyond the reach of GEMM-based emulation.

Title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
Author: Saber Malekmohammadi, Kevin Kuo, Virginia Smith, Golnoosh Farnadi
Text_Content: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.

Title: Uni-Loc: Weakly Supervised 3D CT Pathology Localization via Spatially Grounded Vision-Language Classification
Author: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
Text_Content: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.

Title: Agent-Guided Discovery of Exchange-Correlation Functionals with Physics-based Validation
Author: Achuth Chandrasekhar, Amir Barati Farimani
Text_Content: Accurate, compact exchange--correlation functionals are central to predictive density functional theory. Symbolic search and language-model agents can propose new functional forms, but it remains unclear whether their gains survive self-consistency and external evaluation, whether the new terms carry physical content, whether agents outperform evolutionary search, and how language-model backbones compare. We connect frontier LLM agents to a GPU evaluator through the Model Context Protocol, with training-only fitting, persistent memory, and self-consistent and external evaluation. Opus-5.5 agents passed the screening gate with about 40-fold fewer tokens than Codex (GPT-6-Astra) agents and found a candidate with lower validation and held-out errors; only this candidate advanced to self-consistent evaluation. The resulting 13-parameter functional, O159, multiplies same-spin correlation by a smooth density window. Refitted controls favor a window that scales the entire same-spin factor, reducing it by 15--30\% at its peak, and that acts on reaction energies mainly in near-iso-orbital regions; against a refitted no-window control, it lowers heavy-atom total-energy errors on GSCDB137 by 29\%. With about 400 fits each, SyFES evolution did not improve on its GAS22 seed, whereas the agents found forms 0.10--0.13 \kcal\ lower in validation error by adding an explicit density scale. Self-consistent O159 lowers the held-out MGCDB84 test error of $ω$B97M-V by 11.7\%, and its mean normalized error ratio on 36 GSCDB137 datasets (1.139) is comparable to $ω$B97M-V (1.144) and below GAS22 (1.190). Frontier-LLM agents thus produced O159, a compact functional whose improvement over $ω$B97M-V survives self-consistent, physics-based validation.

Title: Hysteresis and mode switching in FIB engineered random laser diodes
Author: Andrea Martínez Pacheco, Sara Rodríguez Corvillo, Alberto Rivera-Calzada, Antonio Consoli, Jacobo Santamaría, Cefe López
Text_Content: Complex dynamical behavior in laser diodes is commonly induced by external perturbations such as optical or optoelectronic feedback and optical injection. The structural transformation of a stable laser diode into a stand-alone nonlinear dynamical system would provide a practical alternative as a single and compact device. Here we demonstrate the fabrication of such a device by milling, via focused ion beam, the output facet of a Fabry-Perot laser diode with a predesigned mask, obtaining a scattering surface which provide feedback for random lasing. The fabricated random laser diode shows multi-mode emission with current dependent spectral reconfigurations, hysteresis in output power and spectrum and mode switching at constant bias current. We attribute this behavior to the interplay between scattered optical feedback and carrier induced local variations of refractive index and temperature at the output facet surface, where defects are located. The observed phenomena reveal complex nonlinear behavior emerging from a single standalone device, which could be tailored by varying the milling pattern, thereby providing a flexible platform for different applications.

Title: Causal mediation analysis for a time-to-event endpoint in the presence of competing events
Author: Yuhao Deng, Peter Gilbert, Youyi Fong, Bo Zhang
Text_Content: Causal mediation analysis is widely used to decompose a treatment's effect into components operating through distinct causal pathways and to characterize the mediator--outcome relationship. In time-to-event settings, competing events --- events that preclude the primary endpoint --- substantially complicate this decomposition. We provide a unified treatment of causal mediation analysis for a time-to-event endpoint under competing events. We show that the total effect on the cause-specific cumulative incidence decomposes into a direct effect, an indirect effect through the mediator of interest, and an indirect effect through the competing events. We develop this decomposition under the natural effects, stochastic interventional effects, and separable effects frameworks, and show that, in certain settings, all three yield identical statistical functionals despite relying on distinct identification assumptions. We derive efficient influence functions for the counterfactual cumulative incidence curves and the decomposed effects, and propose double-machine-learning-type estimators that are multiply robust and attain the semiparametric efficiency bound, with a sensitivity analysis to address unmeasured common causes of time-to-event endpoints. We further study the mediator--outcome response relationship via kernel-smoothed estimands. We apply the methods to immune correlates analyses of COVID-19 vaccine and HIV-1 prevention trials.

Title: ARIA: An AI-Powered Radio-Channel Inference and Analysis Pipeline
Author: Homa Nikbakht, Mingjun Ying, Dipankar Shakya, Daniel Abraham, Theodore S. Rappaport
Text_Content: Statistical channel models play a key role in the design and standardization of next-generation wireless systems. The models substitute for costly and time-consuming field measurements when fitted distributions accurately reproduce the measured channel impulse responses. Future wireless systems will operate in global spectrum allocations from 1 to 150 GHz. Over the full span, analytically chosen distribution families fitted to scarce measurement data fail to deliver the required accuracy. Generative AI models instead learn each distribution from the radio-propagation data itself, adapt to the measured structure at every frequency, and scale across the entire band. We present ARIA, an AI-powered Radio-channel Inference and Analysis pipeline that learns each channel-parameter distribution from the measurements. The pipeline extracts power-delay profiles and recovers the channel parameters with time-cluster spatial-lobe (TCSL) analysis. Three neural density estimators, namely mixture density networks, neural spline flows (NSF), and denoising diffusion implicit models, learn each parameter's distribution. A composite rank across goodness-of-fit metrics with Friedman-Nemenyi testing identifies the best estimator, and a maximum-likelihood step anchored to the measured samples converts its density into closed-form parametric families. We instantiate ARIA on the NYU WIRELESS 16.95 GHz InH campaign and find that NSF outperforms the other estimators on every metric. We also show that a conditional NSF with feature-wise linear modulation, trained jointly on the 6.75 and 16.95 GHz measurements, improves over single-frequency training. We feed the fitted distributions into the NYUSIM simulator and reproduce the measured omnidirectional RMS delay spread medians within 2 ns, the per-lobe azimuth and zenith spread medians within 1 degree, and the omnidirectional zenith spread medians within 0.5 degrees.

Title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
Author: Henrique Oliveira
Text_Content: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).

Title: Robust Flow Matching under Target Corruption and Label Noise
Author: Mert Can Kurucu, Erik Englesson, Hossein Azizpour
Text_Content: Flow Matching (FM) is a strong framework for generative modeling due to its stable training and efficient sampling. However, FM assumes clean target data and labels, an assumption often violated in practice. We formulate FM training as a time-dependent regression problem over conditional vector fields and analyze how the two corruption types affect the objective: i) target corruption adds a time-dependent residual term that grows with time, ii) label noise causes updates to the wrong class-conditional vector field. Based on this analysis, we propose to improve FM robustness by mapping corruption-specific residual scores to sample weights. For target corruption, we propose the Temporal Residual Score (TRS), which emphasizes residual magnitudes at intermediate-to-late FM times, where clean and corrupted samples are more separable. For label noise, we propose the Comparative Conditional Score (CCS), which compares the residual of the observed class-conditional vector field against alternative class-conditional vector fields for the same trajectory and velocity target. Experiments across controlled corruption settings and real-world noisy labels show that the proposed methods improve robustness over standard FM and robust-training baselines, supporting corruption-specific residual structure as a practical basis for robust FM.

Title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
Author: Nika Zahedi, Fangyi Zhu, Anna Wu
Text_Content: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.

Title: The climate and potential habitability of a warm and oxygenated Mars
Author: Ashwin S. Braude, Edwin S. Kite, Preston Cosslett Kemeny, Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Alexandre Kling, Michael A. Mischna
Text_Content: We present the first 3-D Global Climate Model simulations of an oxygen-rich, terraformed Mars. Assuming an O2-CO2 atmosphere, with additional warming from a well-mixed grey gas, we study (1) how surface temperatures change with atmospheric pressure and grey gas opacity, and (2) how temperature, pressure, and other effects limit life as oxygen builds up. We neglect the climate effects of dust and the water cycle, as well as possible soil-chemistry and nutrient limits to life. We find that (1) increasing grey gas opacity and increasing atmospheric pressure both moderate day-night temperature swings, but only slightly reduce seasonal temperature swings. Climate remains harsher in the Southern mid-latitudes relative to the Northern hemisphere. (2) For an atmospheric pressure of 30 hPa (5 times its present-day value), temperatures on Mars would be consistent with lichen and moss, followed at 60 hPa by forests (initially in the Hellas Basin). However, creating a human-breathable atmosphere through photosynthesis alone, at the oxygen production rates of biomes on Earth today, would take at least thousands of years, and require more oxygen than can be made via photosynthesis of known CO2 reserves on Mars alone (unless CO2 is recycled).

Title: Multicomponent Isotope Engineering of Phonon Polaritons in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
Author: Nihar Ranjan Sahoo, Byung-Il Noh, Brandon Stephanie, Hossein Zandipour, Eli Janzen, James H. Edgar, Siyuan Dai, Thomas G. Folland
Text_Content: Isotopic enrichment provides a non-invasive means of tuning the vibrational and optical properties of van der Waals crystals (vdW) without altering their lattice structure. We investigate two doubly enriched hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) compositions, h10B15N and h11B15N, to determine how isotope substitution on both sublattices modifies mid-infrared hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs). Polarization-resolved room temperature and cryogenic far-field reflectance measurements reveal optical-phonon blue shifts of approximately 35 cm-1 in h10B15N relative h11B15N, translating both Reststrahlen bands (RBs) and their polariton dispersions. For the upper RB, the combined accessible range expands from 1360-1614 cm-1 in natural hBN to 1356-1640 cm-1 across the B- enriched 14N crystals and 1339-1640 cm-1 when the 15N enriched crystals are included. Near-field imaging confirms deeply sub-diffractional propagation and shows that both crystals exhibit lower polariton damping and longer lifetimes than natural hBN, with performance comparable to monoisotopically enriched crystals. Further, we compare the conventional reduced-mass description with a phenomenological two-component inverse-mass model that captures the isotope dependence of the phonon frequencies and LO-TO coupling while resolving the contributions of the individual sublattices. These results establish multicomponent isotope engineering as a materials design strategy for positioning the HPhPs spectral range while preserving low-loss propagation in polar vdW crystals.

Title: Impact of compressiblity approximations on atmospheric gravity wave characteristics
Author: Hrishikesh Sivanandan, Matthew Churchfield, Ben Kravitz, Eliot Quon, Mehtab Khan
Text_Content: Atmospheric gravity waves are a common phenomenon in the atmosphere and are of critical importance to understanding power generation from wind plants. Common sources of atmospheric gravity waves are stratified flow over topography or wind deceleration ahead of wind farms. Simulations to understand atmospheric boundary layer conditions and wind power generation often solve the Navier-Stokes equations in incompressible Boussinesq form, which allows for density variation as a function of potential temperature only; the purpose of this study is to understand how much that simplification matters. In this work, we evaluate simulated internal gravity wave characteristics by modeling stratified flow over bell-shaped hills using three forms of the governing equations: the linearized incompressible Boussinesq form, the full incompressible Boussinesq form, and the fully compressible form. While all formulations predict qualitatively similar wave structures, the compressible equations predict larger parcel displacements at higher altitudes, higher variations in apparent wavelengths, and more differences in wave angle, particularly at low Froude numbers. These differences can be attributed to compressibility and non-linear effects. The physical implications of differing wave characteristics become especially important in low Froude number regimes. These differences can, in turn, lead to differing predictions of wind farm performance and the characteristics of wind farm-induced gravity waves, underscoring the potential importance of compressibility effects in accurately capturing flow behavior in strongly stratified environments.

Title: A probabilistic model of visual segmentation explains early visual cortical dynamics
Author: Tridib K. Biswas, Ruben Coen-Cagli
Text_Content: Neural dynamics are a central feature of biological neural systems. In the visual cortex, the functional role of neural dynamics is poorly understood, particularly for static stimuli. The statistics of still natural images have long been used by models that successfully predict firing in early visual cortex; those models assume that neurons represent inferences about latent image features, but often ignore the dynamics of said inference. Here, we test if inferential dynamics in images explain visual-cortical dynamics. To do so, we present a biologically plausible model of cortical computation which assumes that the inference of features is coupled with inference about how those features are organized into meaningful parts, a function also known as segmentation. Given an input image, our model iterates between inferring the features and the segments, through recurrence and feedback, thus inducing dynamics in the neural representation of features. For these neural dynamics, we derive theoretical and exact predictions. Our model predicts both gain and variability in evoked responses to natural images, and we show that it captures classical single-neuron experimental findings such as gain dynamics and variability decay during stimulus presentation. The model also predicts that those dynamics are organized around inferred segment structure and more heterogeneous than previously thought, reflecting the complexity of inference for natural scenes. Finally, our analytical formulation provides a clear interpretation of our results. Insights from our normative model could generalize to segmentation problems in other experimental modalities, and help address the cost of inference in artificial networks with iterative computation.

Title: Chemotactic recruitment offsets congestion in honeybee trophallaxis
Author: William Magrogan, Orit Peleg, Zachary P. Kilpatrick
Text_Content: Honeybee colonies distribute food by trophallaxis, a sequence of local interactions in which nectar donors transfer resources to hungry nestmates. Efficient transfer requires a searcher to find a donor and then be served. Chemical signals may draw searchers to a donor, though the crowd they form may block the way. We develop a stochastic framework coupling velocity-jump search that depends on chemical signaling to random-order service at donor aggregations, and measure trophallactic efficiency by the time the colony needs to feed a prescribed fraction of its members. Directed recruitment emerges because fed bees linger near donors and strengthen local chemical cues, but lingering also slows service. Trophallactic efficiency is therefore maximized at an intermediate abandonment rate that balances recruitment against congestion. We determine when displaced cues remain useful and how competing donors partition searchers. With two donors of unequal service rate, the faster one produces fed bees sooner and so advertises more strongly, drawing recruitment toward the donor that can sustain more throughput and away from the one that would congest. Together, these results show how feedback between service and signaling can self-organize recruitment to match local service capacity without centralized coordination.

Title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
Author: Akseli Kangaslahti, Milind Tambe, Alastair van Heerden, Cheryl Johnson
Text_Content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

Title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
Author: Mahindra Rautela
Text_Content: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4--9 Euler steps at 5% terminal error and 87--112 at 1%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.

Title: ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking
Author: Xiang Fang, Wanlong Fang, Junhao Dong, Daizong Liu
Text_Content: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.

Title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
Author: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Berent Aldikacti, Angelina Ju, Ian Lumsden, Anirban Mandal, Rajiv Mayani, Kin Wai Ng, Hamza Safri, Michael Stealey, Sai Swaminathan, Michela Taufer, Karan Vahi, Michael Zink, Ewa Deelman
Text_Content: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.

Title: Domain-Adversarial Adaptation from MURA to In-House Radiographs for Improved Adult Elbow Fracture Classification
Author: M. Bolhassani, W. Furtado, D. Duvall, MJ Negahdar, J. Joshi, S. Contractor, A. Amini
Text_Content: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.

Title: Does Haptic Connection to a Healthy Partner Improve Motor Learning in Chronic Stroke? A Pilot Study of Robot-Based Dyadic Training
Author: Erica L. Waters, Natalia Stroutinsky-Sobotka, Reem M. Azar, Frances S. Shofer, Pamela Z. Cacchione, Rochelle J. Mendonca, Michelle J. Johnson
Text_Content: Purpose: Robot-based haptic dyads, where two users exchange forces through robots, have been proposed for robot-assisted neurorehabilitation. This intervention could increase motor learning by promoting motor variability, providing an implicit communication channel, and facilitating social interaction. Despite the potential benefits, few studies have investigated robot-based haptic dyads for neurological populations, and none have included a comprehensive clinical assessment. Design/Methodology/Approach: We present a pilot study investigation of individuals with chronic stroke learning a complex tracking task in solo and dyad conditions. Prior to training, participants completed a battery of cognitive, motor, and sensory assessments. We assessed changes in key kinematic outcomes including tracking error, distance traveled, mean absolute power, and sample entropy. We also performed a correlation analysis of clinical scores with baseline tracking errors. Findings: Baseline tracking error was strongly correlated (r > 0.6) with lower cognitive scores and higher motor scores. Only the solo group demonstrated lower tracking error at assessment (Δ = -5.33, 95%CI [-10.25, -0.40], p = 0.027), but this result was tempered by the removal of an outlier participant. Neither group demonstrated clear retention. The dyad group showed significantly elevated performance, effort, and movement complexity during training. Research Limitations/Implications: The selected task was too difficult to reveal learning for either group, which may be related to its high cognitive demand. Sample size and stroke heterogeneity were also limitation. Originality/Value: Dyadic training increased movement complexity and effort, which are associated with better motor learning. Clinical characteristics such as lesion location, cognition, sensation, and chronicity may influence potential benefits of dyadic training.

Title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
Author: Shenghui Li, Li Ju, Thiemo Voigt
Text_Content: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar, a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to $2.2\times$ under bandwidth constraints.

Title: DUO: Dual Readouts of Diffusion Models for OOD Detection
Author: Alireza Javid, Shirin Shoushtari, Nuria González Prelcic
Text_Content: Diffusion models are powerful generative methods for learning and sampling from complex data distributions. Safely deploying these models requires detecting inputs that fall outside their training distribution. Because diffusion models recover clean samples from noisy inputs, reconstruction error is often used for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This approach assumes that in-distribution (ID) inputs are reconstructed more accurately than OOD inputs. However, OOD inputs may be reconstructed equally well or even better, making this score unreliable. We therefore propose the leading sensitivity spectrum of intermediate denoising features as a complementary OOD signal and demonstrate that it remains informative when reconstruction error is misleading. We introduce DUal-readout of diffusion models for OOD detection (DUO), a fully unsupervised, training-free OOD detector that combines reconstruction error and feature sensitivity. DUO improves average AUROC by approximately 6% points over the strongest baselines while substantially reducing inference cost, and achieves SOTA on near-OOD and high-resolution benchmarks.

Title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
Author: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble
Text_Content: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

Title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Efficient Multipath Parameter Estimation in MIMO Systems
Author: Chaofan Deng, Linyu Sun, Jaeho Lee, Zishen Wan, Arijit Raychowdhury
