We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.

Title: AMSchem: Automated Schematic Visualization of AMS Circuits via Verifiable Agentic Generation
Author: Yichen Shi, Zhiyuan Wang, Jianing Cui, Yao Lai, Jinting Zhang, Zhuofu Tao, Hongyang Wang, Zhiping Yu, Ting Jung Lin, Lei He
Text_Content: For decades, the netlist-to-schematic gap has remained a persistent challenge in design automation, especially for analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits. Netlists encode connectivity, not visual presentation, making their manual conversion into readable schematics time-consuming and dependent on expert conventions. The same gap leaves LLM-based design tools without structured visual feedback, forcing them to iterate on circuits they cannot see. We present AMSchem, a training-free, verifier-guided agentic framework that automatically generates human-readable schematics from AMS netlists. AMSchem separates circuit-aware visual planning (DrawingIntent) from executable schematic geometry (SchematicIR), and applies localized visual feedback with bounded, revalidated repair patches. Deterministic validators enforce device preservation, pin-net consistency, and geometric correctness throughout. For evaluation, we construct AMSchem-Bench comprising 64 circuits of 12 types. On the 40-circuit schematic subset, AMSchem with gpt-5.5 achieves 85.0\% validity (vs. 32.5\% direct generation). When integrated as a visual feedback module in LLM-based analog design, AMSchem resolves all 13 previously failed cases from AnalogCoder benchmark across five models, substantially improving the success rate. Our dataset and benchmark are available at https://www.amschem.com/benchmark

Title: Do Machine Learning Models Predict?
Author: Michele Pizzochero, Emanuele Ratti
Text_Content: Machine learning (ML) models are said to predict. Philosophers draw a line between accommodation and prediction, depending on whether or not the evidence a theory succeeds on was used in constructing it. Does this distinction survive when a theory is replaced by an ML model? We argue so, yet the dividing line becomes fuzzy. Whether an output of an ML model counts as an accommodation or as a prediction hinges upon the relationship between the patterns the input instantiate and those on which the model was selected through its training. Once this relation is taken into account, most successful outputs of ML models, we suggest, bear a strong accommodation character. We further trace the consequences of our account for confirmation, novelty, and scientific realism.

Title: Cut Conditions, Integrality, and Obstructions for Directed Multiflows
Author: Srinwanti Debgupta, Martin Skutella, Philipp Warode
Text_Content: In contrast to the max-flow/min-cut theorem for single-commodity flows, the cut condition is necessary but not sufficient for the existence of directed multiflows, even with only two commodities. Poremba and Shepherd (IPCO 2023) conjecture that the cut condition is sufficient for all capacities and demands on a directed two-commodity topology if and only if it contains neither of two specific topologies as a relevant minor. We prove this conjecture. As a consequence, the fractional and integral flow-cut gaps of every directed two-commodity topology coincide and are either 1 or 2. We then investigate stronger necessary conditions for multiflow feasibility and their implications for integrality. We introduce a hierarchy of five conditions, ranging from the classical cut condition through conditions based on blocking edge sets and binary edge lengths to the linear programming dual characterization of fractional feasibility. The corresponding classes of sufficient topologies are strictly nested. We extend the Nagamochi-Ibaraki theorem: whenever one of the first four conditions is sufficient on a topology, integral capacities and demands satisfying that condition admit an integral multiflow, computable in polynomial time. Finally, we prove that recognizing topologies on which any of these four conditions is sufficient is coNP-complete, even for two commodities.

Title: SpatialSR: Spatial Resolution-Centric Pipeline for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution
Author: Yan Zhang, Runfeng Luo, Liangke Gao, Lin Yuan, Bin Xiao, Xinbo Gao
Text_Content: Although remote sensing image arbitrary-scale super-resolution (RSI-ASSR) methods support reconstruction at arbitrary or continuous scales, they predominantly condition on the relative scale factor and have not sufficiently investigated the absolute spatial resolution itself as a reconstruction prior, thereby disregarding the inherent spatial context of objects, which frequently leads to spatial-related distortions and compromised performance in downstream remote sensing applications. To address these challenges, we introduce SpatialSR, a SRe-centric arbitrary-scale RSISR method that leverages the spatial resolution (SRe) of remote sensing images (RSI) as an essential prior for super-resolution reconstruction. Distinct from existing SR methods, SpatialSR aims to restore high-resolution remote sensing images with a target SRe (typically set to 0.1m/pixel to align with the metadata of commonly used downstream task datasets). Specifically, we design a Spatial Resolution Estimation Module (SREM) to estimate the SRe of low-resolution (LR) images, thereby dynamically determining the required arbitrary scaling factor. Next, we employ a pretrained SRe-to-image diffusion model to extract SRe-specified texture-style codes, which are further incorporated into a carefully designed Resolution-aware Style Consistency Module (RSCM) to constrain the SRe-aware texture consistency of reconstructed images. Furthermore, to overcome the high computational expense inherent in diffusion-based SR methods, we wrap the iterative diffusion process as a Trajectory Consistency (TC) loss, which enables comparable reconstructed texture quality of the generative model in SpatialSR within a single step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SpatialSR achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on commonly used RSISR and downstream (image classification and segmentation tasks) datasets.

Title: Tensor Network Kernel Machines for Nonlinear System Identification
Author: Kim Batselier
Text_Content: Over the past ten years Tensor Network Kernel Machines have enabled efficient nonlinear system identification through the use of low-rank tensor networks. The goal of this article is to provide the reader with a basic understanding of this model class in terms of its two defining properties. Furthermore, both the optimization and regularization of such models are discussed, together with recent developments and starting points for further exploration.

Title: An Explicit Below Half Threshold Bound for the Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir's Secret Sharing Scheme
Author: Cheng Zhang, Xin Wang, Xiangliang Kong
Text_Content: As a fundamental cryptographic primitive, secret sharing distributes a secret among multiple parties and allows certain authorized parties to recover the secret while preventing unauthorized parties from knowing the secret. However, local leakage from each party member allows an adversary to learn partial information from each share, which is not guaranteed by traditional security. In this paper, we study bounds on the reconstruction threshold of Shamir's secret sharing scheme over prime fields against arbitrary 1-bit local leakage. We show that, for all sufficiently large $n$ and every prime $p>n$, the $(n,t)$-Shamir's scheme is $\exp(-Ω(n))$-resilient whenever $t/n\geq 0.489$, for any choice of distinct nonzero evaluation points. Our proof refines the dual-code list recovery analysis and combines complementary Fourier estimates according to the support sizes and biases of the leakage functions, yielding an improved explicit reconstruction threshold bound.

Title: MICRO: A Surgery-Phase Retinal Image Rigid Registration Benchmark and One-Step Frequency-Structure Similarity Registration Learning
Author: Mingdao Gong, Yan Hu, Mingzhen Yuan, Jialu Zhang, Junming Feng, Yiming Jiang, Jing Ma, Jinghua Liu, Huazhu Fu, Hai Lu, Xiaoqing Zhang, Jiang Liu
Text_Content: Precise multimodal retinal image rigid registration (MRIRG) is essential for aligning cross-modal vessel structures, offering critical guidance for ophthalmic surgery. Despite its significance, the advancement of MRIRG is hindered by the lack of publicly available multimodal retinal image rigid registration datasets spanning various ophthalmic surgery phases (e.g., preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative). To address this issue, we introduce the MICRO dataset, a large-scale MRIRG benchmark, comprising 1,365 cross-modal retinal image pairs with standardized annotations across all ophthalmic surgery phases. Moreover, existing deep registration methods achieve competitive MRIRG results via a two-step segmentation-then-detection framework, but segmentation quality heavily constrains their performance. We argue that this dependency stems from an implicit need for keypoint topology constraints, which have not been exploited for MRIRG through a one-step registration framework. Inspired by the above analysis, we propose a novel One-step Frequency-Structure Similarity Registration (OFS2Reg) learning framework for MRIRG that leverages the potential of cross-modal vessel structure similarities to construct keypoint topology constraints under a shared detection network. To be specific, OFS2Reg applies a well-designed frequency-guided structure preservation descriptor to construct coarse keypoint topology constraints in descriptors by highlighting significant vessel structures. Additionally, we develop a new cross-modal vessel structure similarity learning method that refines cross-modal keypoint topology constraints to precisely align pixel-level cross-modal vessel structures by leveraging cross-modal vessel structure similarity priors.

Title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time
Author: Ku Onoda, Haruto Kawano, Shota Takashiro, Kohei Hayashi
Text_Content: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.

Title: Strong Backdoor to Forests is FPT: Tight Linear-Time FPT for Essentially General SAT
Author: Olesia Bilyk, Aidar Munduzbaev, Roohani Sharma, Mamnoon Siam
Text_Content: In a seminal work, Gaspers and Szeider [FOCS 2013] gave a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) approximate algorithm for finding a strong backdoor of size at most $k$ to incidence treewidth at most $t$, for a given CNF-formula $φ$. In particular, their algorithm runs in $f(k,t) |φ|^3$ time, and finds a strong backdoor to treewidth at most $t$, of $φ$, of size at most $2^k$ whenever there exists one of size at most $k$. Determining whether the detection of strong backdoors to bounded incidence treewidth is FPT parameterized by $k+t$ was left open in their work and this has been repeatedly posed as an open question by Gaspers and Szeider, for example in [The Multivariate Algorithmic Revolution and Beyond 2012] and more recently in [Computer Science Reviews 2025], even for incidence forests and when the input is a $3$-CNF formula. We answer this question affirmatively. We show that strong backdoors to forests can be found in linear-FPT time on arbitrary non-tautological CNF formulas (not just on 3-CNF formulas). Given such a formula $φ$ and a budget $k$, our algorithm finds a strong backdoor to the class of forests, of size at most $k$, or correctly reports that none exists, in $2^{2^{O(k)}} |φ|$ time. Moreover, we show that our result is as tight as it can get. First, we show that finding strong backdoors to treewidth $t$ for any $t \geq 2$ is W[1]-hard, even on non-tautological 3-CNF formulas. Second, the running time of our algorithm is tight: it is linear in the input size and a better than double-exponential dependence on $k$ in the running time would imply a $2^{o(N/\log N)}$-time algorithm for solving 3-SAT on $N$ variables, which would beat even the very recently claimed sub-exponential algorithm for solving 3-SAT by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
Author: Junha Ryu, Hoi-Jun Yoo
Text_Content: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

Title: Maximizing Detection Probability in UAV Search Missions using Random-Key Optimizers
Author: Antonio Dantas, Elcio Shiguemori, Antonio Chaves
Text_Content: This paper focuses on the stochastic and real-time constraints of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) path planning in Search and Rescue (SAR) missions. We introduce a configurable data-driven and intelligent routing architecture that combines a closed-loop probability update with the Random-Key Optimizers (RKO). Our problem is mathematically modeled as a dynamic probabilistic variant of the Open Vehicle Routing Problem (OVRP), enabling the solver to switch adaptively between two objectives, thereby balancing probability maximization and resource minimization. The framework degrades elegantly under noisy priors but not under biased ones: a systematically biased map performs about half as well as flying with no prior at all. Computational tests show that the proposed scheme is scalable and competitive with single-path scenarios in terms of solution performance and serves as a strong decision guide for intelligent planning in SAR operations in unstable environments

Title: Beating Rytter's Bound: All-Pairs CFL Reachability in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ Time
Author: Rupak Majumdar
Text_Content: Context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition are fundamental problems in program analysis and language theory. Despite years of effort, the best algorithms for these problems run in time $O(n^3/\log n)$ on a word RAM model; they are based on an observation of Rytter in 1985 for 2NPDA which was adapted for CFL reachability by Chaudhuri in 2008. No better algorithm has been designed since. We give the first improvement to Rytter's algorithm. For both all-pairs context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition, we show a deterministic algorithm running in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ time and $O(n^{2+ε})$ words of space for every fixed $0<ε<1$ on a word RAM. Our improvement is based on a new data structure that reports set differences using batched maintenance of exact intersection counts, allowing saturation to skip regions that contain no new reachability information.

Title: A Modular Perspective for Modeling MARL Systems
Author: Tiziano Maisonhaute, Jean-Christophe Soulié, Fabien Michel
Text_Content: The growing complexity of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has fragmented the literature, obscuring underlying architectural choices behind diverse implementations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to evaluate critical modeling dimensions in isolation, identify how components affect the resulting system dynamics, and compare, reuse, or combine contributions across the literature. This paper proposes a modular perspective for modeling, analyzing, and implementing MARL systems. We decompose them into eight functional modules: agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module, we clarify its role and review representative approaches. We instantiate this decomposition in MARLKIT, a framework whose modules are explicit and interchangeable. MARLKIT demonstrates how the proposed perspective supports transparent experimental assumptions and the controlled variation and combination of MARL mechanisms. Experiments illustrate its ability to prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. Overall, the paper provides a structured perspective on MARL modeling and implementation, offering a common language for making modeling choices explicit, supporting clearer descriptions of MARL approaches, and supporting more controlled experimentation through the systematic isolation and combination of MARL mechanisms.

Title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
Author: Thomas Broholt Knudsen, Christian Høst-Madsen, Vedran Sekara, Jonas L. Juul
Text_Content: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $α$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $α$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $α$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $α$ and more at high $α$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

Title: Cyclically covering subspaces and additive perfect codes
Author: Yangcheng Li, Pingzhi Yuan
Text_Content: Let $h_q(n)$ be the largest codimension of a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ whose cyclic shifts cover the whole space. For $r>0$, we characterize the inequality $h_q(n)\ge r$ in terms of cyclic $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear codes over vector alphabets with covering radius one, no nonzero word of block weight one, and a scalar dual generated by the shifts of one word. For $k,m\ge2$, let $I_q(j)$ count the monic irreducible polynomials of degree $j$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. If $k$ is prime or $m\ge2\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}I_q(j)+2$, we prove that a cyclic $\mathbb{F}_q$ linear perfect code of length $\frac{q^{km}-1}{q^k-1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q^k$ exists if and only if $\gcd(m,q-1)=1$. When this condition holds, we also obtain \(h_q\!\left(\frac{q^{km}-1}{q^k-1}\right)=k(m-1).\) Restriction of scalars gives the same criterion for every $m\ge2$ when $q$ is odd, $q+1$ is a power of two, and $k=2p$ with $p$ prime. We also show that $h_q(q^k+1)=k$ exactly when $q$ is even, for every $k\ge1$.

Title: MNN-Pocket-0.3B Technical Report
Author: MNN Team
Text_Content: This technical report presents MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a compact 300M-parameter dense language model designed for efficient on-device deployment and supporting context lengths of up to 32K tokens. With an INT4 deployment footprint of only 173 MB and decoding throughput of up to 466 tokens/s on iPad Pro M5 (Metal), it can be seamlessly integrated into applications on edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is developed through the co-design of its architecture, data, training pipeline, and inference system. Hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning balance model capability with on-device memory and compute constraints. A four-stage pre-training pipeline covering approximately 4.1 trillion high-quality Chinese and English tokens equips the model with broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. This is followed by a three-stage post-training pipeline comprising instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and quantization-aware training. Finally, hardware-specific optimizations in the MNN inference engine enable fast, memory-efficient inference and long-context processing. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MNN-Pocket-0.3B achieves frontier-level performance among models of comparable size, with particularly strong results in Chinese and English knowledge and reasoning, mathematics, coding, and instruction following. It consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models and even surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks. We release MNN-Pocket-0.3B with open weights and ready-to-use MNN deployment packages. We hope it will provide a practical foundation for capable, responsive, and memory-efficient edge applications while advancing research and development in on-device language models.

Title: The Optimal Rate Constant of Heavy-Ball Momentum on Smooth Strongly Convex Functions
Author: Marcos Hernanz
Text_Content: The heavy-ball method with a constant step size and a constant momentum parameter accelerates gradient descent on quadratics, but no choice of the two parameters does so on the class of smooth strongly convex functions. We determine how much faster than gradient descent it can be made on this class. Writing the best worst-case rate over all tunings as $1-c(κ)/κ$, where $κ$ is the condition number, we prove that $c(κ)$ tends to $8$ in every dimension of two or more. The lower bound on the rate holds for every tuning, because a tuning that is faster than $1-8/κ$ on quadratics follows a slowly decaying spiral on some function of two variables. The matching upper bound comes from an explicit tuning, with nearly the momentum of Polyak's tuning and a step size about $\sqrtκ/8$ times smaller, and from a Lyapunov function whose positivity is verified in exact arithmetic. Optimally tuned heavy-ball is therefore asymptotically four times faster than gradient descent on this class.

Title: Efficient sensitivity analysis for combustion problems via reformulation and adjoint methods
Author: Francesca Loffredo, Raymond Langer, Marco Vivenzo, Sanket Girhe, Heinz Pitsch
Text_Content: Numerical simulations of combustion processes rely on chemical kinetic models, whose predictive capability is typically assessed by comparing measurements of quantities of interest (QoIs) in idealized experimental configurations with the corresponding simulated values. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the influence of model parameters on QoIs, making it a key tool for model development and optimization. Given the large number of parameters involved in detailed kinetic models compared to the number of QoIs, adjoint methods are a promising approach for efficient sensitivity analysis. Ignition delay times (IDTs) and extinction strain rates (ESRs) are among the QoIs of primary importance. However, applying adjoint methods to these quantities is not straightforward and is addressed in this work. The system of governing equations is reformulated via a coordinate transformation that makes the QoI an explicit component of the solution vector. This reformulation enables the application of adjoint sensitivity analysis for both IDT and ESR. A computational complexity analysis demonstrates that the proposed formulation significantly improves algorithmic efficiency compared to conventional approaches. The methodology is verified by comparing adjoint sensitivity coefficients with those obtained from other methods. Execution time measurements show computational cost reductions of up to two orders of magnitude relative to standard direct sensitivity analysis. A benchmark study is conducted across kinetic models of increasing size to assess how far theoretical efficiency gains are realized in practice. While the results show that implementation details can limit performance for smaller problem sizes, the expected asymptotic scaling is observed for larger models. The benchmark thus provides a reference framework for identifying key performance bottlenecks and guiding subsequent optimization efforts.

Title: PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations
Author: Riccardo Cavarra, Lupo Lovatelli, Shaheim Ogbomo-Harmitt, Jakub Grzelak, Adelaide De Vecchi, Andrew King, Oleg Aslanidi
Text_Content: Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

Title: ExoStack: A Modular and Reconfigurable Software Framework for Wearable Robotics Using ROS 2
Author: Debadrata Sarkar, Upamanyu Ray, Soumen Sen, Aman Arora
Text_Content: Wearable robots depend on a software chain that links body-worn sensing to gait interpretation, assistance generation, and actuation. Personalization further requires each measured response to remain associated with the assistance parameters that generated it. This paper presents ExoStack, a modular ROS 2 framework for implementing that chain across embedded hubs and a host computer. Its Embedded Sensing and Actuation (ESA) library configures ESP32 boards as microROS sensing and actuation hubs. ExoCore supplies multi-hub synchronization, gait-event detection, profile generation, motion planning, cost evaluation, and human-in-the-loop (HIL) optimization as configuration-instantiated nodes. The PASE desktop application edits configurations, launches the processing stages, and visualizes ROS 2 topics. Hardware drivers and algorithm plugins can be added through defined interfaces without modifying the generic processing nodes. We characterize hub and planner timing on three embedded computers and demonstrate reuse on two pneumatic exosuits.

Title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
Author: Zixin Su, Yangguang Lin, Zegang Peng, Yuntong Sun, Xuanyi Wang, Jiahao Wang, Qiankai Xu, Bing Yuan, Jingjia Huang, Ruyang Liu, Yanxu Hu, Yufeng Zhou, Yi Lin
Text_Content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

Title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
Author: Hao Kang, Weili Xu, Ziyang Li, Zheng Du, Hanchen Li, Tian Xia, Song Bian, Tushar Krishna, Huizi Mao, Ion Stoica, Song Han
Text_Content: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework. We open-source the system implementation of Evolving Infra at https://github.com/mit-han-lab/EvolvingInfra.

Title: Reconfigurable Action Theories: A Formal Foundation for Dynamically Composable Agent Harnesses
Author: Jianmin Ji
Text_Content: Action theories typically fix their vocabulary and causal laws, whereas agent harnesses can change their tools, providers, and policies during execution. We introduce Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT), in which actions can change the action theory itself. A theory module in RAT contains a vocabulary, causal laws, and an initializer. A RAT configuration records the active modules and the world state. Module loading and unloading are represented by actions governed by ordinary causal laws. RAT retains the standard causal action semantics of its language fragment when the active module set is fixed. We give sufficient conditions for at most one next configuration, preservation of existing behavior when a module is added, and equal results when modules are loaded in either order. We establish the computational complexity of reasoning tasks in RAT and translate finite RAT systems into nonmonotonic causal theories and Answer Set Programming (ASP), preserving bounded executions. Experiments compare finite RAT models with executions of official DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and OpenHands implementations. RAT provides a formal basis for checking how component changes affect a harness's available actions, behavior, and reachable goals.

Title: Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks for Damage Identification in Ultrasonic Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
Author: Lukas Jilke, Caspar Wasle, Norbert Hosters, Florian Raddatz, Marek Behr, Gerko Wende
Text_Content: Ultrasonic guided wave (UGW) inspection has become an effective method in structural health monitoring (SHM). While machine learning has enhanced damage detection capabilities, purely data-driven models remain constrained by extensive labeled datasets and limited physical interpretability. Standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) further suffer from spectral bias (F-Principle) in high-frequency regimes, prioritizing low-frequency components while failing to resolve the high-frequency oscillations critical for UGW reconstruction. Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks (PI-SIRENs) address these limitations by embedding governing partial differential equations directly into the training process. Building upon SIRENs, which utilize periodic activation functions to inherently capture high-frequency spectral content, the proposed framework is designed to operate effectively in sparse ultrasonic measurement regimes. This work introduces a frequency-domain PI-SIREN framework tailored for the Mindlin-Reissner plate theory to reconstruct ultrasonic wavefields without temporal discretization. The model parameters are optimized using a hybrid strategy comprising three phases: first-order Adam, residual-adaptive refinement (RAR) and quasi-Newton L-BFGS. Numerical and experimental evaluations confirm that the model serves as a physics-consistent baseline derived from sparse data, functioning as a computationally efficient surrogate for damage identification in SHM and non-destructive testing (NDT). Integrating the surrogate into a damage identification pipeline detects and localizes a milled notch from sparse experimental measurements with a localization error of 1 % of the plate diagonal. In contrast, data-driven benchmarks and MLPs with hyperbolic tangent activation functions, with and without Fourier feature embedding, are unable to identify damage due to higher reconstruction errors.

Title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
Author: Xiangrui Yang, Yunfeng Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Fangyu Zhang, Enrui Zhao, Liang Zeng, Cheng Peng, Minhui Xie, Jiaqiang Liu, Xiao Liang, Yiming Qiu
Text_Content: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

Title: Be My Eye: Learning to See Beyond a Robot's Own Perspective
Author: Baifu Huang, Shilin Fang, Jianan Wang
Text_Content: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.

Title: Depth as a Candidate Source: Portfolio Allocation for Recurrent Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models
Author: Chaoyuan Hao, Wentao Yue, Yanyan Wu, Boyuan Gao, Tianyou Lai, Maolin Wang, Yongxin Ni, Hanwen Du, Youhua Li
Text_Content: Recurrent latent reasoning in large lanugage models (LLMs) scales test-time computation by increasing recurrent depth, naturally framing inference as a problem of deciding when to stop. We identify a previously overlooked limitation of this single-depth view through systematic preliminary analysis: deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, while depth-specific success sets remain broadly non-nested even after controlling for marginal accuracy. This suggests that depth determines not only computation cost, but also access to distinct candidate solutions. Motivated by this finding, we propose Depth Portfolio Allocation (DPA), which reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. DPA supports both fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP show that mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs, while feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings. Code and data are avaible at : https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM-latent-B7BC/.

Title: Optical frequency combs on thin-film lithium niobate: from principles to applications
Author: Xiangzhi Xie, Tianqi Lei, Zeyu Luo, Binbin Nie, Yanyun Xue, Yikun Chen, Qi-Fan Yang, Yaowen Hu, Cheng Wang
Text_Content: Optical frequency combs, consisting of mutually coherent and equally spaced spectral lines, provide a powerful means of synthesizing, distributing, and processing optical frequencies on chip. Among integrated photonic platforms, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is particularly attractive for comb generation because it combines strong electro-optic (EO) functionality, accessible $χ^{(2)}$ and $χ^{(3)}$ nonlinearities, low-loss nanophotonic confinement, and versatile dispersion engineering. This review summarizes the physical foundations and representative realizations of TFLN combs, and discusses their applications in optical communication, microwave photonics, optical computing, and precision metrology. The integration of nonlinear functionality, EO control, and passive photonic components is expected to advance compact, energy-efficient comb sources and broaden the utility of TFLN in integrated photonics and quantum optics.

Title: Representational Alignment between Deep Neural Networks and Human Brain in Speech Processing under Audiovisual Noise
Author: Cheng Luo, Jian Zhu, Zhoujian Sun, Yunyi Qi, Yu Qi, Wenhui Sun, Wenyuan Yu
Text_Content: Speech comprehension in the human brain is an incremental process that begins with acoustic processing and advances to linguistic processing. While recent studies have revealed that the hierarchy of deep neural networks (DNNs) correlates with the ascending auditory pathway, the exact nature of this DNN-brain alignment remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate how DNN representations align with the brain's acoustic-to-linguistic processing. Specifically, we employed neural encoding models to simulate neural responses to acoustic (i.e., speech and noise envelope) and linguistic features (i.e., word onset and surprisal). By applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), we quantified the similarity between these neural responses and the DNN embeddings generated by a pre-trained automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, both before and after fine-tuning on audiovisual noisy data. Our results demonstrate significant DNN-brain alignment: embeddings from shallow layers exhibit higher similarity to neural responses associated with acoustic features, while those from deeper layers align more closely with neural responses related to linguistic features. Importantly, the fine-tuning process enhances this alignment by improving noise processing in shallower layers and refining linguistic representations in deeper layers. These results suggest that fine-tuned DNN models can naturally develop human-like processing patterns in noisy environments, highlighting a functional alignment between the human brain and DNNs in speech representation.

Title: Ultrafast Liquid Jet X-ray Total Scattering
Author: Adam F. Sapnik, Philip A. Chater, Dean S. Keeble, Tobias A. Bird, John S. O. Evans, Federica Bertolotti, Antonietta Guagliardi, Norberto Masciocchi, Daniel T. Bowron, Lise J. Støckler, Elodie A. Harbourne, Anders B. Borup, Rebecca S. Silberg, Viktoria A. Kaznelson, Stefanie Punke, Mariia Svyrydenko, Maryna I. Bodnarchuk, Dmitry N. Dirin, Simon C. Boehme, Maksym V. Kovalenko, Bo B. Iversen, Emil S. Bozin, Kirsten M. Ø. Jensen, Gabriele Ansaldi, Karen Appel, Alexander Gierke, Jörg Hallmann, Aliaksandr Leonau, Anders Madsen, Johannes Möller, Jan-Etienne Pudell, Angel Rodriguez-Fernandez, Andreas Schmidt, Roman Shayduk, Cornelius Strohm, Joana Valerio, Ulrike Boesenberg, David A. Keen
Text_Content: X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide the temporal resolution needed to extend total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to investigate structural dynamics on femtosecond-to-picosecond timescales. We recently demonstrated that high-quality total scattering data and PDFs can be obtained from individual XFEL pulses; here, we take the next step towards time-resolved studies of structural dynamics in solution. Using the Materials Imaging and Dynamics (MID) instrument at the European XFEL, we obtain total scattering data up to $Q_{\max} = 16.4\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$ from both conventional capillary samples and, critically, from samples delivered by a liquid jet. Despite the large air and solvent backgrounds inherent to this setup, PDFs suitable for quantitative structural analysis are recovered from liquid dispersions and molecular clusters in solution. We further demonstrate pump-probe total scattering from $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_3$ nanocrystals in a liquid jet, resolving a fluence-dependent photoinduced isotropic lattice strain. Additionally, empirical potential structure refinement (EPSR) of XFEL total scattering data from an aqueous Keggin cluster reveals site-specific hydration environments and enables three-dimensional mapping of the surrounding solvent structure. Together, these advances open the door to tracking not only ultrafast structural changes in solution, but also the evolving solvent environments that govern molecular behaviour and reactivity.

Title: ForgeSystem: An Architecture for Demand-Specific Artefact Production with AI Agents
Author: Qingfeng He, Zhui Zhu, Yaojian Chen, Shangzhan Li, Leshan Li, Tingjian Zhang, Qian Xie, Yuxuan Li, Xu Han, Zhiyuan Liu
Text_Content: General-purpose software serves many different demands, but this flexibility costs performance and efficiency on any specific demand. Software tailored to a specific demand avoids these losses, yet developing it requires substantial time and effort from human experts. AI agents offer an alternative: they can design, implement and test artefacts tailored to individual demands. We call this production paradigm Forge. Forging for a demand is economically justified when the cumulative benefit of specialisation exceeds the total cost of construction, verification and maintenance. To make Forge a repeatable production process, we propose ForgeSystem, which consists of a control layer, a forge loop and a recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. The control layer selects which artefact serves each demand and decides which demands to forge, when to forge them and from which starting point; the forge loop iterates between production and verification until a candidate artefact passes verification; and the RSI loop draws on accumulated production records to supply starting points, refine the harness and train models. We implement ForgeSystem for training frameworks, decoding megakernels and individual computational kernels. Forged training engines reach 1.047-1.332x the model-FLOPs utilisation of their reference frameworks, forged megakernels achieve a geometric-mean decoding speedup of 1.21x over SGLang across thirteen configurations, and forged kernels match or exceed expert libraries in eighteen of twenty-two configurations, while satisfying task-specific quality requirements. Controlled comparisons show that explicit quality requirements steer agents towards optimisations that preserve training quality. We also discuss a gradual transition to Forge through service routing, and how demand-specific production may shift value accumulation and trust towards production systems.

Title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations
Author: Tongyu Li, Alexander Giessing
Text_Content: Iterative algorithms are integral to many statistical procedures, whereas sampling uncertainty along their iteration is generally not quantified. We develop simultaneous inference for discrete trajectories generated from high-dimensional estimating equations, with iteration-specific population estimands that preserve algorithmic regularization. Our proposed fixed-Jacobian bootstrap propagates perturbations along the observed trajectory without repeatedly running the original nonlinear algorithm. We establish uniform first-order expansions and bootstrap validity over possibly infinite sets of contrasts and iterations under stability, entropy and moment conditions. Simulations in sparse linear regression, paired Fisher discrimination, and temporal-difference learning demonstrate accurate simultaneous coverage. A micro-randomized trial application illustrates inference for a treatment trajectory with participant-level clustering.

Title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
Author: Yongxuan Lv, Zhen Fang, Lichen Man, Hao Li, Pu Li, Hengyi Wang, Langfeng Cao, Lin Chen, Jie Huang, Xiu Su, Shan You, Fei Wang, Feng Zhao
Text_Content: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.

Title: Learning Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
Author: Xingpeng Gao, Mingyue Cheng, Daoyu Wang, Huajian Zhang, Xiaoyu Tao
Text_Content: LLM-driven time series forecasting has become increasingly promising by leveraging contextual features to generate future values directly or refine forecast priors. However, incorporating contextual features alone does not ensure that models can identify which features matter for forecasting and understand what they suggest about future dynamics. We argue that the fundamental challenge is how to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and when and how to leverage it to guide forecasting decisions. In this paper, we propose CastReasoner, an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. Specifically, CastReasoner uses a structured chain of thought (CoT) to extract predictive evidence from contextual features, infer the future dynamics suggested by this evidence, and assess these dynamics against the forecast prior to guide adaptive forecasting decisions. To enable this capability, we design a reasoning-centric two-stage post-training framework including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, we synthesize reasoning trajectories through controllable multi-teacher guidance and select high-quality ones using a novel student-aware difficulty metric. Second, we design fine-grained multi-objective rewards to further improve reasoning and forecasting. To address heterogeneous learning needs across domains in both stages, we introduce a convergence-guided data balancing strategy. Through this two-stage training, CastReasoner improves both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy. Extensive experiments across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CastReasoner achieves superior forecasting performance.

Title: Probabilistic wavefield decomposition from array covariance
Author: Jack-Andrew Smith, Claudia Elijas-Parra
Text_Content: Inter-sensor coherence loss carries information about the wavefield that conventional array processing discards. The array-covariance matrix is modelled using a mixture of energy distributions over slowness with analytical characteristic functions, e.g., skew-normal and angular-harmonic distributions, and inverted using variational Bayesian inference. The posterior supports uncertainty quantification, experimental design, model comparison and hypothesis testing. For a synthetic hydroacoustic T-phase, information is increased by an additional sensor and decreased by noise; the data favour a distributed source over a point source. For an observed thermospheric infrasound return, energy is skewed back towards the source. The method is implemented in the software Topophone2.

Title: SimpFlow: Transferable Pretraining for Fluid Dynamics via Simplified Physics
Author: Ruijie Li, Tianbai Xiao
Text_Content: Neural surrogates enable rapid fluid simulation, but learning across diverse three-dimensional (3D) geometries requires costly computational fluid dynamics (CFD) labels. We introduce SimpFlow, a pretraining approach that generates supervision from simplified physics on unlabeled geometry libraries. A source-panel potential-flow solver generates velocity and pressure fields for approximately 9,000 3D geometries, capturing geometry-induced acceleration, stagnation, and suction while omitting viscosity and separated wakes. The solver imports only a surface mesh and reuses precomputed velocity fields across inflow directions, enabling inexpensive label generation. In our benchmark, amortized labeling takes 0.111 s per example using four CPU threads. We pretrain a neural surrogate on these labels and fine-tune it on independent CFD datasets. Across five flow tasks, SimpFlow improves over training from scratch in all 24 task-budget settings. With fine-tuning fixed at 200 epochs, interpolation indicates that SimpFlow requires 35-68% fewer CFD training cases to match the error of scratch models trained at each task's largest data budget. These results demonstrate that simplified physical solutions can provide transferable supervision, offering a practical way to reduce the high-fidelity data requirements of fluid surrogates.

Title: Public, Identifiable, and Effectively Immutable: Ethical Lessons from Research on arXiv
Author: Jan Pennekamp, Johannes Lohmöller, Peter Mayer, Arjun Arunasalam
Text_Content: Ethical decision-making is central to safe cybersecurity research. Recent studies, one of which is our own, analyzing the source files of arXiv papers bring this challenge to light - arXiv publicly distributes the source files, to the surprise of many authors. Unique aspects reveal ethical challenges and dilemmas that extend beyond established ethical frameworks, institutional processes, and community best practices. In this work, we examine this case and provide insights for similar research on other public live resources, such as Zenodo or the Wayback Machine. While such empirical studies are particularly realistic, they must account for personally identifiable information, leaked secrets, and other sensitive details that could expose, shame, or otherwise negatively affect individuals, possibly leading to both reputational and practical harm. sDrawing on our collective experience and discussions among researchers, affected authors, and readers, we make three contributions: First, we define the ethical setting and highlight that even intentionally-public data with deliberate real-name attribution can raise ethical concerns when repurposed for empirical analysis. Second, we discuss the ethical issues surrounding the use of arXiv data and derive four higher-level dilemmas that researchers may face when working with similar data. Third, we derive practical guidance for ethically navigating such settings and, in doing so, distill four lessons for research on arXiv and similar public, live datasets: public availability should serve as the starting point of ethical reasoning; research should minimize the amplification it induces on exposed information; disclosure should be calibrated to the harm, confidence, and actionability of a finding; and effective immutability must be accounted for. Together, these contribute to community resources for ethically-sound cybersecurity experiments.

Title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
Author: György Eigner, Patrik P. Süli, Roland Hollós
Text_Content: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

Title: Modelling socio-economic effects of the pandemic in a metropolitan area
Author: Jan E. Snellman, Rafael A. Barrio, Cecilia I. Ventura, Tzipe Govezensky, Kimmo K. Kaski, Maarit J. Korpi-Lagg
Text_Content: One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the consequences of these measures and to predict the infections under different scenarios, for various different countries. In this paper we extend the model, called the BTH--SEIRS-model, to deal with the reduction of mobility in an urban area. The chosen region was the densely-populated metropolitan area around Helsinki, the capital of Finland. This choice obeyed to the fact that there are precise data related to mobility from a mobile telephone company, and that this region was completely isolated from the rest of the country for a short period during the pandemic. We also used public transport data from railways and the accommodation occupation rates in the area of interest. We show that the BTH--SEIRS model is capable of simulating the real infection data as well as the mobility-related economic activity, exhibiting the main trends present in the three indicators used for comparison. Our calculations allow us to highlight the difference of the behaviour of the pandemic in a totally different spatial scale, and to discover the hidden factors that govern the behaviour of people who are forced to commute every day from home to work.

Title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
Author: Guangyan Gan, Jiahao Li, Jiashun Wang, Lin William Cong
Text_Content: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.

Title: Odds-Structured Distributional Regression for Interpretable Time-to-Event Prediction
Author: Jakob Versnjak, Manuel Welte, Titus Kuehne, Marcus Kelm, Grégoire Montavon
Text_Content: Time-to-event prediction is fundamentally challenged by partial observability and aleatoric uncertainty. In clinical medicine, for instance, the timing of disease progression or acute readmission is contingent on highly dynamic and largely latent health trajectories. Rather than forcing a deterministic point forecast, distributional regression offers a principled means to address this complexity by predicting a probability distribution over time. However, explaining these distributional predictions presents a key obstacle: raw distribution parameters output by the model are abstract mathematical quantities that do not align well with domain concepts. To gain interpretability, we propose a novel paradigm where output parameters are designed to be additive in log-odds---a widely established measure in clinical risk modeling. Our approach, called ODDS-DR, moves beyond technical convenience to deliver clear domain alignment as well as the layer-wise computational structure required for robust, time-dependent feature attribution. Validated across two real-world clinical cohorts, our framework matches state-of-the-art predictive performance while resolving distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.

Title: Data-Adaptive Subset-Size Selection for Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimation
Author: Chikun Li, Baisuo Jin
Text_Content: Subset size determines the balance between robustness and efficiency in minimum covariance determinant estimation. Conventional choices fix this balance before the extent and structure of contamination are known. Reweighting does not remove the influence of the initial subset size. We propose a data-adaptive rule based on ordered squared Mahalanobis distances. It selects the first window maximum, with window width proportional to the sample size. For a minimum covariance determinant subset, the statistic equals the smallest squared distance among excluded observations. For smooth elliptical distributions with small one-point contamination, we characterize the first population window maximum. Under suitable conditions, it is the last retained fraction at which excluding the contaminating point remains optimal. We derive a first-order expansion for this boundary and establish sample localization along the full integer path. Without contamination, the selected fraction tends to one. A fast depth-based implementation reuses one ordering across candidate sizes. Simulations under Gaussian and heavy-tailed sampling show gains over fixed subset sizes, most consistently for scatter estimation. Real data analyses show that the initial subset size affects which observations are retained after reweighting.

Title: Beam-beam effects on measurements at electron-positron colliders: LEP neutrino counting and Higgs factories
Author: Brendon Madison
Text_Content: Beam-beam electromagnetic interactions affect the luminosity, collision energy, polarization, and particle backgrounds relevant to precision measurements at electron-positron colliders. We investigate these effects using Fast $e^{\pm}e^{\pm}$ Beam and Luminosity (FeeBL), a new beam-beam simulation framework, and compare its predictions with published results from LEP and proposed future colliders. We reproduce the analytical field-integration calculations of LEP Bhabha scattering and identify an approximately 2% bias in previously published beam-deflection simulations. Applying the corresponding luminosity correction and a revised uncertainty assessment motivated by the observed agreement among the four LEP experiments yields ($N_ν= 2.9965 \pm 0.0040$), compared with the previously reported ($2.9963 \pm 0.0074$). The revised uncertainty is conditional on an assumed common rescaling of experiment specific uncertainties and motivates further investigation of the original uncertainty budgets. We identify and correct implementation errors in the modeling of Breit-Wheeler, Bethe-Heitler, and Landau-Lifshitz pair production, with implications for detector backgrounds at Higgs factories. Simulated beam depolarization and luminosity spectra are compared with existing ILC and HALHF predictions. Finally, we investigate collision energy monochromatization for direct Higgs production, obtaining sub-MeV collision energy peak widths in exploratory linear collider configurations at substantial luminosity cost, while finding significantly weaker narrowing for the FCC-ee configurations studied. We derive a rigid Gaussian beam overlap model and estimate that FCC-ee needs roughly 10 m of horizontal only dispersion to reach widths of $\approx1~\mathrm{MeV}$.

Title: Hierarchical Multi-Channel Tip-Over Prediction via Isolated Temporal Models for Planetary Rover Safety
Author: Siddhant Shete, Raul Dominguez, Frank Kirchner
Text_Content: Reliable tip-over prevention is critical for planetary rovers operating in unstructured environments where communication delays prevent real-time human intervention. Existing learning-based approaches typically optimize a single prediction objective, limiting their ability to capture both gradual instability evolution and abrupt terrain disturbances. This work presents a hierarchical multi-channel tip-over prediction framework based on isolated temporal learning. A multi-horizon Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) learns progressive instability patterns from inertial measurements, while a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based forward dynamics model predicts nominal rover motion and detects unexpected dynamic deviations through prediction residuals. These complementary signals are integrated through decision-level fusion and priority-based arbitration to generate graded safety actions, including early warning and emergency braking. The proposed system is deployed as an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT)-based safety component within the Rock robotics framework, operating at 100 Hz on a planetary rover software stack. Experiments on Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) samples collected across heterogeneous terrains demonstrate 97.58% event prediction coverage with a 1.82s median lead time, outperforming individual prediction channels. The results validate that isolated temporal models combined through hierarchical decision fusion provide a robust solution for real-time rover safety in uncertain terrain.

Title: Variational free complement method with Gaussian expanded complement functions: extensions of general atomic framework including helium and lithium ground states with geminal induced expansion length
Author: Cong Wang
Text_Content: We expand the previous framework of hierarchical-decontraction Gaussian expanded complement functions approach (arXiv: 2603.16262v2) of the free complement (FC) method to $N$-electron atomic systems including general permutations. We consider the possibility that the Gaussian expansion length depends on the presence of the geminal $g$ function. To be more specific, fewer expansion length shall be used when the two-electron $g$ function is combined with the initial wavefunction. The present approach is applied to the ground states of the helium and lithium atoms. The complement function generations via 2s$\rightarrow$1s channel in the lithium ground state are discussed. Symmetries for the associated $N$-electron integrals are analyzed.

Title: A forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models: an EFM3D case study for crime scene reconstruction
Author: Davidson Chisom Onwubiko, Shahana Bano, Carlos Francisco Moreno-García
Text_Content: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.

Title: Predictability of Collective Behavior in Networks of LLM Agents
Author: Fabian Baumann, Michele Starnini
Text_Content: As AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact at scale, anticipating their collective behavior becomes necessary. Unlike humans, individual LLM agents can be probed in {controlled scenarios}; however, the predictability of their collective outcomes hinges on what such measurements capture. We study information cascades on networks of LLM agents that decide whether to share a post given how many of their contacts have shared it. At the same fraction of sharing contacts, an agent's response depends on how many contacts it has and on the post. Responses that ignore the number of contacts mispredict the cascades, increasingly on heterogeneous networks, by an error we derive analytically and that network topology alone cannot reveal. Measured in context, the response predicts, through mean-field theory, the cascades of full LLM simulations, tipping points included. Anticipating the collective behavior of AI agents thus requires evaluating them in their local network context.

Title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
Author: Mohsen Ahmadvand, Piotr Dobaczewski, Camille Bouzerand
Text_Content: Bridge hacks have cost billions, often without exploiting a code bug. In the cross-chain bridge hacks we catalogue from 2021 to 2026, failures of security posture, meaning how a bridge's people, code, controls and off-chain infrastructure are set up, account for 88% of reported losses since 2023, and nearly all repeat earlier failures. Code audits cannot catch these failures, so we propose a bridge security assessment rubric. It scores each bridge deployment from on-chain evidence, and a hard cap drops the score to the lowest value when a fatal risk is present. A token is only as safe as its weakest deployment if all its deployments share one backing. For attacks nobody anticipated, we show that rate limits and an emergency stop still bound the loss. We build an analyzer that applies the rubric to deployed bridges and monitors them for changes, and an agentic analyzer that runs the same checks on any bridge. Operators learn what to fix, and users can compare bridges. Our rubric's controls cut bridge hack losses 105-fold, from \$3.52B to \$33M.

Title: RAIL: Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning for Student-Compatible Teacher Policies
Author: Meraj Mammadov, Pedro Zuidberg Dos Martires, Johannes Andreas Stork
Text_Content: Reinforcement learning (RL) from raw sensory inputs such as images or onboard sensors can be challenging due to high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. A common strategy is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged state information and then distill it into a student policy that acts from raw inputs alone. However, when the teacher relies on information unavailable to the student, exact imitation may be impossible, creating an irreducible imitation gap. Existing approaches typically mitigate this mismatch through careful reward shaping or additional reinforcement learning on the student policy after the teacher has been trained. Instead, we introduce Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning (RAIL), which addresses the mismatch during teacher training itself. RAIL learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations using contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in this space. Because the teacher policy is constrained to operate on this shared space, it learns behaviors that are reproducible from student observations. This substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance. Across multiple environments, RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct reinforcement learning from raw observations. The learned representations further enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. Project site: https://merajmammadov.com/rail/.

Title: Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings
Author: Oshando Johnson, Ranjith Krishnamurthy, Rohith Kumar Shanmuganathan, Goran Piskachev, Eric Bodden
Text_Content: Static application security testing (SAST) tools surface vulnerabilities early and their verdicts are rule-based and auditable. Yet developers routinely dismiss findings they cannot interpret. Large language models can supply the missing explanation, but designs that also hand the model the detection give up the auditability that makes static analysis defensible. We keep detection with the analyser and give the model only the explaining. A preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners yielded five requirements. Guided by these we redesigned SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that explains findings from any analyser reporting in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format.
