The trained policy reaches the optimal cost to within a median gap of $0.4\%$ for seen systems. For unseen systems, a light fine-tuning step brings the median gap to $1.0\%$.

Title: Lensless single-pixel imaging through dynamic coded-aperture illumination
Author: Yuhan Guo, Shilei Li, Tong Zhou, Liming Li
Text_Content: We demonstrate a lensless single-pixel imaging (SPI) system combining dynamic coded-aperture illumination with single-pixel detection. Binary digital micromirror device (DMD) masks generate tailored grayscale intensity fields through coherent propagation, without relay projection optics or temporal grayscale synthesis. Six target-field configurations---uniform, Rayleigh speckle, squared-Rayleigh speckle, and sparse binary fields with $p=10\%$, $5\%$, and $1\%$---are evaluated using binary and grayscale objects. Intensity-correlation and nonnegative total-variation-regularized reconstructions reveal that the preferred illumination depends on the object, reconstruction method, and evaluation metric. By combining rapid binary modulation, programmable grayscale illumination, and single-pixel readout, this implementation provides a flexible architecture for lensless computational imaging and joint design of optical encoding and reconstruction.

Title: Is a CNN-Transformer Ensemble Worth It When a Chest X-Ray Foundation Model Is Available?
Author: Aditya Seelaboyina, Irfan Khan
Text_Content: Ensembles of ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks and Vision Transformers are a common way to improve multi-label chest X-ray classification. We ask whether such an ensemble is still worth its cost when a model pretrained on chest radiographs is available. On the official patient-disjoint split of NIH ChestX-ray14 (25,596 test images, 2,797 patients), we train five ImageNet-pretrained backbones and the EVA-X-S foundation model with validation-only model selection, compare five fusion rules, and estimate every difference with a patient-level paired bootstrap. EVA-X-S alone reached a test macro-AUROC of 0.828; the five-model ensemble reached 0.814 (difference -0.0136, 95% CI -0.0178 to -0.0098) at about 7.8 times the summed backbone latency and ten times the parameters. Averaging the five ImageNet models with EVA-X-S changed AUROC by -0.0056 (-0.0095 to -0.0021). With all five ImageNet backbones trained with the EVA-X-S recipe, their ensemble scored 0.817, still -0.0109 (-0.0142 to -0.0076) below EVA-X-S, and across three seeds EVA-X-S varied by at most 0.001 AUROC. Under the ImageNet models' recipe, however, EVA-X-S fell to 0.798. Our full-stacking configuration never outperformed calibrated averaging. In this setting, the tested ImageNet ensembles did not improve on a single chest X-ray foundation model fine-tuned with its own recipe.

Title: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
Author: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das
Text_Content: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.

Title: khammoon: From a Linguistic Guideline to a Thai Morpheme Segmenter
Author: Warit Sirichotedumrong, Adisai Na-Thalang, Chanakan Wittayasakpan, Kritsadha Phatcharoen, Kunat Pipatanakul
Text_Content: Thai is written without spaces between words, making segmentation a foundational step in most Thai NLP pipelines. Existing tools primarily reproduce the word-level conventions of corpora such as BEST; however, because the notion of a "word" in Thai lacks a unified linguistic consensus, these conventions struggle with productive compounding, leading to arbitrary boundaries and ambiguity in downstream representations. Instead, we propose operating at the morphological level, focusing on khammoon, the smallest atomic unit that carries meaning. Segmenting at the morphemic level provides an explicit, consistent morphological representation that eliminates compounding ambiguity. Crucially, this representation benefits downstream learning: models trained on morphemes perform on par with or exceed word-level baselines across part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment classification, demonstrating that linguistic consistency improves representation quality without downstream performance penalty. To operationalize this representation, we translate linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement ($κ\approx 0.99$), scale annotation with an LLM, and correct systematic errors with human labels. Finally, we train khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, achieving a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text. The guideline, datasets, model, and library are all publicly released.

Title: CaseLaw: A Policy-Decoupled Framework for Training-Free Content Moderation
Author: Qi Lu, Sen Li, Likun Shi, Xiaolong Jiang
Text_Content: Content moderation is inherently policy-dependent: moderation boundaries are often subtle, subjective, and frequently updated, while conventional rule based or fine-tuning based systems require costly rule rewriting, model retraining, or system redeployment. We propose CaseLaw, a policy-decoupled and training-free framework for adaptive content moderation. CaseLaw reformulates moderation as precedent-based retrieval and voting, where multimodal content is transformed into evidence-preserved structured semantics, embedded into a stable semantic space, and classified by thresholded voting over retrieved precedent labels. We train NoteCap on a large-scale corpus of structurally annotated notes to ensure consistent semantic extraction and freeze it during subsequent policy adaptation, which requires no additional training. Policy adaptation is achieved by updating the semantic case library, including case labels and mappings, without retraining models or modifying prompts. To evaluate CaseLaw, we construct MFO-RedNotes, a benchmark for the male-female opposition risk domain. We additionally provide a five category CoPro comparison. Experiments show that CaseLaw consistently outperforms competing baselines in both precision and recall across policy-dependent risk levels and broader safety categories, with category-wise precision/recall reaching up to 86.8%/90.1% on MFO-RedNotes across both policy settings and 94.5%/92.3% on CoPro. Our work highlights the potential of precedent-based reasoning for policy adaptive content moderation and offers a practical direction toward more stable, transparent, and training-free moderation systems.

Title: Rethinking Adaptive Routing on Dragonfly
Author: Ziyu Wang, Dezun Dong, Fei Lei
Text_Content: The Dragonfly topology is widely deployed in leading supercomputers, where adaptive routing is crucial for high-performance interconnection. Despite years of research, a dilemma remains: state-of-the-art adaptive routing algorithms achieve excellent performance but demand hardware budgets far beyond what real router chips can afford -- prohibitive buffers, logically dependent floating-point operations, or exhaustive path-set traversals -- whereas realizable algorithms deliver unsatisfactory performance. Furthermore, existing algorithms fail to exploit the abundant almost-minimal paths in Dragonfly: when only the local channels of a minimal path are congested, they reroute packets to significantly longer global non-minimal paths, wasting global bandwidth and increasing latency. To address both limitations, we analyze intra-group path contention and propose the Decoupled Incremental Adaptive Routing (DIAR) algorithm, which decouples routing into global path selection at the source and incremental local detours onto almost-minimal paths, guaranteeing deadlock freedom without additional virtual channels, escape rings, or turn models. Requiring only a few comparators, shifters, adders, and multiplexers, DIAR reduces buffer overhead by up to four orders of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art algorithms, while achieving comparable or superior performance across all evaluated scenarios: relative to the strongest realizable adaptive routing algorithm in each scenario, DIAR improves saturation throughput by up to 30.0% across synthetic traffic patterns and improves performance by up to 34.9% (13.2% on average) across HPC workloads.

Title: Budget-aware Correspondence-driven View Selection for Real-time 3D Perception of Mobile Robots
Author: Vaishnav Ramesh, Jacob Carter, Shivali J. Patel, Sanjeev J. Koppal, Md Jahidul Islam
Text_Content: 3D visual perception and scene reconstruction are critical for autonomous robots and intelligent transportation, yet real-world deployments often generate long, redundant image sequences that hinder downstream processing. This report investigates BCVS (budget-aware correspondence-driven view sampling), a pose-free view selection algorithm that offers 22+ FPS on a CPU, enabling online filtering for efficient 3D perception by mobile robots. Unlike existing approaches that rely on full structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines or camera pose estimation, BCVS employs a purely correspondence-based scoring strategy that prioritizes view novelty while maintaining sufficient overlap for geometric stability. Given a user-specified budget, BCVS iteratively selects the most distinct frames and suppresses near-duplicates, producing compact subsets that preserve connectivity and minimize reconstruction loss. Extensive experiments on benchmark show that BCVS outperforms CPU-friendly baselines at tight budgets and remains competitive as budgets scale. Field trials with large aerial and marine robotics data further validate its practicality and scalability: BCVS reduces redundancy up to 16% while sustaining robust SfM registration and high-quality 3D reconstructions.

Title: Compile-Gated Lean Proof Refactoring with Enterprise Agent Practices: A Model per Step under a US\$3 Cap, Followed by Programmatic Rewrite Rules
Author: Bobber Cheng
Text_Content: Our closed-track entry (Arena username Vexorium-Agent) scored 86.31 points on the final board (L = 77.07, H = 81.86, Z = 100) over the 60 final problems, against 33.33 for the reference proofs, 8th at the deadline (top: 92.57), for US\$166.33 at list prices with every call counted (per problem: mean US\$2.772, at most US\$2.874; US\$3 cap). Three practices carry the entry. First, each paid stage runs the model that measured best per dollar for it among the 9 we tested in our own harness: GPT-6.1 Sol the early sessions, GPT-6.1 Terra the later ones and the tail at 70% of Sol's cost per turn, and Gemini 4 Argon the review and repair; Sol also runs the style rewrite. Second, what our development and research runs learned ships as compiler-checked programmatic rewrite rules rather than prompt text (+0.93 points from rules fixed before the release; +0.26 and +0.30, in sample, from passes built or switched on after the release). Third, every call is recorded and reviewed before each change (all 9 board scores came within -0.063 to +0.015 points of our meter's prediction). The harness, gate and many of these rules also serve our open-track entry. We report the full bill and the spread of three runs.

Title: Efficient Online Submodular Maximization with Bandit Feedback
Author: Iasonas Nikolaou, Evimaria Terzi
Text_Content: We study online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback. On each round, the learner selects at most $k$ elements from a ground set of size $n$ and observes only the value of the selected set. We develop an efficient algorithm achieving $O\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right)$ expected $(1-1/e)$-regret over $T$ rounds. To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm with $\sqrt{T}$ dependence on the horizon for arbitrary monotone submodular functions in the bandit setting. Our approach uses randomized sampling and a carefully constructed potential to reduce online submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.

Title: Preserving Cultural Records: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Visual-Prior Routing Network for Ancient Book Image Restoration
Author: Shumin Fan, Tianyu Song, Hongming Chen, Xiaodong Zhou, Xiang Chen
Text_Content: Ancient books preserve invaluable cultural heritage, yet their images often suffer from complex degradations caused by long-term ageing, environmental exposure, and physical damage. Existing ancient book image restoration benchmarks are limited in scale and rely on simplified degradation simulations, which cannot fully represent real-world degradation patterns and restrict the generalization ability of restoration models. To address these challenges, we introduce AncBench, a large-scale synthetic paired benchmark containing 100K aligned clean-degraded image pairs. AncBench models realistic composite degradations through a comprehensive degradation pipeline that considers material ageing, paper texture variation, blur, staining, water-induced geometric distortion, and local occlusion. Furthermore, we propose AncRestore, a degradation-aware visual-prior routing network for ancient book image restoration. AncRestore first learns degradation representations from degraded images and then dynamically selects and integrates suitable visual priors according to different degradation characteristics. Guided by these degradation cues, a dynamic routing mechanism combines expert-wise and region-wise routing strategies adaptively adjusts the contribution of these priors across different regions, enabling the model to recover both global appearance and local text details. Extensive experiments show that AncRestore effectively suppresses composite degradations while preserving text structures and enhancing restoration quality against other methods, highlighting its application potential for intelligent ancient book image restoration in cultural heritage preservation.

Title: More particles or the pair? An exact test of how to improve mode-coupling theory
Author: Hu Cang
Text_Content: How a dense liquid arrests into a glass remains a central problem in physics. Mode-coupling theory (MCT), the leading microscopic theory of the glass transition, fails to reproduce mean-field caging. Two routes are proposed to repair it: tracking more-particle correlations, or enforcing repulsion within each colliding pair. Testing both on an exact benchmark liquid, we show that MCT lets touching spheres pass through each other at all orders: adding particles dilutes memory and worsens the transition, whereas restoring pair impenetrability recovers mean-field arrest and the cage size.

Title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
Author: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart
Text_Content: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

Title: Origin of devil's staircases and anomalous Arnold tongues of breathing solitons in optical Kerr resonators
Author: Tianhao Xian, Junsong Peng, Sonia Boscolo, Christophe Finot, Heping Zeng
Text_Content: Synchronization phenomena are ubiquitous across natural and engineered systems, and optical resonators supporting breathing solitons offer a natural platform for their investigation. In driven Kerr cavities described by the Lugiato-Lefever equation (LLE), breathing-soliton dynamics constitute a minimal setting in which such behavior can be systematically analyzed. Despite recent observations of intricate self-synchronization structures in mode-locked lasers-such as subharmonic entrainment, devil's staircases, and holes within Arnold tongues, i.e., regions of unsynchronized dynamics embedded within synchronized domains-their physical origin has remained elusive due to the complexity of laser dynamics. Here, we demonstrate that these phenomena emerge in the universal framework of the LLE. By reducing the problem to this model, we uncover the mechanism responsible for both the devil's staircase and the formation of holes within Arnold tongues. This provides a unified physical picture of synchronization in nonlinear systems, extending beyond optics and providing insight into analogous predictions and observations in fluids and other oscillatory media. In addition, we identify the regimes of high-order synchronization, enabling the generation of ultradense frequency combs, opening new directions for precision photonic applications.

Title: HiddenPathQA: A Benchmark for Knowledge Graph Question Answering When Questions Hide Their Paths
Author: Sumin Jo, Edward Choi
Text_Content: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) systems are typically evaluated on questions whose surface tokens lexically expose the gold KG path. Users, however, may ask questions without knowing the underlying schema: "Which condition could Andrew have due to family history?" compresses a 4-hop chain "Andrew --[father]--> parent --[father]--> grandparent --[medical condition]--> disease --[subclass of]--> hereditary disorder" into a single phrase (family history) that names none of those relations. We identify this collapse of path-question alignment as a blind spot in existing KGQA evaluation. Three major LLM-KG paradigms, hop-by-hop exploration, plan-then-retrieve, and similarity-based retrieval, implicitly rely on such lexical cues, an assumption rarely tested in practice. We make three contributions. (i) We introduce HiddenPathQA, a manually verified benchmark of 1,055 questions spanning 2-6 hops and multiple domains, constructed so that question wording does not reveal the gold path's relations. (ii) We propose Holistic Path Selection, which compares questions against candidate relation chains in the local subgraph as complete units, replacing irreversible per-hop relation scoring with globally informed chain-level reasoning. We develop two implementations, TieredHolistic and FlatHolistic. (iii) We conduct a pseudoword stress test that replaces entity names with meaningless placeholders to distinguish KG-grounded reasoning from entity-level memorization. Holistic Path Selection outperforms six strong KGQA baselines (ToG, PoG, FiDeLiS, R2-KG, KAPING, and KARPA) by 8.8-17.9 accuracy points across two LLM backbones and both original and pseudoword settings. Its advantage under pseudoword replacement shows that the gains cannot be explained by entity-level memorization alone.

Title: Proactive Dimension-Adaptive Denoising for Graph Collaborative Filtering via Representation Coherence
Author: Wenjun Li, Dong Zhao, Jiaying Shi, Juan Zhang, Zhaoming Pan, Zhimin Zhang
Text_Content: Implicit feedback in recommender systems contains noisy interactions (e.g., accidental clicks, impulse purchases) that propagate through user-item graphs and contaminate learned representations. Existing explicit denoising methods uniformly rely on training loss to estimate interaction reliability. However, loss is a fundamentally passive signal: it detects noise only after it has caused prediction errors, and it is heavily confounded by training stage, negative sampling, and hard positives. We propose Noise-aware Dimension Learning (NDL), a proactive dimension-adaptive denoising framework. NDL introduces Representation Coherence Detection (RCD), which evaluates the coherence between an interaction representation and the user's historical preference centroid in embedding space, providing an active noise signal independent of loss. RCD and the loss signal are fused via activity-aware weighting (active users rely more on coherence while cold-start users automatically fall back to loss), and the fused estimate drives an interaction-level dimension-adaptive mask that limits the effective representation capacity of unreliable interactions. A lightweight contrastive regularizer further improves embedding uniformity, stabilizing the geometry on which RCD discriminates. On three public benchmarks NDL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art denoising methods, lifting Recall@5 by +17.95% on Amazon-book, +12.33% on Yelp, and +5.63% on MovieLens-1M over the strongest baseline DAR; the core variant without contrastive learning already surpasses DAR on sparser datasets, confirming representation coherence as the primary driver of these gains. NDL is confined to the training loop and is serving-compatible with LightGCN-based production pipelines, adding no online latency or parameters at inference time. Code: https://github.com/GordonDongZHAO/NDL

Title: Ultrasound-Assisted Biometric Watermarking Against Face Video Deepfakes
Author: Guodong Liu, Lei Wang, Dongxu Liu, Qianran Qiao, Meng Li, Haipeng Dai, He Huang, Guihai Chen
Text_Content: Currently, artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) poses a severe threat to facial video deepfakes, and many AIGC companies employ video watermarking to mitigate unauthorized fake video usage, but its effectiveness is limited due to watermark tampering and private-model forgery. Additionally, some schemes actively add watermarks to user videos. However, current approaches focus primarily on the quality of watermark embedding in offline scenarios, and no existing work offers a solution for protecting human facial videos in real-time online applications. To fill this gap, we propose, to the best of our knowledge, a novel biometric video watermarking method, UltraGuard, for the first time. It uses the smartphone's built-in speaker and microphone to emit ultrasonic signals and capture biometric features, which are then fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into videos in real time, enabling dynamic, content-aware watermarking throughout transmission and propagation. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that UltraGuard can effectively defend against malicious attacks such as forgery and editing, both at the source and during propagation, proving the system's efficacy. In the future, it can be deployed on users' mobile devices to provide real-time protection for users' facial videos, thereby preventing security and privacy breaches caused by various malicious attacks.

Title: PAIR: Proprioception-Aligned Image-Ray Representations for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
Author: Sung-Wook Lee, Xuhui Kang, Dylan Losey, Yen-Ling Kuo
Text_Content: While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Visuomotor policies rely heavily on visual inputs, yet images provide an inherently ambiguous signal under viewpoint change: similar scenes may appear markedly different across viewpoints, while distinct states may share certain visual overlaps. A policy must therefore infer not only the task-relevant state, but also how it is visually projected under a particular camera configuration. This entanglement of viewpoint-dependent appearance and task-relevant state can make learning inefficient and limit generalization to unseen viewpoints. Recent work has begun to address this challenge through camera-ray conditioning and representation learning using geometric cues to induce invariance. However, providing camera information as additional context does not by itself ground visual representations in how the task scene is visually projected, while geometric alignment without camera context can introduce spurious correspondences by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection. We propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework that aligns joint image-ray representations using robot proprioception. PAIR encourages observations with similar robot states to remain close in representation space across viewpoints, providing a structured grounding signal for learning viewpoint-robust features. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train Diffusion Policy (DP) or post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. In simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks with camera variation, PAIR consistently outperforms the behavior cloning baseline without ray conditioning by 12.7% and 26.7% points, respectively, demonstrating stronger generalization to unseen viewpoints. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io.

Title: Wide Field 3D Color Topography for Steep-slope Structures
Author: Yuchen Lin, Mengrui Wang, Fan Li, Jingxiang Zhang, Manming Shu, Jiajing Yan, Chang Liu, Tianyu Zhao, Yansheng Liang, Ming Lei
Text_Content: Three-dimensional (3D) topography measurement is essential for industrial inspection and scientific research. However, existing techniques are limited by an inherent trade-off between resolution, speed, color imaging capability and the ability to measure large-angle surfaces. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method that integrates ring light illumination based wide-field 3D imaging with an iterative shape-from-focus (SFF) algorithm. The system employs coaxial epi-illumination combined with ring light illumination to simultaneously acquire information from flat regions and steep slopes. The proposed iterative SFF algorithm achieves high-resolution 3D topography measurement. Full-color 3D reconstructions of electronic chips and PCBs demonstrate that the proposed method enables fast scanning and sub-micrometer resolution and significantly extending the measurable inclination range for large-angle structures. This method fills a critical gap in existing technology for fast, natural-color, 3D imaging and measurement of samples with steep topographies.

Title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
Author: Yiqun T. Chen, Jan Matthias, Jianing Yao, Hongyu Eric Zhao, Stephanie C. Hicks
Text_Content: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

Title: ChemInsight: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating and Diagnosing Chemistry Understanding and Reasoning in Large Language Models
Author: Changyu Hu, Yiming Zou, Xin Tang, Yiru Pan, Zicheng Huang, Deng Zhao, Qing Cui, Zhenduo Zhang, Wang Ren, Xiao Li
Text_Content: We introduce ChemInsight, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on chemistry tasks that require multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding. We propose a two-dimensional scoring system (scope and depth) to assess both task coverage and reasoning completeness. ChemInsight consists of 203 challenging chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles, which support the two-dimensional scoring evaluation scheme. We evaluate ten representative LLMs using ChemInsight and observe consistently low performance across models, with scope scores below 30% and depth scores below 11%, substantially lower than human expert performance. We then proceed to ask (1) What factor limits the advancement of current LLMs in chemistry? (2) To what extent are statistically driven language-model training methods effective at modeling chemistry symbolic language such as SMILES? And (3) Can LLM performance in chemistry be improved through intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora?

Title: Benchmarking CNNs, Vision Transformers, and Foundation Models for Explainable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: Calibration, Decision Analysis, and External Validation
Author: Akwasi Asare
Text_Content: Deep learning models for brain tumor MRI classification are usually compared by accuracy alone, on public datasets whose independence is rarely checked. We benchmarked six architectures: two convolutional networks (EfficientNetV2-M and ConvNeXt-V2-Tiny), two vision transformers (Swin-V2-S and ViT-L/16), and two foundation models (DINOv2-L and MedSigLIP-448), for four-class classification of 7,216 public MRI images. We assessed accuracy, calibration, explainability, ensembles, and decision curves, with every fitted quantity estimated on validation data only. Pixel-verified duplicate screening showed that 36% of the test images had a near-duplicate in the training data. Test accuracy ranged from 94.5% to 95.6%, with no pairwise difference after Holm correction, and fell to 90.3% to 91.7% on the 773 test images free of duplicates and shared patients. Ensembles did not outperform the best single model. Attribution maps passed a model-randomization test but localized expert-annotated tumors poorly. On 1,675 external BDNeuro-MRI images that did not duplicate the training data, accuracy ranged from 77.6% (MedSigLIP-448) to 95.0% (ViT-L/16), and 12 of 15 pairwise differences were significant. Internal accuracy on this public collection therefore did not distinguish the architectures, whereas the duplicate-filtered external test did.

Title: APO2CS: Advantage-Aware Preference Optimization for Two-Level Constructive Search in Combinatorial Optimization
Author: Kaixi Yang, Linbo Qiao, Wei Shang, Yanqi Shi, Dongsheng Li
Text_Content: Preference optimization has emerged as a promising alternative to reward-based training for neural combinatorial optimization. However, existing methods typically rely on binary pairwise labels, which discard the magnitude of solution-quality differences and provide supervision only at the complete-solution level. We propose Advantage-aware Preference Optimization for Two-level Constructive Search (APO2CS), a preference-based training objective for constructive neural solvers that integrates both macro-level and micro-level supervision. At the macro level, APO2CS enriches pairwise preferences with an advantage term derived from objective-value differences. At the micro level, it compares partial trajectories, thereby providing denser supervision throughout the sequential construction process. The resulting objective can be used either to train a policy from scratch or to fine-tune a pretrained one. Experimental results show that APO2CS improves the expressiveness and search capability of preference learning for combinatorial optimization, while demonstrating strong effectiveness and adaptability across multiple combinatorial optimization tasks.

Title: FMA-Net: Flexible Modality Adaptation for Robust Multimodal Face Presentation Attack Detection
Author: Yuhao Gao, Yichen Shi, Zitong Yu, Hongyang Wang, Hongrui Li, Ruixin Zhang, Shouhong Ding, Jun Feng
Text_Content: Multimodal face presentation attack detection (fPAD) improves robustness using complementary RGB, depth, and infrared (IR) cues, but deployment remains challenging when modalities are unavailable or incomplete. Existing flexible-modality methods mainly use zero-filling or modality omission, potentially discarding cross-modal information and introducing modality-dependent bias. We propose the Flexible Modality Adaptation Network (FMA-Net), a unified framework that compensates for missing modalities through instruction-guided latent-space translation. The Face Modality Instruct Translator (FMIT) estimates target modality observations from RGB inputs, while context-aware category enhancement uses learnable text prompts as modality-invariant semantic anchors. A Facial Feature Adapter (F2A) integrates global facial structure and local spoof-relevant cues to enhance discriminative representations. Synthetic-to-Real Face Domain Alignment (SR-FDA) reduces feature discrepancies between translated and real modalities, with benefits depending on the missing-modality pattern and data domain. Experiments on WMCA and PADISI-Face validate the framework. On WMCA with a 70% modality missing ratio, FMA-Net achieves a mean ACER of 3.22% across four intra-domain missing-modality protocols, compared with 4.24% for the strongest baseline by the same criterion. When both depth and IR are entirely unavailable, it achieves 5.23% ACER, compared with 5.99% for the best competing result. Cross-domain experiments also reveal limitations of synthetic-to-real alignment under dataset shifts. These results support FMA-Net as a practical approach to fPAD with flexible and incomplete modalities.

Title: HolidayFactory 1.0: Simulating, Generating, and Evaluating Industrial Robot Tasks
Author: Holiday Robotics, :, Jeongmin Lee, Taehyeon Kim, Dohyun Jang, Minji Lee, Seonghun Oh, Dongwoo Park, Geonhyup Lee, Jaehyung Kim, Jaemin Yoon, Jinseop Bok, Jungwoo Kim, Minseok Yang, Philsik Chang, Soomin Lee
Text_Content: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.

Title: Payoff-Aware Prediction of Population Game Dynamics
Author: Kang Wang, Xiao Wang, Bo Li, Renzhe Xu
Text_Content: Population game dynamics describe how aggregate behavior evolves in response to payoff signals. In many applications, the payoff function may change, and the goal is to predict the population trajectory induced by a new payoff design before trajectory data under that design are available. We study this problem as $\textbf{payoff-aware prediction of population game dynamics}$. Standard dynamics learning methods fit the motion observed under training payoffs, but do not separate the payoff-dependent incentive from the payoff-independent response structure needed for prediction under new payoffs. Building on the existing framework of Riemannian game dynamics, we propose PA-RmD, a payoff-aware learning method that keeps payoff information explicit and learns the payoff-independent response structure from data. Theoretically, we show that the learned model preserves fixed-payoff Nash equilibria and derive finite-time one-step prediction bounds under shared-response and payoff-coverage conditions. Empirically, we evaluate PA-RmD on synthetic zero-sum and potential games, as well as a YouTube Trending multi-country dataset, showing that our method performs well under changing payoff designs.

Title: On the robustness of locally D-optimal designs under parameter uncertainty in single-factor generalized linear models
Author: Osama Idais
Text_Content: Local and Bayesian approaches to optimal experimental design specify information about the regression parameters through a nominal value and a prior distribution, respectively. A practical question is whether accounting for parameter uncertainty justifies replacing a locally optimal design. We investigate when locally D-optimal designs remain Bayesian D-optimal in single-factor Poisson, gamma and logistic regression on the unit interval. Analytical arguments and numerical comparisons under normal and uniform slope priors examine how prior form and dispersion affect the optimal support and the Bayesian D-efficiency of retaining a local design.

Title: Three-dimensional polarization of thermal fields at arbitrary distances from thin-film emitters
Author: Xiaohong Zhang, Wenshan Cai, Zhuomin Zhang
Text_Content: Recent advances have shown that thermal radiation can exhibit strong polarization in both the near and far fields. However, most existing studies focus on paraxial far-field emission, where polarization can be described using conventional two-dimensional (2D) Stokes parameters. Non-paraxial thermal radiation, with three nonzero vector components, requires a fully three-dimensional (3D) polarization description. This work develops a generalized theoretical method for analyzing thermal-radiation polarization at arbitrary distances from an emitter. Fluctuation-dissipation theory is employed to determine the $3\times3$ coherence matrix of the thermally emitted electromagnetic field, from which generalized 3D Stokes parameters are obtained. This method is applied to planar slabs composed of isotropic, anisotropic, and nonreciprocal materials. The results reveal distinct polarization behavior across the near- and far-field regimes. Near-field polarization is strongly influenced by evanescent waves and polariton dispersion, whereas far-field polarization is primarily governed by polarization-dependent radiative properties, including differences between transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) emission. Slab thickness further modifies polarization by controlling supported modes and interference effects. In addition, circular polarization, which vanishes in reciprocal slabs, is observed in n-type doped InAs under an external magnetic field that breaks reciprocity. This work provides a unified framework for characterizing the polarization of thermal electromagnetic fields from the extreme near field to the far field.

Title: CABrain: A Correlation-Aware Brain Foundation Model for EEG Decoding
Author: SuGil Choi, Mooseop Kim, Chi Yoon Jeong
Text_Content: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models have emerged as promising paradigms for decoding brain activity through large-scale self-supervised pretraining. Notably, most existing approaches employ masked patch reconstruction, in which randomly selected EEG patches are masked and recovered by the network. However, purely random masking may limit representation learning as informative patches from highly correlated channels often remain unmasked, causing the network to underutilize weakly correlated channels or serial dependencies. Furthermore, because these models are typically based on transformer architectures, their performance is influenced by the choice of positional encoding. Although positional encoding has been extensively explored in natural language processing and computer vision, few studies have adapted it to the unique characteristics of EEG signals. To address these limitations, this study introduces a conditional positional encoding method based on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to explicitly model inter-channel correlations, along with an adaptive masking strategy that enhances representation learning by modulating the difficulty of masked patch reconstruction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate graph-based representations into conditional positional encoding and introduce adaptive masking within EEG foundation model pretraining. Experimental results on ten benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed GCN-based positional encoding and adaptive masking strategies, both individually and in combination, achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance, highlighting their effectiveness in EEG foundation modeling.

Title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
Author: Yong Hwi Song, Keon Myung Lee
Text_Content: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.

Title: Towards Trustworthy Mobile Speech Interaction: Ensuring Voice Authenticity and Transmission Integrity
Author: Guodong Liu, Lei Wang, Dongxu Liu, Qianran Qiao, Haipeng Dai, He Huang, Guihai Chen
Text_Content: The rapid progress of generative speech models has made high-fidelity voice cloning and editing cheap, fast, and widely accessible, weakening the security of voiceprint-based authentication in mobile speech interactions. Existing speech watermarking techniques focus on offline protection or watermarking synthetic speech, and thus cannot verify whether a live utterance originates from the genuine speaker at capture time. We present \textit{MoBiMark}, a real-time \textbf{mo}bile \textbf{bi}ologic speech water\textbf{mark}ing system that binds ultrasonic articulatory signatures to speech content and embeds a dynamic watermark during capture. MoBiMark emits a multi-frequency ultrasonic probe on commodity smartphones, extracts echo features from the vocal tract, and fuses them with a content-dependent speech embedding to produce a dual-layer dynamic watermark combining a persistent user identifier (UID) and a per-utterance speech identifier (SID), enabling both source authentication and propagation-time tamper detection. A jointly trained embedder and detector injects the watermark while preserving perceptual quality, and system-level optimization with INT8 quantization enables lightweight on-device deployment. Evaluated on 50 users across four smartphone models, MoBiMark achieves an average 99.79% accuracy in source and propagation attacks, with negligible impact on speech quality and intelligibility.

Title: Wireless AI Networks: Co-Adapting Communication Resources and Distributed Intelligence
Author: Ziqiang Ye, Yue Xiao, Qiyan Zhan, Yulan Gao, Xianfu Lei, Vladimir Poulkov
Text_Content: Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on wireless networks, where communication and computing resources shape how AI tasks are configured and executed. However, resource availability alone does not determine how effectively these tasks can be supported, since different information selections and transmission strategies may yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints. To address this challenge, this article presents Wireless AI Networks as a unified design perspective for bidirectional adaptation between wireless communication and distributed intelligence. Specifically, an AI-executable resource budget characterizes candidate AI configurations, while task-level information value guides their selection and wireless resource allocation. Building on these principles, a wireless-AI co-adaptation framework coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback. Two complementary experiments illustrate this perspective: update selection and statistical correction improve federated learning under identical model-update payload budgets, while sensitivity-aware power allocation reduces model accuracy degradation under the same average transmit-power constraint. Together, these results highlight the importance of coordinating resource feasibility and task-level information value in distributed AI execution.

Title: ARMOR: Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise-Robust RAG Reasoning
Author: Yan Wang, Yuxin Zhang, Shenyu Zhang, Yongrui Chen, Sheng Bi, Guilin Qi
Text_Content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.

Title: Towards Rotation-Only Imaging Geometry: Multi-View Pose Estimation
Author: Xinrui Li, Qi Cai, Yuanxin Wu
Text_Content: Global structure-from-motion (SfM) commonly refines relative poses on individual image pairs and then estimates global rotations by rotation averaging. Pairwise refinement does not explicitly combine feature-level constraints with multi-view consistency during rotation initialization. We introduce Global Rotations from Aggregated Matches (GRAM), which estimates global rotations directly from initial relative rotations and inlier matches by minimizing edge-wise rotation-only algebraic residuals. GRAM replaces two-view relative-pose optimization and rotation averaging with a single stage. We further extend rotation- only imaging geometry to multiple views and develop Multi-view Optimization with Rotation-only Reprojection Error (MORE) for nonlinear global rotation refinement. Analytical Rotation-guided Translation (ART) derives locally scaled triplet translations from Linear Global Translation (LiGT) constraints and recovers global translations using weighted least squares. Synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and efficiency of the proposed methods.

Title: LangDepth: Vision-Language Scene Priors for Semantic Binning and Cross-Domain Monocular Depth Estimation
Author: Reyhaneh Ahani Manghotay, Jie Liang
Text_Content: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.

Title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection
Author: Ping Zhao, Qianya Sun, Long Feng
Text_Content: Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. Heavy-tailed returns and dependence across funds complicate this task. We propose a robust selection procedure based on radially weighted alpha estimation in linear factor pricing models. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. For radial weights fixed conditional on the factor design, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control under elliptically symmetric errors and show that the proportion of sufficiently strong positive-alpha funds selected tends to one. The theory accommodates comparable cross-sectional and time-series dimensions and nonvanishing alphas. We also develop a smoothed implementation and assess its finite-sample properties. Simulations show higher true discovery proportions than least-squares and spatial-sign methods under heavy-tailed distributions and improved numerical stability from smoothing. An application to U.S. equity mutual funds examines the subsequent performance of portfolios formed from the selected funds.

Title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
Author: Payman Behnam, Debopam Sanyal, Pranav Ponnusamy, Kusum Meda Ravi, Pranav Sastry, Mani Chandana Bandaru, Alind Khare, Myungjin Lee, Alexey Tumanov
Text_Content: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.

Title: Calibrated Alarm Thresholds for Compact Fire and Smoke Detectors
Author: Vikas Sandireddy
Text_Content: Compact object detectors such as YOLOv8n are a common choice for camera-based fire and smoke detection on low-power devices. These detectors are usually evaluated with box-level metrics such as mean average precision, and their outputs are turned into decisions with a fixed confidence threshold such as 0.25 or 0.5. A fire monitoring system, however, makes one decision per image: raise an alarm or not. In this paper we evaluate two publicly available compact detectors on the D-Fire test set at the image level. We compare three simple rules for turning box detections into one alarm score per image, and we use a split conformal procedure to choose the alarm threshold from held-out images so that the expected fraction of missed fire and smoke images stays below a chosen target. We find that the same fixed threshold leads to very different miss rates for the two detectors, 17.3 and 8.4 percent at a threshold of 0.5, while the calibrated threshold meets miss-rate targets of 10, 5 and 1 percent for both detectors and all three rules. At a 5 percent target, the false alarm rate on images without fire or smoke stays between 1.2 and 3.0 percent. We also find that smoke-only images stay below the target even when the overall target is met, and we describe the main failure cases.

Title: Causal Resolution of Undefined Answers in Datalog with Negation
Author: Ratan Bahadur Thapa
Text_Content: Unstratified negation may leave the answer to a Boolean Datalog query undefined under the well-founded semantics. We study database causality in this setting by asking which fact insertions and deletions realize a prescribed transition and which other changes preserve the observed query answer while making a designated fact pivotal. Such a set of changes to other facts is a contingency for the designated fact and the prescribed transition. Our game representation assigns one shared move to each mutable fact and preserves query values and intervention distances. Pairing source and target certificates characterizes all minimum contingencies for the six transitions among true, false, and undefined. When inserting or deleting a move resolves a draw, a directed tree traces the newly winning and losing positions along alternating paths to the source of that move. For the fixed one-rule win--move program, deciding whether a contingency of size at most $k$ exists is $\mathrm{NP}$-complete for each transition, even on bounded-degree graphs. Computing the minimum size is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}[\log]}$-complete, and counting minimum contingencies is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. When only one of true and false is reachable, the prime implicants of undefinedness satisfied at the observation cover every undefined state, and their supports induce nonempty subtrees of a common tree, we compute a minimum resolving intervention in polynomial time from the game instance. From the explicit tree and these implicants, we construct an equally large family of disjoint supports, certifying optimality.

Title: Graph-Sparse Distributed Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning vianEdge-Consensus ADMM
Author: Josep Borras-Borras, Pablo Segovia, Carlos Ocampo-Martinez
Text_Content: This paper presents a distributed model predictive control (MPC) architecture for collision-avoiding motion planning of planar robots with double-integrator dynamics. To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. Execution is selectively supervised by a centralized high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) QP when the distributed candidate does not satisfy the direct-execution conditions. Evaluated in C++ simulations involving 8, 16, and 32 robots, the proposed architecture achieves collision-free execution and substantially improves computational scalability while maintaining task-level performance comparable to a centralized complete-graph baseline.

Title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
Author: Luis Adrián Lizama-Pérez, José Mauricio López-Romero
Text_Content: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.

Title: SpinSCI: Mask-Conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer for Video Snapshot Compressive Imaging
Author: Seungki Hong, Zhishuai Zhang, Taekwang Jang
Text_Content: Video snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) recovers multiple frames from one spatiotemporally coded measurement. This paper proposes SpinSCI, a mask-conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer whose Mask-Conditioned Ising Refinement Block (MC-IRB) combines attention logits and sensing information to form signed spin couplings. Finite mean-field updates gate residual feature refinement. Physics-guided initialization and final data consistency incorporate the measurement model. Compared with HiSViT$_9$, SpinSCI achieves average PSNR gains of 0.51 dB, 0.23 dB, and 0.04 dB on small-scale gray, mid-scale color, and large-scale color benchmarks, respectively, with 16.9% fewer parameters, 21.0-21.6% fewer FLOPs, 17.1-49.9% lower latency, and 62.3-63.3% lower peak memory. Relative to DU-9stg, average PSNR differs by at most 0.13 dB across these benchmarks, with 28.2-28.7% fewer FLOPs, 64.6-71.7% lower inference latency, and 30.1-35.0% lower peak memory. Qualitative comparisons on the real benchmark further show recovery of fine details and textures. Code and reference checkpoints are available at https://github.com/skethz/SpinSCI.

Title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
Author: Khurram Khalil, Khaza Anuarul Hoque
Text_Content: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $σ_i \propto i^{-α}$ with $0 < α\leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.

Title: GeoPilot: Diagnosis-Guided Interventions and Geometric Evaluation for Aerial Reconstruction
Author: Pengyu Yin, Jie Pan, Junxiang Tan, Mengqi Fu, Kun Cheng, Yifan Liu
Text_Content: When a mesh reconstructed from aerial remote-sensing imagery disagrees with reference geometry, deciding what to change requires a diagnosis of the reconstruction process. We present GeoPilot, a workflow that turns diagnostics and prior observations into executable program or camera-configuration interventions. A large language model proposes the change, numerical tools reconstruct the mesh, and an external evaluator measures its geometry under a stated coordinate and reference protocol. The main case tests a shared-intrinsics hypothesis proposed before the comparison. On 224 Metashape-raster development images, shared intrinsics improved all six native-coordinate measures and reduced mean surface-to-reference distance by 7.04%. Reference-assisted alignment fitted and evaluated on separate within-scene checkerboard samples reversed the mean-distance ranking, limiting that gain to native-frame delivery. A separate matched comparison on publisher-undistorted images favored fixed published cameras on all six measures, reducing mean distance by 12.11%; the cameras retain upstream image and laser-scanning adjustment information. With one reconstruction per configuration, these comparisons provide conditional evidence for camera handling. Three end-to-end runs each delivered a mesh and six-metric evaluation from all 327 images of a second development scene.

Title: Instance-preserving graded semantic reporting for surgical action triplets
Author: Yanchong Xue, Wanting Zhang, Lingtao Yu, Guochao Zhang
Text_Content: Complete-or-reject reporting of surgical action triplets can discard a correctly identified instrument and action when the target is uncertain. We introduce instance-preserving graded semantic reporting, which separates instance selection from the choice of semantic detail. Each selected instance retains its predicted mask and labels while hierarchical correctness scores guide instrument (I), instrument-verb (IV), or complete instrument-verb-target (IVT) reporting. The utility-increment rule DELTA weighs the expected gain from finer reporting against its error cost. We compare three decision rules on 5,641 test frames from eight surgical videos using fixed predictions and scores. At the 10% development calibration target, DELTA retains correct partial reports for 80.0% of candidates rejected by a matched complete-or-reject baseline (5,329/6,662). Adding IV increases source-normalized weighted correct-report yield by 19.13 to 23.13 per 100 frames across all three rules relative to separately recalibrated I/IVT controls. Weighted reporting risk changes by -0.77 to +1.01 percentage points, with complete correct-triplet counts unchanged or reduced. Graded reporting makes partial surgical predictions available as localized descriptions, with an explicit trade-off between report utility and completeness.

Title: Bounds and Constructions for Optimal Wide-Gap Frequency Hopping Sequences
Author: Jiwen Zhang, Haitao Cao
Text_Content: In a frequency-hopping (FH) system, to reduce interference to the received signal, each user's frequency hopping sequence (FHS) shall have wide-gap property. In this paper, we update the upper bounds on the minimum gaps of optimal uniform wide-gap frequency hopping sequences (WGFHS) with parameters $(v,s,λ;e)$ where $v=ks, k\ge 3, λ=k$ and $s\ge k(k-1)+1$ is odd. We completely prove the existence of such WGFHSs for $k\le 3$.

Title: Reproducible quantum clustering for single-cell transcriptome atlases
Author: Henry Han
Text_Content: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and can yield inconsistent clusters across random seeds. We introduce KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework for reproducible whole-transcriptome clustering. KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, enabling exact feature evaluation on classical hardware and direct checks on a quantum processor. Theoretically, we prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally. Practically, while retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, KQE-2 delivered identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes, the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79. KQE-2 scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, outperforming the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases (and within the best method's run-to-run range on two), and leads on six even under standard downstream clustering.

Title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
Author: Jiajun Liang, Linxuan Wang, Guang Lin, Qifan Song
Text_Content: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/ε^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $ε^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/ε^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC

Title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle
Author: Fei Jiang, Lei Yang
Text_Content: Measurement systems generate uncertain information that downstream manufacturing decisions often consume as if fixed. This structured integrative review examines how measurement error, uncertainty, GR\&R estimates, calibration evidence, and drift information are handed off into capability inference, retrospective Phase I reference estimation, prospective Phase II monitoring, operational action, and requalification. Studies are compared by the upstream uncertain object, whether it is known, calibrated, or estimated, its propagation mechanism, the downstream decision, and the validation boundary. The synthesis distinguishes recorded production data from latent-process targets: measurement-system information calibrates limits, uncertainty statements, replication, guard bands, or losses, but does not reveal the realized random error in an individual record. Within the retained literature, measurement-to-capability and measurement-to-monitoring mechanisms are more extensively represented by model-based studies, whereas prospective evidence is thinner where statistical results must support source attribution, cost-sensitive action, and requalification. A decision-handoff spine separates measurement generation, statistical inference, and operational validation so that capability, stability, attribution, and intervention effectiveness are not conflated. The review is integrative rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is an auditable measurement-science framework that preserves provenance, information status, validity conditions, and downstream use while identifying claims that are model-supported, conditionally calibrated, or not yet operationally validated.

Title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
Author: Pedro Malo
Text_Content: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

Title: Creative Priming: Decoupling Process from Product to Escape the Creative Paradox
Author: Alon Albalak, Sebastian Gabriel, David B. D'Ambrosio, Joel Lehman, Kenneth O. Stanley
Text_Content: Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response.

Title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
Author: Georgii Kliukovkin
Text_Content: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes and evicts 26 bystander pods, because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single io.MultiWriter. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.

Title: Dense Flow from Adaptive Correspondence
