Text_Content: General-purpose state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems fail systematically for speakers with moderate to severe speech disabilities. This paper describes the design, implementation, and evaluation of a customized ASR system built for the first author, a researcher with cerebral palsy and dysarthria. We fine-tuned OpenAI's Whisper medium and large-v3 models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on audio samples recorded from the first author's own speech on consumer-grade hardware. On a held-out test set of 100 previously unseen utterances, the corresponding transcriptions resulted in a Word Error Rate drop from 49% to 17% for medium and from 30% to 12% for large-v3, while the Character Error Rate fell from 26% to 7% for medium and from 16% to 5% for large-v3, indicating that the residual errors are minor phonemic substitutions. Based on these models, the first author developed AVoz, a mobile application that acts as a real-time interpreter, converting his speech into synthesized voice for the listener. All processing is performed locally, ensuring that no audio data leaves the user's machine. We argue that the methodology is replicable. Moreover, we publish the full LoRA configuration, the implementation, and a step-by-step recording and training protocol, so that other people with speech disabilities, or their family members and caregivers, can build their own systems with a few hours of labeled audio data and a couple of days of GPU time.

Title: Conditional Diffusion-Based Proxy Representation Recovery for BCVA Prediction with Missing SLO Modality
Author: Chuyi He, Hua Zou, Fei Luo, Zixian Yang
Text_Content: Preoperative prediction of postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) can support prognosis assessment and individualized decision-making in cataract surgery. Multimodal learning can integrate preoperative optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) images, and clinical text to characterize patient status. However, SLO images are often missing in real-world clinical data due to acquisition or data-management issues, resulting in incomplete multimodal inputs. To address this problem, this paper proposes a conditional diffusion-based method for SLO proxy representation recovery and fusion prediction. Instead of reconstructing raw SLO images, the proposed method formulates SLO missingness as proxy representation recovery in the latent feature space. Specifically, OCT image features and clinical text features are first fused to construct an OCT-text conditional representation, which guides the reverse denoising process of the diffusion model to estimate sample-specific SLO proxy representations. The recovered SLO proxy representation is then used as a substitute for the unavailable SLO modality and incorporated into the downstream multimodal fusion prediction network for postoperative BCVA prediction. Experiments were conducted on 2,141 preoperative multimodal cataract samples, with an SLO missing rate of 58.80%. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 0.9714 under the criterion of an absolute prediction error within 0.1 LogMAR and a mean absolute error of 0.0423, outperforming representative postoperative visual acuity prediction and missing-modality learning methods. These results indicate that representation-level proxy recovery can alleviate the impact of SLO modality missingness on postoperative BCVA prediction.

Title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
Author: Po-Ming Law, Jianheng Ouyang, Nguyen-Truong Thinh, Weizhi Li, Arpit Narechania
Text_Content: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

Title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
Author: Chung-I Huang, Wen-Yi Chang
Text_Content: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

Title: Stanley Deser 19th March 1931 - 21st April 2023
Author: M. J. Duff, K. S. Stelle
Text_Content: Stanley Deser was Ancell Professor Emeritus at Brandeis University and Visiting Professor at the California Institute of Technology. He was a world-renowned theoretical physicist whose accomplishments include the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formulation of general relativity, supergravity with Zumino, the dynamics of flat space with Jackiw and 't Hooft and many other contributions to the quantum theory of gravity. In the 1980s he was instrumental in securing National Science Foundation approval of the LIGO gravitational wave experiment against much opposition. He was awarded the Einstein Medal in 2015 for important contributions to general relativity, in particular the development of the ADM formalism. Other awards include: The Dannie Heineman Prize 1994; Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences 1994; Honorary Member of the Torino Academy of Sciences 2001; Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1979, Fellow of the American Institute of Physics.

Title: Beyond Similarity Entropy: A Rank-Guided Data-Free Quantization Framework for Vision Transformers
Author: Runqing Jiang, Ye Zhang, Pengpeng Yu, Zhuo Song, Changjun Li, Longguang Wang, Yulan Guo
Text_Content: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at https://github.com/Runqing-forMost/rankq-vit.git

Title: ZeroPoint: Lightweight Energy-Based Decision Model
Author: Javier Marín
Text_Content: Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to every joint value of the observed and predicted variables. In decision models, the prediction is chosen from a finite list of options provided with each input. Inference then reduces to comparing the energies of the options, and training lowers the energy of the correct option relative to the others. A complete decision must also account for the possibility that no option is acceptable. However, the energies learned by a standard EBM define only relative compatibility: adding the same input-dependent quantity to all energies leaves the predictions, the Gibbs distribution, and the usual training losses unchanged. The model therefore has no learned reference level against which to decide whether any option fits. We propose ZeroPoint, an EBM that makes the empty answer a state of the model with energy zero for every input. This fixed state provides an explicit reference for the energies of all listed options, whose non-negative depths measure their compatibility with the input relative to the empty answer. The options and the empty answer share one distribution, in which an option at zero depth receives no probability. The decision to select an option or to abstain is thus part of ordinary inference, trained with the negative log-likelihood loss, rather than a separate rejection rule. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input together with all the options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax, while leaving the choice among options unchanged.

Title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
Author: Devanshu Jha, Gaurav Kumar, Agniva Chowdhury, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Aditya Desai
Text_Content: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.

Title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
Author: Minseo Yoon, Minseong Bae, Sojin Lee, Hyunwoo J. Kim
Text_Content: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

Title: Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
Author: Yuxuan Hou, Di Yu, Linshan Jiang, Jin Zhang
Text_Content: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.

Title: ReGKG-2025: A GKG-Compatible Reconstruction of the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph for the Missing Period of 14 June to 2 July 2025
Author: Nikita A. Klimin
Text_Content: The June 2025 outage in the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG), interrupting article-level news metadata used in downstream research. ReGKG-2025 is an archive-derived sample of 281,620 reconstructed article records covering all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches. Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalized, non-English bodies were translated, and flagged records were manually reviewed. Eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout. The versioned package includes record-level provenance, archive replay and WARC locators, source summaries, source-by-day calibration weights, and the complete manual decision journal. The sample reaches about 14% of modeled native volume and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records; field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). The dataset supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates; its tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG, and it does not support exhaustive counts. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964265.

Title: Flash evaporation Riemann Problem: Thermodynamic Relaxation and Oscillation-Free Real Fluid Finite Volume Method
Author: Haotong Bai, Ping Yi, Yixin Yang, Guoyan Zhao, Wenjia Xie, Mingbo Sun
Text_Content: The Flash evaporation Riemann problem (FeRP) formulated the wave structures of flash evaporation in the vapor-liquid homogeneous equilibrium limit. However, physical flash evaporation involves finite-rate interphase heat and mass transfer, inducing the wave structure to deviate from the equilibrium state. To solve such a non-equilibrium Riemann problem, this paper first derives the governing equation of mechanical equilibrium evolution in a relaxation system, based on which an oscillation-free Homogeneous Relaxation Real Fluid (HRRF) finite volume method is developed. In addition to the Euler equations with mass relaxation, the HRRF method evolves advection equations for the internal energy--pressure affine parameters and the vapor volume fraction, in order to eliminate numerical pressure oscillations inherent in conservative methods while preserving phase-transition-induced pressure changes, and consistently degenerate into a completely pressure-equilibrium method in supercritical flows. The HRRF method is then employed to comprehensively evaluate how thermodynamic relaxation affects the FeRP solution. Results indicate that the non-classical expansion shock of the FeRP loses its traveling-wave characteristics with increasing relaxation time, continuously degenerating into a self-similar rarefaction wave. Compared with the equilibrium limit, an increased mass transfer relaxation time smooths the expansion branch of the RP solution, lowers the intermediate pressure and velocity, and induces a pseudo-splitting of the rarefaction wave as well as a pseudo-advance of the phase transition onset. Meanwhile, the heat transfer relaxation time primarily dictates the temperature difference in the vapor-liquid mixture, thereby modulating the liquid superheat and in turn influencing the mass transfer rate.

Title: Shape-Adaptive Subspace-Constrained Quadratic Matrix Factorization
Author: Zheng Zhai, Zhuan Liang, Sujun Guo
Text_Content: Quadratic manifold fitting provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear low-dimensional structures embedded in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing methods typically employ prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, limiting their adaptability to varying noise characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose an alternating maximum likelihood estimation method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization, termed AMLE-SQMF, which jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the underlying noise distribution. Specifically, we model the residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD), whose shape parameter controls the tail behavior and determines the associated fitting loss. By exploiting the closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter, we eliminate the scale variable and derive a profile negative log-likelihood. Based on this formulation, we develop an alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively updates the manifold parameters and estimates the noise shape parameter. This enables adaptive loss selection within a unified likelihood-based framework, without requiring prior specification of the noise characteristics. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMLE-SQMF in quadratic manifold fitting and its robustness to diverse noise distributions.

Title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
Author: Carlo Berzuini, Luisa Bernardinelli
Text_Content: A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them. METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy. SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them. CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.

Title: SkillCODER: Towards Auditing and Attribution of Copyright Infringement in LLM Agent Skills
Author: Enhao Huang, Chunshu Xia, Yiming Li, Yuchen Yang, Bingrun Yang, Zhan Qin, Dacheng Tao, Kui Ren
Text_Content: Agent skills package reusable workflows and task-specific procedures into deployable natural-language artifacts for LLM agents. Their scale and readability make them valuable but vulnerable to unauthorized redistribution and repackaging. Existing prompt copyright auditing methods struggle with long skills and introduce token-level perturbations that compromise readability. We propose SkillCODER for copyright auditing and buyer attribution in a black-box, content-only setting. During embedding, SkillCODER parses a skill into a section-aware intermediate representation, SkillIR, to identify structural anchors. It distributes conditional instructions across these anchors to form an Artifact-Gated Capsule, designed to activate under verification queries and remain dormant otherwise. Controlled-Vocabulary Error-Correcting Codes encode buyer-specific fingerprints through controlled lexical choices within the capsule. During verification, the defender issues paired positive and negative probes, extracts capsule evidence, and recovers ownership and buyer identity through error-correcting decoding. Across three domains, six models, and three agent frameworks, SkillCODER achieves 99.2% owner verification and 99.3% buyer Top-1 attribution accuracy while preserving task fidelity, substantially outperforming prompt-level baselines. Embedded signals remain robust under paraphrase, compression, clause deletion, and reorganization. Under five adaptive attacks, including a method-aware LLM sanitizer and multi-buyer collusion, ownership evidence remains reliably detectable while buyer attribution degrades gracefully.

Title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records
Author: Liyao Zhou, Xinwei Sun
Text_Content: Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.

Title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
Author: Joseph Marvin Imperial, Daniel Slate, Noam Kolt
Text_Content: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots$.$txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (below 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots$.$txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

Title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
Author: Doron Shavit
Text_Content: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.

Title: TransArt3D: From Two States to Articulated 3D Reconstruction with Video Transition Priors
Author: Chenhao Guan, Liying Yang, Xinxing Yu, Hao Mo, Tianshun Han, Renjun Gao, Yanyan Liang
Text_Content: Reconstructing interactable articulated assets from a few images is key to robotics and simulation, yet highly underconstrained. Existing optimization-based methods fit an articulated asset under a static 3D prior that scores each state independently, so per-state reconstruction errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D. To this end, we present TransArt3D, an optimization-based framework that reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from two endpoint images by translating this video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics. It first lifts frames generated between the endpoints with a transition-coupled 3D consensus that applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames, stabilizing unchanging regions and initializing the parts and joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement then lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field over the whole transition, while part assignment and a shared joint constrain the field throughout optimization, keeping per-state errors out of the articulation. Finally, a motion-aware canonical appearance fusion uses the recovered articulation to map both endpoint images onto one canonical surface, texturing regions that only one state reveals. On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D outperforms methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy, and surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.

Title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
Author: Hanan Shteingart, Amedeo Sapio, Chen Avin, Devendar Bureddy, Manjunath Gorentla Venkata, Srivatsan Krishnan, Shie Mannor, Sreeram Potluri, Gil Shabat, Zsolt-Alon Wertheimer
Text_Content: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

Title: EASE-KV: Diagnosing the Gap Between Memory Availability and Effective Use
Author: Di Lu, Zechen Li, Xuanyu Yue, Jiabo Fan, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
Text_Content: Reusable key-value (KV) memory avoids repeatedly prefilling retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence. We present EASE-KV, a controlled framework for understanding this gap under fixed candidates and a frozen language model. EASE-KV separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding, whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation, and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations. Matched experiments show that causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, while the tested inference-time bridging methods fail to recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, diagnostic evidence-guided allocation improves LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%, demonstrating that memory influence can be controlled without re-encoding. However, controllability does not guarantee learnability: binary correctness provides informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, compared with 73.6% under the evaluated shaped-reward setting. These findings show that effective KV memory requires more than retrieval and injection: the required relations must be encoded, preserved memories must receive appropriate influence, and supervision must distinguish better allocations from worse ones.

Title: Specializing Meta Multi-Objectivization as Baseline for Software Engineering Optimization
Author: Chengjie Chuan, Pengzhou Chen, Tao Chen
Text_Content: Given the discrete nature of many software engineering (SE) optimization problems, trapping at local optima remains a crucial issue in the optimizer designs. Meta Multi-Objectivization (MMO) is an optimization model for overcoming local optima by introducing an extra, auxiliary objective. Yet, MMO is originally designed only for configuration tuning, leaving its suitability for other SE problems in doubt, particularly regarding the choice of the auxiliary objective. In this paper, we study the possibility and resolution for specializing MMO as a general baseline across a range of SE optimization problems, making it a fundamental counterpart for future SE optimizers that seek to mitigate the issue of local optima. We do so by providing both theoretical remit and empirical evidence: we analytically show how the choice of the auxiliary objective is crucial while demonstrating the effectiveness of MMO under nine SE optimization problems comprising 212 cases when the right one can be chosen, i.e., MMO is able to outperform the other state-of-the-art and general-purpose optimizers in 79% and 94% of the cases, respectively. Drawing on the theoretical understanding and empirical findings, we then propose L2RAC, a tool that automatically recommends the best auxiliary objective choice for a given SE problem/case, hence helping to specialize MMO therein. Through extensive experiments, we reveal that, in general, L2RAC can more accurately rank the choice of auxiliary objective for MMO under a case than other guesses by up to 60%, saving as much as 99% of the cost that would otherwise be required to conduct trial-and-error when using MMO.

Title: Single-Radar Bilateral 3D Near-Field Imaging for Mobile Robots
Author: Yingqi Wang, Tingwei Chen, Zhongqin Wang, Min Xu
Text_Content: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.

Title: Samyama-SDG: A Declarative GraphQL @count and Regex/Ontology Synthetic Data Compiler with $O(1)$-Memory Referential Integrity and Causal Ground Truth
Author: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru
Text_Content: Synthetic data generators face a divide between declarative relational mockets and domain causal simulators. Declarative generators specify entities, regexes, and foreign keys via schemas, but buffer parent primary-key pools in RAM ($O(N)$ memory) and lack ontology bindings or causal ground truth. Conversely, domain simulators emit realistic streams and ground-truth labels, but require thousands of lines of procedural code per domain. We present Samyama-SDG (sdg-rs), a Rust synthetic data compiler unifying declarative schema compilation with ontology-bound causal simulation. At Layer 1, Samyama-SDG compiles Cardinality-Extended GraphQL schemas (@count, @pk, @ontology, @regex, @dist, @fk, @after) and an Attribute Data Dictionary into a topologically sorted DAG. Combining stateless counter-based seekable PRNGs (SplitMix64 over $(\text{seed}, \text{entity}, \text{row}, \text{field})$) with index-bijective primary keys $f_{\text{PK}}(s, E, i)$ lets child tables resolve uniform or Zipfian foreign keys and multi-hop @after constraints in $O(1)$ memory without buffering parent tables. At Layer 2, causal processes layer fault propagation and machine-scorable ground truth (ground_truth.jsonl) over the same seekable PRNG and samyama-ontologies binder. Across three schemas, Samyama-SDG generates $1{,}000{,}000$ records in $128.79\text{ ms}$--$172.43\text{ ms}$ ($5.80\text{M}$--$7.76\text{M}$ rows/s) and $5{,}000{,}000$ records in $676.12\text{ ms}$--$808.56\text{ ms}$ at flat $31.4\text{ MiB}$--$35.1\text{ MiB}$ memory, with $0$ conformance errors across $1{,}150{,}000$ foreign keys and $900{,}000$ temporal constraints.

Title: AWS Serverless Infrastructure from WebAssembly Components
Author: Philipp Vollmer
Text_Content: The infrastructure definitions and the code for serverless applications are often only loosely connected. This yields a large error class: the referenced infrastructure components might not exist. It is also hard to keep the application and its permissions in sync. To address this problem we present an infrastructure from code solution where we provision cloud infrastructure from Wasm Interface Type (WIT) - the language defining the interface of WebAssembly components. We limit ourselves to the basic example of an AWS Lambda function accessing S3 buckets. We build two interpreters for the WIT language: one that derives the definition of S3 buckets as infrastructure as code and least-privilege IAM permissions, and a generic runtime that runs the component as a Lambda function and provides access to the S3 buckets as capabilities. We formulate consistency properties that ensure the existence of the S3 buckets and correct permissions of the Lambda, and provide evidence that our interpreters satisfy them. We show how selected failures for deployment of such cloud components can be prevented using our technique and how a baseline setup fails at this task. Together with the strict sandboxing of the WebAssembly runtime we achieve an instance of capability-based security for access to AWS infrastructure as a further result.

Title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
Author: Saurabh Kumar, Dewant Katare, Prakriti Jain
Text_Content: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.

Title: Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers
Author: Rui Xue, Tianfu Wu
Text_Content: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.

Title: A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition
Author: Saurabh Kumar, Dewant Katare, Prakriti Jain
Text_Content: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

Title: A Markovian SuASR epidemic framework with stochastic external factors
Author: Vasileios E. Papageorgiou, Georgios Vasiliadis
Text_Content: Epidemic waves are often shaped by uncertain external drivers, such as environmental variability or behavioral and policy changes, that can randomly amplify or dampen transmission. Capturing this randomness requires models whose dynamics evolve under time-varying, stochastic influences. In this paper, we introduce a stochastic Susceptible-Asymptomatic-Symptomatic-Removed (SuASR) framework that embeds random external factors directly into the epidemic mechanism through an extended continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). The proposed framework is flexible enough to represent epidemic dynamics both with reinfection and with infection-induced immunity, depending on the epidemiological setting under study. Unlike standard Markovian epidemic models, our formulation explicitly tracks two concurrent infectious sources (asymptomatic and symptomatic), yielding coupled infection pathways and substantially richer transient behavior. A key contribution is analytical tractability, where we derive computable expressions for the joint distribution of asymptomatic and symptomatic infection-event counts and develop tools tailored to extreme-outbreak risk, including the distribution of the maximum infectious burden. These results enable probabilistic quantification of epidemic severity beyond mean trajectories, providing direct estimates of the likelihood of rare but consequential surges. We validate the model through extensive sensitivity analysis and an application to the H1N1 influenza epidemic, illustrating how stochastic external influences reshape outbreak profiles, total infections from both sources, and the probability of extreme epidemic scenarios

Title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
Author: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
Text_Content: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.

Title: Cable construction effects on the lateral forces and wakes of helically stranded cables under oblique inflow
Author: Tielin Ma, Junlin Zhang, Jingcheng Fu, Chongwen Jiang, Chuan Ye
Text_Content: Helically stranded cables in aerial towing systems experience oblique inflow, but are often modeled as smooth cylinders, neglecting three-dimensional cross-stream coupling and surface texture. We perform large-eddy simulations and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition for a smooth cylinder and four stranded cables at four inclinations from $22.5^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, all stationary, with $Re \approx 1.0 \times 10^4$. Aerodynamic differences are governed mainly by cross-sectional symmetry and strand-scale groove depth. Force-source decomposition shows that surface pressure contributes 94.9%--98.3% of the mean normal force and dominates the mean lateral force. High-symmetry, quasi-circular envelopes maintain balanced circumferential pressure, whereas deep-grooved, low-symmetry tri-lobed geometries produce asymmetric separation and a persistent lateral pressure imbalance. In the wake, high-symmetry cables sustain spanwise-synchronized Karman shedding at moderate-to-high inclinations, concentrating fluctuation energy in a dominant low-rank mode. Deep grooves disrupt shedding coherence, deflect the recirculation zone laterally, and spread energy across broadband scales. Mean lateral force and lateral-force fluctuations are therefore decoupled: the quasi-circular $(1 \times 19)$ cable has minimal mean lateral force but strong periodic fluctuations, while the deep-grooved $(3 \times 7)$ cable has weak fluctuations but appreciable mean lateral force. These results support construction-dependent cable selection and aerodynamic load modeling.

Title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes
Author: K. Debicki, E. Hashorva, S. Novikov
Text_Content: We investigate the upper tail of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$, where $X$ is a centred Gaussian process (GP) with continuous sample paths on a nonempty compact metric space $\mathcal T$. As suggested by the findings of [1], the exponential rate is governed by an optimal-measure problem, while the exact prefactor depends on the local geometry of the corresponding contact set. In the full-contact regime, we strengthen the known Gumbel max-domain of attraction property of the distribution of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$ by establishing the von Mises condition. For fractional Brownian motion on $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, with Hurst index $H\in(0,1/2)$, we also determine the order of the logarithmic correction to the leading Gaussian exponential. For finite contact sets, we distinguish dominated, smooth-critical, and rough-critical regimes and derive exact asymptotics of $P\{\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)>u\}$ as $u\to\infty$ under suitable local assumptions. We illustrate our findings with examples including fractional Brownian motion and the fractional Brownian sheet.

Title: WarBias: A Bilingual LLM Benchmark of Stereotypes About Internally Displaced People and Veterans
Author: Viktoriia Makovska, Tetiana Zakharchenko, Oleksandra Ostafiichuk
Text_Content: This paper contains examples of stereotypes about veterans and displaced people that may be offensive or distressing. Social bias benchmarks for language models commonly examine categories such as gender, race, and religion, often drawn from lists of legally protected characteristics. Veterans and internally displaced people (IDPs) fall outside these lists, and stereotypes about them, which can undermine access to employment, housing, and social participation, remain largely absent from language model evaluation. We introduce WarBias, a Ukrainian-English benchmark of stereotypes about these two groups. Built from a taxonomy of 120 stereotype claims grounded in research and monitoring reports, WarBias contains 1,007 stereotype-counter-stereotype-unrelated sentence triplets and 240 multiple-choice questions per language. A Ukrainian language model selected in a blinded human pilot generated the Ukrainian triplets. At least two independent annotators reviewed each triplet in the annotation cohort. The authors revised items in response to the reviews, and the final release was machine-translated into English. Each claim carries a human severity rating. In a baseline evaluation of six models, four prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences about at least one group, most strongly about IDPs, while English scores are mostly balanced. WarBias supports complementary evaluations of stereotypical preferences and context-sensitive judgments, and provides paired forget/retain material for unlearning-based bias mitigation. We document the benchmark's construction, intended uses, and limitations, and offer its construction method as a template for analogous benchmarks in other conflict-affected societies.

Title: Real-Time Arbitrary Resampling for Phase-Continuous Microtuning in Audio Streams
Author: Andreas Falkenberg
Text_Content: This paper develops an output-driven resampling formulation for fine pitch adjustment of recorded signals. A fractional input-position increment combines the desired frequency ratio with independently specified input and output sample rates. Each output sample is evaluated from neighboring input samples, and gradual rate changes preserve the current input position. Musical interval mapping and direct sine synthesis are treated as distinct layers. The formulation separates tuning resolution, numerical accuracy, interpolation quality, and streaming correctness. Optional rational-factor representations use freely chosen approximation parameters; numerical illustrations do not define constants required by the algorithm. Linear interpolation provides a low-cost evaluation kernel but does not establish a universal signal-quality or frequency-accuracy guarantee.

Title: Impropriety and resilience of the chromatic number
Author: Ross J. Kang, Colin McDiarmid
Text_Content: We show that, for $p$ bounded away from $1$ and $np\to\infty$, the chromatic number of the binomial random graph $G_{n,p}$ is resilient to removal of a subgraph $H$ with $o(n \log(np))$ edges. It follows that the same assertion holds with $H$ being a subgraph of maximum degree $o(\log(np))$; and both these results are best possible up to a constant factor. We also prove corresponding results for the random $r$-regular graph $G_{n,r}$, when $r\to\infty$ and $r/n$ is bounded away from $1$, where $H$ has $o(n\log r)$ edges or maximum degree $o(\log r)$. Our results rely on a natural connection between chromatic resilience to edge removal and improper graph colouring. This work provides counterpoint to the work of Sudakov and Vu (2008) and Alon and Sudakov (2010), which treated chromatic resilience for $G_{n,p}$ subject to the addition, rather than removal, of edges.

Title: How Efficient Is Your Agent? Online Predictive Bounds under Budget Constraints
Author: Roy Maor Lotan, Shai Feldman, Yaniv Romano
Text_Content: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.

Title: An Adaptive, Context-Aware, and Stacked Attention Network-Based Recommendation System to Capture Users' Temporal Preference
Author: Jung-Hsien Chiang, Chung-Yao Ma, Chi-Shiang Wang, Pei-Yi Hao
Text_Content: Recommendation systems have become more important since the widespread use of the Internet. The large amount of information means that it is difficult for users to discover they really need. However, users' preferences can change over time because of the age and the impact of social networks. Recommendation systems must capture users' preferences and recommend suitable items, which is a difficult challenge. This study proposes a novel recommendation system that adapts to the changing preferences of users. By learning and adapting to users' changing preferences better recommendations are provided. This study uses context factors as additional information to model users' preferences more precisely. For the proposed recommendation system, the context is based on users' interaction items within each defined time interval. This study proposes two novel attention mechanisms for the recommendation system. The contextual item attention module captures contextual information, changing pattern in users' preference and the importance of items. The multi-head attention module extends the diversity of users' preferences and adapts to changing preferences. The recommendation performance is improved using additional item's temporal information to model the contextual item's representation. Experiments compare the proposed algorithm with several state-of-the-art recommendation methods using three real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware recommendation model outperforms traditional methods and demonstrate the effectiveness with which contextual information is captured by the attention mechanism.

Title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning
Author: Yaxin Yu, Long Chen, Minfu Feng
Text_Content: Stochastic first-order methods use sampled gradients to reduce per-iteration costs, but estimation errors can slow convergence and, in some settings, cause divergence. To improve gradient accuracy while retaining acceleration, we develop scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG for smooth stochastic convex optimization. The methods combine STORM-type recursive estimation, Adam-style preconditioning, and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction, using at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes. Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, polynomial steps with prescribed initialization yield $O(1/K)$ mean-square gradient-estimation error and expected objective-gap bounds combining $O(1/K^2)$ initial-energy decay with an $O(1/\sqrt K)$ stochastic term after $K$ iterations. These guarantees require neither monotonicity of the preconditioner nor a uniform positive lower bound on its eigenvalues. The analysis also establishes polynomial-step convergence of projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s, filling a gap in its original theory. Experiments compare the methods at matched sample-gradient budgets. In every tested setting, at least one of the two versions achieves the lowest mean terminal objective gap among all compared methods.

Title: Zero Replacement and Latent Profiles in Short Media Diaries: Checking Recording Status Before User Segmentation
Author: Eunjeong Song, Sehee Hong
Text_Content: Short media diaries contain many zeros because many activities go unrecorded during the observation period. Log-ratio analysis of time allocation requires these zeros to be replaced with small positive values; as a result, all respondents who did not record an activity receive nearly the same value. We examined how such zero replacement affects classification in latent profile analysis and propose checks to perform before profiles are interpreted. Three-day diaries of 8,089 adults from the 2025 Korea Media Panel Survey were converted into nine-part time-use compositions. Gaming was not recorded by 88.9% of the respondents, and in every model with two to eight profiles and a covariance matrix held equal across profiles, respondents who recorded gaming and those who did not were classified into different profiles. Even when the replacement value equaled the minimum recording unit (5 min/day), the two-profile classification largely matched gaming recording status, and the two groups separated more sharply as the replacement value decreased, until the separation was complete. Before naming profiles, researchers should therefore check the proportion of respondents who did not record each activity and its replacement value, the same proportion within each profile, and the distribution of usage time among those who recorded the activity.

Title: Task-adaptive anonymisation enables privacy-preserving sharing of clinical speech data
Author: Ziyun Cui, Haoyu Niu, Wen Wu, Hao Sun, Sihan Zhang, Chang Lei, Yun Zhang, Chunyun Sun, Yang Luo, Liangliang Cao, Ji Wu, Runsen Chen, Lian Zhou, Yongsheng Tong, Chao Zhang
Text_Content: Clinical speech is increasingly used for disease screening and clinical assessment, but directly distributing speech recordings poses privacy risks because they contain both speaker-identifying voiceprints and sensitive spoken content. Existing speech anonymisation approaches are primarily developed for general speech applications or task-specific clinical speech and overlook that different clinical tasks rely on distinct speech characteristics, necessitating task-adaptive anonymisation strategies to protect patient privacy while preserving clinical utility. Here we introduce CASA, a clinically adaptive speech anonymisation agent that transforms anonymisation from a fixed processing procedure into a task-guided optimisation process, dynamically tailoring voiceprint and content anonymisation to task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements. Through recursive self-improvement (RSI), CASA iteratively evaluates and refines anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements, while learning from these outcomes to guide more efficient planning in subsequent clinical tasks. CASA is validated across 14 clinical tasks encompassing five languages, diverse elicitation paradigms, and mental health, cognitive and voice disorders. CASA preserved disease-related classification performance while meeting speaker-anonymisation requirements across all clinical tasks, versus only 8/14 for the strongest fixed method. Assessments of resistance to speaker re-identification by external attackers and identification and redaction of sensitive personal information in clinical speech further demonstrated CASA's dual protection of speaker identity and sensitive spoken content. Clinical expert assessments further supported the preservation of clinically relevant information and the acceptability of anonymised speech for controlled research sharing.

Title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
Author: Peng Zheng, Deng-Ping Fan, Binglu Wang, Nicu Sebe
Text_Content: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet-V2.

Title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
Author: Riya Bharathwaj, Akshara Prabhakar, Roshan Ram, Avni Kothari, Sarah Tan, Huan Wang, Silvio Savarese
Text_Content: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.

Title: DuSS-PET: Self-Supervised Low-Dose PET Reconstruction Using Pseudo-Dual-Domain Consistency Without Paired Data
Author: Shuijin Lin, Yuzhu He, Yongbo Wang, Jianhua Ma, Fan Wang
Text_Content: Positron emission tomography (PET) is pivotal in medicine and healthcare, but requires high radiation doses for quality imaging. Although deep learning has shown promise for low-dose PET reconstruction/enhancement, existing methods primarily rely on fully supervised learning, which requires paired low- and full-dose scans that are clinically impractical to obtain. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose DuSS-PET, a novel self-supervised PET reconstruction framework that operates without any paired low- and full-dose data. Our method is built upon a computational Noisier2Noise (Nr2N) paradigm, featuring a Bernoulli corruption strategy that serves as an image-space approximation to emulate low-count noise patterns in image-derived pseudo-sinogram representations. The DuSS-PET framework integrates three core components: an adaptive Swin transformer for pseudo-sinogram restoration, a plug-and-play module for image enhancement, and a consistency-constrained SSL strategy that enforces agreement between the pseudo-sinogram and image representations. Extensive experiments on multi-center datasets demonstrate that DuSS-PET achieves superior reconstruction performance, outperforming state-of-the-art SSL methods and achieving comparable or even better results than fully supervised approaches across various dose levels. In particular, it exhibits exceptional generalization across different scanner vendors. This work is among the first self-supervised low-dose PET reconstruction framework that enforces consistency between reconstructed images and pseudo-sinograms, where the pseudo-sinogram generated in the image space serves as a solid computational consistency constraint for enhanced imaging without full-dose training scans. The source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/ladderlab-xjtu/DuSS-PET.

Title: Global Trends and Heterogeneity in Modified Adjusted Net Savings
Author: Xin Xiao
Text_Content: Modified adjusted net savings is a derived weak sustainability indicator obtained by subtracting education expenditure from adjusted net savings (ANS). Because ANS equals net national savings plus education expenditure minus natural-resource depletion and carbon dioxide damage, MANS isolates the savings and depletion components and is useful when education expenditure would otherwise dominate cross-country comparisons. This study documents the global distribution, long-run trends, and cross-country heterogeneity of MANS excluding particulate emission damage over 1990-2021. The accounting base is the World Bank World Development Indicators series NY.ADJ.SVNX.CD, and MANS is constructed by subtracting education expenditure from this series. We combine global maps, aggregate time series, country-level heatmaps, distributional statistics, and income group comparisons. The results show that global MANS has increased substantially in aggregate, but its evolution as a share of nominal GDP has been more volatile and uneven across countries. Per capita MANS and global MANS totals remain concentrated in high-income and large economies, whereas low-income and lower-middle-income groups display persistently lower and more volatile outcomes. Country rankings are highly persistent, and some populous countries exhibit pronounced fluctuations associated with natural-resource dependence and structural change. The study provides a reproducible descriptive benchmark for monitoring sustainable development and highlights the need to interpret MANS in current US dollars alongside income-group and country-specific contexts. The findings are relevant for macroeconomic policy, natural-capital accounting, and the design of sustainability-oriented investment strategies.

Title: Beyond Node Attributes: A Controlled Evaluation and Ablation of Local Interaction Statistics for Ethereum Phishing Detection
Author: Thanh Dat Tran, Duy Loi Duong, Duy Luu Hoang, Minh Huy Tran, Vo Minh Thu Le, Nhat Tung Le
Text_Content: Methods for detecting phishing accounts on Ethereum are usually evaluated as complete pipelines that differ in features, architecture, and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate. This paper evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), a block of 12 local interaction statistics computed from each account's incoming and outgoing call and transfer edges without reading class labels. UFE is appended to the 14 source features of HEIG-Phish and tested with six model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE, and Meta-IFD. Within each pair of Baseline and Plus variants, the data partition, model configuration, random seed, decision threshold, and sampled neighborhoods are identical; only the input feature block changes. Across 20 predetermined stratified partitions of the same 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts, UFE increased test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improved on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreased for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 predetermined partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute; once this feature is present, an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established. The results support reporting feature-augmented baselines alongside graph models, but they show stability under re-partitioning of one static, transductive benchmark rather than temporal or cross-dataset generalization.

Title: Improving the Trifference Lower Bound via Non-Perfect Hashing
Author: Chen Yuan, Ruiqi Zhu
Text_Content: We strictly improve the Körner-Marton lower bound $\frac14\log \frac{9}{5}$ on the asymptotic rate of trifferent codes. We obtain this improvement by constructing non-perfect $(9,3)$-hash codes with rate above $\log(9/5)$ and then applying the Tetra-code construction, which gives $R_3\ge\frac14R_{9,3}$. More generally, for every $q\ge4$, we prove $R_{q,3}>B_{q,3}+\frac1{250000}$. We also extend the method to $(p,2,3)$-list recovery. For every $q\ge4$ and $0\le p<\frac{q-2}{12(q-1)}$, we prove $R_q^{\mathrm{LR}}(p)>B_q^{\mathrm{LR}}(p)$. Here $B_{q,3}$ and $B_q^{\mathrm{LR}}(p)$ denote the respective probabilistic lower bounds. For every fixed $0\le p<1/18$, the rate improvement is bounded below by a positive constant independent of $q\ge4$. For every fixed $0\le p<1/12$, we also obtain a positive rate improvement independent of $q$ for all sufficiently large $q$.

Title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
Author: Yibo Miao, Yichuan Cao, Xiao-Shan Gao, Yinpeng Dong
Text_Content: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

Title: Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has
Author: Anqi Qu
Text_Content: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

Title: Auto-GlaKG: Automated Biomarker Reasoning for Explainable Glaucoma Detection
Author: Cheng Huang, Zeyu Han, Yian Hu, Yaopeng Ding, Jingxi Qiu, Yadi Liu
Text_Content: Interpretable glaucoma detection requires a transparent connection between fundus images, clinically meaningful biomarkers, and diagnostic predictions. Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning provides this structure, but performance measured using annotated biomarkers does not establish performance when only images are available. We present Auto-GlaKG, an automated framework that combines image-based biomarker prediction with fixed clinical-prior rules. A ResNet50 network predicts the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) and six morphological signs using biomarker supervision, and a KG reasoner aggregates their signed rule contributions into a glaucoma score. On 689 fundus images evaluated using stratified, group-aware five-fold cross-validation, Auto-GlaKG achieves a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.951 (95\% confidence interval: 0.931--0.969), with sensitivity of 0.970 and specificity of 0.779. The matched image classifier also achieves an AUC of 0.951, while the rule stage adds 0.2~ms per image. Replacing predicted CDR with its annotation increases fold-mean AUC from 0.953 to 0.995. The framework provides an explicit rule-level account of image-based predictions and identifies CDR estimation as a priority for validation using independently measured biomarkers.

Title: Learning calibrated probabilistic forecasts using Koopman mode decomposition and the continuous ranked probability score
Author: Benjamin M. Kent, Richard E. Turner
Text_Content: Well-calibrated forecasting for non-linear dynamical systems is essential in science and engineering applications such as fluid dynamics and weather prediction. We present a forecasting method combining probabilistic machine learning with the structured linear dynamics of Koopman mode decomposition.
