Text_Content: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

Title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
Author: Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
Text_Content: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

Title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses
Author: Yuta Nonomiya
Text_Content: In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term's effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.

Title: Towards Sustainable Federated Learning via Carbon-Aware Client Selection
Author: Wentao Gao, Omid Tavallaie, Albert Y. Zomaya
Text_Content: The Information/Communication Technology (ICT) industry is severely challenging the global environment due to the sharply rising carbon emissions generated by machine learning (ML) workloads. Federated Learning (FL) is one of the prominent distributed ML systems used in applications with billions of client devices, such as Google Gboard and Apple Siri. Nearly half of the total carbon footprint in FL originates from client-side computation during local training. However, existing client selection strategies in FL primarily focus on minimizing energy consumption rather than carbon emissions, despite the fact that carbon impact depends not only on computational load but also on the underlying carbon intensity of the energy source. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a carbon-aware fair client selection strategy (CA-FCS) designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with model training on client devices. In contrast to existing approaches for reducing carbon emissions in FL, we incorporate hourly carbon intensity and a realistic energy consumption model developed using empirical measurements from Google Pixel smartphones to estimate client-side carbon emissions in FL. Since repeatedly selecting low-carbon clients may reduce data diversity and degrade global model performance, particularly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data settings, CA-FCS incorporates fairness into client selection to mitigate this issue. We conduct extensive experiments under realistic FL settings for mobile devices, where client participation is constrained by device availability conditions, such as charging status and Wi-Fi connectivity. The results demonstrate that our method reduces client-side carbon emissions by up to 46% while maintaining competitive model accuracy.

Title: Deliberate Pacing for Human Oversight in Agentic Software Development
Author: Tobias Reichel, Michèle Stassen, Anamaria Mojica-Hanke, Maria Teresa Baldassarre, Sebastian Baltes, Alexander Serebrenik, Steffen Herbold
Text_Content: Agentic AI increasingly enables software development activities to proceed without continuous human involvement. While this autonomy may accelerate development, it also raises questions about when developers can meaningfully oversee software development done by agents. We propose deliberate pacing: intentionally adjusting when and how autonomous development proceeds to preserve opportunities for meaningful oversight. Drawing on an exploratory multivocal literature review of 20 sources, we identify three factors motivating this vision: changing relative costs of human involvement, the timing of oversight opportunities, and interdependencies between pacing decisions across the software development life cycle. We argue that neither uninterrupted autonomy nor frequent human intervention is universal. Instead, pacing should balance opportunities to understand and influence consequential decisions against costs in human attention, development time, and rework. We outline a research agenda to investigate when deliberate pacing is beneficial, how intervention timing affects oversight, and how pacing decisions interact across development activities.

Title: CoMoFlow: Controllable Protein Conformational Ensemble Generation via Explicit Collective-Mode Modeling
Author: Yusong Wang, Zheyuan Gu, Ailiang Lin, Minghao Shao, Yicheng Xu, Jiang Cai, Prayag Tiwari, Mingkun Xu
Text_Content: Protein conformational ensemble generation aims to efficiently characterize the structural variations accessible to a protein beyond a single static structure. Recent flow-based methods efficiently generate conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation implicitly, which can limit ensemble fidelity and hinder direct control. To address this limitation, we propose CoMoFlow, a controllable framework for generating protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation. CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.

Title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
Author: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
Text_Content: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.

Title: Mode interaction in inclined-layer convection: a physical interpretation
Author: Zheng Zheng, Laurette S. Tuckerman, Tobias M. Schneider
Text_Content: We carry out a numerical investigation of the Oberbeck--Boussinesq equations in a fluid layer inclined against gravity. Equilibria containing different numbers of co-rotating rolls are computed. Mixed-mode branches connect branches containing states with four and six identical co-rotating rolls. These branches display two contrasting routes to reducing (or increasing) the number of rolls, one in which rolls disappear (or appear) and another route in which rolls merge (or split). These results are interpreted in light of the $(2,3)$ mode interaction scenario.

Title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning
Author: Nataly Brukhim, Steve Hanneke, Amirreza Shaeiri, Maximilian Thiessen
Text_Content: We study the problem of multiclass classification within the framework of marginal-nonuniform learning, where the constants in the learning rate may depend on the unknown marginal distribution generating the unlabeled data, but not on the target concept. This notion naturally lies between classical PAC learning, where the constants are independent of both the marginal distribution and the target concept, and more recent universal learning, where the constants may depend on both. We give a complete characterization of the optimal marginal-nonuniform learning rates, establishing a fundamental trichotomy: exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates. This characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, termed the uncentered DS-eluder dimension. A key ingredient in the upper-bound proofs is a set of new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension and may be of independent interest.

Title: CID: Measuring Cognitive Work Through Semantic State Change
Author: Ron Fulbright
Text_Content: Traditional information theory provides powerful tools for analyzing statistical properties of information but offers limited insight into meaning and semantic transformation. It has never been possible to quantify the meaning of an arbitrary piece of information. Large language models represent information as vectors embedded within high-dimensional semantic spaces, enabling meaning to be analyzed geometrically. This paper defines semantic state as the vector representation of information within a model's semantic space and defines cognitive work as the transformation between semantic states, movement through semantic space. To quantify this transformation, we introduce the Contextual Information Differential (CID), a covariance-aware metric based on Mahalanobis distance measuring semantic displacement relative to the structure of the embedding manifold. By treating meaning as a geometric property of semantic space, CID provides a practical method for measuring semantic change, cognitive transformation, and information processing. This framework establishes a foundation for analyzing cognitive processing, learning, reasoning, knowledge generation, synthetic expertise, and human/AI collaboration through implementation-independent measurement of semantic state change in both human and artificial systems.

Title: Portable Glass-RPC Telescope for Muography and Future Applications at Laser Wake Field Accelerators
Author: S. Ikram, D. Ahmadi, U. Chaulagain, A. Cimmino, E. Cortina Gil, P. Demin, A. Giammanco, G. M. Grittani, M. Lagrange, M. Nevrkla, J. Sisma, M. Tytgat, R. Versaci, F. Vitha
Text_Content: We report a 2025 beam test at ELBA, the multi-GeV laser wakefield accelerator at ELI Beamlines, using a Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) telescope with an active area of 16 * 16 cm2. The portable design sup- ports autonomous operation in challenging environments. Previous cosmic-ray measurements established its tracking capability for muography. During the campaign at ELBA, 30 f s long, 0.5 PW laser pulses in- teracted with a plasma target at a 0.2 Hz repetition rate, where a tungsten converter upstream of the beam dump enhanced muon production. This was the first deployment of an RPC telescope in a high-power laser environment. The detector remained operational in the presence of radiation and electromagnetic interference. Although parasitic running and limited statistics prevented definitive identification of beam- induced muons, the measurements offered insight into background activity and showed evidence of re- constructed tracks. They establish the feasibility of a dedicated campaign with controlled beam conditions and improved muon sensitivity. This contribution forms part of the International Muography Workshop 2026 proceedings.

Title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity
Author: Swati Shukla, Subhra Sankar Dhar, Shalabh
Text_Content: This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.

Title: Multimodal Training with Knowledge Traction for Video Anomaly Detection
Author: Xiao Tan
Text_Content: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.

Title: Graph representations of dislocation networks
Author: Gaurav Lathiya, Markus Stricker
Text_Content: The mechanical response of a crystal is governed by the evolving network of dislocations it contains, yet quantitatively linking the `state of that network' to its yield stress remains challenging. Here we represent the dislocation networks obtained from discrete dislocation dynamic simulation as graphs, using five distinct graph representations, characterize each network through a compact set of topological properties, and predict the yield stress from these graph properties and the applied strain rate using a standard random forest model evaluated with strain rate stratified cross-validation. The model predicts the yield stress with $R^2\approx0.86-0.90$ across all box sizes and $R^2\approx0.91-0.94$ for larger box sizes, and this accuracy is consistent across all five representations, indicating that the topology-stress relationship is a robust feature of the graph properties rather than an artefact of any single graph representation. We propose graph topology as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response in addition to established variables.

Title: Pangenome Peeling: Decomposing Weighted Adjacencies into Path-Forest Genomes
Author: Alitzel López Sánchez, Jiazhen Leng, Natasha Ivanova, Lingling Jin, David Sankoff
Text_Content: One aspect of pangenome analysis that has received little attention is the recovery of the individual genomes that gave rise to a pangenome graph. While substantial effort has focused on constructing pangenomes from collections of genomes, the inverse problem remains largely unexplored: given a pangenome represented as a set of weighted adjacencies, can we reconstruct the constituent linear genomes that underlie it? Thus we introduce the pangenome peeling problem, which seeks to decompose a weighted adjacency graph into a collection of linear genomes whose combined adjacencies reproduce the observed edge weights. This problem is particularly relevant when considering ancestral pangenomes, where the graph structure may be known or inferred, but the underlying genomes are not. As a first step toward addressing this problem, we formally define pangenome peeling and derive a lower bound on the minimum number of genomes required to explain a given weighted adjacency graph. We then present two reconstruction methods: one based on the sequential addition of edges and a second based on extracting maximum-spanning-tree structures. Both methods produce genome collections that exactly explain the input adjacency data. To evaluate the recovered sets of genomes, we compare them to the set of input genomes using a maximum-weight matching framework based on the double-cut-and-join distance with indels. Here the maximum-spanning tree approach is superior, producing sets of constituent genomes close to the simulations while the sequential addition of edges approach yields constituent genomes increasingly divergent from the input as genomes sizes increase.

Title: Violent relaxation redux
Author: Michael L. Nastac, Yonadav Barry Ginat, Robert J. Ewart, Michael Barnes, Alexander A. Schekochihin
Text_Content: Collisionless self-gravitating systems, such as merging galaxies, have long seemed an exception to the statistical-mechanical principle that chaotic many-body systems relax to maximum-entropy states: Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of their "violent relaxation," constrained by exact conservation of phase-space volume -- equivalently, of infinitely many collisionless "Casimir" invariants -- has appeared not to be a good description. We propose that violent relaxation does give rise to Lynden-Bell's maximum-entropy equilibria, but that both are underpinned by gravitational turbulence, in which large-scale gravitational fluctuations drive chaotic phase-space mixing of the particles' distribution function. We derive the universal small-scale (sub-Jeans) spectra of this turbulence and show that it leads to phase-space-volume conservation being broken on a timescale only logarithmically longer, in the particle number N, than the dynamical (violent-relaxation) time. This timescale separation lets the system relax "adiabatically" through a sequence of Lynden-Bell equilibria, each corresponding to instantaneous values of the Casimirs. At long times, it approaches an equilibrium close to its "ground state": a distribution whose Casimirs have adjusted so that the system's energy is now its minimum possible energy. Thus, the system's universal tendency is toward a minimum-energy, maximum-entropy state. We corroborate this picture with 1D N-body simulations and hypothesize that it can explain the universal equilibria of galaxies and dark-matter halos.

Title: PreForceVision: Physics-Guided Optical Estimation of Bolt Preload from Bolt-Head Deformation
Author: Nehal Afifi, Klaus Rappenecker, Florian Peinhardt, Gerhard Kachel, Alfred Isele, Sven Matthiesen
Text_Content: Bolt preload is a decisive functional quantity in bolted joints because it determines whether external loads are transmitted primarily through frictional clamping or directly through the bolt. Existing preload measurement techniques, including strain-gauge bolts, force washers, ultrasonic methods, and bolt-length measurements, are effective in certain applications but require additional hardware, coupling, calibration, or joint modifications. This limits their scalability for large numbers of standard fasteners and motivates a non-contact optical approach. This paper proposes PreForceVision, a physics-guided optical framework for estimating bolt preload from preload-induced surface deformation of the bolt-head front face. The method treats preload estimation as an inverse deformation-to-force problem, where deformation of the optically accessible bolt-head surface is extracted from reference-loaded image pairs and related to the internal preload state. Preliminary results for an M16 strength class 8.8 bolt show an approximately \SI{12}{\micro\meter} simulated head-face depression at \SI{90}{\kilo\newton}, strain-gauge measurements of comparable magnitude, and an optical 3D measured central depression of approximately \SIrange{10}{20}{\micro\meter}. The contribution is a physics-guided optical methodology combining controlled image-pair acquisition, DIC- or optical-flow-based deformation extraction, multimodal validation, and uncertainty-aware regression for rough preload estimation under controlled conditions.

Title: StockASkill: A Local-First AgentSkill for Intelligent Stock Selection
Author: Xiangjing An, Zhibin Jiao, Aiting Chen
Text_Content: Quantitative equity selection and portfolio construction in emerging and cross-border markets frequently suffer from computational bottlenecks, remote API fragility, survivorship bias, and rigid execution constraints such as discrete board lots and investor-mandated drawdown limits. In this paper, we present StockASkill, a local-first, full-data-driven AgentSkill engineered as a specialized Quant Co-Processor for autonomous AI agents and quantitative researchers. Tailored for agile portfolios (10^5 ~ 10^7 RMB) where discrete lot execution and capital protection are mandatory, StockASkill embeds a columnar DuckDB OLAP engine over 42.44 million historical price records and 186,432 financial disclosures spanning 26 years across China A-shares, Hong Kong, US equities, and ETFs. By eliminating ad-hoc network dependencies during analysis, StockASkill reduces cross-sectional screening latency across 5,400+ equities from over 25 seconds to sub-0.5 seconds (a 95%+ reduction). We formalize an end-to-end mathematical pipeline integrating a 7+1 factor alpha model, an SLSQP convex optimizer under smooth CVaR drawdown surrogates with exact path projection, dynamic 100-share board lot integer quantization, and an autonomous thesis lifecycle finite-state machine. Furthermore, we provide a zero-disk, strongly-typed JSON streaming interface designed for high-throughput LLM tool-calling. Open-sourced at https://github.com/axjing/stockaskill, comprehensive empirical benchmarks from 2018 to 2024 demonstrate that the architecture achieves annualized Sharpe ratios exceeding 1.48 and Calmar ratios up to 2.17, while reducing max drawdown by up to 85% relative to benchmark indices.

Title: ExQuery: Explicit Structured Query Priors for Temporal 3D Object Detection
Author: Honglin Sun, Yifei Zhang, Junyang Zhang, Kenji Hashimoto
Text_Content: Sparse query-based 3D detectors commonly encode heterogeneous semantic, geometric, and motion information into unified latent queries, including when explicit 3D anchors are used. We introduce ExQuery, an explicit structured query framework for temporal 3D object detection. Each decoded query is organized into a shared semantic context slice and physical-state-specific slices for center, dimensions, orientation, and velocity. This structure is preserved from prior encoding to branch-specific regression and is reused to reconstruct temporal queries: predicted physical states are transformed by ego motion, classification scores form soft semantic priors, and the reconstructed query is fused with the stored latent instance feature through gated affine modulation. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark show that our method achieves competitive detection performance, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our proposed modules.

Title: Secondary neutron beam production at Jefferson Lab
Author: A. Fulci, P. Ambrozewicz, M. Battaglieri, M. Bondi, R. De Vita, M. Filippini, G. Foti, S. Grazzi, G. Mandaglio, T. Nagorna, A. Pilloni, M. Spreafico, S. Vallarino
Text_Content: We investigate secondary neutron production by an 11 GeV electron beam in the Hall A beam dump at Jefferson Lab and their transport to a downstream experimental area. This secondary beam could operate opportunistically with the primary electron-scattering programme. The neutron energy spectrum extends from thermal energies to several GeVs, offering a distinctive opportunity for irradiation at energy grater than 1 GeV. We considered three configurations: the current setup, the planned BDX facility, and an optimized BDX layout with a dedicated neutron extraction pipe. We also studied how radiators made of different materials and placed upstream of the beam dump increase neutron production.

Title: RadarDINO: Distilling a Visual Foundation Model into mmWave Radar for Human Mesh Reconstruction
Author: Furkan Mert Algan, Zhifan Ni, Eckehard Steinbach
Text_Content: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a privacy-preserving and illumination-robust alternative for human mesh reconstruction (HMR). However, high-fidelity radar HMR remains challenging. Sparse point cloud-based methods suffer from information loss and missed detections, while raw radar tensor methods like RT-Mesh lack fine-grained semantics and explicit local body modeling. In this paper, we propose RadarDINO, a radar HMR framework that distills visual semantics from a DINOv3 teacher into 3D radar representations and introduces explicit geometric supervision. DINOv3 descriptors are transferred to radar voxels via calibrated RGB-radar geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations. We further incorporate vertex- and joint-losses to directly constrain reconstructed geometry. On the M4Human dataset, our method outperforms the SOTA baseline across all three evaluation splits.

Title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
Author: Ahmed Zeer, Erkan Uslu
Text_Content: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.

Title: Embedding Predictive Adaptation and Refinement for Multi-Modal Industrial Anomaly Detection
Author: Jaeho Cho, Jinsik Bang, Taehwan Kim
Text_Content: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) has evolved from 2D image-based approaches to multi-modal methods that leverage the complementary nature of RGB images and 3D point clouds. Among these, memory bank-based methods, which identify anomalies by the discrepancy between each query patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, have proven particularly effective. However, two limitations remain: (i) employing frozen pretrained encoders yields insufficient discrimination between normal and anomalous features due to the domain gap, while existing contrastive learning-based adaptation struggles to capture the spatial relationships required for precise localization; and (ii) pixel-level anomaly maps interpolated from patch-level distance scores remain coarse, lacking fine-grained detail. To address these limitations, we propose EPAR (Embedding Predictive Adaptation and Refinement). We adapt encoders by predicting the embeddings of masked regions to capture spatial relationships, together with patch-level Variance-Invariance-Covariance (VIC) regularization, resolving the poor discriminability between normal and anomalous features caused by the domain gap. We further propose a Noise Suppression Network that refines coarse maps by learning the relational discrepancy between each patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, rather than the anomaly's appearance. This relational signal remains valid for unseen real defects, despite being learned from synthetic anomalies. EPAR demonstrates strong practical applicability, excelling in few-shot settings and improving AUPRO@1% on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies by +1.8% and +1.9%, respectively.

Title: Active Learning of Robust Models
Author: Mizu Nishikawa-Toomey, Andreas Kirsch, Laurent Charlin, Dhanya Sridhar
Text_Content: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. In addition to the high costs of acquiring data in such domains, there is the added complexity of data distribution shifts that can occur between training and deployment. For example, the features of cancerous skin cells taken in one country may be different in another region of the world. These two challenges - efficient labelling of data, and learning models robust to distribution shifts have been studied separately but not together, even though these challenges often co-occur in real-life settings. We identify failure modes of standard active learning approaches when the distribution of data at deployment is different from the distribution in which the data is sampled for labelling. We propose a new strategy for efficiently learning classifiers that generalise under specific forms of distribution shift, namely subpopulation shift. Drawing on work in learning from heterogeneous data, we aim to train models that perform well across subpopulations of the data, through active learning. To handle this challenging setting, we exploit the fact that many datasets include metadata about data collection that can serve as a noisy proxy for each sample's underlying subpopulation. We demonstrate how to leverage these noisy labels during active learning selection, and demonstrate empirically that our approach improves classifier accuracy across subpopulations.

Title: Memory as a Temporal Resource: Lifetime Contracts for Multi-Retention Systems
Author: Adrian Jackson
Text_Content: Computers move and rewrite data whose useful lifetimes range from inner-loop iterations to years, yet memory systems usually hide retention as a fixed physical property. We argue that required lifetime should become a first-class resource across algorithms, programming systems, controllers, and devices. Building on prior lifetime-aware placement, we propose an event-based validity contract that links application completion events to retention-class selection and renewal of protection. Applications would be enabled to express semantic contracts such as ``until this tile completes'' and the system will map data to homogeneous arrays engineered for ephemeral, epoch, or durable retention and preserve correctness through margins, ECC, refresh, migration, or recomputation. We present a trace-based simulator and FPGA prototype that exercises class migration.

Title: The PICO-40L detector
Author: PICO Collaboration, E. Adams, B. Ali, R. Anderson-Dornan, D. J. Auty, E. Behnke, M. Bai, M. Bressler, B. Broerman, G. Cao, W. C. Chen, U. Chowdhury, K. Clark, J. I. Collar, J. Corbett, C. B. Coutu, D. Cranshaw, M. Crisler, C. E. Dahl, M. Das, S. Fallows, R. Filgas, A. García-Viltres, C. Gaudreau, F. Girard, G. Giroux, P. Grylls, C. Hardy, O. Harris, H. Hawley-Herrera, R. Hill, T. Hillier, C. B. Krauss, M. Laurin, I. Lawson, A. Leblanc, H. Leng, I. Levine, Q. Malin, A. Mathewson, D. Maurya, S. Meister, V. Monette, C. Moore, R. Neilson, A. J. Noble, H. Nozard, A. Ortega, S. Pal, M. -C. Piro, A. Plante, S. Priya, M. Rangen, C. Rethmeier, M. Robert, A. E. Robinson, J. Savoie, S. J. Sekula, N. Starinski, I. Štekl, T. Sullivan, M. Tripathi, E. Vázquez-Jáuregui, E. Weima, U. Wichoski, W. Woodley
Text_Content: The PICO collaboration has designed and constructed a novel bubble chamber to search for evidence of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, a leading dark matter candidate. The PICO-40L detector is the successor to PICO-60, and uses a fully redesigned system for pressurization of the active volume after a bubble nucleation event. Pressure in PICO-40L is transferred to the target fluid through a set of two nested synthetic quartz vessels connected by bellows below the active volume. This is in contrast to the design of earlier detectors in which the pressure was transferred through a buffer fluid atop the target fluid, within a single synthetic quartz vessel connected to a bellows above the active volume. Removing the buffer fluid removes the potential for backgrounds arising from the interface between the two fluids, and moving the bellows below the target fluid suppresses potential backgrounds from particulates originating from the bellows. The newly designed detector concept of PICO-40L is referred to as the Right-Side-Up (RSU) design and requires a dedicated thermal system to keep the lower region of the detector cold while the upper region is stably superheated. The main goal of PICO-40L is to establish the performance characteristics of the RSU detector concept, which will inform the operating configuration of the final generation PICO dark matter detector, PICO-500, which is currently under construction at SNOLAB. This paper reviews the design, installation, and performance of the PICO-40L detector.

Title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
Author: Chih-Hao Hsu, Feng-Chun B. Chou, Pin-Hao A. Chen
Text_Content: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

Title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
Author: Abhishek Gautam
Text_Content: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.

Title: A Physics-Informed Learning Framework for Linking Microscopic Surface Degradation to Bolted Joint Functional Behavior
Author: Nehal Afifi, Gerhard Kachel, Sven Matthiesen
Text_Content: Returned products in circular engineering often have heterogeneous degradation histories, making remaining function difficult to assess. For bolted joints, corrosion alters surface morphology, contact, friction, preload retention, and mechanical response. This paper presents a physics-informed multimodal framework for linking microscopic and camera-based degradation observations to functional indicators of corroded bolted joints. The workflow defines the corrosion failure mode, generates synchronized inspection and functional-response records, preprocesses image, roughness, exposure, and joint descriptors, aligns microscopy and camera observations through similarity learning, and constructs a calibrated corrosion-severity field. Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery is applied to this field to identify candidate effective mesoscale laws rather than complete electrochemical mechanisms. The corrosion-evolution model is coupled to a separate functional model, with friction coefficient as the primary target and preload loss included when clamp-force data are available. The contribution is a reproducible pathway for physically constrained assessment of degraded bolted-joint behavior.

Title: V-STORM: A Structure-Aware Grounded Chain of Thought Dataset for Faithful and Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Video Reasoning
Author: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
Text_Content: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

Title: Pelletization Pressure Engineering of the Superconducting Properties of Fluorine-Doped PrFeAsO
Author: Jayant Kumar, Konrad Kwatek, Tatiana Zajarniuk, Taras Palasyuk, Yaroslaw Konopelnyk, Tomasz Cetner, Cezariusz Jastrzębski, Shiv J. Singh
Text_Content: We investigate the influence of the pelletization pressure on the structural, microstructural, and superconducting properties of fluorine-doped PrFeAsO0.7F0.3 (Pr1111). Precursor powders are pressed into pellets at pressures ranging from 174 to 1131 MPa, after which the applied pressure is released and all samples undergo an identical two-step conventional synthesis process at ambient pressure (CSP-AP). All samples predominantly exhibit the tetragonal P4/nmm structure, and the lattice parameter a and unit-cell volume V decrease with increasing pelletization pressure up to an intermediate-pressure range (~900 MPa) before increasing at higher pressures. The actual fluorine-content derived from energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) also increase with pelletization pressure, while Raman spectra show only modest variations in the characteristic vibrational modes associated with Fe and As. The superconducting response exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the pelletization pressure. Among the investigated samples, the sample pelletized at 870 MPa exhibits the most favorable overall superconducting properties, with a superconducting onset temperature of 44.2 K, ~5 K higher than that of the lowest-pressure sample. It also displays a narrower superconducting transition, the highest relative sample density, a favorable effective magnetic critical current density at high fields, and a relatively large effective thermally activated flux-flow activation energy. At higher pelletization pressures, the superconducting response deteriorates, coinciding with increases in the lattice parameters, increased secondary-phase contributions, and reduced relative density. These findings establish the pelletization pressure as a relevant processing parameter for modifying the structural, microstructural and superconducting properties of Pr1111 during CSP-AP.

Title: On the Effectiveness and Limitations of Open-Weight LLMs for Low-Resource Offensive Language Detection in Danish
Author: Elnur Adl Zarabi, Amit Kumar, Adi Singh, Sierra Nelson, Megan Stubbs-Richardson, Taoran Ji
Text_Content: We study the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight large language models (LLMs) for Danish offensive language detection, an underexplored low-resource task. We evaluate four model families (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen) across eleven prompting strategies spanning five design categories, cross-prompt generalization, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions. We compare against three BERT-family baselines with distinct pre-training strategies, evaluated via both masked language model prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs can surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight finetuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates, underscoring that prompt design interacts with model pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, while format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalize. ASCII transliteration of Danish-specific characters (æ, ø, å) generally degrades performance, indicating these characters encode meaningful signal. At the same time, the gap between a balanced test set (best F1 of 0.84) and the corpus's natural class skew (0.62 trained on skewed data, 0.70 trained on balanced data) -- relative drops of 26.2\% and 16.7\% -- shows that class imbalance remains a critical open challenge. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/PASHAADC/Danish-LLM-HateSpeech.

Title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
Author: Gonçalo Gomes, Bruno Martins, Chrysoula Zerva
Text_Content: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

Title: TimeOmni-Live: Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding with Long-Term Memory
Author: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
Text_Content: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.

Title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
Author: Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou
Text_Content: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

Title: Selection versus residuals: deep-learning solvers for the Dubreil-Jacotin-Long equation and application to mode-2 internal solitary waves
Author: Qiang Li, Yaoyin Zhang
Text_Content: Neural solvers offer structural flexibility for the Dubreil-Jacotin--Long (DJL) equation of internal solitary waves, which also admits the trivial state, oscillatory wavetrains and broadened near-solutions. A solver must select the physical wave before resolving it. Turkington's variational principle selects the wave through the nonlinearity of the available potential energy (APE). An exact virial partition shows that every localized wave carries more kinetic energy than APE, so a quadratic APE would favour a broadened field. The nonlinear APE enhancement, $1.27$--$2.06\times$ for the computed waves, reverses this ordering, although the preferred width remains weakly selected. From a shared KdV-derived start, a constrained Deep Ritz objective recovers the mode-1 wave, whereas strong- and weak-form residual objectives, which vanish at every exact solution and therefore do not favour the physical wave over other roots, lose the prescribed APE within one descent round. The recovered wave is under-resolved because its residual is dominated by high-wavenumber error that the energy barely penalizes, and a residual refinement at exact APE then meets every acceptance criterion. Structurally excluding mode 1 from the trial space, we compute mode-2 waves on four stratifications. A computed wave core qualitatively reproduces the two-lobe structure observed on the South China Sea shelf. In the deep basin, the selected core misses the residual criterion, and residual refinement widens it with little change in the energy objective. The two resolved linear estimates suggest weaker relative mode-1 radiation at larger ratios of wave half-width to resonant wavelength.

Title: Hardness of Unique Shortest Vectors and Bounded Distance Decoding
Author: Sergei Kudria, Jason Luo
Text_Content: We prove randomized NP-hardness of the unique shortest vector problem (uSVP) at every constant uniqueness factor greater than one, and of bounded distance decoding (BDD) at every fixed positive fraction less than one half of the minimum distance, in both their threshold decision and search versions. Both results hold in every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $1\le p<\infty$. Previous Euclidean NP-hardness results for the search versions reached uniqueness factors tending to one and decoding radii greater than the minimum distance divided by $\sqrt2$. For linear codes over every fixed finite field and each fixed ${0<ρ\le1/2}$, the decision version of BDD with radius strictly less than $ρ$ times the minimum distance is equivalent under deterministic polynomial-time reductions to satisfiability for circuits promised to have at most one satisfying input. It is therefore NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions. Earlier hardness for decoding general codes applied beyond half the minimum distance. For every fixed $p>2$ and for $p=\infty$, there is a constant $ε>0$ such that, under randomized polynomial-time reductions, uSVP in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at uniqueness factor $n^ε$, and BDD in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at radius $λ_1/n^ε$, where $n$ is the lattice rank and $λ_1$ is its minimum distance.

Title: fNIRSAtlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Classification
Author: Kalle Mäkelä, Tuukka Ruotsalo
Text_Content: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a promising modality for brain-computer interfaces and cognitive state decoding, but progress in machine learning for fNIRS has been limited by small, isolated datasets and inconsistent evaluation protocols. We introduce fNIRSAtlas, the largest open benchmark for fNIRS classification to date, comprising 23 classification tasks from 19 public data collections, spanning diverse experimental paradigms, including motor execution, motor imagery, mental arithmetic, working memory, and emotion recognition. fNIRSAtlas provides a fully automated pipeline from raw data to evaluation and defines standardized benchmark tasks for both cross-subject and within-subject classification, ensuring reproducible comparison of methods. We evaluate a variety of baseline models from fNIRS and related neuroimaging and time-series machine learning literature on the benchmark. Our results demonstrate that performance varies substantially across tasks and that methods validated on limited data -- especially deep learning approaches -- often fail to generalize beyond their original evaluation. fNIRSAtlas serves as an extensible, open, and reproducible benchmark to support more robust and cumulative progress in machine learning for fNIRS data. Our code and data can be found at https://fnirsatlas.github.io.

Title: Mosaic:montage-agnostic self-distilled graph learning for subject-independent ieeg seizure detection
Author: Arya Jalali, Mahsa Shoaran
Text_Content: Intracranial EEG provides high signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution for detecting epileptic activity, but patient-specific electrode placement leads to substantial variation in channel count and montage across subjects. This heterogeneity limits the generalization of existing detectors under subject-independent evaluation. We propose MOSAIC (MOntage-agnostic Self-distilled Adaptive Inter-channel Connectivity learning), a lightweight graph-learning framework for subject-independent iEEG seizure detection. MOSAIC pairs a shared convolutional channel encoder with a patient-agnostic channel-attention module that infers a weighted inter-channel adjacency matrix from the encoded features, requiring no fixed montage graph. An exponential moving average self-distillation objective regularizes each prediction toward a slowly updated per-patient teacher. Across four public iEEG corpora (SWEC-ETHZ long- and short-term, Mayo, FNUSA), MOSAIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in F2 and Cohen's $κ$ while learning more stable inter-channel adjacencies, demonstrating that self-distilled connectivity learning transfers across unseen implantations.

Title: FusionCLIP: Multimodal Contrastive Pretraining for Fusion Plasma Diagnostics
Author: Qiang Chen, Xiao Wang, Qingquan Yang, Hao Si, Zikang Yan, Guosheng Xu, Jin Tang
Text_Content: Visible-light videos and multivariate diagnostic signals provide complementary observations of tokamak discharges. However, existing fusion pretraining methods, primarily learn representations by reconstructing or predicting observations, leaving the correspondence between these modalities underexplored. Representation learning is further challenged by the fact that plasma-related regions occupy only part of each video frame and diagnostic variables have substantially different sampling rates. We propose FusionCLIP, a multimodal contrastive pretraining framework. Spatiotemporal Stability Selection retains informative visual tokens, while a Temporal Query Encoder integrates asynchronous diagnostic signals using their observation timestamps. Contrastive learning then aligns the two modality representations. We construct EAST Multimodal Diagnostics (EAST-MMD), comprising 1307 EAST discharges, and evaluate the model on three independently fine-tuned tasks: disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) classification, and $H_{98}$ regression. FusionCLIP achieves an aggregate score of 89.07\%, exceeding the best general-purpose pretraining configuration and an in-domain contrastive pretraining configuration without Spatiotemporal Stability Selection by 6.27 and 2.12 percentage points, respectively. Ablations and attention visualizations further support the contributions of its key components.

Title: An Effective Spoken Language Understanding Approach Leveraging Query-Adaptive Intent Detection
Author: Bing-Long Kuo, Yu-Hsuan Fang, Tien-Hong Lo, Hsueh-Wei Liao, Berlin Chen
Text_Content: Large language models enable fine-tuning-free spoken language understanding (SLU) through in-context learning, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar yet intent irrelevant demonstrations. This paper presents Query-Adaptive Intent Detection via Prototype Extraction (APEX), a two-stage retrieval framework that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves contextual exemplars within the selected intent space. Experiments on the SLURP dataset evaluate joint SLU performance using Exact Match Accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, with additional retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts. Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B, respectively, on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs, APEX also yields EMA gains of 7.66 and 2.13 percentage points. Retrieval analysis further indicates that prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.

Title: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4
Author: Manveen Kaur, Rajmeet Singh, Saeed Mozaffari, Majid Ahmadi, Shahpour Alirezaee
Text_Content: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline (YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterize both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46-0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57x, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214x, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37x. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5x more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy-throughput-energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.

Title: The ATAR, a dense and compact vertex detector for the PIONEER experiment
Author: Tilman Rohe, for the PIONEER collaboration
Text_Content: PIONEER is an approved experiment at the Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI) in Villigen, Switzerland that aims to measure the charged-pion branching ratio to electrons vs. muons with an accuracy of 0.01%. This is an order of magnitude improvement in precision compared to its predecessors and approaches the accuracy of the standard model prediction. The key elements of PIONEER are a high resolution calorimeter built concentrically around the high granularity active target (ATAR). The ATAR is composed of a stack of 48 low gain avalanche strip detectors (LGADs) to stop the beam pions and provide detailed information of the event topology. This will include precise timing (in the order of 200ps), spatial information (to an accuracy of about 60 micro meter) and pulse height information with a high dynamic range to separate pion stops from muons and MIPs. To avoid affecting the energy measurement of the positrons, the readout electronics is placed outside the acceptance angle of the calorimeter. It is composed of a fast amplifier and a fast sampling chip digitizing the LGAD wave form for real time analysis. The paper describes the PIONEER-experiment with focus on the ATAR and its readout. The status of the development and activities in 2026 will be reported.

Title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data
Author: Haojie Dong, Xinyuan Song, Xinghui Wang
Text_Content: Nonparametric expectile regression methods face new challenges from streaming data, where retaining the full dataset for batch processing becomes increasingly impractical. In this paper, we develop a scalable nonparametric expectile regression framework for varying coefficient models. We estimate the coefficient functions online via functional stochastic gradient descent with Polyak--Ruppert averaging in a product reproducing kernel Hilbert space, requiring only gradient information and one pass over the data. For this online estimator, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds, prove its optimal nonparametric convergence rate under the proposed step-size schemes, and derive its Berry--Esseen bound for pointwise asymptotic normality. To perform online inference for the varying coefficient expectile regression models, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure that perturbs the stochastic gradients with independent random weights and recursively constructs bootstrap trajectories. We establish the bootstrap consistency of the online inference procedure, yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals. Simulation studies and a real data application confirm the performance of the proposed methods.

Title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
Author: Miroslav Stibůrek, Tomáš Pikálek, Petra Ondráčková, Kristina Herzánová, Adrian Lorenz, André Gomes, Julia Henschke, Endre Levente Marosi, Bhargavi Murthy, Petra Kolbábková, Hongbo Jia, Sanja Bauer Mikulovic, Janelle Pakan, Alessio Attardo, Hana Uhlířová, Tomáš Čižmár
Text_Content: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

Title: Resolving non-neutrality across scales in a hyperdiverse tropical forest
Author: Pietro Zgaga, Pablo Villegas, Tancredi Caruso, Tommaso Gili
Text_Content: Different ecological processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Macroscopic regularities can therefore be captured by descriptions that ignore microscopic details, even when those details are mechanistically relevant to ecological processes. Here, we develop a framework inspired by statistical mechanics to track interspecific spatial correlations under spatial coarse-graining. To do so we combine random-matrix filtering with a spatially explicit neutral model. Applying this approach to eight censuses of the Barro Colorado Island tropical forest, we observe a continuous crossover from an interacting to an effectively neutral organization. Below a few tens of metres (20--35~m), the empirical correlation spectrum differs from neutral expectations, revealing scale-dependent species-specific structure. Part of this structure can be attributed to environmental heterogeneity. However, residual spatial associations provide candidate signatures of biotic interactions or other unmeasured ecological, non-neutral processes. With increasing spatial coarse-graining, empirical and neutral correlation spectra progressively converge, and above the crossover scale the neutral model provides an accurate description of the measured collective organization. Neutrality thus emerges as an effective description of the collective organization of the forest above a characteristic scale, without implying that species are equivalent at the individual level. Our framework provides an operational way to locate that scale.

Title: LEMMO: A Large Electromagnetic Model leveraging Pretrained LLMs for Million-Sample Signal Understanding
Author: Mingkai Li, Jiajun Wu, Yihan Mao, Zilin Sang, Taosong Yu, Yuan Ma, Minghe Liu, Qianqian Yang, Zhiguo Shi
Text_Content: Large language models have expanded beyond text to vision, audio, and other modalities, but understanding raw electromagnetic (EM) signals remains challenging. Wideband recordings can contain millions of samples, whereas existing waveform-based EM models are primarily evaluated on short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, leaving long-recording understanding and detailed description insufficiently explored. We introduce LEMMO, a large EM model for instruction-driven recognition and description of long raw IQ recordings. LEMMO combines a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased temporal resampling to process up to eight million complex samples. Its EM-text interaction module conditions learnable queries on instructions before retrieving signal evidence. Compact queries support recognition, while structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision organize scene-level properties, signal attributes, and cross-signal relationships for detailed description. We also construct and release a unified 1.38-TB corpus of real-world and synthetic EM signals, including LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc. Compared with MERLIN-LoRA, LEMMO improves mean EM-Bench perception accuracy by 15.77 %, mean strategy-generation ROUGE-L F1 by 4.38 points, and mean LEMMO-ShortQA accuracy by 14.31 %. It also improves categorical and numerical fact F1 on both LEMMO-LongDesc tasks while preserving its language backbone's MMLU performance. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO and https://huggingface.co/datasets/DaftJun/RFLAS, respectively.

Title: Nebula: Distributed Position-Independent Caching for LLM Serving
Author: Yifei Liu, Junbin Pan, Junhao Hu, Yang Liu, Junyi Chen, Juntong Wu, Chen Chen, Haiyuan Zhao, Xiaoxu Chen, Weihang Chen
Text_Content: Modern LLM workflows, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and LLM agents, build long prompts from multiple independent text segments, making prefill a major source of computation. Reusing KV caches is therefore important for reducing serving costs and latency: distributed caching systems spread KV cache across a cluster to increase aggregate capacity, while position-independent caching (PIC) enables reuse of recurring segments under different prefixes. However, existing systems distribute KV caches but still rely on prefix caching (PC), while existing PIC methods enable position-independent reuse without cluster-wide resource management. We present Nebula, the first distributed LLM serving framework to treat PIC segments as first-class citizens, enabling remote PIC reuse and parallel prefill. To track PIC's fine-grained, asynchronous state changes, Nebula combines optimistic accounting with event-driven updates to provide a timely and truthful cluster view for cache management and prefill scheduling. To accommodate diverse reuse patterns across workloads, Nebula leverages cluster-wide ghost-hit feedback to automatically tune the allocation of shared cache capacity between PC and PIC. Finally, Nebula incorporates queueing, computation, and KV transfer costs into a unified prefill completion time model to guide elastic parallelism adjustment and locality-aware compute placement. Across four models and four real-world RAG and agentic workloads, Nebula reduces median TTFT by an average of 61.4% compared with the strongest existing baseline and recovers an average of 76.1% of the tokens missed by prefix caching.

Title: ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation
Author: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
Text_Content: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.

Title: Interface-driven second harmonic generation in indium tin oxide/gold nanolayers: density and mass discontinuities matter
Author: J. Arya, D. Ramonell, J. Trull, N. Akozbek, M. Scalora, C. Cojocaru
Text_Content: Second harmonic generation from transparent conductive oxides and metals is traditionally attributed to Coulomb, magnetic Lorentz, and convective sources. We show that this picture is incomplete in deeply subwavelength indium tin oxide/gold bilayers. Measurements reveal two robust spectral features, a broad maximum near 1000 nm and an epsilon-near-zero peak near 1350 nm, that persist across wide variations in material and excitation parameters. Hydrodynamic-Maxwell simulations identify an interface-specific convective mechanism activated by freeelectron density and effective-mass discontinuities at the oxide-metal boundary. As electronic homogenization develops across the bilayer, the response evolves toward one described by conventional Coulomb, Lorentz, and leading convective terms. These results establish second harmonic generation as a sensitive probe of interface-driven nonlinearities and suggest a broader role for electronic discontinuities in shaping nonlinear optical processes at surface and buried material interfaces.

Title: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
Author: Mohammad Mashreghi, Mohammad Hossein Badiei, Md. Jalil Piran
Text_Content: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.

Title: Mechanical Interaction Sensing for Robotic Kiwifruit Handling with an Optoelectronic Soft Suction Cup
Author: Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Alessio Mondini, Samuel M. Youssef, Cosimo Della Santina, Gualtiero Volpe, Barbara Mazzolai
Text_Content: Robotic handling of delicate fruit benefits from compliant contact and quantitative sensing of the mechanical interaction at the end-effector. This study investigates an optoelectronic soft suction cup with a kiwifruit-specific bicomponent design for estimating interaction forces during contact with real fruit.
