Text_Content: Tuning the electron beam of a MeV-scale $γγ$ collider, first in the design and later in a digital twin of the machine, requires the beam parameters at the interaction point (IP) for many injector states. Start-to-end particle tracking is too slow for this and needs the full particle distribution, which an operating machine cannot measure. We address this problem for the 200-MeV transport line of the collider with two fast predictors. For design, second-order transfer maps from the transport entrance to the IP are applied to every particle. For a digital twin, an extremely-randomized-trees (ExtraTrees) model predicts the IP parameters from the means and rms widths of the beam at the transport entrance. On 89 held-out start-to-end simulations, the map predictor reproduces Elegant tracking for the mean energy, momentum spread, bunch length, transverse rms sizes and normalized emittances with coefficients of determination ($R^2$) of 0.97--1.00 and is ten times faster. The ExtraTrees model reaches an average $R^2$ of 0.88, compared with 0.58 when the injector settings are used as input, and performs similarly with eleven inputs that can be measured or reconstructed. Under a 2% input perturbation, the average $R^2$ of the six parameters other than the mean energy decreases only from 0.917 to 0.895, whereas the mean energy requires an accurate momentum calibration. The two predictors provide the IP-beam evaluation for the collider design and the prediction layer of a future digital twin.

Title: Should We Pay This Much for Robustness? Efficient Proxy Certificates with Marginal Guarantees
Author: Soroush H. Zargarbashi, Mohammad Sadegh Akhondzadeh, Aleksandar Bojchevski
Text_Content: Modern classifiers remain sensitive to small input perturbations, while strong model-agnostic robustness certificates such as randomized smoothing are often too expensive for deployment, requiring an extensive number (e.g. 2000) of model forward passes per input. We propose a framework that delegates certification to a cheap proxy function while statistically controlling its deviation from the original sound certificate. Given an exchangeable unlabeled calibration set, we tune the proxy via robust conformal risk control to guarantee a bounded marginal (rather than pointwise) false-approval rate: the probability, over future inputs, that the proxy accepts an input whose prediction is flipped due to perturbation. The resulting proxy certificate can be used either as a standalone marginal certificate or as a fallback mechanism that invokes the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects. We provide both single-sample and sample-heavy calibration recipes. Empirically, as a standalone certificate our method reduces the test-time certification cost to a single model forward while retaining much of the certified performance of randomized smoothing at small radii, and as a fallback it recovers the certified ratio of randomized smoothing at a more modest speedup. This enables cheap yet effective robustness guarantees for larger architectures such as vision transformers and language models.

Title: Reproducing Kernel (Quasi-)Banach Spaces with the $\ell^p$ Coefficient Norms
Author: Tianfang Wang, Guohui Song, Haizhang Zhang
Text_Content: This paper advances the theory of reproducing kernel Banach spaces (RKBSs) by investigating the general $\ell^p$ regularization framework, with a particular focus on the non-convex regime $0<p<1$. While our preceding work established the foundation for RKBSs with the $\ell^1$ norm, the pursuit of stronger sparsity---closer to the $\ell^0$ pseudo-norm---naturally motivates this exploration into $\ell^p$ quasi-norms. For $0<p<1$, we construct reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces (RKQBSs) with $\ell^p$ quasi-norms and establish existence and sparsity results for interpolation and regularized learning under appropriate assumptions. We characterize the linear and relaxed representer theorems in terms of a generalized Lebesgue constant and derive bounds under kernel decay, sample spacing, and stability assumptions. For $p>1$, we construct RKBSs using a fixed countable dictionary, establish minimizer existence, and identify the optimal relaxed representer factor through an off-sample coefficient operator. These results reveal fundamental differences between the regimes $0<p<1$, $p=1$, and $p>1$. Numerical experiments compare the accuracy and sparsity of solutions for these three cases.

Title: Precision - Preserving Subtensor Inference for a 22B Joint Audio - Video Generator under a Fixed GPU Working Set
Author: Hanyue Shen, Xinling Liao
Text_Content: Complete-block offloading reduces model residency but requires each transferred block to fit the GPU budget. We present Precision-Preserving Subtensor Inference (PSI), a fixed-arena runtime that combines sub-block weight streaming with separately managed intermediate state for the BF16 LTX-2.5 22B joint audio-video transformer. The contribution is a construction whose managed GPU footprint is determined by reusable pages, live state, and bounded workspace, together with controls that separate resource use, transport correctness, and numerical fidelity. Its partitioned operators preserve the dense real-arithmetic construction under stated assumptions. Across nine matched full-prompt cases on RTX A6000, modified PSI reduces sampled transformer-process peak memory from 8,578 to 360 MiB relative to official MATH, while mean time for the eleven transformer invocations rises from 247.11 to 349.00 s. Its managed arena is 80 MiB. Complete native generation and a complete-block FLASH path both succeed under a fixed 3 GiB available-memory cap. The matched A6000 comparison and separate DGX Spark service suite both achieve 100% success in complete audiovisual decoding. FFN reuse lowers mean block time by 4.0% with unchanged BF16 outputs; a fixed-arithmetic one-token transport control preserves all saved states bitwise. Targeted bias and attention changes improve local and one-token numerical comparisons, while mean endpoint error increases across nine full-prompt cases. The construction enables BF16 audiovisual inference with an explicit transformer-memory budget and makes numerical fidelity a separate, testable property of the implementation.

Title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
Author: Guangyu Chen, Jingyun Zeng, Hui Jiang
Text_Content: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL

Title: Zero-Point Renormalization Reshapes the Shift Current: The Role of Electron-Phonon Coupling
Author: Yang Li, Zuzhang Lin, Zhikuan Wang, Chengzhi Wu, Zeyu Jiang, Bing Huang
Text_Content: Shift current (SC) drives the bulk photovoltaic effect, holding promise for near-instantaneous, low-dissipation photodetection and energy conversion. The current understanding of SC relies primarily on a single-particle picture, in which the SC is determined purely by band dispersion. While many-body effects from directly excited quasiparticles, such as excitons, magnons and phonons, have been explored, the renormalization of electronic states by quantum virtual-phonon coupling --- inherent in essentially all solids and particularly decisive for transport --- remains unaddressed. Here, using first-principles calculations, we identify this missing channel --- band-renormalized shift current (BRSC) --- in monolayer MoS2. We find that the zero-point renormalization alone, without any polarization-carrying photoexcited phonons and with barely any alteration of the band dispersion, dramatically reshapes the SC spectrum: emergent low-energy peaks arise from phonon-assisted optical transitions between momentum-distinct states, with a pronounced redshift of higher-energy features. A mere 1.0% strain sharply tunes the BRSC, whereas raising the temperature enhances it. Our findings overturn the band-structure-only paradigm, establishing electron-phonon coupling as an indispensable ingredient for nonlinear photocurrent and opening a strain-thermal route for engineering next-generation optoelectronic responses.

Title: Closed analytical formulas for the Ashley-Ritchie-Brandt and Jackson-McCarthy polarization functions
Author: J. M. Fernández-Varea, A. Fernández-Mrosko
Text_Content: The $Z_{1}^{3}$ correction in the Bethe-Bloch formula that quantifies the electronic stopping power of matter for heavy charged particles is revisited. This correction accounts for the Barkas-Andersen effect. Ashley, Ritchie and Brandt (ARB) wrote it in terms of a non-relativistic polarization function, and Jackson and McCarthy (JM) obtained the relativistic counterpart. Both expressions involve intricate triple integrals. The present manuscript describes how the polarization functions of JM and ARB can be reduced to compact analytical formulas. The corresponding asymptotic behaviours are also found. The accuracy of two currently-used empirical fits to the ARB and JM polarization functions is assessed.

Title: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
Author: Guan Zhe Hong, Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Liang Chen, Yangchen Pan, Junchi Yu, Jialin Yu, Philip Torr, Yi Ren
Text_Content: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD's learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.

Title: Probabilistic Relevance Decisions for Semantic Retrieval
Author: Bahadır Tatar, Cevat Şener
Text_Content: Dense similarity supplies reusable corpus representations, while probabilistic relevance decisions offer query-dependent document scoring. We compare dense-only BGE-M3 with TypeSafe Jev Noul and OpenAI Decisions Predicate scores on the official BEIR SciFact test benchmark. The study evaluates 300 official test queries using identical positive-enriched 100-document pools and full-corpus dense retrieval followed by reranking at candidate depths of 50 and 100. Unlike the controlled pools, neither dense prefix receives positive injection. Jev has the highest observed Recall@5 and nDCG@10 under the evaluated conditions. At depth 50, full-corpus nDCG@10 is 0.6413 for BGE-M3, 0.7545 with OpenAI and 0.7805 with Jev. Extending depth from 50 to 100 increases known-positive candidate recall but produces small, uncertain final-effectiveness changes. All four paired-bootstrap depth intervals include zero. Unique-condition API scoring cost approximately doubles, while compatible cached decisions reduce incremental expenditure. OpenAI returns many exact-zero scores, and secondary exact-tie randomization reveals ranking sensitivity without replacing deterministic primary results. Top-100 latency mixes cached and new execution. Historical hybrid latency is a saved-component sum under different execution environments and timer boundaries. These exploratory, unadjusted analyses support relevance decisions as a complement to dense retrieval within this protocol, without establishing general superiority, probability calibration or equivalence between depths.

Title: Development of Anthropomorphic Arm for collaborative and Home Service Robot CHARMIE
Author: Hafiz Adil, Tiago Ribeiro, Antonio Ribeiro, Carolina Lopes, Joana Coelho, Gil Lopes, Fernando Ribeiro
Text_Content: Service Robots are becoming a reality and are progressing by leaps and bounds. Alongside this avenue of robotics is also the field of prosthetics, which is evolving rapidly. These topics are hot cakes in the industry and are widely developed. Some have one quality, and some have others, but are making a shoreline towards success. The development of arm and hand as individual or as a package is becoming common as more and more advanced collaborative robots come to the surface and join their human counterparts in the real world. This dissertation presents an open-source 3D-printed arm which was assembled and programmed on two fronts. The first is the control of the hand by utilising teleoperation with a camera and ML-based hand pose estimation. Secondly, it is the control via kinematics utilising the Denavit-Hartenberg method to define the motion and to find the position of the end effector in 3D space.

Title: Symmetry-Aware Surrogate-Assisted Testing of UAVs
Author: Anas Shrinah, Chris Bennett, Kerstin Eder
Text_Content: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by trans- forming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordi- nate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.

Title: Route-DMD: Distribution Matching Distillation with Task-Routed Mechanism for Speech Foundation Models
Author: Yanru Huo, Zhikang Niu, Wenming Tu, Junxi Liu, Tian Tan, Shan Yang, Yipeng Kang, Ziyang Ma, Xie Chen, Zilong Zheng
Text_Content: Speech foundation models built on flow matching handle generation, editing, and processing in one system, but every request costs 20-50 iterative steps, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) doubles each of them. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains a student that approaches the teacher's quality in a few steps, yet existing speech distillation work applies it to generation alone. We show that a distribution-matching objective does not serve every task: in separation, the noised states of erroneous student outputs deviate far from the teacher's training distribution, where its prediction is unreliable. Route-DMD therefore makes the objective task-dependent, routing the affected tasks to a regression loss and keeping decoupled distribution matching elsewhere. The student is initialized by consistency distillation, and teacher rollouts use adaptive projected guidance (APG) instead of CFG. Without CFG, the 4-step student matches the 32-step teacher on generation, editing, and processing tasks at a 4.5$\times$ end-to-end speedup.

Title: Quantum transport of vortex electrons in bending magnets and circular accelerators
Author: D. Karlovets, I. Pavlov, A. Murtazin, D. Grosman, X. Chen
Text_Content: Controlling the sizes and phase structure of single-particle wave packets in accelerators remains an experimental challenge and requires understanding how bending magnets transform these states. An important example is transporting relativistic vortex electrons through the magnets to a collision point while keeping a narrow orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) distribution. We derive an effective Hamiltonian that accounts for the packet acceleration, employ it to obtain a generalized BMT-like equation, match the electron state at both magnet boundaries, and calculate the mean OAM and its variance. A half turn can reverse the mean OAM relative to the momentum while broadening its distribution, so recovering the mean does not ensure state recovery. We identify windows in packet sizes and bend angles for a small OAM spread and show that weak bends can produce narrow distributions with the mean OAM tilted relative to the momentum, making these states candidates for spatiotemporal vortices. For a few MeV electrons, we propose to use half-turn magnets that leave the mean OAM nearly antiparallel to the momentum while keeping its distribution narrow. For a circular orbit in a uniform field, the OAM variance after the exit grows as $N^2$ over $N$ turns, favoring linear accelerators, such as LINAC at JINR, for first experiments in MeV range.

Title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
Author: Adnan Takriti, Mahmoud Sadeq, Quentin Rouxel, Daniele Cafolla, Michael Mistry, Carlo Tiseo
Text_Content: Physical human--robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.

Title: Automatic keyphrase extraction and annotation: modern theoretical approaches and practical solutions for text and speech
Author: Daria Guseva, Olga Mitrofanova
Text_Content: The exponential growth of textual and audiovisual information has made the task of automatic keyphrase extraction (KE) increasingly significant. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of contemporary theoretical approaches and practical solutions for KE across both text and speech modalities. The primary contribution of this work is its systematic synthesis of these often-disparate research strands into a unified analytical framework, highlighting the evolution of the field from statistical methods towards large language models (LLMs) and end-to-end speech processing. We examine the stages of KE, the characteristics of keyphrases in written and spoken language, and terminological nuances. Various methods for automatic KE are discussed and analyzed in detail: statistical, hybrid, machine learning-based, and structural. The review dedicates substantial attention to emerging paradigms, including keyphrase generation using LLMs, and provides a detailed overview of methodologies and challenges in automatic corpus annotation. Furthermore, we specifically analyze current directions and inherent difficulties in KE for spoken language, comparing transcript based and end-to-end acoustic approaches. This synthesis leads us to conclude that the field is moving towards a more integrated, context-aware paradigm. Future progress will depend on addressing key challenges such as data scarcity for low-resource languages, effective multimodal fusion, and the nuanced evaluation of generative KE systems.

Title: Deformable Contact-Aware 3D Object Placement
Author: Songhe Wang, David Miller, Charles A. Kamhoua
Text_Content: Current language-guided 3D object placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose, ignoring the physical reality that indoor placements are dictated by contact. Consequently, predicted poses often float, interpenetrate supports, or fail to deform soft surfaces. We propose Deformable Contact-Aware Placement (DCAP), a framework that reframes placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process. Rather than predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale, and deformable components, allowing a coupled rigid-deformable simulator to settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization. Evaluated on a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases, DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements, it improves VLM Physics & Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, while reducing mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared to simulated rollout baselines, DCAP reduces residual speed by 72.1%. Ultimately, our results prove that physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.

Title: When GeoFMs Meet VHR: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Very High Resolution Earth Observation Imagery
Author: Kshitij Raj Sharma, Pierre Adorni, Minh-Tan Pham, Dirk Tiede, Sébastien Lefèvre
Text_Content: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.

Title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
Author: Makoto Takamoto, Chaitanya Sampara, Viktor Zaverkin, Daniel Oñoro-Rubio, Mathias Niepert
Text_Content: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

Title: Atomic Parity Violation: Standard Model Tests
Author: Jacinda Ginges, Anastasia Borschevsky
Text_Content: Atomic parity violation (APV) offers a sensitive high-precision, low-energy test of the Standard Model and a powerful probe of new physics. It played a significant role in confirming the nature of the neutral weak currents, and gives unique information about fundamental weak parameters and possible new physics, reaching energies well into the TeV scale and beyond. In this chapter, we provide a pedagogical introduction to the fascinating field of APV. The underlying mechanisms are introduced, an overview of past and ongoing experiments is presented, including prospects for measuring parity violation in molecules, and the critical role of electronic structure theory in interpreting the experiments is described. The importance of the nuclear anapole moment and other nuclear-spin-dependent parity-violating contributions for understanding nuclear structure and weak nuclear forces is highlighted. We discuss the current challenges and identify the most important and pressing goals in this field, which promises exciting discoveries in the coming years.

Title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
Author: Jiming Su, Feng Zhu, Yuhao Xiao, Miao Zhang
Text_Content: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.

Title: Ultra-Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation via Knowledge Distillation in Label-Scarce Domains
Author: Rahim Ullah, Hasan Abbas, Syed Waqar Nabi
Text_Content: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: https://github.com/2802990u/tinyunet3d-dist-kd.

Title: Reviving the Discarded High-Resolution Feature for Transformer-Based Tiny Object Detection
Author: Zehao Wang, Si Wu, Guiping Cao, Xin Li, Yaowei Wang
Text_Content: Tiny object detection remains challenging because tiny instances occupy only a few pixels, and their fine-grained details are easily lost during feature downsampling. Although the highest-resolution feature preserves rich local details for tiny objects, DETR-like detectors often discard it due to its large computational cost, while directly reintroducing this feature also brings dense background noise. To address this problem, we propose ReDHF, a novel framework that Revives the Discarded High-resolution Feature for tiny object detection. ReDHF has three cooperative components. Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion (CSDF) first constructs a semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature and injects its fine-grained details into the shallow feature under a moderate cost. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) then guides the enhanced feature to learn more reliable classification and localization priors by applying geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision. Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI) further enables decoder queries to access both low-level details and high-level semantic information, allowing them to aggregate richer cues for tiny objects. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks. The best ReDHF variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone, and +1.5 AP on SODA-D, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects.

Title: Direct calculation of dipole moment surfaces through second-order symmetry-adapted perturbation theory for properties
Author: Bartosz Tyrcha, Marcin Stachowiak, Konrad Patkowski, Piotr S. Żuchowski
Text_Content: Interaction-induced dipole moment surfaces are vital for calculating line intensities and collision-induced absorption coefficients for van der Waals complexes. We introduce the perturbative corrections, of second order with respect to the interaction operator, to the dipole moment (or, in general, any one-electron property) change due to noncovalent interactions. These are obtained in the spirit of the symmetry-adapted perturbation theory for properties (propSAPT) method, developed recently by some of us [B. Tyrcha et al., JCTC 21(9), 4562--4578 (2025)]. When orbital relaxation effects due to the external property field are properly introduced, these can be understood as analytical derivatives of the second-order SAPT interaction energies. We apply the newly introduced formalism to calculations of dipole moment surfaces for three light van der Waals complexes: He...Ar, He...H$_2$ and the H$_2$ dimer. The propSAPT method is compared against finite-field SAPT calculations and finite-field supermolecular CCSD(T) as the reference.

Title: Orientation and slip statistics of spheroids settling in turbulence
Author: Anubhab Roy
Text_Content: Small spheroids settling through turbulence are turned broadside-on by fluid inertia and tilted away by velocity gradients. We describe their orientation and slip statistics through the crossover from random orientation to alignment, in the overdamped limit. With quasi-static Stokes drag the leading inertial torque is an exact gradient flow on the orientation sphere, its potential quadratic in the cosine of the tilt and only rescaled by mobility anisotropy. The orientation performs an overdamped random walk in a quadratic well, and isotropic Gaussian white noise gives exactly a Boltzmann distribution. For forcing of finite correlation time, a closure keeps this form with its width set by linear response; it recovers the uniform density as settling vanishes and, for fixed-orientation forcing statistics, the aligned coefficient of rapid-settling theory, and errs most in the crossover. The root-mean-square lateral slip peaks where the alignment rate approaches the Kolmogorov rate, as faster settling strengthens the sideways drift at a given tilt but suppresses the tilt; the nearly shape-independent ratio, which tensor-forced simulations reproduce, lets a measured peak constrain the torque coefficient or dissipation rate for given forcing statistics. Dissipation intermittency enters as a lognormal superposition of Boltzmann distributions, which fattens the tails but leaves the leading aligned mean-square tilt unchanged. The superposition reproduces the shape of plate orientation distributions from direct numerical simulations, where a single Boltzmann distribution fails; published moments confirm the predicted spread beyond the weakest torques, and at strong alignment the measured fourth-order tilt moment lies between the two predictions.

Title: Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation for Wind Energy Predictive Analysis
Author: Purbak Sengupta, Aparna S. varde, Emil Jørgensen Njor
Text_Content: Resource-constrained cyber-physical decision systems often apply fixed sensing, knowledge, and computational pipelines despite state-dependent information needs. We introduce Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation (MSKC), a resource-aware computing principle: select the least-costly route meeting decision-risk and deployment constraints, escalating only when cheaper routes are insufficient. As proof of concept, we isolate adaptive knowledge routing, the decision underlying Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (KGML), which conventionally injects external knowledge unconditionally rather than only where needed. We instantiate this for wind ramp-event predictive analysis, an edge-oriented decision-support task, evaluating local, relational, and physics-informed routes with a state-aware gate on publicly available real data from two wind farms. We establish conditions for feasibility preservation, cost dominance, and strict expected savings over always-on routing. At a 35.9% relational-knowledge injection rate, adaptive routing is statistically indistinguishable from always-on injection on the reported metrics while reducing knowledge calls by 64%, supporting sustainable, Green-IT-aligned deployment. These results support MSKC's premise that uniformly maximal intelligence is unnecessary. This offers intelligent data analysis for big data streams: the analysis itself decides, per state, how much knowledge and computation the data warrant.

Title: Compression Through a Context Lens: Evaluating Adaptation, Quantization, and Distillation in Arabic Legal LLMs
Author: Md. Rafiul Biswas, George Mikros, Wajdi Zaghouani
Text_Content: Model compression can facilitate the deployment of large language models in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain-specific performance may depend on the evaluation protocol. We investigate this issue using ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, under both with-context and no-context evaluation. The former provides supporting legal passages, while the latter assesses performance without external context. Removing the context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. We examine three stages: domain adaptation, quantization, and knowledge distillation across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Four-bit quantization reduces model memory by 64-71%, with changes in no-context MCQ accuracy ranging from -3.2 to +1.6 percentage points. Distillation produces more variable results, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR achieves 76.6% no-context accuracy, compared with 77.2% for its teacher. Our findings suggest that no-context evaluation provides a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing the effects of adaptation and compression on Arabic legal language models.

Title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
Author: Charalampos M. Liapis, Epameinondas Panagopoulos
Text_Content: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

Title: How Far Can Lightweight LLMs Go in Intent-to-SLO Translation?
Author: Sabbir Ahmed, Hazem Abbas, Salimur Choudhury
Text_Content: Intent-based networking (IBN) promises QoS provisioning in which the network derives the configuration from operator-stated goals. Its first step, translating a natural-language intent into enforceable service-level objectives (SLOs) grounded in a live snapshot of the network state, increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs). These large models add cost and energy to the management loop and typically require multi-GPU, cloud-hosted infrastructure. Can lightweight open LLMs take over this step dependably? We answer this question with a five-dimensional evaluation of ten LLMs with <10B parameters from five families, under four prompting setups, on 716 placement intents. We evaluate translation performance, intent validation, hallucination, energy impact, and robustness to diverse phrasing. The best configurations translate intents with a strict F1 of 0.943 and reject up to 191 of 195 invalid intents. With few-shot reasoning, the strongest models hallucinate unsupported QoS requirements in only about one response in a hundred, whereas the zero-shot setup struggles. A translated intent costs 0.044-0.148 Wh of GPU energy without reasoning, and added energy cost for reasoning pays off for the weaker models. Furthermore, we show that realistic rephrasing lowers the rejection of invalid intents in 15 of 16 configurations for the best-performing models, leaving robust intent validation as a key open challenge for reliable IBN. Our code and data are available: https://github.com/ggck43/intent2slo.

Title: Solving Linear Programs in the Matrix Multiplication Time
Author: Zhao Song
Text_Content: We give a randomized algorithm for feasible bounded-box linear programs with $n$ variables and $d\le n=O(d)$ linearly independent equality constraints. For additive accuracy $ε$, its expected running time is $O((n^ω+n^2\log n)\log(1/ε))$, where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. This answers the matrix-multiplication-time open question posted in Song's Ph.D. thesis [Son19] in this setting.

Title: Perception Over Geometry: Rethinking Gaussian Allocation in Mesh-based Splatting
Author: Yuting Wang, Yang Zhao, Shanding Diao, Penglin Wang, Yuan Chen, Wei Jia, Ronggang Wang
Text_Content: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel-view synthesis but lacks explicit topology for geometric editing. Existing mesh-based methods enable geometric manipulation by associating Gaussians with triangular mesh faces, typically assigning a fixed number of Gaussians to each face. However, the representation capacity required for appearance reconstruction depends on local appearance complexity rather than merely on mesh tessellation density. To address these limitations, we propose P-MGS, a framework that separates appearance modeling from geometric control to achieve high quality rendering, compact representation, and flexible mesh editing. P-MGS introduces a perceptual complexity guided allocation strategy that distributes Gaussians according to surface appearance demand estimated from multiview observations. To preserve reconstruction flexibility, Gaussians are optimized without mesh constraints and subsequently associated with the original mesh through post hoc binding, retaining adaptive refinement while preserving mesh topology. During mesh editing, local affine deformation transfer updates Gaussian centers and covariances under mesh deformation, reducing misalignment and floating artifacts. Experiments demonstrate superior average novel view synthesis quality with fewer Gaussians and coherent mesh editing.

Title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
Author: Yingjie Tan, Haiquan Qiu, Quanming Yao, Manyi Zhong, Xianzhi Yu, Yaqing Wang
Text_Content: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.

Title: Stealthy Malicious Interference Detection in UAV Formations: A Power-Domain Signaling Game Approach
Author: Jianle Ba, Shaolong Guo, Yuntao Wang, Xin Wu, Zhou Su, Zhendong Li
Text_Content: Reliable intra-swarm communication is fundamental to cooperative sensing, control, and mission execution in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms. In open low-altitude shared-spectrum environments, coexisting UAVs may cause benign interference through spectrum reuse and signal leakage, while jamming UAVs may deliberately degrade critical intra-swarm links. Since a jamming UAV can adjust its transmit power to disguise signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) degradation as link fluctuation in benign interference, stealthy jammer UAV detection remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel belief-driven stealthy jammer UAV detection scheme from the perspective of Bayesian security game. To capture stealthy interference in shared-spectrum UAV swarms, the interfering UAV is modeled as a hidden benign or jamming type, whose transmit power strategy induces the SINR observed by the defender. The defender updates its posterior belief from the observed SINR and decides whether to maintain normal operation or trigger defensive power boosting. We characterize pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) conditions under separating structures with distinguishable type and pooling structures with indistinguishable observations. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme improves the defender's expected utility compared to the conventional schemes.

Title: GMD-Mamba: Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation Using a Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba
Author: Rahim Ullah, Hasan Abbas, Hazrat Ali, Syed Waqar Nabi
Text_Content: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.

Title: An Overview of Classical Scattering by a Lennard-Jones Potential
Author: Tiago Kroetz
Text_Content: We present a numerical and conceptual overview of classical scattering under a Lennard-Jones potential. All results were obtained by direct integration of particle trajectories in the two-dimensional plane for varying impact parameters and energies. From these trajectories, we compute deflection functions, identify critical values associated with unstable circular orbits, and visualize non-monotonic behavior in the angular deflection. We construct color maps representing the deflection angle and interaction delay time as functions of energy and impact parameter, and determine the differential cross section from the deflection function, accounting for multi-valued contributions. These results are displayed both as individual plots and as a full color map in the energy-angle plane, providing a detailed picture of the scattering behavior in this central potential.

Title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Maximum Number of Linear Regions of Piecewise-Linear Kolmogorov--Arnold networks
Author: Ye Su, Yong Liu
Text_Content: Schoots et al.~\citep{schoots2025relating} (AISTATS 2025) established a generally loose upper bound on the number of linear regions of continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), without providing a lower bound. We consider a $T$-layer network with width vector $\mathbf n=(n_0,\ldots,n_T)$, input dimension $n_0=d$, output width $n_T=1$, and at most $k\geq2$ affine segments per edge. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the tight growth order $Θ_{\mathbf n}(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}ρ_{\ell-1}})$ in $k$, where $ρ_{\ell-1}:=\min_{0\leq s\leq\ell-1}n_s$. When every hidden width is at least $d$, the tight order simplifies to $Θ_{\mathbf n}(k^{dT})$. The upper bound of \citep{schoots2025relating} is $k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell}$. Our upper bound improves it by a factor of $Θ_{\mathbf n}\!\left(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell-\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}ρ_{\ell-1}} \right)$, with strict asymptotic improvement whenever a hidden layer has width greater than one. We further compare CPWL KANs with rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks using dense parameterizations with at most $Λ$ parameters per model and the same fixed nonlinear depth $T$. Counting trainable knot locations and optimizing the widths and $k$, we prove that the maximum region count of CPWL KANs divided by that of ReLU networks is $Θ_{d,T}(Λ^{d\lfloor T/2\rfloor})$ as $Λ\to\infty$, yielding a polynomial advantage for KANs when $T\geq2$. These tight bounds characterize the attainable geometric complexity of CPWL KANs, providing a foundation for understanding their expressive power and guiding architectural design.

Title: A Little Derandomization Goes a Long Way: Unconditional Circuit Lower Bounds using Low-Degree PIT
Author: Nikolai Chukhin, Karthik Gajulapalli, Alexander Golovnev, Ivan Mihajlin

Title: ArcadeDB in Python: An In-Process Multi-Model Database
Author: Taewoon Kim
Text_Content: Some Python workflows need transactional reads and writes over documents, traversals over a graph, and similarity search over vector embeddings. In practice these are split across separate systems (a document store, a graph engine, and a vector index), and the data is copied between them and kept consistent by application code. ArcadeDB is an open-source multi-model database engine, written in Java, that supports all three access patterns and can be embedded in a host process. We present arcadedb-embedded, a Python package that runs ArcadeDB inside the Python process via JPype, using a Java Runtime Environment bundled in the wheel. One pip install gives a database with documents, a property graph, and vector search, and needs no Java installation. Query results can be returned as Python lists, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, or Arrow tables. We demonstrate a hybrid retrieval workflow that chains vector search, SQL filtering, and graph traversal over one dataset. We benchmark arcadedb-embedded against SQLite, DuckDB, LadybugDB, and Chroma, and report its costs.

Title: Estimating Vertical Ocean Velocity from Horizontal Currents: Linear and Depth-Conditional Neural-Network Approaches on a High-Resolution Regional Ocean Model
Author: Francesco M. Ventrella, Cristóbal López, Emilio Hernandez-Garcia
Text_Content: The vertical component of the ocean velocity, w, is several orders of magnitude smaller than the horizontal components u and v, yet it controls vertical tracer transport, upwelling, and mixed-layer ventilation. Because w is extremely difficult to measure directly and is normally obtained only diagnostically from the continuity equation, predicting it from the horizontal velocity field is a problem of both practical and physical interest. We address this problem with two data-driven methods, a physically-motivated linear baseline and a convolutional neural network conditioned on depth through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). Both methods are applied to a high-resolution regional simulation of the Coastal and Regional Ocean Community model over the Western Mediterranean, using a sub-region of the south-west Mediterranean Sea as a training region and two independent, out-of-sample regions for validation: the Alboran Sea, with a distinct dynamical regime driven by Atlantic inflow through the Strait of Gibraltar, and a transition region between Almería and Cartagena, between the Alboran Sea and the open western Mediterranean. Once the FiLM network is regularized enough to avoid overfitting to a single training domain, we find that its comparison with the physically interpretable linear baseline is domain- and depth-dependent rather than uniform: near the reference depth, essentially all of the achievable out-of-sample performance on both validation domains is already captured by the linear model, but at the deepest levels tested the FiLM network outperforms the linear baseline on the transition domain, whereas on Alboran it does not.

Title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
Author: Jona Nagerl, Younes Naceur, Natalia G. Berloff
Text_Content: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.

Title: High resolution 3D localization of ultrasound sparse sources using a SAGE algorithm
Author: Sophie V. Heymans, François Rottenberg, Tatiana Gelvez-Barrera, Adrian Basarab, Barbara Nicolas
Text_Content: Reliable localization and characterization of cavitation activity are central to many ultrasound imaging and therapy monitoring applications. Passive acoustic mapping (PAM) can estimate cavitation distributions without prior assumptions but remains limited by the system point spread function. While advanced PAM methods improve spatial resolution, their performance may degrade for transient emissions with uncertain emission times. In this work, we propose a parametric source localization framework based on the Space-Alternating Generalized Expectation-Maximization (SAGE) algorithm to estimate source positions and emitted waveforms directly from array channel data. A greedy source extraction and localization procedure is first used to initialize the model order and source parameters, after which SAGE iteratively refines each source estimate. The proposed method was validated on 49 simulated acquisitions containing up to seven simultaneously emitting sources with emission time uncertainties of 12 microseconds, achieving a source localization precision of 0.24 mm (standard deviation of the total localization error). Experimental evaluation on proton-induced nanodroplet vaporization data acquired with an ultrasound matrix array demonstrated improved spatial resolution compared to a beamforming-based approach and sub-millimeter agreement between vaporization maps and the proton distribution in all three spatial dimensions. These results highlight the potential of parametric source localization for high-resolution proton therapy monitoring and provide a general framework for the localization of simultaneously emitting sparse ultrasound sources.

Title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
Author: Adam Y. Shavit
Text_Content: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.

Title: Time-Indexed Skill Success Models for Latency-Aware Skill Selection and Timing in Dynamic Manipulation
Author: Mohsen Omidi, Maria Chiara Leva, Brian Vaughan
Text_Content: Robots that manipulate moving objects act on observations that are outdated when the chosen skill starts, and the best skill can change within a few hundred milliseconds. Skill competence models, however, predict success for a launch at the moment of observation. We propose time-indexed skill success models, which predict whole-task success when a skill is launched after a given delay. Trained on rollouts branched at a grid of launch delays, they let a receding-horizon planner select both the skill and its launch time under fixed or random latency. In a MuJoCo study in which a UR5e captures a sliding puck with three skills, the planner exceeded a static competence model by 2.8 to 6.2 percentage points at 100 to 300 ms of latency, including when that model was evaluated on point or sampled forecasts of the launch state. Across five complete runs (three training seeds and two distribution shifts), all 80 paired 95% intervals against four baselines excluded zero. On delayed launches, the time-indexed model was calibrated (expected calibration error 0.009 against 0.239), and pausing the world during latency overstated success by up to 23 points. On a real UR5e that captures a rolling ball after 0.2 s of injected latency, a static model trained in a hardware-matched simulator predicted 99% success on a prespecified subset of 35 delayed launches that it rated at least 0.8. Of these, 63% succeeded (95% interval 46 to 77%), and the time-indexed model predicted 56%. In this single-skill, predictable regime, a matched physics-based forecast was also well calibrated.

Title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
Author: Yifan Luo, Zhengying Liu, Yang Yuan, Zhilin Yang, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao
Text_Content: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $ρ=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

Title: Bri3D: Bridging the Object-Scene Gap in Single-Image 3D Generation via Scene-Anchor
Author: Hongye Hou, Shuai Zhang, Hongjie Li, Zhuoxiao Li, Haiping Wang, Yuan Liu, Wufan Zhao
Text_Content: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.

Title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
Author: Guhan Chen, Bohan Li, Jun Rao, Hejin Wang, Songtao Tian, Yexin Xie, Xiaojun Meng, Peng Yuan, Jiansheng Wei, Xuebo Liu, Zixiong Yu
Text_Content: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.

Title: Rotation Is Token-Blind: A Structural Criterion for Post-Training Quantization of Feed-Forward Geometry Transformers
Author: Huanfei He, Bohao Zhang, Jiaxin Zhang, Wei Sui, John See, Zeyd Boukhers, Cong Yang
Text_Content: Feed-forward 3D models use Transformers to predict camera poses, depth, and structure in one pass, avoiding iterative multi-view optimization. Long sequences and deep attention incur high compute and memory costs, motivating Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) for deployment. Existing PTQ methods mainly suppress channel-wise outliers by smoothing or orthogonal rotation. Geometry Transformers introduce a different challenge: heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid. A few special tokens may exert high leverage over global outputs and be updated by only a subset of blocks. Token-blind transforms, which apply the same transformation to every token, reduce overall quantization error but cannot remove differentiated degradation across token types. We propose QMapAnything, a structure-aware PTQ framework. We cast floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing as a token-blind reparameterization group, and prove that they yield common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. We introduce a statistic $Γ$ that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage and output leverage to predict whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation. Experiments on geometric benchmarks show that W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by $2.2$--$3.1\times$ versus FP32, with up to $3.1\times$ speedup on real hardware. These results provide a principled and efficient approach to deploying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models in resource-constrained edges.

Title: Phase-Matched Design of Pinching-Antenna Elements on a 60-GHz Dielectric Rod Waveguide
Author: Stylianos D. Asimonis, Dimitrios Tyrovolas, Spyridon Daskalakis, Nikos C. Sagias, Donal P. Lynch, George K. Karagiannidis
Text_Content: The radiation of pinching antennas, dielectric elements placed on a dielectric waveguide, depends on the element shape. We explain it with a phase-matching, or prism-coupler, picture: the guided rod mode couples into the denser antenna plate at an angle set by the plate-mode effective index, about 31 degrees at 60 GHz, and radiates through the face it reaches first. This yields a simple sizing rule linking element height to contact length. Rectangular, isosceles and right-triangular elements of equal contact length and height are compared from 53 to 67 GHz in full-wave openEMS simulations including the waveguide-to-rod transitions. The rectangle peaks sharply at the rule, reaching 15.9 dBi. The right triangle keeps its gain within 0.7 dB and its side lobes at least 10 dB down over a two-to-one height range. At the rule, both outperform the isosceles element by 1.2 to 2.1 dB, and all remain matched.

Title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
Author: Yao Huang, Yichi Zhang, Yifan Wang, Yitong Sun, Haoyu Dong, Jifan Ma, Jinzhe Tu, Xiaojian Li, Sören Mindermann, Wei Xu, Yinpeng Dong
Text_Content: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.

Title: The Containment Polytope of a Triangle and a Convex Polygon
Author: Yoonsung Choi, Sunghee Choi
Text_Content: The containment polytope $\mathcal{C}$ for a triangle $P$ and a convex $n$-gon $Q$ is a four-dimensional polytope representing the similarity transforms (translation, rotation, scaling) that place $P$ inside $Q$. While it is known that the complexity of $\mathcal{C}$ and its silhouette $Λ$, which represents all the largest placements of $P$ inside $Q$ for all orientations, can be quadratic in $n$, we show that the silhouette can be partitioned into a linear number of planar convex chains and steps in $O(n \log n)$ time. Based on the linear number of convex chains and steps, we can compute the complexity of silhouette $Λ$ in $O(n \log n)$ time and query the largest placement of $P$ inside $Q$ for a given orientation in $O(\log n)$ time. We explain geometrically how the triangle $P$ rotates while continuously scaling and translating to be maximal inside $Q$, leading to a parameterized algorithm for containment problems.

Title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
Author: Hardik Rajpal, Dan Goodman
Text_Content: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.

Title: Requirements Nobody Wrote Down: Emergence in a Public-Sector ML Pipeline
Author: Ronivaldo Ferreira, Vinicius Costa Girard, Cleidson de Souza, Igor Steinmacher, Carla Aguiar, Filipe Roseiro Cogo, Gustavo Pinto
Text_Content: Governments increasingly use machine learning (ML) to handle data volumes beyond their analytical capacity, yet little is known about how requirements arise and evolve as an ML experiment moves toward operational use. Requirements Engineering (RE) for ML often assumes that requirements can be elicited upfront; in the public sector, however, demands arrive vague, stakeholders speak different professional languages, and what counts as a ``good'' result is unknown in advance. We report a 15-month case study of a thematic classification pipeline for Brazil's national digital participation platform, which holds over 60,000 citizen proposals, triangulating 43 project artifacts with interviews of six project participants. Institutional demands arrived as broad goals, endorsed but not sponsored, and only 40\% of the 95 reconstructed requirements and criteria were ever formalized. The pipeline's key requirements emerged largely from experiments, model outputs, and integration work, shaped by technical decisions and institutional constraints; the central one, the classification categories, was settled by a government taxonomy chosen for its institutional legitimacy. Acceptance relied on technical metrics, domain judgment, and political assessment, without shared thresholds or validation of usefulness in practice. In public-sector ML, technical and institutional artifacts thus act as elicitation instruments, and experimentation and integration belong to the requirements process.

Title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
Author: Dang-Khoa Bui, Quang-Huy Tran, Minh-Khoi Nguyen-Bui, Duc-Tuan Ngo, Thanh-Trong Tran, Tuan-Khoi Nguyen, Hoang-Anh Ngo
Text_Content: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

Title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse
Author: Shimaa Ibrahim, Mabrouka Bessghaier, Md. Rafiul Biswas, Insaf Elouard, Wajdi Zaghouani
Text_Content: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $κ= 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($κ= 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($κ= 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.

Title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
