Sequential composition multiplies both components, while aggregation selects a derivation by its credible grade, the product of grade and reliability, with ties resolved by grade. On the canonical carrier, in which the weights of zero grade or zero reliability are identified with zero, the resulting structure is a commutative selective semiring, isomorphic to a subsemiring of a lexicographically ordered product, and its credible-grade projection is a homomorphism onto the Viterbi semiring. We compare several alternative combination rules and identify the carriers on which the relevant algebraic laws hold. Standard results on weighted automata then yield a rational characterization and closure properties. We prove that positive credible-grade cuts and selected-run reliability filters of finite automata are regular and effectively constructible for rational weights and thresholds, and we exhibit distinctions that the scalar projection cannot see: a reliability filter that no scalar reweighting of the same one-state automaton implements, nonmonotonicity under the addition of runs, and an unambiguous automaton with no deterministic equivalent although its scalar projection is deterministic. A count-based example illustrates an attestation penalty for grammar rules. The construction concerns scalar pairs, and its extension to arbitrary fuzzy-valued Z-numbers remains open.

Title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
Author: Ziang Cui
Text_Content: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.

Title: Flexible Piezoelectric Tactile Sensing System for Intelligent Object Recognition
Author: Razan Khalifeh, Mohamad Yaacoub, Christian Gianoglio, Moustafa Saleh, Maurizio Valle, Yahya Abbass
Text_Content: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.

Title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
Author: Dikshant Kukreja, Gautam Gupta, Avni Mittal, Avinash Anand, Kritarth Prasad, Zhengkui Wang, Timothy Liu, Rajiv Ratn Shah, Aik Beng Ng, Simon See, Erik Cambria
Text_Content: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.

Title: Adapters as Data: The Latent Space of LoRAs
Author: Moritz Grävinghoff, Konstantin Wehmeyer, Aron Asefaw, Boris Knyazev, Damian Borth
Text_Content: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts rather than as a data modality. Prior work has shown that LoRA adapters populate a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes well enough to support different operations such as sampling, editing, and inversion. We ask what a learned, nonlinear latent adds beyond this. We train a transformer autoencoder on the same population of LoRA identity adapters, mapping each into a latent space and compare every operation against the identical operation applied directly to the raw adapter weights. The latent preserves the capabilities already available in weight space, sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes. Beyond preservation, we show that the latent is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture. Fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot natively host adapters of more than one rank, so we extend our sequential autoencoder to hold mixed-rank adapters within one shared latent. This gives a path toward treating adapter weights of varying architecture as a single, general modality rather than one tied to a fixed rank, and points to a learned, nonlinear latent as the mechanism that could carry this generalization further, toward heterogeneous populations of adapters.

Title: Unobserved Consideration and Consumer Welfare
Author: Debopam Bhattacharya, Ryan J. Martin
Text_Content: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers' consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. The result permits unrestricted income-effects, preference heterogeneity, and dependence between preferences and consideration. Within this class, limited consideration admits a full-consideration representation preserving choice-probabilities and money-metric compensation: consideration/preferences can remain unidentified while demand and welfare are identified. When consideration sets contract as prices rise, the welfare distribution can be bounded using demand and a bound on choice-set attrition.

Title: Optimal Learning in Games with Arbitrary Delays: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Self-Play and Adversarial Opponents
Author: Emmanuel Esposito, Andrew Jacobsen, Hao Qiu, Alexander Ryabchenko, Mengxiao Zhang
Text_Content: We study learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback. We introduce Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm which obtains optimal fast rates in self-play on smooth games, while simultaneously maintaining minimax optimal guarantees against arbitrary opponents. In particular, in smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary and unknown feedback delays, MAO-OMD obtains $O(σ_{\max}+1)$ social and individual regrets when used by both players, where $σ_{\max}$ denotes the maximum number of outstanding gradients, while also guaranteeing minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T+d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$ individual regret against arbitrary opponents, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. Moreover, we show that these optimal rates cannot be obtained simultaneously using the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting. We also extend our results to multi-player games, and to games with player-dependent delay sequences.

Title: Adapt the Object to the Subject: Representative Study Material for Empirical Software Engineering
Author: Max Unterbusch, Julian Frattini, Michael Mircea, Alexander Korn, Kurt Schneider, Jonathan Ullrich, Andreas Vogelsang
Text_Content: External validity is a central concern in empirical software engineering, yet the debate has largely focused on whether study participants are representative. How well the study objects they reason about - code, models, or requirements - are representative of each participant's own work is often overlooked. Practitioners' own artifacts would be ideal, but are often out of reach, so researchers sample from public datasets or construct objects artificially. Whether this lack of subject-object fit affects participants' ability to act on the material remains unknown. We take a first step toward answering this question for requirements. We propose an approach that uses an LLM to generate context-adapted synthetic requirements just-in-time during an online survey from a short, participant-supplied context description, optionally injecting requirements smells as controlled stimuli. To validate the approach, we conducted a controlled experiment with 31 industry practitioners in a 2x2 design that crosses stimulus generation (static vs. synthetic) with quality (clean vs. smelly). Each participant rated the perceived representativeness and assessability of 20 requirements. Using Bayesian data analysis within a statistical causal-inference framework, we find that perceived representativeness has a strong positive effect on assessability. Synthetic requirements are rated as more representative and, primarily due to this gain, more assessable than static ones sourced from public datasets; smell injection leaves both perceptions unchanged. Our results support treating a lack of study-object representativeness as a first-class validity threat and position context-adapted synthetic study objects as a practical addition to the empirical methodology toolbox.

Title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
Author: Abraham Yeung
Text_Content: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, naïve per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

Title: BiGrounder: Bidirectional Training Unlocks the Potential of GUI Grounding
Author: Dengyao Shi, Tianyu Fu, Fei Hu, Anyang Su, Hanning Wang, Shuo Wang, Minghui Wu, Chenxu Zhao, Zhen Lei
Text_Content: Graphical User Interface (GUI) grounding aims to map natural language instructions to precise operational coordinates, serving as a critical task for autonomous agent interaction. Current approaches formalize GUI grounding as predicting action-coordinate pairs from instructions, with end-to-end training supervised solely by final coordinates. Training datasets typically provide only a small number of descriptions per target coordinate, whereas real-world scenarios involve a much larger set of varied descriptions for the same target, which limits robustness to linguistic variation. While recent GUI grounding paradigms have begun employing reinforcement learning to enhance localization accuracy, models with limited exploratory capability before reinforcement yield constrained improvements even with identical training data during the reinforcement phase. To overcome these limitations, we propose a bidirectional reward paradigm that enables model self-reinforcement. During SFT, bidirectional training equips the model to generate action descriptions from target coordinates. During RL, the model samples semantically consistent instruction variations on-policy and grounds each variation back to its target. A cycle-consistency gate couples semantic quality to grounding success, turning the model's own instruction policy into a source of continually refreshed reinforcement trajectories. Our 4B-parameter model achieves competitive accuracy across five grounding benchmarks in our evaluation, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed training paradigm. https://github.com/Spell-shi/BiGrounder

Title: Bringing Dark States to Light after Frustrated Tunneling Ionization
Author: Yu He, Eleni Tzima, Gergana D. Borisova, Noah L. Wach, Aaron T. Bondy, Juan C. Del Valle, Klaus Bartschat, Christian Ott, Thomas Pfeifer
Text_Content: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gases is typically regarded as a sub-laser-cycle process, well described by the semiclassical three-step model. In this work, we report the extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission observed in an HHG experiment arising from a longer temporal process associated with dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization. The emission exhibits a larger spatial divergence than typical high-order harmonics, resembling the polarization decay of optically bright states. Supported by the time-frequency analysis of the theoretical calculations, we show that the emission originates from the nonradiative capture of the tunneling electrons into excited dark states of the neutral atom, followed by Floquet-like laser-dressing effects induced by the extended tail of the driving pulse. Our results reveal a largely unexplored pathway for XUV generation through laser-dressed dark states, thereby enabling the enhancement of coherent XUV emission at targeted wavelengths with high repetition rates.

Title: Fast Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Methods on Software Logs - An Empirical Study
Author: Jesse Nyyssölä, Mika Mäntylä, Yuqing Wang
Text_Content: Anomaly detection on software logs ensures system reliability through failure identification, root cause analysis and fault localization. While supervised models show excellent performance, in a practical setting there rarely are labeled training data available. This calls for the use of unsupervised models. We study effects of data preprocessing, anomaly detection method, and the dataset. For preprocessing, we examine three options: The use of anomaly-free training data, using randomized as opposed to chronologically selected training data, and the use of a custom loader to extract log message from the log line. Regarding anomaly detection we use four models (KMeans, IsolationForest, RarityModel, Out-Of-Vocabulary Detector) and three representations (Words, trigrams, and parsed events). We evaluate these approaches on seven datasets: BGL, HDFS, Hadoop, Spirit, Thunderbird, Liberty, and LO2Token. We run each combination of the selected factors and measure performance with AUCROC and F1-score metrics. Then we utilize a generalized linear model to establish relationships between the factors. Furthermore, we address execution times. Our evidence reveals large variability across all datasets, preventing us from making recommendations that apply universally. For instance, log parsing enhances performance on some datasets but reduces it on others. The evidence suggests that using anomaly-free data for training unsupervised models can improve anomaly detection performance, though this requires extra effort to identify such data.Previous work has argued that shuffling data leads to unrealistic model performance (data leakage). Yet, our results show this does not hold for the unsupervised models we tested, while it remains true for supervised models in the same setup. For fast execution of the pipeline, use word representation and avoid IsolationForest model.

Title: ReConMem: A Graph-Based Dual Memory System for Repository-Oriented Conversations
Author: Zhishuo Yang, Li Zhang, Yang Liu, Donghao Yang, Fang Liu
Text_Content: LLM-based code assistants are increasingly used in iterative repository-level development, where effective assistance requires jointly leveraging evolving conversational history and repository context. Existing memory systems, however, are primarily designed for general-purpose conversations and do not sufficiently coordinate conversational information with the structured code entities to which it refers. We propose ReConMem, a graph-based dual memory system for repository-oriented conversations. ReConMem organizes distilled conversational memories and conversation-relevant code entities into interconnected semantic and structural memory graphs, while maintaining their cross-graph associations as interactions evolve. For memory recall, ReConMem combines natural-language and code-aligned retrieval through code-draft-based query grounding, expands retrieved information over intra- and inter-graph relations, and compresses retrieved code according to its structural granularity. We evaluate ReConMem on two repository-oriented conversational benchmarks spanning long-horizon context management and realistic project-grounded multi-turn assistance. On LoCoEval, ReConMem improves Pass@1 over the strongest baseline by 7.917 and 7.292 percentage points on single-hop and multi-hop subsets, respectively, with comparable context compression. On CodeAssistBench, it achieves 27.61% Correct and 44.03% Partially Correct, exceeding Full History by 4.10 and 7.09 percentage points, respectively, while improving interaction quality. These results demonstrate that aligning conversational memory with repository structure improves context management for repository-oriented multi-turn interactions.

Title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
Author: Yifan Chang, Yunze Li, Feifei Jiang, Juntao Wu, Xin Chen, Han Hu, Yucheng Wu, Wei Tang, Mingqian Ma, Wanli Ouyang, Kaipeng Zhang, Lei Bai, Hongting Tang, Feiran Li, Yuchen Ren
Text_Content: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

Title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
Author: Nikita Koriagin, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov
Text_Content: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.

Title: Automated Video-to-QA Pipeline: End-to-End Question Generation and Verification Using Large Language Models
Author: Jaival Chauhan, Vikram Singh, Pruthwik Mishra
Text_Content: The exponential growth of educational and informational video content on platforms like YouTube presents a challenge for efficient knowledge retrieval and assessment. This paper proposes an end-to-end automated pipeline for extracting structured summaries and generating high-fidelity Question-Answer (QA) pairs from video streams. The framework integrates a cascade of state-of-the-art models: audio extraction is handled via FFmpeg, followed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Whisper (A library in Python) to generate accurate transcripts. Due to the token constraints of Large Language Models (LLMs), transcripts are segmented and summarized using Facebook's BART. A key innovation of this work is a Self-Verification and Fine-Tuning Loop. We utilize meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct to generate candidate QA pairs from transcript chunks, which are then fed back into the model to rigorously assess their relevance and importance. Only verified, high-quality pairs are retained to construct a synthetic dataset. This dataset is subsequently used to fine-tune the Llama model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), resulting in a specialized model capable of generating domain-aligned assessment questions. This approach demonstrates a scalable method for creating self-improving educational tools without the need for manual data annotation. The proposed model can be downloaded from Kaggle with all the codes from GitHub.

Title: Uncovering Systematic Blind Spots in Graph Database Testing through Integration and Process-Level Analysis
Author: Tinghan Li, Aoyang Fang, Longbin Lai, Zifan Xie, Hongbo Zhao, Yu Shao, Ying Zhang, Pinjia He
Text_Content: Graph databases are becoming foundational infrastructure for connected data, and a growing body of automated testing techniques has uncovered many bugs across mature graph database systems. Each technique checks a different aspect of correctness and exposes a different class of defect. Combining them is the natural next step, but each technique is judged by the real bugs it finds, not by useless reports or tests that can never fail, and that is what decides whether a developer can afford to fix the problems. To identify the remaining gaps, we integrated test capabilities from 8 testing methods and conducted an empirical study of their behavior, during which we found two blind spots. First, 12 hours of testing produce thousands of bug reports, far more than the number of genuine defects a mature database is likely to contain. Most reports are false positives caused by dialect or pattern-matching differences, and many of the remaining reports are duplicates. Second, analysis of process-level data reveals that many equivalence-based metamorphic test cases lose their ability to detect defects because of the optimization mechanism. Based on these findings, we summarize and realize these guidelines in GraphWeave, an integrated testing platform for graph databases. This includes a multi-agent system that analyzes the flood of bug reports to produce gating rules for issue filtering and adapter rules for dialect adaptation, and a plan-aware triage routes metamorphic pairs by plan, skipping those that share a plan on the same graph state and therefore cannot detect defects. We apply GraphWeave to NeuG, a recently open-sourced industrial graph database that has not been covered by prior graph database testing work. With modest manual effort, GraphWeave uncovers 19 previously unknown bugs, all of which have since been confirmed.

Title: Neural Collapse on Imbalanced Datasets and Open-Set Scenario
Author: Qiufu Li, Huibing Xiao, Linlin Shen, Yongdong Huang
Text_Content: Neural collapse (NC) describes the elegant geometric structure that sample features and classifier vectors exhibit when a classification model's loss reaches its minimum. Class imbalance, however, generally distorts standard NC. In this paper, we theoretically reformulate NC on imbalanced datasets and in open-set settings. Our analysis is based on an optimization problem over class-wise averaged losses, rather than the global averaged losses used in prior NC studies. We prove that when class-wise averaged losses attain their minima, standard NC is achieved on balanced or imbalanced datasets, for both cross-entropy (CE) and binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses. We further extend the analysis to an open-set-inspired scenario, where some classes contain no training samples yet are still assigned classifier vectors in the losses. We find that in this scenario, when class-wise averaged losses reach their minima, standard NC still emerges on the known classes with training samples, while the classifier vectors of unknown classes without training samples overlap with each other and become orthogonal to those of the known classes. Finally, we analyze Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency, proving that at their minima on balanced or imbalanced datasets, sample features of different classes likewise form standard NC.

Title: Adjustment-Anchor Dependence in Formulaic Alpha Languages: A Certified Grammar and a Re-Anchoring Audit
Author: Zhengkai Tu, Xinyue Xiang, Jimmy Huang
Text_Content: Several public scripts for formulaic alpha mining store prices adjusted to the snapshot's last day, so a past day's stored price changes with every later split or dividend and formulas that do not cancel the adjustment factor depend on future corporate actions. We formalise a change of adjustment anchor as a per-stock group action and give a two-sorted type system that soundly certifies anchor invariance from a formula's syntax, under a declared field-adjustment contract and idealised operator semantics; its second sort admits log-returns, and a linear-time checker plugs into any miner. In a re-anchoring audit on Chinese A-shares, pools that five published methods mined in our benchmark pipeline score a mean information coefficient (IC) 0.005 higher on the stored representation than on a cutoff-anchored one, about 14% of their IC. The mean signed change for certified pools is about -0.001, and pools mined on past-anchored data stay sensitive. On the Chinese development folds, certification shows no detectable predictive cost or gain; the estimated minimum detectable difference is about 0.017 IC across cells on pool ICs of 0.03-0.04. We also trace an erroneous index-membership entry to public Qlib data snapshots and show that re-mining exposes the effect of such data defects, which re-evaluating fixed pools understates.

Title: Foresee to Trade: Forecast-Augmented Policy Optimization for Portfolio Management
Author: Zeyu Liu, Xuanzhi Feng, Haoran Xu, Lai Sing Kwong, Yang Li, Hualei Zhang, Hao Chen, Jie Zhang, Xiaoyi Pang, Song Guo
Text_Content: Online investment services must translate asset opportunities into investment outcomes for users' accounts, yet the same market opportunity can warrant different account actions. We study how supervision from future asset opportunities can strengthen account-level trading decisions and propose Forecast-Augmented Relative Policy Optimization (FRPO). FRPO separately supervises asset opportunities and account decisions through a jointly learned representation: a Financial State Head (FSH) learns future relative-return targets to provide asset-level opportunity supervision, while Same-Path Group-Relative Optimization compares trading trajectories under the same market path and initial account to provide account-level relative-outcome supervision. An Adaptive Gate coordinates auxiliary supervision using predictive variance and gradient alignment. FSH is used only during training; inference uses the encoder and policy for trading. Across DJIA30, TOPIX Core30, and three investment-style portfolios, ten-seed evaluations show that FRPO achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among the compared methods in all five settings. These results support strengthening investment agents' trading decisions through joint supervision from asset opportunities and trading outcomes.

Title: ConvPE: Convolutional Position Embedding Improves Transformers
Author: Zehao Wang
Text_Content: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.

Title: Wedge-Jamming Mechanism for String Configuration
Author: Taro Tako, Takanori Jin, Hiroshi Kaminaga, Taisuke Kobayashi
Text_Content: Variable stiffness mechanisms that achieve both flexibility and rigidity are important technologies for robotic systems. Recently, wire-based jamming mechanisms have attracted significant attention. In the wire-based jamming mechanisms, modules are chained by a wire, and the overall stiffness is controlled by changing the friction between the modules through wire tension. These mechanisms have been widely studied due to their simple structure and controllability. However, conventional wire-based jamming mechanisms mainly focus on holding torque along the joint axis, and the resistance against disturbances in other directions has not been sufficiently explored. In this study, we propose a wedge-jamming mechanism that introduces wedge-shaped contact surfaces into the modules of wire-based jamming structures. By changing the wedge angle, the holding characteristics against disturbances in different directions can be adjusted. Experimental results show that an out-wedge configuration improves resistance to vertical disturbances, while an in-wedge configuration enhances resistance to torsional disturbances. These results demonstrate that the anisotropic holding performance of wire-based jamming mechanisms depend on wedge geometry.

Title: Volatility Heredity in Multivariate Time Series: A Statistically Guided Temporal Convolutional Approach to Variable Ordering
Author: Kaoutar El Azaar, Mohamed Hamlich, Moncef Garouani, Franck Ravat, Asmae Chakir, Mohamed Tabaa
Text_Content: Volatility heredity concerns the information that past fluctuations in one series may carry about another after accounting for the target's own persistence. QS-TCN compares this dependence in both directions to estimate an order of temporal precedence. For each series, quasi-maximum likelihood estimation yields a persistence coefficient, and the matrix pencil method extracts temporal modes from the autocovariances of squared observations. These estimates define filters in a temporal convolutional network. The network models the target's squared observations from their own past and scores the association between the residuals and the filtered history of a candidate source. Differences between the two directional scores are aggregated into a global order. In an exploratory simulation with 100 systems in each of four volatility regimes, an ensemble of ten models trained with fixed seeds achieved higher mean ordering quality than CCF-AUC, a lead--lag method based on distance correlation, in every regime. Against CCF-AUC applied to squared standardized observations, the mean gains were 8.69 percentage points under positive linear coupling and 7.81 points when nonlinear coupling depended on the target's state. In the other two regimes, paired 95\% bootstrap intervals for the gains included zero. Mean agreement with reference constraints was 71.55\% across nine Finance systems and 54.02\% across 27 simulated functional magnetic resonance imaging systems, compared with 50\% expected under random ordering. In a panel of daily currency and gold returns, the estimated order placed the dollar--franc and dollar--yen exchange rates before gold.

Title: Laser fabrication of vibrating microcavities on silicon: Formation dynamics and frequency tunability
Author: Belen Valiente, Gonzalo Gomez-Munoz, Mario Garcia-Lechuga, Irene Solana, Fernando Agulló-Rueda, David Grojo, Angel Rodriguez-Fernandez, Javier Solis, Jan Siegel
Text_Content: Laser processing of silicon has long since become a standard method for wafer dicing, surface texturing, re-crystallization after ion implantation, as well as surface amorphization, to name a few examples. Here, we introduce a novel concept, the fabrication of vibrating microcavities in a commercial platform, Si wafers covered by a thick SiO2 layer, acting as a membrane. We demonstrate that by exposing our material system to single ultrashort laser pulses above the evaporation threshold of Si, a controlled delamination of the cover layer without fracture can be achieved, leading to the formation of a microcavity accompanied by a surface bulging up to 1.5 micrometer. The formation dynamics of the microcavities has been investigated by time-resolved optical probe techniques. Ultrafast pump-probe microscopy resolves the initial stages of substrate melting, the onset of layer expansion followed by relaxation. Real-time reflectivity measurements with nanosecond resolution resolve the long lived, highly complex oscillation process of the membrane, extending over tens of microseconds. The formed cavities can be re-excited at low fluence without damage or degradation, featuring vibrations at single frequencies with high Q factors. The frequencies can be tuned continuously from 8 MHz up to 19 MHz by adjusting the fabrication fluence. A simple classical model is found to well describe the behavior of the membranes. Our results pave the way for applications in micro- and nanooptics and acoustics, in great part due to the commercial availability of the Si-SiO2 platform and the simplicity of the fabrication method. An extension to the field of microelectromechanical system (MEMS) of this technology is proposed.

Title: Comparing Classification and Feature Learning by Analyzing Their Loss Functions in Normalized Spaces with Different Scale Factors
Author: Qiufu Li, Huibin Xiao, Linlin Shen, Weijia Fan, Xi Jia, Yongdong Huang
Text_Content: Classification and feature learning are two closely interrelated fundamental tasks. Feature learning in supervised settings is typically achieved by training classification models, under the common assumption that higher classification accuracy implies better feature quality. In this paper, we first point out that classification accuracy reflects the sample-wise local properties of a model on a dataset, whereas feature learning aims to learn features with good dataset-level global properties, such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. From the first principle of feature learning, we redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, a counterpart of the cross-entropy (CE) loss used in classification. Then, in normalized feature space, we analyze the minima of the BCE and CE losses and show that both can lead to neural collapse, where sample features from different classes become maximally compact and maximally separated. More importantly, by investigating the convergence behaviors of the two losses as the scale factor $γ$ varies in the normalized space, we reveal how classification accuracy and feature quality change differently across spaces of different sizes. Under a fixed training strategy, a very large $γ$ achieves perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, whereas a very small $γ$ makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. A moderate $γ$ is therefore necessary for simultaneously achieving reliable classification and well-structured features. Extensive experiments validate these findings and demonstrate that BCE loss exhibits advantages in long-tail and open-set recognitions, as it better aligns with the global requirements of feature learning.

Title: Fix One, Miss Another: Leveraging Historical Bug Fixes to Uncover Residual Bugs in Database Systems
Author: Yankai Rong, Zhaoyang Zhang, Shuang Liu, Wei Lu, Xiaoyong Du
Text_Content: Database management systems (DBMSs) implement SQL constructs through grammar-driven dispatch handlers. Although handlers for syntactic siblings implement different SQL constructs, they often share a common implementation pattern, including argument extraction, type checking, and permission validation. Consequently, a bug fix that hardens the handler exercised by a historical bug may leave the corresponding logic in sibling handlers vulnerable to the same semantic flaw. We refer to such defects as sibling bugs. Despite the structural similarity among sibling handlers, existing bug-finding techniques rarely exploit historical fixes to systematically uncover these related defects. We present Reaper, a novel approach for detecting sibling bugs guided by historical bug fixes. Reaper first analyzes a bug fix to infer a trigger profile, which characterizes the conditions under which the defect is exposed, and a validation profile, which captures the semantic evidence needed to distinguish buggy behavior from correct behavior. It then projects the trigger profile onto syntactic siblings through grammar-guided test mutation, generating tests that exercise corresponding semantic paths in sibling handlers. Finally, Reaper validates suspicious behaviors using the inferred validation profile through a staged validation process, reducing false positives caused by complex DBMS behavior. We evaluate Reaper on four widely used DBMSs, including MariaDB, MySQL, OceanBase, and CockroachDB. Reaper uncovers 61 previously unknown bugs, of which 57 have been confirmed by developers and 13 have been fixed at the time of writing. These results demonstrate that historical bug fixes contain actionable semantic knowledge that can be systematically transferred across syntactic siblings to uncover otherwise overlooked defects.

Title: A continuum model of a diffusive compressible gas - Kinetic theory and real gases
Author: Magnus Svärd
Text_Content: Using kinetic theory of gases, we derive the diffusive compressible Euler (dcE) model for ideal gases. The derivation covers all steps from the particle description of a gas, to macroscopic averages, to a discrete system of conservative balance equations in finite volumes, to the system of partial dif- ferential equations. Along the way, we discuss the modelling assumptions, and derive approximations of the diffusion coefficient. In the next part, we discuss the modifications needed to model real gases. In particular, we propose a tentative model for intermolecular friction forces.

Title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping
Author: David Berghaus, Arber Zela, Behzad Shomali, Markus Frey, Mehdi Ali, Rafet Sifa, Volkan Cevher
Text_Content: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

Title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
Author: Nils Schwager, Simon Münker, Alistair Plum, Achim Rettinger
Text_Content: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.

Title: Beyond Hash Matching: AI-Based Detection of Previously Unidentified CSAM and its Legal Implications in the EU
Author: Emmanouela Kokolaki, Georgios Samaritakis, Paraskevi Fragopoulou
Text_Content: The detection of previously unidentified Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) remains a significant challenge for law enforcement authorities, online service providers, and child protection organizations, as traditional hash-matching technologies are primarily designed to identify previously verified material. This paper reviews and classifies existing AI-based technologies that could complement hash-based approaches and support the detection, analysis, and prioritization of potentially harmful content. The reviewed approaches are organized into three categories: real-time image and video analysis, image and video classification and tagging, and AI-based behavioral monitoring. A comparative analysis examines the capabilities, limitations, and potential integration of general-purpose computer vision platforms, content moderation services, and specialized CSAM detection tools within existing detection workflows. An experimental evaluation was conducted using Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine to investigate sexual-content classification and child-adult age estimation. The results highlight differences in classification taxonomies and outputs across providers, as well as significant limitations in age classification, particularly for adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of using AI-based assessments as complementary tools for analysis and prioritization, rather than as definitive determination of CSAM. Finally, the paper examines the relevant European Union regulatory framework, with particular attention to the EU AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), fundamental rights, transparency, accountability, and human oversight. The legal analysis highlights how regulatory obligations and safeguards may differ depending on the deployment context, potentially creating inconsistencies across interconnected detection and reporting workflows.

Title: Over-the-Scene Computation: Illumination-Programmed Functional Sensing of Unresolvable Populations
Author: Seyed Mohammad Azimi-Abarghouyi, Christopher G. Brinton
Text_Content: Decisions about dense populations depend on how much will cross a boundary by a deadline and when the first member arrives. Conventional radar forms a range-Doppler map, whose cells add noise and whose detections merge unresolved members. We introduce over-the-scene computation, where illumination makes the scene compute such functionals without resolving members. With random echo phases, a correlator's mean output energy sums member reflectivities weighted by a kernel set by the waveform and template. The waveform's ambiguity function is this computation's transfer function, determining computable functionals and their noise cost. One readout aggregates members over a small delay-Doppler area but along a line segment growing with duration, longest for the chirp of matching slope among constant-envelope waveforms. Members predicted to share a range lie on such a line, so a chirp's mean beat spectrum is the predicted range profile at a look-ahead horizon set by its rate. For unbiased estimation, a Cramer-Rao bound over all equal-energy waveforms favors resolving members above unit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and grouping weaker ones into unit-SNR sets. At 0.65 members per cell, -10 dB member SNR, and one sweep, the chirp's bin sum inside the boundary comes within 16% of this bound in root-mean-square error and, with 77 times fewer samples per horizon, outperforms every unbiased estimator from a coherent processing interval of equal dwell, bandwidth, and energy. No finite set of waveform-template probes determines an unconstrained Rayleigh-fluctuating population's first arrival, but bisection localizes it if first arrivals outweigh later arrivals' sidelobes.

Title: O$^2$PD: Overlap-Gated On-Policy Distillation on Reliable Prefix
Author: Shuaishuai Zu, Jihao Zhao, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Yuhan Liu, Biao Qin, Baochuan Yang
Text_Content: On-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision by aligning a student to the teacher's next-token distribution on its own generated rollouts. Existing works mostly implement top-$k$ OPD, applying reverse Kullback-Leibler ($\RKL$) divergence between the teacher's and the student's renormalized distributions over teacher top-$k$ support. However, the teacher scores student-generated rollouts that are inherently off-policy for itself, leaving the reliability of its next-token guidance unclear. Restricting the divergence to the teacher top-$k$ support also discards the remaining mass outside that support. These gaps leave two questions implicit: 1) which tokens to align, and 2) how to align those tokens. To answer these questions, we propose Overlap-gated On-Policy Distillation (O$^{2}$PD). As for 1), we quantitatively analyze the reliability of teacher supervision and find that alignment on the student's trajectory prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context. Therefore, our O$^{2}$PD is applied only to the 20\% prefix tokens of each student rollout. As for 2), we theoretically characterize two problems of top-$k$ OPD: the \emph{Teacher-support Uncovering} and the \emph{Dominant-Mode Mismatch}. Based on these analyses, we propose two support strategies: the \emph{Reset Support} strategy attaches a reset atom to every token, pooling mass outside the teacher top-$k$, and the \emph{Support Convergence} strategy converges the support to the already aligned intersection. Our O$^{2}$PD employs the designed overlap-gated $α$-divergence to interpolate between mode-covering and mode-seeking for per-token alignment, where the overlap is used as a gate to switch the support and adaptively modulate $α$.

Title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
Author: Seong-Eun Hong, JuYeong Hwang, Jinhyun Kim, Hanyoung Jang, HyeongYeop Kang
Text_Content: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/

Title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
Author: S. -Y. Tseng
Text_Content: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $χ$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2χdz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.

Title: Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning: A Multi-Objective Framework for Learning Local Distance Functions in Nearest Neighbor Classification
Author: Isaac Touza
Text_Content: Nearest neighbour classifiers inherit the geometry of their distance function. Fixed distances and globally learned metrics apply the same geometry throughout the input space, although relevant feature directions may vary across regions. We propose EAML (Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning), a framework that learns instance-dependent positive-definite metrics through a low-dimensional parameterization. Each local metric combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, generated by softmax interpolation between anchor points, with a global low-rank correlation component. A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters using a scalar objective combining leave-one-out prediction error, robustness, metric smoothness, and regularization. We establish positive definiteness, metric equivalence, existence of an optimal solution, and Lipschitz continuity of the metric field. We further investigate prediction stability, generalization bounds, and evolutionary convergence under explicit assumptions. Experiments on synthetic data with region-dependent feature relevance show that EAML can recover local metric variations and outperform global metrics. Evaluation on thirteen public datasets using nested 5-fold cross-validation reveals a more nuanced picture: EAML improves performance on selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall. Additional experiments show that global diagonal metrics can be preferable under nuisance features and test-time noise. These findings identify the conditions under which evolutionary local metric learning is beneficial and highlight its practical limitations.

Title: Dual-Arm Tabletop Rearrangement with Movable Stacking and Gap-Aware Push Transfers
Author: Mohammadreza Firoozalizadeh, Zakiye Rostamirad, Arman Barghi, Ahmad Kalhor, Mohammadreza Nayeri, Mehdi Tale Masouleh
Text_Content: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.

Title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
Author: Emile de Bruyn, Moritz Schäffler, Jannik Schneider, Sebastian R. Schmidt, Chanwoong Hwang, Aleena Siji, Utkarsh Upadhyay, Stefan Bauer, Alexander Schug, Stefan Kesselheim, Artur Yakimovich, Alina Bazarova
Text_Content: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

Title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
Author: Bozhen Fang, Linhao Zhong, Xuehao Wang, Huanyi Zheng, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
Text_Content: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses. We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.

Title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
Author: Jiawei Jiang, Zhaoxiang Zang, Zhengtao Yu
Text_Content: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. Continuous MSE evaluates a predicted vector obtained by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities; different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under this objective. We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF), which applies squared supervision directly to token identities when continuing pretrained language flows. TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. With fixed token embeddings, we show that the squared error between predicted token probabilities and the true posterior bounds the squared errors of continuous denoising predictions and flow velocities. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. We also establish convergence to token embeddings under ideal predictions and sufficient conditions for local convergence with prediction error. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF achieves Gen.PPL values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE continuation controls. It attains the lowest Gen.PPL at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, together with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B.

Title: Evaluating Language Model Features for Zero-Shot Time-Series Anomaly Detection Under Isolation Assumption
Author: Romain Hermary, Nesryne Mejri, Djamila Aouada
Text_Content: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamentally challenging task: it is unsupervised, requires high local precision capabilities, and suffers from limited labelled data. Recent work has explored adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series via cross-modal transfer. However, existing approaches are poorly suited to Multivariate TSAD (MTSAD), as tokenisation often obscures fine-grained temporal and variables structures, and most methods optimise auxiliary objectives such as forecasting or reconstruction. We posit that these surrogate objectives become unreliable as model capacity increases. Highly expressive models risk reconstructing or forecasting anomalies, undermining the foundations of both strategies. Instead, we propose to use LLMs purely as feature extractors and directly analyse their induced feature spaces. In this work, investigate the ability of LLMs to provide useful representations for MTSADs in a zero-shot setting through classification. To this end, we study the separability of the extracted features, under the assumption that anomalous features should be isolated from normal ones. We analyse their temporal and contextual discriminative ability using simple step-wise tokenisation schemes, with one time-step per token, which preserve fine-grained local information. Their usability for MTSAD is assessed using an unsupervised Isolation Forest, enabling a direct evaluation of the resulting representation quality. We further investigate whether the observed performance can be attributed to the language-related pre-training of the LLMs or arises independently of it. Our results provide empirical insight into the ability of LLMs to represent multivariate time-series for anomaly detection and highlight broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.

Title: Graph Symbolic Distillation: Decoding Graph Data into Interpretable Formulas across Materials and Chemistry
Author: Yuxuan Yao, Karsten Reuter, Wenbin Xu
Text_Content: Graph data provide a natural representation of the interconnected structures and interactions underlying many chemical and materials systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn complex relationships from such data, yet translating these representations into interpretable descriptors and scientific insights remains challenging. Here we introduce graph symbolic distillation (GSD), a framework for decoding graph data into interpretable symbolic formulas. GSD identifies task-relevant message-passing architectures and distills their learned transformations while preserving graph connectivity and aggregation operations. Across three case studies spanning bulk materials, molecules, and surfaces, GSD not only recovers expert-defined descriptors from elementary node and edge features, but also reveals relationships emerging from their organization in complex graphs: extremal local geometric descriptors for band gap variations in $γ$-CsPbI$_3$, a local polarity--size relationship underlying hydration free energy, and site-specific electronic-connectivity coupling in multidentate adsorption. GSD thus provides a general route from graph data to interpretable descriptors and new, testable scientific insights.

Title: Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck for Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning
Author: Liangjian Wen, Jiangtao Zheng, Jiang Duan, Qun Dai, Yong Dai, Jianzhuang Liu, Jun Wang, Shu-Dong Huang, Xinwang Liu, Zenglin Xu, Zhao Kang
Text_Content: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wanglingzaishi/MIIB.

Title: Pediatric ECG foundation model via adult-to-pediatric fine-tuning: downstream tasks and clinical evaluation
Author: Yu Cao, Haiyan Xu, Xiaohan Li, Jian Yang, Yuqing Feng, Wei Wang, Haomin Li
Text_Content: Pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is complicated by age-dependent electrophysiological changes that limit direct transfer of adult AI models. We asked whether an adult ECG foundation model could be adapted to pediatric ECGs. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, we compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch under an identical architecture. Direct transfer was poor (mean AUC 0.8256). Fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above de novo training (0.9661), and attained 0.9079 using only 1% of training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels. It generalized to age regression (MAE 1.12 years) and congenital heart disease classification (AUC 0.9562). Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when AI erred. Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation; fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.

Title: Selective Event Evidence and Persistent Temporal Priors for Event-Based Point Tracking
Author: Xiaokai Song, Zhang Li, Leqi Liu, Yibin Ye, Kun Wang, Xichao Teng
Text_Content: Event cameras enable tracking under fast motion and challenging illumination. However, stable long-term point tracking remains challenging: event activity is sparse and varies with scene content and motion, complicating correspondence, while trajectory estimates can drift over long sequences. Together, these challenges motivate a tracker that selectively uses informative event evidence and retains trajectory constraints across temporal windows. We propose Selective Event Evidence and Persistent Temporal Priors (SEPT), an event-only framework for tracking any point (TAP) over long sequences. SEPT introduces two complementary modules: Task-Adaptive Event Evidence Modulation (TEEM) and Persistent Trajectory Prior (PTP). Using only tracking supervision, TEEM learns a bounded reliability field that weights the event tensor across space, time, and channels before feature extraction. PTP carries geometric information across overlapping windows by marginalizing a fixed local quadratic trajectory model with a Schur complement. Its visibility-aware correction refines overlap coordinates, while a clipped terminal velocity initializes coordinates at newly exposed timestamps. SEPT builds on the ETAP architecture. SEPT is trained exclusively on synthetic EventKubric data and evaluated on five datasets across TAP and feature tracking. Results show that SEPT outperforms the retrained ETAP baseline in average Jaccard for TAP and in feature age and expected feature age for feature tracking; it also surpasses several methods combining event and frame inputs on EC and EDS. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/SEPT.

Title: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human-Humanoid Social Interaction
Author: Nikita Kuzmin, Georgii Demianchuk, Mariya Lezina, Yara Mahmoud, Iana Zhura, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
Text_Content: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.

Title: Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation in Pixels, Interaction and World Space
Author: Jinkun Cao
Text_Content: Monocular hand mesh estimators commonly predict rig parameters and project the mesh to obtain 2D keypoints. We find that directly predicted 3D joints agree better with 2D predictions, and fitting a mesh to predicted points reduces mesh error. We present FAH (Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation), a family of models built on SAM 3D Body's hand branch through fine-tuning and feature distillation. The models predict corresponding 2D and 3D joints and surface points, fit MANO or MHR-Hand, and optionally estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference. Causal refinement reduces acceleration error, and camera estimation places the hands in world space. Experiments show improvements in image-space alignment, hand geometry, contact estimation and world-space tracking over the evaluated baselines. The default ViT-L model runs at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, or 49 fps with parts and contact enabled. The smallest ViT-S model reaches 125 fps without mesh fitting, parts or contact. Code: https://github.com/noahcao/FAH.

Title: AffineGS: Unlocking Accurate Geometry in 3DGS via Spatially Varying Affine Rectification
Author: Tze Ho Elden Tse, Jizong Peng, Richard Chen, Angela Yao
Text_Content: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.

Title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
Author: Orhun Görkem, Athanasios Vasilopoulos, Georgios Pagonis, Victoria Clerico, Hadjer Benmeziane, Irem Boybat, Hsinyu Tsai, Abu Sebastian, William Andrew Simon
Text_Content: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

Title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
Author: Junjun Pan, Yixin Liu, Yu Zheng, Fuyi Li, Alan Wee-Chung Liew, Shirui Pan
Text_Content: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision.
