We therefore formulate hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem and present Gaussolve, a subtract-and-refill framework that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content before residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. We introduce a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field, parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians, to learn where and from which viewing directions mesh content should be dissolved. A continuous transmittance fusion rule progressively exposes residual Gaussians behind the dissolved mesh, preserving their reconstruction gradients and avoiding hard visibility discontinuities. Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes demonstrate higher visual fidelity with fewer Gaussian primitives and faster rendering. Project page: https://ooosn.github.io/gaussians-can-subtract/

Title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
Author: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
Text_Content: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

Title: Polynomial Lower Bounds for Steiner Shortcuts via Test Functions
Author: Aaron Bernstein, Henry Fleischmann, Bernhard Haeupler, Gary Hoppenworth, Thatchaphol Saranurak
Text_Content: The Steiner shortcut problem asks whether every directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges admits an augmentation $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+o(1)}$ edges such that $G_+$ has the same reachability structure as $G$ (i.e. for all $s,t\in V$, $s$ reaches $t$ in $G$ iff $s$ reaches $t$ in $G_+$), and the diameter of $G_{+}$ is $m^{o(1)}$. This is a core combinatorial question underlying many reachability algorithms in the dynamic, streaming, and CONGEST models, and all parallel algorithms with almost-linear work and sublinear depth. A sequence of works ruled out such a shortcut $G_{+}$ in the non-Steiner setting where $V_{+}=\emptyset$. However, as recently shown by Bernstein et al. [STOC '26], all known non-Steiner lower-bound constructions fail once Steiner vertices $V_{+}$ are allowed. This paper rules out almost-optimal Steiner shortcuts: we show an infinite family of graphs $G=(V,E)$ with the property that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, a Steiner shortcut $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+\varepsilon}$ edges must have diameter at least $n^{1/56-O(\varepsilon)}$. Our construction strengthens the standard non-Steiner lower-bound framework via an additional structure that allows Steiner vertices to be replaced by original vertices; we can then reduce back to the standard arguments without Steiner vertices. This new structure is achieved via a new general strategy based on test functions, which is quite flexible and can potentially be extended to applications beyond our work. We also generalize our lower bound to exact Steiner hopsets in undirected graphs and to depth reduction for monotone circuits. The latter significantly strengthens the classical lower bound based on Sylvester matrices.

Title: Follow the Policy, Fail the Benchmark: Auditing and Revising Policy-Based Decision Benchmarks
Author: Yanru Xiao, Yifei Cai
Text_Content: Policy-based decision benchmarks evaluate whether systems apply written rules to financial and operational cases. Yet a rule-following response can be marked wrong when the benchmark misstates the required decision. We audit nine public policy-based decision benchmarks through source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks. We find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate as solved steps, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions. To measure the scoring impact, we rescore unchanged model responses. On the 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises acceptance by more than 80 percentage points for each of three models, without changing references or responses. In RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references and narrows an observed model gap. A controlled federal-exemption task with explicit ownership and eligibility assumptions also shows that errors in supplied intermediate answers can affect final decisions. We present BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and revisions for reevaluation.

Title: An LLM-Orchestrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Verifying Diagnostic Signal Reachability in Electronic Systems
Author: Heba Jaradat, Mohammed-Khalil Ghali, Saurabh Kulkarni, Rohan Kulkarni, Sangwon Yoon
Text_Content: Diagnostic Signal Reachability (DSR) captures whether board-level health signals are observable by management controllers, including baseboard management controllers (BMCs), complex programmable logic devices (CPLDs), and other smart controllers. Verifying DSR is essential for field diagnosability in datacenter fleets, where one design is deployed at massive scale, yet it remains largely manual, since each signal is traced by hand across schematic sheets, renamed nets, series components, and monitoring devices. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive but unreliable at structural connectivity reasoning, where over-claiming can silently hide a rare coverage gap. We present NetFlow-DSR, a neuro-symbolic framework in which an LLM orchestrates the DSR pipeline and resolves device roles mainly from part-name families and library pin names, consulting specifications only for ambiguous parts. Pin directionality is read from the design library, and deterministic graph engines verify connectivity over the authoritative netlist. The pipeline detects diagnostic nets, canonicalizes renamed net fragments, and performs controller-seeded, power-aware breadth-first search over an admissibility graph that credits device-mediated monitoring. Each verdict carries an auditable trace card whose proof path is the witness. Across five production boards from an AI platform, covering 421 expert-graded signals, a three-stage ablation improves pooled F1 from 0.578 to 0.944. Because a monitored verdict is emitted only with a proof path, the verifier is sound by construction, and precision and specificity were 100% in the evaluated data. In a cross-model study on the system-controller module, precision remained 100% across three LLMs while recall tracked each model's device-semantic extraction. Precision therefore depends on the netlist-grounded verifier and correct device semantics rather than on any single LLM.

Title: Topological Transitions of Evanescent Waves
Author: Ignacio Pavez, Tom Sheppard, Yoonseok Hwang, Hannah M. Price, Frank Schindler
Text_Content: We study the band structure of evanescent waves, that is, the decaying or growing solutions that live within the gaps of tight-binding Hamiltonians. Although the underlying Hamiltonian is Hermitian, these modes carry complex wavevectors and therefore exhibit a non-Hermitian dispersion. Using the transfer matrix formalism in one dimension, we show that, in addition to the standard exceptional points that appear at the band edges, a different type of exceptional point can arise inside the gap, protected by spinless time-reversal symmetry. Tuning model parameters drives a topological transition where such in-gap exceptional points are nucleated in pairs, mediated by a crossing between purely imaginary momentum branches. We show that this spectral structure is diagnosed by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index assigned to every energy inside the gap, with the in-gap exceptional points arising as its domain walls. A generic bound state in the system has a tail that is purely exponential when its energy lies between a band edge and the nearest exceptional point, but becomes oscillatory - with a wavevector differing from the band-edge momentum - when its energy lies between the pair of in-gap exceptional points. We illustrate these results using continuum and tight-binding models, as well as an anisotropic photonic crystal.

Title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
Author: Teresa Delgado, Hugo Hazard, Martin Benfeghoul, Jun Wang, Zafeirios Fountas
Text_Content: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

Title: TraCE: Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding
Author: Wooil Lee, Junpyo Hong, Jongseo Lee, Tuomas Oikarinen, Tsui-Wei Weng, Jinwoo Choi
Text_Content: Video understanding models often rely on motion, yet their explanations can obscure which motion sources support a prediction. We identify motion-source under-specification as a limitation of existing video XAI: region-centric explanations can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete. We propose TraCE (Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding), a concept-based framework that discovers source-flexible motion concepts by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos. These concepts represent dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions, while object and scene concepts account for static context. The resulting typed trajectory/object/scene interface supports class prediction for action recognition and question-conditioned concept matching for video question answering (VQA). We evaluate TraCE across five random seeds on six benchmarks: NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, and STAR. Relative to non-interpretable baselines, TraCE maintains competitive task performance, with an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA. Motion perturbation and concept-removal tests provide complementary evidence of directional semantic alignment and decision faithfulness, while sample-level interventions illustrate targeted model debugging. Our project page is available at https://leewooil.github.io/TraCE_project_page/.

Title: From Pixels to Actions--Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
Author: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
Text_Content: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

Title: Resolving Tusnády's Problem
Author: Nicola Wengiel
Text_Content: We prove a lower bound of $Ω_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusnády's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $Θ_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors. The matching upper and lower bounds are also formalized in Lean 4.

Title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
Author: Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
Text_Content: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

Title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
Author: Balakumar Sundaralingam, Adithyavairavan Murali, Stan Birchfield
Text_Content: We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated planner that reduces both planning latency and execution time for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited motions. B-spline trajectory optimization reduces the required iterations, while accelerated robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics reduce refinement cost and accommodate changing payloads. TimeOpt optimizes traversal speed along the fixed path under sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque constraints, exploiting local spline support to solve banded Newton systems efficiently on the GPU. With a 3,kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieves 4.4 ms mean planning time on RTX 5090, 14.7x faster than cuRoboV2. Our method on Jetson AGX Orin plans faster than cuRoboV1 + TOPPRA on RTX 5090. A stereo-camera-based deployment on YAM achieves 5.93 s mean completed pick-and-drop cycles, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2. Code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/NVlabs/curobo , Project Page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/curobov2-fast .

Title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
Author: Nicolas Tricard, Linzheng Wang, Jason Chen, Sili Deng
Text_Content: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.

Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
Author: Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Ji Dai, Dong Li, Yining Jiang, Qinghua Ni, Jun Huang, Qiang Zhang, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Yonglin Tian, Fei-Yue Wang, Xue Yang
Text_Content: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

Title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
Author: Bingran You, Wenjun Ke, Ria Rosenauer, Bo Liu, Wenbo Chen, Min Chen, Shuqi Xu, Yue Ma, Jiechao Feng, Bo Chen, Xiangkai Sun, Jiarui Liu, Jinen Guo, Zeyu Zhou, Xu Huang, Zhuohan Li, Haoyu Li, Heguang Lin, Lijie Ding, Yadong Zeng, Kangqi Zhang, Xinge Liu, Hanwen Liu, Zhenghong Li, Alexander von Recum, Yuchen Zhu, Felix Schwarzfischer, Yizhou Zhao, Jicheng Wang, Binxu Li, Qian Yu, Chan Li, Cheng Dai, Di Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Jiankai Sun, Kaituo Feng, Mian Qin, Ruihong Yin, Yiqun Luo, Weiwei Wu, Shihong Pan, Tsung Yeh Hsieh, Xiao Huang, Yan Zhang, Sihan Li, Zirui Ren, Zengji Tu, Kyoung Whan Choe, Ke Sun, Vincenzo Galia, Vaisakhi Mishra, Jiashu He, Hongyang Wang, Zhiheng Yang, Shubham Gaur, Yifan Gu, Shuyi Wang, Zihao Zuo, Steven Dillmann, Yiyou Sun, Xinyang Han, Hanchung Lee, Molei Tao, Yue Zhao, Shilong Liu, Yuchen Wu, Xuandong Zhao, Xiangyi Li, Florian Brand, Gerbrand Ceder, Hartmut Haeffner
Text_Content: AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

Title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
Author: Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
Text_Content: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.

Title: A Simple Subquadratic Cut Query Protocol for Directed Reachability
Author: Henry Fleischmann, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Swagato Sanyal
Text_Content: We study $s$--$t$ reachability in an unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices, accessed through a directed cut oracle: given $S\subseteq V$, the oracle returns the number of edges directed from $S$ to $V\setminus S$. Directed cut functions are submodular, and reachability asks whether the minimum $s$--$t$ cut has positive value. This connects the problem to the query complexity of submodular function minimisation. Whether or not reachability can be solved in truly subquadratic query complexity has been an outstanding open question for a decade. We give a simple algorithmic blueprint with two randomised implementations. The first uses $\widetilde O(n^{9/5})$ outgoing-cut queries; the second improves this bound to $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$. The common idea is to construct an alternative orientation with the same underlying undirected graph and vertex-wise degree imbalances, thereby preserving reachability. We first approximate the target imbalances using an averaging and rounding procedure, then correct the remaining error with a flow. An earlier manuscript, made available in August 2026 in an online AI repository, reports an $\widetilde O(n^{3/2})$ query bound. Our contribution is a simple and comprehensible alternative approach that already achieves a polynomial saving over quadratic query complexity.

Title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
Author: Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf Römer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As, Pranav Vignesh, Manan Agarwal, Leander Diaz-Bone, Piotr Zalewski, Mikołaj Czarnecki, Lenart Treven, Shashwat Saxena, Sreyas Venkataraman, Sarvesh Patil, Zhiyuan Zhou, Daniel Marta, Oier Mees, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Carmelo Sferrazza, Bhavya Sukhija, Angela P. Schoellig, Andreas Krause, Max Simchowitz, Andrew Wagenmaker
Text_Content: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

Title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models
Author: Yiwen Chen, Qiqi Hou, Jisoo Jeong, Yinhao Zhu, Huaizu Jiang, Amir Said
Text_Content: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.

Title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
Author: Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
Text_Content: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.

Title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
Author: Ahsan Habib Shihab, Imre Felde, Ramis Akhmedov, Stefan Gubo, Berik Sabdenaliyev, Madina Mansurova, Amir Mosavi
Text_Content: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.

Title: 3D Printed Monolithic Optomechanical Chassis for an Unbalanced Field-Widened Interferometer
Author: Ramy Tannous, Dogan Sinar, Sagar Patel, Tabitha D. Arulpragasam, Issa Rishmawi, Mark Kirby, Vlad Paserin, Mihaela Vlasea, Thomas Jennewein
Text_Content: Additive manufacturing is increasingly being explored as an approach for producing complex structures for optical hardware. In this work, we present a fully monolithic optomechanical chassis fabricated using laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. The structure was fabricated from thermally stable Invar36, a low-thermal-expansion alloy that enables high dimensional stability under varying environmental conditions. Our monolithic design incorporates embedded optical mounts, flexures, and alignment features directly into the chassis geometry that exceed the practical limits of conventional subtractive manufacturing. By integrating the optomechanical support structure into a single compact unit, the system achieves a reduced footprint compared to traditional optomechanical assemblies. The results demonstrate the potential of additive manufacturing to produce lightweight, and highly customized optical systems, opening the possibility of new pathways for next-generation quantum sensors and optical instrumentation.

Title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity
Author: Khalid Tounoussi, Mohammed Sayagh, Ali Ouni, Yutaro Kashiwa
Text_Content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcp-research-alliance/mcp-ecosystem Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7TqnNneSfU

Title: Online Edge-Weighted Matching Beyond 0.55
Author: Alireza Farhadi, Mohammad Hajiaghayi
Text_Content: We give a $0.556195$-competitive randomized algorithm for edge-weighted online bipartite matching with free disposal, improving the $0.5368$ guarantee of Blanc and Charikar. The result holds for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights and any input sequence fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. Our algorithm builds on online correlated selection, introduced by Fahrbach, Huang, Tao, and Zadimoghaddam, and its multiway extension due to Blanc and Charikar. Our main contribution is a state-dependent primal--dual analysis of correlated selection. At each weight threshold, we track the state of the selection process jointly with an auxiliary failure event. The analysis accounts for arrivals below the threshold, which change the state without improving the matching value at that threshold. A potential function bounds the dual increase in both cases. We instantiate the analysis with an explicit win map that assigns a common score to an initial range of states. Its selection inequalities are verified by a finite computer-assisted proof covering every required candidate multiplicity and every real threshold; the verifiers are available in an accompanying repository. Triangular unit-weight inputs asymptotically attain the guarantee of the underlying ideal algorithm, proving that its analysis is tight.

Title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
Author: Christof Fehrman, Jacob J. Morra, Eva A. Naumann
Text_Content: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

Title: Nonuniform Buy-at-Bulk Network Design: Improved Approximation and LP Integrality Gap
Author: Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Text_Content: In nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design, we are given an undirected graph and $h$ terminal pairs with positive demands, and we must route every demand at minimum total cost when each network resource has two independent parameters: a fixed buying price paid once if the resource is used, and a per-unit rental cost (or physical length) paid proportionally to the traffic it carries. Unlike the uniform-cost or single-sink variants, the general multicommodity problem allows unrelated buying and rental metrics across arbitrary source--sink pairs, arbitrary demands, and both edge and node resources. We give a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$-approximation algorithm for undirected nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design. The guarantee holds for edge costs, node costs, and their combination, and applies to arbitrary positive rational demands with no dependence on the number of vertices or the numerical demand ratio. This improves upon the $O(\log^4 h)$ bound of Chekuri, Hajiaghayi, Kortsarz, and Salavatipour (2010) for unrestricted instances. Our result also establishes the same $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$ upper bound on the integrality gap of the natural affine multicommodity flow LP, bounding integral buying and rental costs separately against their fractional counterparts and preserving zero rental budgets exactly.

Title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
Author: Darion Cassel, Ariana Azarbal, Anna Soligo
Text_Content: A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension. We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.

Title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Separation at 1-1/e and a 0.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights
Author: Hossein Esfandiari, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Text_Content: Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for matroid prophet-secretary and prophet-secretary with XOS valuation functions. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements. We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a $0.6767$ competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d.\ nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive. For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

Title: Procedural Adversarial Learning
Author: Jack Nugent, Jia Deng
Text_Content: For many computer vision tasks, neural networks can be trained to produce a low average error, yet they still fail on seemingly simple scenes. Reducing these failures requires first finding them, but they may not be in a fixed dataset. We study procedural adversarial learning (PAL), a framework of minimax training and adversarial evaluation which searches the input space of a procedural generator for difficult instances. The procedural generator is an interpretable program mapping a low-dimensional vector of control parameters (e.g. layout, lighting, pose) to a rendered image and its label. We introduce the Simple-PAT algorithm, which uses zeroth-order optimization in the procedural generator's parameter space to propose adversarial training samples that are generated on demand. We also create PAL-Dojo, a collection of efficient procedural generators for surface normal estimation, image segmentation, and human pose estimation. Against a cross-model black-box adversary with 50M aggregate queries, Simple-PAT reduces worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x compared to standard training and 2.63x compared to the strongest robust training baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/princeton-vl/procedural-adversarial-learning.

Title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
Author: Siyi Yu
Text_Content: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

Title: Odd Capillarity
Author: Nadia Bihari Padhan, Axel Voigt
Text_Content: Capillarity governs interfacial relaxation and hydrodynamic motion in binary fluids through parity-even mechanical stresses. Here, we introduce \emph{odd capillarity}, a parity-breaking interfacial mechanical response, by incorporating a symmetric, nonvariational, parity-odd capillary stress into the Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes (CHNS) equations. This stress generates forces along interfaces, transverse to ordinary capillary forces, and performs mechanical work that is not balanced by changes in the composition free energy. Direct numerical simulations reveal that odd capillarity arrests domain coarsening while sustaining turbulent fluid motion without a conventional inertial energy cascade, as energy injection is predominantly balanced by viscous dissipation. In asymmetric mixtures, odd capillarity driven deformation and breakup interrupt droplet growth, producing dynamically arrested emulsions with composition hyperuniformity and suppressed large-scale vorticity fluctuations. These findings establish odd capillarity as a distinct interfacial mechanism for controlling phase separation and sustaining nonequilibrium fluid motion.

Title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
Author: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Uksang Yoo, Xinyue Zhu, Meadow Shen, Jaimyn Drake, Eugen Solowjow, Lionel Gulich, Alexander Millane, Rafael Cathomen, Tuur Stuyck, Sangeeta Subramanian, Yichao Pan, Bruce McGowan, Michael Benedict, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg
Text_Content: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

Title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
Author: Benjamin Jacob Bodner
Text_Content: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).

Title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
Author: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
Text_Content: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $τ^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.

Title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
Author: Bálint Gyevnár, Simon DeDeo
Text_Content: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

Title: Learning to Decode Linear Codes with Generalized Belief Propagation Network
Author: Samira Malek
Text_Content: Error correcting codes are a fundamental component of communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Recently, neural decoders have demonstrated notable performance gains over classical iterative algorithms. In this paper, we propose a Generalized Belief Propagation Network (GBPNet) that preserves message-passing symmetry while enhancing the decoder's learning capability. The architecture uses cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling while retaining the Tanner graph structure. We also introduce two training strategies, progressive training and high-SNR training, that improve decoding accuracy. Experimental results on several linear codes show that GBPNet achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated state-of-the-art neural decoders.

Title: Pixie: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Large Language Models (LLM) Architecture for Digital Marketing
Author: Vivek Vishwas Vichare, Akshat Singhal, Kirill Dubovikov, Vivek Kumar, Sreyas Chaithanya, Saurabh Verma, Humeil Makhija, Mrunal Nasery
Text_Content: We present Pixie, a context-aware, multi-agent large language model (LLM) architecture designed to enhance digital marketing operations across real-time and offline activities. Pixie uses a primary orchestration agent alongside task-specific and reconciliation/reviewer agents to support a broad range of marketing tasks. These agents combine zero-shot and few-shot prompting with marketing data, proprietary expert strategy guidelines, and documentation for proprietary statistical models. We experiment with agentic workflows ranging from single-agent to multi-agent systems. We evaluate them using assessments by trained marketing experts and measurements of LLM output variance, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and domain-specific problem-solving. Results show that Pixie's multi-agent framework improves decision quality and operational efficiency in digital marketing workflows. We assess Pixie on common digital marketing processes, including root-cause analysis and reporting, campaign research, and planning. The framework is designed to support additional specialized agents for other marketing tasks and adapt to evolving digital marketing needs.

Title: When optimized geometries are not optimal: Implications for inverted singlet-triplet gap predictions
Author: Atreyee Majumdar, Elamathi Selvan Samynathan, Raghunathan Ramakrishnan
Text_Content: Pseudo-Jahn-Teller distortions can substantially alter singlet-triplet gaps, potentially reversing the predicted excited-state ordering in molecules proposed to exhibit inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) gaps. In this study, we benchmark geometry optimization methods for 13 azaphenalenes against CCSD(T)-quality reference geometries, assessing their ability to reproduce symmetry lowering and its consequences for singlet-triplet gaps. Among the methods examined, $ω$B97M-D4 reliably describes the distorted geometries and corresponding gaps, whereas the commonly used methods B3LYP and MP2 retain high-symmetry structures, potentially leading to false-positive INVEST assignments. We further assess $ω$B97M-D4 geometries across 337 molecules comprising azaphenalenes, boron/nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and non-alternant hydrocarbons. Subsequent L-CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ calculations predict negative singlet-triplet gaps for 85 molecules and identify discrepancies with previously reported INVEST assignments. These findings demonstrate that the choice of geometry optimization method is crucial for reliable INVEST screening, particularly in systems susceptible to symmetry-breaking distortions.

Title: PixelSpline: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution via Endpoint-Anchored Shared Pixel Trajectories
Author: Wanqi Yuan, Nianyi Li
Text_Content: Existing continuous space-time video super-resolution methods often infer motion from only two endpoint frames and model the two motion directions independently, making them vulnerable to ambiguous correspondence and inconsistent trajectories. We introduce a continuous STVSR framework that combines long-context encoding, continuous HR feature lifting, and an endpoint-anchored PixelSpline. Long-range observations provide more reliable endpoint representations, while continuous upsampling constructs detailed appearance features directly on the requested HR grid. PixelSpline explicitly models each pixel's motion as a single continuous trajectory shared by both endpoints. Using this trajectory, our method warps endpoint colors into a coarse intermediate frame and aligns the HR features for residual reconstruction. Experiments across spatial and temporal upsampling settings demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a favorable quality--efficiency trade-off.

Title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
Author: Jalaj Bhandari, Dhawal Gupta, Hongli Zhan, Zhenting Wang, Varad Pimpalkhute, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric Xing, Rupesh Srivastava
Text_Content: In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.

Title: GH-AWTrace: A Large-Scale Dataset of GitHub Agentic Workflow Execution Logs
Author: Jasem Khelifi, Hao Li, Ali Ouni, Mohammed Sayagh, Mohamed Aymen Saied
Text_Content: Agentic workflows enable AI agents to perform recurring repository tasks on schedules or in response to repository events. Existing studies examine workflow definitions and outputs, but provide limited evidence of what happens during execution. We present GH-AWTrace, a dataset linking 25,014 verified GitHub Agentic Workflows across 5,051 repositories to 4,112,526 run records and 562,877 nonempty execution log archives. The dataset preserves execution evidence subject to GitHub's log-retention limits and links it to repository metadata and generated workflow configurations. Illustrative cases show how the logs expose tool denials, provider failures, changes in an agent's approach, and delegation among agents. These observations enable research on execution failures, tool use, and the relationship between reported run outcomes and visible task progress. Coverage varies across workflows, and the logs provide partial observations rather than complete agent trajectories. Video: https://youtu.be/KIlfmZhHxtA

Title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
Author: Ankit K. Upadhyay, Aleksandr Algasov, Ekaterina Nepovinnykh, Fedor Zolotarev, Tuomas Eerola, Heikki Kälviäinen, Charles V. Stewart, Lukas Picek
Text_Content: Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.

Title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
Author: Siddharth Aphale, Ayushman Singh
Text_Content: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

Title: Batch-Conditioned Semantic Anchors for Robust Transductive Adaptation of Vision--Language Models
Author: Mohammed Rahman Sherif Khan Mohammad, Ardhendu Behera, Sandip Pradhan, Swagat Kumar, Amr Ahmed
Text_Content: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models at test time by refining predictions on an unlabeled batch, but current methods face a key trade-off. Aggressive approaches exploit batch structure but can drift when batches are sparse, have prior shift, or cover little of the label space. Conservative methods better preserve CLIP text semantics, but fixed semantic references can under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence. We propose JPTA (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation), a prior-aware framework that casts transductive VLM adaptation as batch-conditioned semantic reference estimation. Instead of treating CLIP text prototypes as fixed priors or freely replaceable, JPTA views them as semantic references that shift toward image-side batch structure only under calibrated evidence. It estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references whose impact is scaled by batch reliability. Across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation, and online streams, JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches. Anchor-drift, active-support, and absent-class-mass diagnostics show that JPTA fixes effective-class mismatch without unconstrained transductive drift, indicating that robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choose between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/JPTA.git.

Title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
Author: Kai Ponel, Marco Polignano, Erasmo Purificato, Aylin Julia Temizkan, Marco Levantesi, Giovanni Semeraro, Ernesto William De Luca
Text_Content: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

Title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
Author: Xinrui Zhong, Zhifeng Li, Zhiming Wang, Xinze Feng, Yongqi Liu, Shanglin Yang, Yang Zhou, Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen
Text_Content: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

Title: Deterministic Fault-Tolerant Connectivity Oracles with Subquadratic Space
Author: Merav Parter, Elad Tzalik
Text_Content: A fault-tolerant (FT) connectivity oracle for an $n$-vertex graph $G=(V,E)$ determines whether $G- F$ is connected for any query set $F\subseteq E$. When the number of failures is unrestricted, prior constructions exhibited a sharp contrast between randomization and determinism: randomized oracles use only $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space [Duan and Pettie, SICOMP 2020], whereas no deterministic construction was known to improve upon storing $G$ explicitly, requiring $Θ(n^2)$ bits in the worst case. The promise that $F\subseteq E$ is essential for subquadratic space: allowing arbitrary queries $F\subseteq V\times V$ forces quadratic space. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, Khanna, Konrad, and Putterman [SODA 2027] recently constructed deterministic oracles using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{f}n)$ space that also report approximate distances with polylogarithmic stretch. Their result improves upon the classical $O(fn)$ space bound for deterministic connectivity oracles [Pătraşcu and Thorup, FOCS 2007], but offers no space savings over storing $G$ when $f=Θ(n^2)$. We present the first deterministic connectivity oracles with subquadratic space for failure sets of unrestricted size, using $\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ space. We also establish the first polynomial separation between deterministic and randomized connectivity oracles, proving that every deterministic oracle requires $\widetildeΩ(n^{3/2})$ bits in the worst case. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, we obtain deterministic connectivity oracles using $\widetilde{O}(f^{2/5}n)$ space, improving the dependence on $f$ in the bound of Khanna et al., and prove a lower bound of $\widetildeΩ(f^{1/4}n)$ bits.

Title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
Author: Haoxiang Cao, Yuxuan Zhang, Penghui Du, Bo Li, Jiajiong Cao, Yingying Fan, Zimeng Wu, Yifu Luo, Mingzhe Zheng, Junwen Miao, Huaisong Zhang, Yang Yao, Yu Wang, Dongfu Jiang, Ping Nie, Wenhu Chen, Chaoqun Wang, Changqian Yu, Kelsey R. Allen
Text_Content: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

Title: Regression with Many Generated Controls
Author: Timothy Christensen, Daniel Vebman
Text_Content: We consider linear regression when some covariates are endogenous, a variable sufficient to control for endogeneity exists but is latent, and the practitioner can generate many proxies for the latent control. For instance, one could cheaply but imperfectly impute the latent control using different AI/ML methods, each generating a different proxy. There are several options the practitioner might consider in this scenario: including all proxies or factors computed from the proxies as controls, instrumental variables estimation, and some nonlinear variants thereof. We use a transparent model to derive the implicit estimand each approach targets, determine when these estimands recover the parameter of interest, and provide some practical recommendations. We show that with a sufficiently rich set of generated controls, practitioners can consistently estimate the parameter of interest without relying on validation data.

Title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
Author: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
Text_Content: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr

Title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos
Author: Hanyu Chen, Noah Snavely
Text_Content: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$Ω$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.

Title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
Author: Austin C. Kozlowski, Avital Mintz, Madison Lee
