Text_Content: Common methods for monitoring features in large language models (LLMs) such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features maintain a consistent representation across contexts. LLMs, however, can flexibly adopt different perspectives or "personas" that suggest different underlying systems of conceptual relations. In this paper, we examine whether prompting an LLM to adopt a persona alters the representational geometry of the model's latent space. We extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare these against two neutral baselines. We find that persona conditioning systematically alters both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes themselves in directions consistent with the specified ideology. We then test the implications of this reorganization for two safety-relevant features: truthfulness and morality. Linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and classifiers built from manually selected word representations, all trained without a persona, produce divergent results when applied to models conditioned on political personas, producing politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements. These findings suggest that internal representations, as they are conventionally extracted, can exhibit different geometric relations when the model adopts personas, potentially undermining monitoring efforts.

Title: Inherited Local Shrinkage for Adaptive Functional Form Discovery
Author: Jacob C. Schultz, Daniel Taylor-Rodriguez
Text_Content: Statistical models frequently employ nonlinear effects, interactions, and multiresolution basis expansions to represent complex relationships between predictors and responses. Determining the appropriate level of model complexity, however, remains a fundamental challenge. This paper introduces \textit{Inherited Local Shrinkage} (ILS), a Bayesian global-local shrinkage framework for adaptive functional form discovery that incorporates strong heredity among hierarchically related predictors. ILS propagates shrinkage through directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encoding relationships among predictors, allowing increasingly complex terms to contribute only when supported by their simpler ancestors. This construction provides a common prior framework for a broad class of hierarchical regression models. We demonstrate its application to polynomial regression, as well as multiresolution modeling with two-dimensional Haar wavelet and eigenvalue-ordered spline (EVOS) bases. Although these examples illustrate specific basis systems, ILS is not tied to any particular basis construction and can be applied to any regression model in which relationships among predictors can be represented by a DAG, regardless of the graph's size or topology. Simulation studies demonstrate that ILS achieves competitive predictive performance relative to existing heredity-constrained methods while recovering underlying functional structure. Spatial applications further illustrate its ability to adaptively regulate model complexity across multiple resolutions, identifying where finer-scale detail is supported by the data. Together, these results establish ILS as a flexible framework for hierarchical complexity control and adaptive functional form discovery in Bayesian regression.

Title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness
Author: Grant Shanklin, Jiří Němeček, Asia Biega
Text_Content: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.

Title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
Author: Yingying Yan, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Wei, Qianzhou Wang, Lei Zhang, Jianmin Chen, Yuyang Xia, Botong Geng, Jinjian Wu, Qifeng Chen
Text_Content: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.

Title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
Author: Eliane Younes, Elie Hachem, Marc Bernacki
Text_Content: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

Title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
Author: Xinrui Zhong, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu, Zhaohui Wang, Shanglin Yang, Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen
Text_Content: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

Title: Same Layout, Different Count: What Number Words Do Past Ten in Text-to-Image Models
Author: Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
Text_Content: Ask SD3.5-Medium for twelve of an object and then, from the same starting noise, for twenty-five. The picture keeps its layout, but the count changes about as much as it would under a new random seed, and in no consistent direction. We study what number words do once a request passes about ten objects, in five open text-to-image models. Holding the object and the starting noise fixed, we change one thing at a time, and people who never see the request count 3,088 of the images. Every model follows the number for small crowds, but only up to a point, its reach: SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev stop following it soon after ten, while FLUX.2 [klein] and Qwen-Image follow it loosely up to twenty-five. Beyond SD3.5-M's reach, the coarse part of the starting noise fixes the composition of the picture but not how many objects it holds: redrawing only the noise finer than an eighth of the image keeps the layout as well as a new number does, and already moves the count two-thirds as far. The number word still reaches the denoiser and acts in its first steps, but nothing we tried gives it a clear direction. Shown instead as a noised grid in the starting latent, the count is drawn: people find it in 59% of images, against 4% when it is only told. Past ten, an exact-match score barely separates a model that follows the number loosely from one that ignores it, and a relative-error score can even prefer a constant guess of sixteen. A same-noise test with a few requests per object tells them apart.

Title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
Author: Peidi Dong, Yunze Xiao, Yu-Lin Tsai, Yichen Zheng, Heyuan Huang, Weihao Xuan, Mark Dredze, Jen-tse Huang
Text_Content: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

Title: Context-Aware Autoregressive Image Generation for Emerging Reasoning Properties
Author: Jixuan Ying, Haoyu Liu, Timing Yang, Tingyu Zhu, Predrag Neskovic, Anand Bhattad, Cihang Xie, Zeyu Zheng, Alan Yuille, Feng Wang
Text_Content: Autoregressive image generation has recently emerged as a competitive visual generation paradigm, yet its generation order is often predefined or heuristic, such as next-patch prediction, random-order prediction, or one-step generation for specific scales. We observe that these strategies can cause models to overlook important structural dependencies in images, thereby limiting both structural robustness and reasoning capability. In this work, we propose a context-aware autoregressive generation framework, where the model dynamically determines the next token location based on global context and current local information. Rather than following a fixed or random order, our method allows the generation process to adapt to image structure and semantic dependencies. Extensive experiments show that context-aware generation significantly improves structural robustness across different image AR paradigms, including masked autoregressive and scale-wise autoregressive models. Beyond quantitative improvements, we further observe emerging reasoning properties: the model can better understand complex semantic instructions and generate images that more faithfully follow the given guidance. These findings suggest that generation order is a critical yet underexplored factor in image autoregressive modeling, and that context-aware decoding can unlock stronger reasoning-aware visual generation capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/Hpesojyjx/Saccades-AR.

Title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
Author: Hongcheng Gao, Weiheng Li, Yipeng Wei, Yu Lei, Shuo Sun, Yi Li, Yajiao Wang, Jie Luo, Jianwei Wen, Xinyi Zhou, Hongda Li, Yibing Zhang, Henghui Sun, Yufan Zhou, Tianfang Hao, Naihao Xue, Hailong Qu, Jingjing Zhou, Peng Xu, Yongzheng Wei, Yichen Zhu, Ziying Wang, Yibo Wang, Jianshu Zeng, Yuhang Lei, Zeqiang Wang
Text_Content: We introduce Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter model for engineering with native multimodal input, deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window. We design the Micius data pipeline as a knowledge-tree-driven data flywheel comprising three stages: knowledge tree construction and expansion, data synthesis, and quality validation with hard-example augmentation. From this data, we train expert models for semiconductor knowledge and reasoning, hardware coding, and semiconductor multimodal understanding, along with agentic experts. Subsequently, we employ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to supervise training on sequences generated by Micius itself, thereby integrating the capabilities of these expert models into a unified model. On more than 20 datasets with about 15K records, Micius-Flash averages 64.2% on hardware code benchmarks, 15.0 points above a same-size baseline. It scores 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, exceeding the same-size baseline by 17.2 points. We further develop Micius Harness for industrial applications, connecting the model to specialized tools, including EDA tools and KiCad, as well as execution environments. Case studies in PCB design, chip design workflow automation, and software development demonstrate the model's ability to use tool execution feedback for multi-step planning, code debugging, and iterative verification. We release Micius as an open-source model to advance the development of agents for science and engineering.

Title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
Author: Tommy He, Thomas Jiralerspong
Text_Content: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.

Title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
Author: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
Text_Content: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.

Title: Experimental evaluation of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis for shear-dependent viscosity fluids
Author: Luciano Hergenreder, Serge Simoëns, Wernher Brevis
Text_Content: We experimentally investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis to shear-dependent viscosity fluids. We assess whether dissipative range statistics exhibit a self-similar behavior in nearly homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, using stereo particle image velocimetry in aqueous Carbopol solutions across two concentrations and a range of forcing conditions. We observe that, when normalized by the mean viscosity and mean dissipation rate, second- and third-order structure functions collapse across the different experimental conditions and exhibit functional forms compatible with classical Newtonian results. These observations are in general agreement with the recent numerical results of Rosti [J. Fluid Mech. 1012, R5 (2025)], who proposed that Kolmogorov's similarity hypotheses can be extended to shear-thinning fluids by considering dissipation scales based on the mean viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the flow index.

Title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
Author: Brandon Gower-Winter, Georg Krempl
Text_Content: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous. Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.

Title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
Author: Andrey Rybakov, Marco Marino, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Eugenio Coronado, Jaime Ferrer
Text_Content: In the field of magnetism within condensed matter physics, magnetic systems are microscopically described by a spin Hamiltonian. Its parameterization is accessible through both ab initio calculations and fits to experimental data. Frequently, this is achieved via multi-stage calculations that either relate the parameters to observable material properties or map a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto an effective spin model. In this realm, accurate and flexible methods are essential for simulating the physical properties of the latter. The present study focuses on one such method: spin wave theory. The approach is applied to a new formulation of the spin Hamiltonian, named polynomial localized spin model (PLSM), which includes terms of arbitrary order in the spin operators. This enables the direct application of linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to the analysis of the energy landscape and spin-wave spectrum of arbitrary collinear and non-collinear phases in any realistic magnetic material. Moreover, the classical and quantum parts of the PLSM are cleanly separated. Finally, an open-source implementation of LSWT, named Magnopy, is presented. It interfaces with modern parameterization software, supports arbitrary collinear and non-collinear systems, and is designed for both scripting and standalone use.

Title: Coexistence-Aware Antenna Tilt and Resource Allocation for Cellular-Connected UAV Corridors
Author: Tarun Singh Rawat, Pradyumna Kumar Bishoyi
Text_Content: Cellular-connected UAV corridors reuse terrestrial infrastructure to provide predictable aerial connectivity, but coexistence with ground users (GUEs) creates competing demands on antenna tilt and physical resource blocks (PRBs). Prior work optimizes tilt for signal quality alone and does not address joint tilt-PRB planning under corridor rate and GUE delay constraints, nor the allocation policy needed when combined resource claims exceed the PRB budget. We address both gaps by formulating a joint antenna-tilt and PRB-allocation problem that maximizes GUE sum-log-rate subject to a minimum UAV corridor rate and an $ M/G/1$-based GUE mean-delay bound. We decompose the problem into two subproblems: antenna tilts are adapted via projected gradient ascent, while PRB allocation follows a techno-economic approach. Under resource scarcity, we cast the PRB scarcity as a bankruptcy problem and apply the weighted Talmud rule to balance GUE and UAV claims. Simulation results demonstrate that relaxing the GUE delay bound consistently reduces UAV rate dissatisfaction under the proposed allocation.

Title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI
Author: Remi Denton, Aida Davani, Cynthia L Bennett, Michael Madaio, Roma Patel, Himabindu Lakkaraju
Text_Content: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

Title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
Author: David Rostcheck
Text_Content: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

Title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
Author: Gagik Amirkhanyan, Nuojin Cheng
Text_Content: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

Title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2
Author: Nguyen Minh Thang, Trinh Thi Phuong
Text_Content: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.

Title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device
Author: Luciano Hergenreder, Serge Simoëns, Cristián Escauriaza, Wernher Brevis
Text_Content: We investigate the interscale energy dynamics of nearly homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) generated in a spherically forced, propeller-driven device. From a spatial perspective, by employing the Kármán-Howarth-Monin (KHM) framework, we analyze the scale-by-scale energy transfer without isotropy assumptions. In contrast to other forcing strategies, where regions with inverse and forward cascades often coexist in scale space, we show that spherical forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across the entire scale space. While the energy distribution remains highly isotropic and orientation-averaged structure functions align with Kolmogorov's two-thirds law, the energy flux exhibits a directional dependence, suggesting a higher sensitivity to residual forcing asymmetries. Regarding the temporal dynamics, the reduced mean flow generated by this device allows us to investigate the temporal variability in conditions where Taylor's frozen turbulence hypothesis does not apply. Our results provide experimental validation of Tennekes' Eulerian frequency spectrum, where intermediate scales evidence an inertial-convective range with statistics determined by the integral velocity scale and the dissipation rate. Finally, we adopt a global approach to investigate whether the main turbulent scales can be linked to external experimental parameters. We propose a framework that captures the propeller frequency dependence of the main turbulent variables obtained in our measurements and those of previously reported HIT chambers. These findings contribute to the understanding of how external forcing influences the complex interscale energy dynamics of turbulent flows from a spatial, temporal, and global perspective.

Title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
Author: Tanishq Bhatia, Jose A. Perea, Tarek M. Zikry
Text_Content: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.

Title: Nanopath: Fast, Fair, Open Experimentation for Pathology Foundation Models
Author: Paul S. Scotti, Hassan Muhammad, Ryan Kim, Nima Ashjaee, Ratna Sagari Grandhi, Saman Rahbar, Raymond Biju, Anish Dulal, Chao Feng, Connor Lane, Benjamin Warner, Tanishq Mathew Abraham
Text_Content: We introduce nanopath, an open-source framework and benchmark for rapidly training and evaluating small-scale pathology foundation models. Using a single H100 GPU, a typical nanopath model trains in a little over an hour on up to one million TCGA pathology tile presentations and evaluates within 25 minutes on a broad suite of tile-level and slide-level tasks. Nanopath enables rapid exploration of research ideas at small scale, so promising training recipes can subsequently be tested with more data and compute. To enable fair comparisons between ideas, we constrain submissions to fixed data and compute budgets while keeping the downstream evaluation protocol fixed. Anyone may clone the codebase, automatically download the data, reproduce or modify existing models, and submit a run to Labless, our public experiment ledger where researchers and AI agents can search through prior attempts. Since its public release in June 2026, nanopath has received 1,269 experiments from 20 contributors. Here, we detail its design and assess how well its rapid evaluation tracks standardized THUNDER, HEST, and PathoBench (CPTAC) benchmarks across six nanopath and 14 reference foundation models. Nanopath's fast evaluation suite strongly tracked these standardized benchmarks, and a few 22M parameter nanopath models even outperformed giant 1.1B parameter models on a subset of downstream tasks. We subsequently discuss how we have since optimized nanopath's evaluation suite to be an even more faithful, quick proxy for external benchmarking. Nanopath provides an accessible testbed for students, researchers, and AI agents to explore pathology foundation modeling through fair, transparent, and directly comparable experiments.

Title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
Author: Nuno Batista, Gabriel Falcao, Penousal Machado
Text_Content: Choosing a quantum error-correcting code for a real device means scoring candidates with circuit-level simulations so slow that only a few hundred can be run. So every evaluation counts, and a search is judged by how many good codes it finds per paid evaluation. Quantum LDPC codes built from a few group elements protect many logical qubits, but good ones are rare in a huge space. We introduce GFlowQEC, to our knowledge the first generative flow network (GFlowNet) for quantum code design. It builds a code one group element at a time and learns to propose codes in proportion to a power of their score. We train it once on scores from earlier searches, freeze it, and let it propose lifted-product codes with 180 physical qubits, scored by their distances. Ranking ten of its draws per paid call, it finds more than twice as many new top-scoring codes (inequivalent to any it was trained on) as tuned parallel tempering, even when tempering starts from GFlowQEC's training codes. It finds more than three and a half times as many as a supervised screen ranking ten random candidates per call. When both rank a hundred, the screen beats GFlowQEC, and does best ranking GFlowQEC's draws. Soft Q-learning, which shares the GFlowNet's optimal policy, does as well at one noise bias and better at the other, so the gain does not depend on the GFlowNet's training loss. Trained proposers can make a budget of expensive evaluations go further when good codes are rare.

Title: Linear-time erasure recovery for quantum expander codes
Author: Anirudh Krishna, Christopher A. Pattison
Text_Content: Erasures are used to model faults at a subset of known locations in various platforms used to construct fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond the utility in erasure recovery, efficient decoders for erasures are useful to both understand error decoders and as a subroutine for error decoding. Classical expander codes, which belong to the family of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, can be equipped with the Peeling decoder which works in linear time. Our main result is the algorithm Small-Set-Peeling, a quantum generalization of the classical Peeling decoder for erasures, that applies to quantum expander codes (Tillich, Zémor, IEEE T-IT 2013; Leverrier, Tillich, Zémor, FOCS 2015). This decoder can correct up to $D-1$ erasures, where $D$ is the (design) distance of the code and, importantly, is the first decoder that is guaranteed to do so in linear time. Combining with the erasure-conversion algorithm Small-Set-Find (Krishna, Livni-Navon, Wootters, SODA 2024), our result also implies the existence of a novel graph-local linear-time decoder for Pauli errors.

Title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
Author: Juncheng Ma, Jiaxin Li, Jiankai Tu, Bo Liang, Guodong Lv, Yufan Deng, Junzhe Tang, Liangzhu Yang, Chen Bian, Shukai Gong, Ye Huang, Yintianrun Zhang, Zicong Cao, Baohao Zhu, Jianxin Bi, Tengfei Yan, Yinyuan Zhang, Kewei Zhang, Xinglong Chen, Kaiqi Chen, Duomin Wang, Xiaotian Tang, Liang Tan, Li Li, Yuan Xu, Haosen Yang, Yuqi Wang, Jingfei Xia, Songyan Huang, Zhiyang Dou, Zhen Dong, Enze Xie, Wojciech Matusik, Tat-Seng Chua, Daquan Zhou
Text_Content: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

Title: Boxicity of Power Graphs of Finite Nilpotent Groups
Author: L. Sunil Chandran, Jinia Ghosh, Suraj Kumar Sahoo
Text_Content: The \textit{boxicity} of an undirected graph $Γ$, denoted as $\operatorname{box}(Γ)$, is the smallest non-negative integer $d$ such that $Γ$ can be represented as the intersection graph of axis-parallel rectangular boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The \emph{power graph} of a group $G$, denoted as $\operatorname{Pow}(G)$, is an undirected graph whose vertex set is the group itself, with two elements being adjacent if one is a power of the other. We determine the exact boxicity of power graphs of finite nilpotent groups. For a cyclic group of order $n=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i^{e_i}>1$, where the $p_i$ are distinct primes, we prove that its power graph has boxicity $\sum_{i=1}^{r}e_i-\max_i e_i$. For a finite nilpotent group $G$, let the number of noncyclic odd Sylow subgroups be denoted by $t(G)$. If $G$ has odd order or if $G$ has a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup, then $\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(G))=\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(\mathbb{Z}_{\operatorname{exp}(G)}))+t(G)$, where $\operatorname{exp}(G)$ denotes the \emph{exponent} of a group $G$. When the Sylow $2$-subgroup is noncyclic, and the odd part is nontrivial, the boxicity equals this value or one more, and we characterise precisely when each of these values is attained. The boxicity of power graphs of arbitrary finite groups and the exact boxicity of the comparability graph of the Boolean lattice were posed as open questions in Discrete Mathematics, 349(7):115017, 2026. As a consequence of our results, we answer the latter question completely and the former question partially, by computing the exact boxicity of the power graphs of nilpotent groups.

Title: The 3-Uniform Hyperclique Hypothesis is False
Author: Timothy M. Chan, Reina Itakura, Zhiyuan Ma, Yuancheng Yu
Text_Content: We present truly subquartic algorithms for detecting or counting 4-hypercliques in a 3-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices, disproving a popular hypothesis in fine-grained complexity. The result immediately implies a faster algorithm for finding a $k$-hyperclique in a 3-uniform hypergraph for all constant $k\ge 4$, and a faster exponential-time algorithm for Max-3-SAT.

Title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
Author: Man-Ling Sung, Hemanth Kandula, Jeff Ma, William Hartmann, Matthew Snover
Text_Content: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

Title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
Author: Aditya Raghavan, Sergei V Kalinin
Text_Content: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

Title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
Author: Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Xueqing Peng, Yupeng Cao, Yuechen Jiang, Zhuohan Xie, Anke Xu, Wenbo Cao, Jiarui Chen, Zehan Li, Jimin Huang, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Yuehua Tang, Sophia Ananiadou, Jian-Yun Nie
Text_Content: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

Title: CMS ECAL Phase-2 upgrade: characterisation and stability analysis of a three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system
Author: Liv Anke Richter, Günther Dissertori, Werner Lustermann, Krzysztof Stachon
Text_Content: As part of the High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider, the front-end electronics of the Compact Muon Solenoid electromagnetic calorimeter barrel are being replaced. A three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system supplies the upgraded electronics. As the cascade dynamics require characterisation to ensure stable operation, interactions between the three converter stages are assessed at their two interfaces using the Nyquist criterion. A validated shunt-injection setup using a Bode 100 frequency-response analyser provides in-situ impedance measurements under load to assess the accuracy of the averaged converter models. Results show that both interfaces are stable over the evaluated configurations, with modelled minimum distances to the critical point of 0.76 and 0.79, respectively. A turn-on study identifies capacitor charging at Stage 3 as the main cause of inrush currents triggering Stage 2 overcurrent protection. Two Stage 3 board variants stagger converter enables within and between boards, keeping the measured two-tower current below 5 A, within the 8.0 A protection threshold.

Title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
Author: Nil-Jana Akpinar, Eugenia Kim, Natalie Isak, Amanda Minnich, Victoria Westerhoff, Matthew Dressman
Text_Content: Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.

Title: Monadically Dependent Graph Classes Have Almost Bounded Merge-Width
Author: Jan Dreier, Nikolas Mählmann, Michał Pilipczuk, Szymon Toruńczyk
Text_Content: A graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is monadically dependent if one cannot interpret all graphs in vertex-colored graphs from $\mathcal{C}$ using a fixed formula of first-order logic. We prove that every monadically dependent graph class has almost bounded merge-width, thereby confirming a conjecture of the first and the last author [STOC '25]. Our proof is algorithmic and the witnessing decompositions in the form of merge sequences can be computed in nearly-cubic time. This is a step towards the proof of fixed-parameter tractability of model checking first-order logic on monadically dependent graph classes, which is achieved in a companion paper.

Title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
Author: Ben Johnson, Hayden Helm
Text_Content: Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

Title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
Author: Kendra Givens, Taylor T. Johnson, Bryan C. Ward, Thomas Beckers
Text_Content: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

Title: Message-passing graph persistence
Author: Jorge Luiz Franco, Arthur Queiroz Moura, Moacir Ponti, Amauri Souza
Text_Content: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test. Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors that can complement GNN representations, but existing approaches typically compute persistence separately from the representation learning process. In this paper, we introduce Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations. At each filtration step, node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events. These embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation. We prove that MGP is invariant under graph isomorphism and that it is strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends. We evaluate MGP on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets. Experiments show that MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of these datasets.

Title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
Author: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
Text_Content: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

Title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
Author: Harsidak Singh Banwait
Text_Content: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.

Title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
Author: Mohamed Azzam, Ziyang Xu, Quinlan Couch, Zoe Keese, Andrea Cadlo, Christine Sedze-DeWolf, Micaiah Uhrmacher, Madelyn Graff, Catherine Fox, Lauren Vatter, Paige Jeffryes, Jason Christensen, Neil Hamill, Shibiao Wan, Ling Li, Jieqiong Wang
Text_Content: Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation. Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference. Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed. Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

Title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
Author: Vivek Acharya
Text_Content: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

Title: Open-shell Configuration State Functions as trial states for phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
Author: Don Danilov, Hugh G. A. Burton, James Shee
Text_Content: The accurate description of open-shell states in molecular systems poses challenges for approximate electronic structure methods. One emerging approach is to variationally optimize the orbitals of a single user-selected Configuration State Function (CSF), i.e., a linear combination of Slater determinants that is constructed as an eigenstate of the total spin operator. In this work we explore the use of these orbital-optimized single CSFs as trial wavefunctions in phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC), a stochastic method that recovers electron correlation by evolving an initial state in imaginary time, subject to a constraint imposed by the trial state. We investigate the symmetric stretch of H-He-H, a series of small $p$-block compounds with diradicaloid singlet states, twisted ethene conformers, and a bimetallic iron-sulfur complex. We find that accurate energetics are obtained for states dominated by open-shell character, and that for certain atoms and diatomics the accuracy can be significantly improved when the trial is made to also preserve the relevant angular momentum symmetries. Furthermore, our study reveals that the open-shell CSF trial is suboptimal when the target electronic state reflects a significant mixture of ionic and covalent character, e.g., at shorter bond lengths in H-He-H and for the superexchange-stabilized ground state of [2Fe-2S]$^{2+}$. Our findings suggest that ph-AFQMC using CSF trial states is a promising method for many (but not all) strongly correlated molecular states, especially given its relatively low computational cost, and that it provides a reasonable non-perturbative way to recover some of the dynamic correlation that is otherwise missing in the CSF.

Title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
Author: Shaoliang Yang, Jun Wang
Text_Content: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

Title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
Author: Yu Zhang, JingQi Liu, Shuangrui Zhao, Yuanyu Zhang, Yulong Shen, Xiaohong Jiang
Text_Content: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions increasingly require both semantic reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy SemCom designs mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source identity protection. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation perspective for integrated SemCom-identity protection that leverages task-level error tolerance to coordinate semantic information and source identity information carried by the same waveform. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for different identity protection objectives, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism with two operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic reconstruction quality is maintained to support anonymous transmission. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.

Title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
Author: Andrea Cambiaghi, Marco Tarini
Text_Content: The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants. We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays. We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

Title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence
Author: Songbin Liu, Hanyu Yang, Junren Chen, Arian Maleki
Text_Content: We study the fundamental limits of jointly estimating the signal amplitude and the atmospheric phase distortion in complex-valued multi-look coherent imaging, where the measurements are corrupted by multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise, all looks share a known Gaussian sensing matrix, and both parameters belong to structured classes. By analyzing a constrained maximum likelihood estimator, we establish an upper bound on the joint minimax risk that holds uniformly over the admissible parameter classes, while oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments yield worst-case lower bounds over the admissible parameter classes. These results quantify the effects of structural complexity, signal and measurement dimensions, the number of looks, and the noise level, and establish matching minimax rates in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension. We also construct a two-stage estimator for signal recovery under arbitrary diagonal sign distortions in the real-valued analogue. Under additional conditions, it recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the dependence of the joint, signal, and phase errors on the model parameters and provide further support for the theoretical analysis.

Title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
Author: Quan Minh Nguyen, Hoang M. Ngo, Bhakti Chowkwale, Yasaman Keshtkarjahromi, My T. Thai
Text_Content: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

Title: Target PageRank: Matching Prescribed PageRank Scores via Budgeted Edge Additions
Author: Parth Gupta, Abhinav Jain, Avishek Mukhopadhyay, Amitabha Bagchi, Sayan Ranu, Abhijnan Chakraborty
Text_Content: PageRank is widely used to quantify the importance of nodes in directed networks. In applications such as recommendation systems, it is increasingly important that the PageRank distribution provides a fair representation of node exposure. This motivates the problem of making minimal changes to a graph so that the PageRank values of a given set of target nodes $T$ match a desired vector $\boldsymbol{t}$. In this paper, we study this problem under an edge-addition budget $B$, where exactly $B$ edges may be added to the graph. We show that deciding whether a multiset of exactly $B$ added edges can make the target nodes attain their desired absolute PageRank scores is NP-complete. After this, we define the $\ell_1$ Target PageRank problem in which we seek to minimize the $\ell_1$ distance between the target vector and resultant vector. We show that this optimization problem admits no polynomial-time multiplicative constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$. Motivated by these hardness results, we propose two greedy heuristics for approaching the target PageRank vector. We additionally propose a Random Walk Hungarian (RWH) heuristic that addresses the addition of edges between dissimilar nodes by incorporating a penalty for such edges. Finally, we evaluate the proposed heuristics on several real-world and synthetic datasets and compare their performance in terms of PageRank accuracy, computational efficiency, and the relevance of the added edges.

Title: Semantic Residual Vector Quantization for Sign Language Generation
Author: Chang Liu, Ke Han, Niccolò Biondi, Gloria Isotton, Elisa Ricci, Davide Talon, Nicu Sebe
Text_Content: Sign language generation (SLG) maps written sentences into signing motion while preserving both lexical content and fine-grained articulation. This requires a model to decide what signs should be expressed and to realize them through precise handshape, trajectory, facial expression and body coordination. Existing pose-based systems and reconstruction-only motion tokenizers often entangle these two decisions, leaving the generator without an explicit text-aligned intermediate target for what to sign before refining how to sign it. To address this issue, we introduce Semantic Residual Vector Quantization (SRVQ), a framework for SLG that frames generation as a two-level process moving from semantics to kinematics. The newly introduced SRV Quantizer learns a hierarchy in which the first residual level encodes sign content and subsequent levels refine pose, handshape, trajectory, and body coordination, all within a single quantizer and without separate semantic representations or external planning stages. Through word-aware conditioning for hierarchical code generation, a masked semantic generator predicts semantic codes and a kinematic generator completes the residual codes for full SMPL-X motion synthesis. We evaluate using retrieval and FID in a shared text-motion embedding space, alongside standard geometric metrics. On CSL-Daily and Phoenix-2014T, SRVQ achieves R@1 of 82.3 and 70.3, outperforming the previous SOTA by 30 and 46 points, respectively.

Title: Machine Learning the Complete Active-Space Wavefunction Reconstruction
Author: Aniruddha Seal, Bhavnesh Jangid, Helen S. Clifford, Andrew L. Ferguson, Laura Gagliardi
Text_Content: Machine-learned interatomic potentials enable multireference-quality reaction dynamics but do not retain the electronic structure underlying the predicted energies and forces. Recovering this information by independently performing complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) calculations is both expensive and potentially inconsistent. We introduce the Complete Active-Space Wave Function Reconstruction (CAS-WR) model, which learns the geometry-dependent electronic structure from CASSCF data and reconstructs the CAS wave function without repeated orbital optimization. Combined with uncertainty-based active learning, CAS-WR is demonstrated for the Diels--Alder reaction and \ce{TiC+}-catalyzed C--H activation. The approach enables trajectory-resolved analysis of multiconfigurational electronic structure across reactive ensembles. Preliminary applications to excited-state proton transfer and transition-metal photocatalysis suggest that CAS-WR can provide a general route toward recovering electronic structure along complex ground- and excited-state reactive dynamics.

Title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
Author: Omar Hagrass, Bharath K. Sriperumbudur
Text_Content: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $χ^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $Δ$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $λ$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $Δ^{-1/(2s)}$.
