Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.

Title: Constant-Time Dynamic Edge Coloring via Dynamic Splitting and LLL
Author: Mohsen Ghaffari, Sijin Peng
Text_Content: We give a dynamic algorithm that maintains a near-optimal edge coloring in constant expected time per update. For every fixed $ε>0$, the algorithm maintains a $(1+ε)Δ$ edge coloring under edge insertions and deletions in $\mathrm{poly}(1/ε)$ worst-case expected update time against an oblivious adversary, provided $Δ\geΔ_ε=\widetildeΘ(1/ε^2)$. The previous constant-time algorithm of Bhattacharya, Costa, Panski, and Solomon (BCPS) required $Δ\ge(\log n/ε^4)^{Θ(\log(1/ε)/ε)}$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. We remove this dependence on $n$, answering their open question. Our approach differs substantially from that of BCPS, which relied on coloring in locally tree-like subgraphs. Instead, we draw on distributed algorithms that organize partial coloring through successive applications of the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL). We develop a dynamic LLL solver with worst-case expected update bounds and a dynamic splitting algorithm that partitions edges into low-degree subgraphs. A key technical contribution is a bottom-up method for iterative splitting, which avoids the logarithmic overhead of maintaining successive levels. It achieves constant expected update time by adaptively choosing which levels to inspect and repair, rather than inspecting every level after each update. We believe these dynamic splitting and LLL tools can be of interest beyond edge coloring.

Title: Alternatives to Shallow Autoencoders for Collaborative Filtering
Author: Mario Mallea, Angela Nebot, Francisco Mugica
Text_Content: Collaborative filtering (CF) is a cornerstone of recommender systems and plays a relevant role in many modern applications. CF uses user-item interaction data to discover future preferences. Although deep learning models have shown promise in CF, Embarrassingly Shallow Autoencoders for Sparse Data (EASE) has gained attention for its outstanding ranking accuracy provided by its closed-form solution. EASE relies primarily on relationships among items to fit a full-rank high-dimensional linear mapping. We hypothesize that this design limits its capacity to capture similar but not equivalent fine-grained user relationships, consequently limiting its recommendation accuracy. This paper introduces an alternative formulation based on EASE that takes advantage of user-user information. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid model that combines both user-user and item-item adjacency distributions. Our experiments reveal that the proposed models outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks, highlighting the significance of including the user alternative in shallow autoencoder studies for CF.

Title: A Width Hierarchy of Monotone Algebraic Branching Programs
Author: Julian Dörfler, Alexander Rogovskyy
Text_Content: It is well known that $\mathsf{VF} = \mathsf{VBP}_{3}$ (Ben-Or-Cleve'92), i.e. the width of any constant-width algebraic branching program can be reduced to width $3$ with only a polynomial overhead to size. We prove that this is not the case for the monotone equivalents. In particular, we prove that there is an infinite hierarchy $\mathsf{mVBP}_{2} \subsetneq \mathsf{mVBP}_{3} \subsetneq \ldots$ by showing that $\mathrm{imm}_{k,n}$ requires width $w$ mABPs to have depth at least $\left(\frac{k}{w-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}\left\lfloor n^{\frac{1}{(w-2)}} \right\rfloor - 1}$ whenever $3 \leq w < k$. We prove this lower bound using support-based techniques. Since this lower bound is exact instead of asymptotic, it allows some width separations even for superconstant width. Moreover, it allows us to show that the expressive power of poly-sized monotone formulas of depth $2d$ is not reached by poly-sized mABPs of width $d-1$ but a width of $2d+1$ is sufficient. We contrast this to unbounded-depth monotone formulas, which are proven to be stronger than constant-width mABPs, but weaker than $\log$-width mABPs and incomparable for most widths in between. Finally, we generalize Snir's framework (Snir'80) for showing lower bounds on the number of leaves of monotone formulas to monotone formulas of multiplication depth $d^{\times}$, giving a lower bound of $n \cdot k^{d^{\times}(n^{\frac{1}{d^{\times}}} - 1)}$ for the iterated matrix multiplication polynomial and $\left(\left(e+o(1)\right) \ln^{\circ(d^{\times}-1)}(n)\right)^n$ for the permanent.

Title: Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency: Test-Time Reasoning with Imperfect Generators and Verifiers
Author: Ekaterina Fadeeva, Xueyan Li, Mrinmaya Sachan, Maxim Panov
Text_Content: Large language models can solve many multi-step reasoning problems, but their reasoning remains brittle: plausible intermediate steps often lead to incorrect answers. Improving reasoning at test time requires balancing two imperfect signals: the generator, which provides diversity, and the verifier, which guides correctness. Existing approaches largely favor one side of this tradeoff. Verifier-weighted voting relies on trajectories sampled from the generator and cannot steer generation toward correct ones. By contrast, beam-style verifier-guided search can steer generation, but may over-concentrate on narrow trajectory sets and amplify verifier errors. We propose Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency (VGSC), a stochastic decoding framework that combines step-level correctness and future-outcome estimates to guide reasoning during generation. VGSC repeatedly proposes candidate next steps from the base language model and uses both signals in an acceptance/resampling procedure, while maintaining multiple trajectories for final answer-level self-consistency. We provide a probabilistic interpretation of VGSC as approximate sampling from a verifier-tilted trajectory distribution. Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, generator models, and verifier families, VGSC achieves higher average accuracy than representative baselines.

Title: A Sub-$3^n$ Upper Bound on the Number of Stable Matchings
Author: Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hikaru Wada, Masataka Yoneda
Text_Content: We study the problem of determining the maximum number of stable matchings. This classical counting problem was posed by Knuth and has been studied for five decades. We obtain a new $2.999^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings with $n$ men and $n$ women. This improves the best-known previous result by Palmer and Pálvölgyi. This result gets much closer to the well-known lower bound $\frac{2.28^n}{\text{poly}(n)}$. We refine their entropy-based framework by capturing broader structural relationships among stable matchings. To capture these relationships, we introduce new frameworks, including cones and supports. This establishes the $3.332^n$ bound. We also exploit relationships among local structures and use a charging argument to improve the bound to $2.999^n$.

Title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life
Author: Haibin Tong, Luming Guo, Nana Cui, Jiang Yu
Text_Content: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.

Title: Unraveling Primary Energy Conversion Dynamics in Intact Cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica
Author: Julian Lüttig, Ajeet Kumar, Maurice Schenker, Alastair T. Gardiner, Michal Koblížek, Donatas Zigmantas, Jennifer P. Ogilvie
Text_Content: Photosynthetic bacteria have evolved specialized light-harvesting structures to efficiently capture sunlight. Here, we investigate the ultrafast dynamics in intact cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica, featuring unique double-ring LHh-LH1 photosynthetic complexes containing bacteriochlorophyll a. Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with lock-in detection allows us to directly observe primary energy-conversion processes, from excitation-energy transfer within the antenna system to the formation of a charge-separated state in the reaction center, taking place on 50 ps time scale. Through comparison with Rhodospirillum rubrum, which lacks the outer antenna ring, we use a combination of global analysis and nodal/center line slope analyses to resolve LHh-LH1 excitation energy transfer which occurs on a ~1-2 ps timescale in Gemmatimonas groenlandica.

Title: AtomicFaaS: Offloading Side-Effect Compensation to the Serverless Platform
Author: Jonas Heisterberg, Sebastian Koch, Trever Schirmer, David Bermbach
Text_Content: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) simplifies distributed application development by offloading operational concerns to the platform, but developers remain responsible for recovering from failures. Retries require idempotent functions, which means that developers have to write complex, error-prone code that undoes or skips the already completed operations of a failed function. To address this, we propose AtomicFaaS, a platform extension that provides semantic atomicity for the external side effects of a function invocation, whether the function fails or its instance crashes, without developer-written compensation code. AtomicFaaS intercepts outbound calls and records their effects in a fault-tolerant log, from which the platform compensates leaked effects outside the failed instance. Compared with a manually implemented saga, AtomicFaaS eliminates compensation code and leaves no compensatable effects after any tested failure, while adding ~1 ms per intercepted call. Under load, it lowers the sustainable throughput of CPU-bound functions, while its latency overhead becomes negligible once calls to external services dominate the invocation time.

Title: Brueckner Orbitals in Local Pair Natural Orbital Coupled-Cluster Theory: DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)_Lambda2
Author: Andy Jiang, Tibor Gyori, Elizabeth C. Toth, Gabor Czako, Henry F. Schaefer
Text_Content: In this work, we implement closed-shell Brueckner orbitals for the efficient domain-based local pair natural orbital DLPNO-CCSD(T) and DLPNO-CCSD(T)$_Λ$ methods of the free and open-source \textsc{Psi4} package. We introduce a new algorithm that allows Brueckner orbitals to be computed within the DLPNO framework, resulting in the novel DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ methods. We show that DLPNO-BCCD(T) approximates its canonical BCCD(T) counterpart with significantly lower errors relative to the errors incurred by DLPNO-CCSD(T) over CCSD(T). Through a test on the S22 set of noncovalent dimers, the peak error across the set is reduced from 0.36 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.25 kcal mol$^{-1}$ using normal cutoffs, and 0.28 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.13 kcal mol$^{-1}$ at tight cutoffs. In addition, we show that BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$, a ${Λ_2}$-only implementation of Brueckner orbitals for the asymmetric triples method, generally produces the best agreement with CCSDT, compared to the (T), (T)$_Λ$, and B(T) perturbative triples corrections. This is established through benchmarks on thermochemistry tests on the barrier heights of semibullvalene and bullvalene Cope rearrangement, while the robustness of DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ is demonstrated along bond-breaking potential energy curves, where it matches the orbital-optimized quasi-variational asymmetric renormalized-triples OQVCCDAR(T) method closely for single-bond breaking, and approximates DLPNO-CCSDT respectably even when triple bonds are stretched, at a fraction of the computational cost.

Title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
Author: Joey David, Paul Caillon, Alexandre Allauzen
Text_Content: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter's leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter.

Title: When the Plan Changes: A Strategic World Testbed for Dynamic Multi-Agent Coordination
Author: Joon-Seok Kim, Eugene Agichtein, Kai Shu, Liang Zhao, Andreas Züfle
Text_Content: Changing an objective does not automatically revise agents' earlier plans or delegated tasks. Acknowledgment can coexist with obsolete execution, while misleading instructions can redirect work or discard retained constraints. We present a Strategic World simulation testbed that separates authoritative objectives, local plans, notice receipt, and consequential action. Six intervention families vary objectives, conditions, authority, membership, and communication. Matched protocols and deadlines establish feasibility for the tested disturbances. Controlled trajectories demonstrate that identical completion and acknowledgment summaries can conceal uninformed obsolete work, obsolete work after receipt, or blocked unsafe intent. Local language-model trials and instructed action probes reveal competence limits that constrain interpretation of dynamic failures. A further 16-episode comparison evaluates an engineered guard that prioritizes pending notice submissions over local work. It completes 4/4 held-out settings, compared with 1/4 for a calibrated assisted baseline. Each episode contains one large language model actor and two fixed peers. These results establish diagnostic distinctions and bounded policy feasibility under explicit simulation assumptions; they do not establish frontier-model reliability or autonomous team adaptation.

Title: A trust layer for fast pedestal-stability surrogates: calibrated error bars, out-of-distribution alarms and few-shot recalibration
Author: Amin Vakhshouri
Text_Content: Machine-learning surrogates of linear peeling-ballooning stability now run in milliseconds, but they are mostly deployed as point estimators: they do not say how wrong they may be, or when a query lies outside what they were trained on. For a fusion company designing a new device, every equilibrium of interest is outside the training data of existing surrogates, so this is the case that matters. We describe a model-agnostic trust layer for stability surrogates, made of conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms that route doubtful cases to the physics code, and recalibration from a few simulations of a new design, and we test it with pre-registered hypotheses. On a large public dataset of JET-like equilibria with ideal-MHD growth rates, the error bars hold their nominal coverage in distribution and fall short under a shift in plasma shape; a few dozen simulations of the new shape, or routing the cases the alarms flag, restore it. On resistive BOUT++ surrogates, the bars stay calibrated on held-out runs, the alarm flags tokamaks absent from training, and a scenario scan is screened in seconds instead of hours. Across equilibria from the SPARC library and the DIII-D coil set, a surrogate trained on our own graded BOUT++ labels beats the baseline on unseen equilibria, while a surrogate trained elsewhere ranks the same cases backwards and its alarm declines them. Building our own neural-operator surrogate, the harness exposed two input defects whose fix closed its gap to a simple network. For every surrogate tested, the trust layer keeps coverage near target, with a bar width set by that surrogate's own error. Not every pre-registered hypothesis held, and we report those results and the limits of all of them.

Title: Limited knowledge exchange across biological subfields in agent-based modelling: an LLM-assisted bibliometric analysis
Author: Kira Pugh, Rebecca M Crossley, Sara Hamis
Text_Content: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used across the biological sciences. While applications differ between biological subfields, the mathematical and statistical methods underlying ABMs largely do not, raising the question of how much knowledge is exchanged between subfields. We address this question by developing a bibliometric pipeline that combines a database keyword search with coarse- and fine-grained classification by a large language model (LLM). We apply the pipeline to the Web of Science Core Collection, classifying 22,936 ABM articles into ecology, epidemiology, oncology, other-biology, or not-biology. Using citation patterns and author overlap as proxies for knowledge exchange, we find that 83%, 81%, and 69% of citations from ecology, epidemiology, and oncology articles, respectively, go to articles in the same subfield. Furthermore, 91% of authors with at least two articles across these subfields publish exclusively within one subfield. Both proportions far exceed those expected under random assignment of subfields (permutation tests, $p \leq 0.001$). Terminology also differs, with "individual-based model" used mainly in ecology and "agent-based model" in epidemiology, oncology, and outside biology. Taken together, our results suggest limited knowledge exchange between biological subfields in ABM research, leading us to discuss opportunities for increased exchange through conferences, journals, and training.

Title: On Competing Sellers with Substitutable Goods
Author: Moshe Babaioff, Yuval Grofman, Brendan Lucier, Raghuvansh R. Saxena
Text_Content: We study mechanism design by an incumbent seller facing competition from an entrant seller of a substitute good. The incumbent commits to a potentially randomized mechanism before her competitor responds. A unit-demand buyer with fixed, publicly known values for the two goods observes both mechanisms and may interact with them in either order. How should a revenue-maximizing incumbent design her mechanism when her product is superior or inferior to her competitor's? We determine the incumbent's exact optimal revenue and characterize all mechanisms that obtain it. Commitment and randomization allow her to earn strictly positive revenue even against an arbitrarily superior product, despite earning nothing under posted-price (i.e., Bertrand) competition. Optimal mechanisms can require a continuum of lottery options, even though the buyer selects only one in equilibrium: unselected options shape the competitor's incentives rather than screen private buyer information. We also show that the buyer's ability to choose the interaction order can be strictly beneficial to the incumbent, even though the incumbent is always visited first at equilibrium. Finally, we show that without commitment, every pure Nash equilibrium yields Bertrand revenues even with randomized mechanisms.

Title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation
Author: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
Text_Content: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.

Title: BudgetSplat: Budget-Controllable Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
Author: Yuxi Hu, Jun Zhang, Wei Mao, Yuchen Rao, Friedrich Fraundorfer
Text_Content: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.

Title: Thermodynamics-Informed Learning Captures Hierarchical Hydrogen-Bond Networks in Deep Eutectic Solvents
Author: Yanpeng Ye, Chaoran Duan, Mian Xu, S. Mani Sarathy
Text_Content: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) offer a tunable platform for lignocellulose refining, but their solvation behavior depends on multicomponent hydrogen-bond networks rather than individual constituent properties. We develop TiNN, a thermodynamics-informed neural network that hierarchically represents HBA-HBD association and solute accommodation through a learned free-energy pathway. Trained on 938 records, TiNN achieves a test-set $R^2$ of 0.917 and generalizes to new HBA-HBD combinations and sparse conditions. Ablation identifies solute-specific stabilization as the largest contributor to prediction accuracy, while the importance of hydrogen-bond compatibility depends on the dissolution mechanism. Experimental measurements of glucose, xylan, and Kraft lignin in acidic, basic, and neutral DESs show that TiNN reduces the geometric mean solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to approximately 1.5-fold. Without training on fractionation data, TiNN also distinguishes DES formulations with high and low lignin and hemicellulose removal from corn stover. These results support chemically grounded solvent screening for lignocellulose fractionation.

Title: Competitive Equilibrium for Linear Chores is CLS-complete
Author: Qian Liu, Shinuo Ma, Yixin Tao, Minji Yang, Weiqiang Zheng
Text_Content: The competitive equilibrium (CE) is a fundamental concept for markets, with applications to efficient and fair allocation of resources. We consider the fundamental question of computing a CE in the most basic Fisher market model where agents have linear preferences. While it is known that we can compute a CE in strongly polynomial time with linear goods, there is no known polynomial-time algorithm for CE with linear chores. Computing a CE for linear chores is known to be in CLS with no hardness results. In this paper, we prove that computing an exact CE in Fisher markets with divisible chores and linear disutilities is CLS-hard and thus CLS-complete. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first CLS-completeness result for a market equilibrium problem. On the technical side, we use the nonconvex dual Eisenberg-Gale (EG) program whose Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) points are CE [Chaudhury, Kroer, Mehta, and Nan, 2024], and the CLS-complete problem of computing a KKT point of a quadratic program [Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender, and Savani, 2024]. We show that from any exact equilibrium of the constructed market, we can recover in polynomial time an $\varepsilon$-KKT point of the input quadratic program over the unit box.

Title: FOSCo-Net: Ego-centric Voxel Completion for Forest LiDAR Occlusions
Author: Iman Esfandiyar, Dominik Belter
Text_Content: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.

Title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains
Author: Yichiet Aun, Mohammed A. Alhartomi, Jing Jie Tan, Waqas Nadeem, Adeb Salh, Shankar Karuppayah, Sin Chee Tan
Text_Content: AI agents rely on third-party tools, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, whose publishers can be authenticated and whose execution can be restricted by runtime security policies. Yet authenticity does not guarantee benign behaviour: a legitimately signed tool may perform its advertised function while concealing malicious code that leaks confidential information. We demonstrate this trust failure with a signed MCP tool that embeds sensitive data in requests to a policy-allowed destination. Meta's MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run, yet fails to prevent this attack in every trial. We introduce germline execution, which limits information disclosure without inspecting or trusting tool implementations. Each tool invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, each receiving only information authorised for its destination. Even if malicious code executes, what it can disclose is bounded by the data available to its copy. Under explicit assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline, we prove sink noninterference for every signed release and, for releases deterministic within our replay model, show that a verified witness establishes a flow violation. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defences and an ablation. Invocations served by a single copy completed in 10-49 ms, 2-28x faster than restarting the tool for every invocation, the conventional way to clear state. These results show that data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software.

Title: Informing research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing: insights from a citizens' panel
Author: Hannah Dalgleish, Rafael Mestre, Heidi Wheatley, Angela YT Chan, Mariya Yanishevskaya, Duncan Grimes, Sophie Hart, Sergey Astakhov, Matt Ryan, Dianna Smith, Alexandra Anikina, Ceri Davies-Tyrie, Gianluca Audone, Mohammad Belal, Louis Cook
Text_Content: This report presents findings from a Citizens' Panel convened by the SOUNDSCALE project (www.soundscale.ac.uk) to inform research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). Across three online and in-person workshops, 48 residents from Hampshire and London explored the technology's potential uses, risks, governance, and societal implications. The report summarises their deliberations and priorities, and reflects on the challenges of involving citizens in early-stage research on an unfamiliar technology.

Title: PatchCon: Patch-aware Weighted Supervised Contrastive Learning for Vulnerability Detection
Author: Chaomeng Lu, Pooya Rostami Mazrae, Bert Lagaisse
Text_Content: Automated vulnerability detection is critical for securing modern software systems, yet existing learning-based approaches often treat functions as independent samples and underuse the supervision provided by vulnerability-fixing patches. In this paper, we propose PatchCon, a CodeBERT-based patch-aware contrastive learning model for function-level vulnerability detection. PatchCon jointly optimizes vulnerability classification and supervised contrastive learning, and treats vulnerable-patched function pairs as hard negatives with larger contrastive weights to capture subtle security-relevant differences introduced by fixes. To evaluate patch-level discrimination, we use two pairwise metrics that measure whether a model can correctly distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts. We evaluate PatchCon on PairVul-Linux through extensive experiments, including state-of-the-art comparisons, ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical significance testing. We also conduct fine-grained analyses by Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) type, function length, and patch size, and further evaluate PatchCon on Linux kernel vulnerabilities disclosed after the training data cutoff. On PairVul-Linux, PatchCon outperforms representative pretrained code models and contrastive learning baselines on both classification and pairwise metrics, improves pairwise accuracy over the strongest reproduced baseline from 0.2060 to 0.3264, and achieves pairwise accuracy comparable to that of a GPT-4o-based large language model (LLM) method at a substantially lower cost. Among the reproduced models, PatchCon also achieves the highest pairwise accuracy on test pairs from Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries unseen during training and on newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

Title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks
Author: Arn Caesar
Text_Content: Deep neural networks train best when they are initialised at the edge of chaos, the critical line in the plane of weight and bias variances on which the distance between two inputs neither grows nor shrinks with depth. The line is known for infinitely wide networks; at finite width it moves, and how it moves has been disputed. We treat the logarithm of the distance between two inputs through a network of width $N$ as a random walk and compute its drift and variance to order $1/N$. The edge of chaos moves to a larger weight variance, by $Δσ_w^2=-a_1/(N\,\partial_{σ_w^2}\lnχ_1)$, about $8/N$ for $\tanh$ networks at a bias variance of $0.05$, confirmed by simulations of the exact finite-width recursion. The shift describes a typical network; the average over many networks is dominated by rare networks in which the distance grows, and its critical point moves the other way, which explains why calculations and simulations have disagreed. Backpropagation follows the same random walk, so the shift applies to gradients unchanged. Along the edge of chaos, the information about the similarity of two inputs is constant until the compression over the depth exceeds about one nat, which fixes where to sit on the line. The results give an initialisation rule, Crinit, that places a network on its finite-width edge of chaos without a search. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at width $64$ it is more accurate than the standard rules at their usual settings, by a small margin in shallow networks and a large one in deep networks, where most standard rules fail; it trains in fewer steps, and it matches or beats the standard rules with a tuned gain.

Title: Exact periodic electrostatics for latent-charge machine-learning potentials
Author: Eslam Ibrahim
Text_Content: Machine-learning interatomic potentials of the latent Ewald summation (LES) type learn atomic charges from energies and forces and evaluate their electrostatic energy in reciprocal space. I formulate this long-range term as a smeared Epstein-Hurwitz lattice sum and derive its exact periodic structure: a decomposition isolating a net-charge artefact and a local self-energy, an image theorem for cells of any shape, and the forces and virial. Full charge equilibration, LES with induced charges, constrained and unconstrained LES models and fixed-charge force fields follow as successive approximations of one variational problem, whose diagonal-hardness limit is a projection of the latent charges onto fixed total charge, which I call projected latent Ewald summation (pLES). Energies and forces determine the latent charges only up to a gauge, so fragment-level rather than atom-level charge quantization is the consistent target. The latent channel is guaranteed to be a dielectric only if charge is conserved locally; charges that are local functions of the environment and conserved only globally can screen like a conductor. pLES is implemented in the atomic cluster expansion and in LAMMPS, and the exact identities hold to machine precision, also for trained models. For charged NaCl clusters, pLES recovers the total charge that an unconstrained model misses by up to 1.8 e and reduces the test errors of a short-range model from 1.44 to 0.42 meV/atom and from 37 to 13 meV/Å. In two water datasets, constrained and unconstrained models learn the same latent charges up to sign and scale. In molecular dynamics of pLES water, fluctuating molecular charges dominate the screening at all accessible wavelengths; a crossover model excludes a conductor and gives a latent dielectric constant between 19 and 71; molecular charges are compensated over about 1 nm, beyond the training cells.

Title: Does Personality Persuade? Investigating Personality Trait Prompting and Persuasion in Large Language Models
Author: Ruben Boone, Gilles Eerlings, Sebe Vanbrabant, Davy Vanacken, Kris Luyten
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) can be prompted to express different personality profiles, but it remains unclear how reliably they do so or whether personality affects their persuasiveness. We investigate these questions in two evaluations. First, we assess Big Five personality prompting using the IPIP-NEO-120, examining reproducibility, trait controllability, cross-trait effects, and unconditioned model profiles. Second, we conduct a within-subjects user study (N=32) in which participants discuss moral dilemmas with LLM agents whose personalities are aligned, mismatched, neutral, or unconditioned. We find that prompted profiles can be reproducible and responsive to requested traits, although controllability varies across models and changes to one trait can affect others. Unconditioned models also exhibit systematic personality profiles rather than neutral baselines. In the user study, personality alignment did not significantly affect perceived persuasiveness, stance switching, or confidence changes. Participants switched their initial stance in only 8 of 128 conversations, while confidence changes were more common. Participants' Big Five traits were not significantly associated with susceptibility to persuasion, but higher self-reported AI persuasion literacy was associated with less frequent confidence changes. Exploratory analysis showed that logical appeals dominated agent messages. These findings distinguish technical control over prompted LLM personality from observable influence on users and motivate evaluating persuasive interactions beyond explicit changes in decisions.

Title: One Scale, Four Texts: Gaps, Overlaps and Silent Repairs in Published Grading Schemes
Author: Elisa Rovai, Fabio Rovai
Text_Content: Category systems often reach their users as text, and readers apply them with tacit repairs. We ask what such a text determines once the repairs are removed, using diabetic retinopathy grading, where one international scale circulates in several documents. We transcribe four texts (the English screening definitions of 2025, the international scale as tabulated in 2017 and as published in 2003, and an Italian guideline of 2015) into one rule language over 24 finding variables, and make every point a text leaves open a named precisification. Exhaustive enumeration of 1,425,807,360 finding profiles, re-derived by an SMT solver and spot-checked by an OWL reasoner, shows that every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category under every reading; that the 2017 tabulation has a proliferative class that is empty when read literally and a macular gap that the 2003 text lacks, so that no function maps the 2003 grades onto the 2017 grades; and that on image findings alone the English and Italian texts order some pairs of eyes in opposite ways. On 927 annotated photographs from three public datasets, with retinal thickening assumed absent, the English text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of the eyes of one dataset (DDR) on which both decide, and in a pre-registered experiment classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. Thickening cannot be seen on a colour photograph; left free, every disagreement involving England becomes undecidable, so it rests on what the camera cannot show. In a second pre-registered study, language models that answered without deliberating repaired most gap and overlap items even when told to read literally, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reported the defects far more often; within two models, deliberation reduced silent repair without removing it.

Title: A comparison of three models of a whirling string as it becomes chaotic
Author: Nicholas B. Tufillaro
Text_Content: A stretched wire driven near its fundamental frequency can leave the plane of the driving force and whirl. At larger amplitudes the whirl becomes modulated, reverses its direction, and becomes chaotic. Three models of this motion are in common use: the geometrically exact string equations; a two-mode model -- the Kirchhoff-Carrier equation with one transverse mode in each plane; and the averaged equations for the slow amplitudes of those two modes. We integrate all three under similar conditions and compare them along the route to chaos, which starts with a Hopf bifurcation of the steady whirl and passes through period doublings to chaotic attractors organized by a Shil'nikov homoclinic orbit. The small parameter of the averaging, the ratio $\varepsilon = c/ω_1$ of the modulation rate to the fundamental frequency, runs from 0.005 to 0.02. Qualitatively the three models agree in the sequence of bifurcations, the coexisting attractors, the return maps and the Lyapunov exponents. Quantitatively, averaging places each local bifurcation $0.7\varepsilon$ to $1.2\varepsilon$ higher in the scaled detuning. The geometrically exact and two-mode models agree with each other to within 0.002 at the local bifurcations for $\varepsilon \le 0.01$. The Shil'nikov ratio, which decides whether chaos accompanies the homoclinic orbit, agrees among the three models to within 1.5% for $\varepsilon \le 0.01$, yet the homoclinic bifurcation itself moves by about $\varepsilon$ at the lower damping and by 6 to 9 times $\varepsilon$ at the higher; the difference is set by how quickly the return of the homoclinic loop changes with detuning.

Title: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
Author: Haoyu Shao, Yunshen Wang, Jingze Zhang, Shaohang Zhu, Yong-Lu Li, Tianzhu Zhang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
Text_Content: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.

Title: EPISTEME: Trustworthy Coding Agents Through Tool Call Intent
Author: Sofia Bobadilla, Carmine Cesarano, Raphina Liu, Javier Ron, Martin Monperrus
Text_Content: Coding agents change software through tool calls. Tool calls mutate the local state. For good? For bad? Nobody knows. Agents never say why a tool call is made. We propose the epistemic agent design, in which the harness guarantees that the model declares why a tool call is made. The harness then records what the command actually did and checks the self-reported declaration against these effects. The result is a journal 1) that can guard calls before they run and 2) that supports audits and forensics. For evaluation, we use ImpossibleBench, whose tasks can be passed only by cheating, and demonstrate that forcing the agents to say why results in exposed cheating. Across 49 reward-hacking runs of two open-weight models, the journal exposed 90%.

Title: Mortality Is Undecidable for $2 \times 2$ Integer Matrices
Author: Thanin Quartz, Ivan O. Shevchenko, Hans De Sterck, Jun Liu
Text_Content: The matrix mortality problem asks whether a given finite family of matrices can be multiplied, in any order and with possible repetition, to get the zero matrix. It is one of the most basic decision problems about matrix products, and it arises naturally in the study of switched linear systems and of finite automata. Mortality is trivially decidable in dimension one and has been known to be undecidable for integer matrices in dimensions three and higher since 1970; only the problem in dimension $2$ is left open. We resolve this problem by proving that mortality is undecidable for families of 5,799 distinct $2\times2$ integer matrices. All but one of the matrices are fixed and nonsingular, with determinants $\pm p$ for a single fixed prime $p$. The input affects only the remaining rank-one matrix, which encodes this input into its kernel. Our proof encodes the computation of a fixed universal machine into products of $2\times2$ matrices. We represent each configuration of the computation by a single rational number, which we identify with a line through the origin in $\mathbb{Q}^2$, and each nonsingular matrix carries out a small piece of one computation step. The main difficulty is that the matrices may be multiplied in any order, so we design them to check their own work: a "wrong'' step puts a factor of a prime number $p$ into the denominator of the rational number corresponding to the current computation step, where no later matrix can remove it. As a result, products of these matrices can go from one encoded configuration to another only by following a valid computation. The rank-one matrix then turns the question of whether the machine halts into the question of whether some product equals zero. A companion formalization in the Lean proof assistant verifies the complete reduction.

Title: From Fixed Defaults to Calibrated Activation Policies for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
Author: Shijie Xu, Boyan Tang, Kai He, Jianghua Wu
Text_Content: Long-term time-series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, and other applications where reliable predictions are needed beyond the observed data. Although forecasting research has advanced model architectures, fixed activation configurations provide limited guidance on how activation choices should vary across datasets and prediction horizons. This study aims to establish when task-specific activation choices improve forecasting accuracy and how previous experiments can guide the selection of suitable configurations for new tasks. We develop a calibrated selection policy that learns a reliable default from prior experiments, adapts the activation function and its location to each task, and retains the default when evidence for a change is insufficient. In an evaluation supported by 1,225 Informer training runs across 17 dataset variants and 51 forecasting tasks, the policy reduces mean squared error by 7.86% on average relative to the conventional fixed-activation baseline and improves 72.55% of tasks. These findings establish activation choice and placement as practical opportunities for improving existing forecasting models and show how accumulated experimental evidence can guide configuration decisions without repeating an exhaustive search for every task.

Title: LungMend: A Healthy-Only Latent Diffusion Shape Prior for Lung Mask Correction in Severe Tuberculosis CT
Author: Rezkellah Noureddine Khiat, Pierre-Yves Brillet, Catalin Fetita
Text_Content: Lung segmentation models such as R231 are widely used, but they fail on severe tuberculosis (TB) CT: cavities and consolidations look like non-lung tissue and are left out of the mask. We present LungMend, a post-processing model that corrects such masks using only healthy anatomy. A latent diffusion model, trained on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks, learns to recover the complete lung from the faulty mask and the bone anatomy, without any pathological data or CT intensities. LungMend recovers cavities and consolidations that R231 misses and improves accuracy on expert-annotated slices. Code: https://github.com/noureddinekhiati/LungMend

Title: FA-Agent: An extensible multimodal agent framework for first-arrival picking in mountainous seismic data
Author: Wenda Li, Congcong Yuan
Text_Content: First-arrival traveltimes underpin near-surface velocity modeling and static corrections, but in low signal-to-noise mountainous land data the first arrival is often weak, intermittent, and masked by strong direct waves and noise. Energy-based pickers then pick later arrivals or noise, and deep-learning pickers usually require retraining for a new survey. Because erroneous picks bias first-arrival tomography, many difficult zones are still inspected and corrected manually. We present FA-Agent, an agent framework for first-arrival picking built on a multimodal large language model. It combines a model that performs visual recognition and makes decisions, tools that process the data, and skills that carry experience of processing mountainous data. The framework is open and extensible: new pickers, denoising methods, and quality-control tools can be added, and new experience can be written into the skills. It is restricted neither to mountainous data nor to a particular model. Emulating a seismic data processor, the agent first surveys the whole gather to find zones needing attention, then examines them in enlarged views, and finally keeps, corrects, or removes the initial picks. On semi-synthetic gathers with known first arrivals and real mountainous noise, the agent picked the first arrival with high accuracy where it was clearly visible and removed the picks where it was invisible and could not be judged. Applied to randomly sampled gathers from a mountainous survey, it corrected picks onto weak first-arrival branches and removed picks where no first arrival could be confirmed, and it performed well on the most difficult data. Cases reviewed by experts are added to the skills automatically, so the agent improves with use, and a locally deployed model keeps confidential data on site. FA-Agent can thus become an essential component of future automated seismic data processing workflows.

Title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management
Author: Shreya K. Chari, John S. Vardakas, Kostas Ramantas, Christos Verikoukis
Text_Content: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using MathΣtral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.

Title: Addition by Subtraction: Toward Mitigating Fragile Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
Author: Hamid Dashtbani, Alexandra Dmitrienko
Text_Content: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to prevent harmful generations, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Recent work reveals a deeper structural weakness: safety alignment can be highly sparse, such that pruning a small number of safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behavior. In this work, we take the first steps toward strengthening safety alignment such that it is less dependent on sparse model components. We propose Addition by Subtraction, which gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimization to re-establish safety-aligned behavior through other parts of the model. Our results show that the resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks. Remarkably, these benefits generalize beyond the white-box attacks motivating our design: Addition by Subtraction improves robustness against other sparsity-based interventions, including refusal-direction ablation, as well as a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also exhibit improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four models from three vendors demonstrate consistent improvements in safety robustness, reducing attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.

Title: Who Gets Counted? Large Language Models, Informative Refusal, and Downstream Bias in Name-Based Demographic Classification
Author: Christian Pipal, Morgan Wack, Eva-Maria Vogel
Text_Content: Researchers routinely infer gender, race, and ethnicity from names, yet the standard tools used for this task misclassify the groups that diversity research most needs to measure. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a remedy because they label diverse names accurately. We ask whether that accuracy carries over to the estimates researchers report. Across 10,000 Chinese names, 19,998 North Carolina voters with self-reported race, and 300 political science authors with human reference codes, we compare three LLMs with seven traditional tools and link the voter sample to party registration and age. Selective labeling explains part of the LLMs' accuracy advantage. Claude Haiku labels half of the voters, and a traditional tool limited to its most confident half is more accurate. Hard labels from every tool understate the White--Black gap in Democratic registration by 36% to 65%, while BIRDiE estimation on BISG posteriors comes within 0.03 of it. Haiku's missing labels select on age, inflating the age gap by six years. Combined with BISG, LLM answers sharpen individual labels without a demonstrated gain in BIRDiE accuracy. Classifiers should be judged by the estimates they produce, including the consequences of missing labels

Title: Adapting Sleep Foundation Models for Dense Sleep Spindle Localization
Author: Alexis Bollengier, Abel Díaz Berenguer, Olivier Pallanca, André Anjos, Hichem Sahli
Text_Content: Adapting sleep foundation models to dense electroencephalography (EEG) event localization is challenging because multi-second representations may not preserve sufficient temporal detail for precise boundary recovery. We address sleep spindle localization by adapting a frozen SleepFM encoder with a local time-frequency pathway that preserves spindle-relevant spectral content and intra-token position. The local representation drives localization, while residual cross-attention incorporates SleepFM temporal context. Dense predictions are obtained through localized token-to-sample reconstruction and temporal refinement. Tested on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA), the proposed model achieves an event-level $F_1$ of $0.8080 \pm 0.0040$ at IoU 0.2 across six folds. Ablations show that localization primarily depends on local spectral and sub-token temporal information, while the pretrained representation provides complementary context. These results indicate that dense adaptation benefits from preserving information below the pretrained token scale. Code will be released upon acceptance.

Title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
Author: Wenhui Chu
Text_Content: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit

Title: MKD2World: A Typed Spatial MarkDown World Model For Web Agents
Author: Zhihao Nan, Sifan Zhou, Yiming Cheng, Jinkai Zheng, Zheng Zhu, Si Shi, Ming Li, Fei Yu
Text_Content: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM), a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI, a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World, a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a ``digest'' step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World.

Title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
Author: Shumao Wu, Kongcheng Zhang, Jianqiang Huang, Baisheng Lai
Text_Content: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD.

Title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation
Author: Ximo Zhu, Ruiqi Liu, Yi Han, Zhengan Wu, Gengsheng Li, ZiAn Wang, Zhu Yuantian, Jin Jiang, Wenhao Wang
Text_Content: Proprietary language models exhibit strong reasoning and coding capabilities, but their output distributions are inaccessible, making fine-grained distillation methods that rely on teacher logits difficult to apply directly to black-box models. We observe that rich textual feedback from a black-box teacher can be treated as privileged information (PI) and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision signals on the student's own trajectories. However, what PI should be acquired from the teacher to most effectively support student learning remains unclear. PI strategies that differ in where they focus, what information they request, and how much detail they provide can have substantially different effects on the current student, and their relative effectiveness can further change as training progresses. Based on this observation, we propose Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation (EvoOPD), which treats PI acquisition itself as an optimization problem and maintains a PI Strategy Bank that evolves with the student state. EvoOPD uses the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt the focus, information type, and granularity of teacher feedback, allowing the acquired information to continually match the student's learning needs. We systematically evaluate EvoOPD on mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students. EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code. Further analysis shows that the relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, making a fixed strategy difficult to sustain as the best choice throughout distillation.

Title: Spatially and Compositionally Controlled Multimodal Glioblastoma MRI Synthesis with Latent Diffusion
Author: Steven Glass, Max Van Puyvelde, Marija Pizurica, Mia Meyer, Olivier Gevaert, Willie Brink
Text_Content: Glioblastoma exhibits substantial heterogeneity in tumour morphology and composition across MRI modalities, often making available clinical datasets highly unbalanced in terms of patient pathologies. We propose a two-stage latent diffusion model (LDM) framework for the generation of explicitly controllable 2D glioblastoma MRI scans. First, a segmentation LDM generates tumour maps conditioned on location, spatial extent, axial position, and subregion composition. Second, a modality-conditioned LDM with ControlNet generates T1, T1Gd, T2, and FLAIR images adhering to the requested segmentation. On a held-out test set, generated segmentations achieved a mean centroid error of 0.842 pixels and a subregion proportion error of 0.795 percentage points. ControlNet improved Fréchet inception distance (FID) across all four modalities, reducing pooled FID from 42.59 to 36.12. An expert reader study yielded mean quality ratings of 6.60 for real images, 6.83 for ControlNet-generated images, and 6.77 for fully synthetic images.

Title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
Author: Thomas Wilder, Ranjini Swaminathan, David Storkey, Till Kuhlbrodt
Text_Content: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.

Title: Vertex-subgraph eigenvector centrality for connected induced subgraphs
Author: Qingying Zhang, Haotian Zeng, Changjiang Bu
Text_Content: Eigenvector centrality evaluates the importance of vertices through adjacency relations, while higher-order subgraph structures provide additional information for centrality analysis. This motivates the simultaneous evaluation of vertices and subgraphs within a unified spectral framework. In this paper, we propose vertex-subgraph eigenvector centrality (VSC), which jointly determines the centralities of vertices and connected induced subgraphs of order three. The vertex centrality depends on the centralities of the subgraphs containing it and those of the other vertices in these subgraphs, whereas the subgraph centrality depends on the centralities of its constituent vertices. To distinguish induced paths P3 from triangles K3, the capacity of each subgraph is defined as its number of edges. The resulting coupled nonlinear eigenvalue equations are represented by a fourth-order symmetric nonnegative tensor. We prove that this tensor is weakly irreducible for every connected graph with at least three vertices, which guarantees the existence and uniqueness, up to scaling, of a positive Perron eigenvector. Numerical experiments on four real-world networks compare VSC with classical centrality measures and show that capacity weighting has a greater effect on subgraph rankings than on vertex rankings.

Title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
Author: Maxime Le, Ryan Benazzouk, Jan Brandejs, Andre Severo Pereira Gomes
Text_Content: In this manuscript we outline a computational strategy to leverage a vendor-optimized implementation of the Ozaki scheme I for floating point emulation as part of an implementation of the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) pattern for tensor contractions, and assess its potential to accelerate two of the most expensive tensor contractions appearing in relativistic coupled cluster theory in high-end accelerators such as the NVIDIA Blackwell B200 system in which there is a strong differential in the performance of computations for double and lower precision datatypes. Our results indicate that this emulation-based TTGT strategy can provide significant speedups compared to runs without emulation, and can be competitive with state-of-the-art, vendor-optimized tensor contraction libraries using native double precision as compute datatype. More importantly, our scheme provides a path towards easily allowing users to tune the desired accuracy in the tensor contraction steps, including cases where precision between single and double is sufficient for the application.

Title: Online Control of the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) for Multi-stage Platform Trials
Author: Jiangyue Yao, David S. Robertson, Thomas Jaki
Text_Content: In platform trials, multiple intervention arms can enter or leave the study at any time, which brings the challenge of how to control the type I error rate. Online testing procedures, where a stream of hypotheses are tested over time and the total number of hypotheses is unknown, might be a viable choice for error rate control in platform trials. Interim analyses in a multi-stage design offer the opportunity of early stopping for success or futility in clinical trials by testing the same hypothesis at different time points. Some methods targeting false-discovery rate (FDR) or family-wise error rate (FWER) control for multi-stage platform trials have been proposed. However, a method which controls the FWER and allows new arms to be added at any time without prior information is yet to be established. The ADDIS-Spending (ADaptive DIScarding Alpha-spending) procedure controls the FWER in an online setting. We propose the group sequential ADDIS-Spending algorithm to enable interim analyses for each hypothesis in platform trials. The developed method can update the error level of an individual hypothesis at all (interim) analyses whenever new decisions on other hypotheses are made. We compare alternative approaches with our method in a simulation study. The proposed method yields competitive results in the conducted simulations.

Title: Emergent regularity of walking patterns: evidence from Swiss cities
Author: Guo-Shiuan Lin, Martin Hendrick, Maider Llaguno-Munitxa, Gabriele Manoli
Text_Content: Human travel behaviour is characterised by high temporal and spatial regularity, as demonstrated by the Exploration and Preferential Return (EPR) mechanism, whereby individuals alternate between exploring new locations and preferentially returning to previously visited places. Yet, existing evidence is based on aggregated mobility data that cannot distinguish short trips or separate active mobility (i.e., walking and biking) from other mobility modes. This limits our ability to assess the benefits of walking activities and proximity-based policies such as the 15-minute city. Here, we analyse the spatial distribution and duration of walking habits of 1,318 participants, tracked during a 4-week time use survey in major Swiss cities - which are very close to the 15-minute city model. We find that walking activity is highly concentrated around individuals' home and work locations. These two attractors create walking patterns that are fundamentally different from other transport modes, which are instead used for longer trips and to connect home-workplace. We then introduce a dual-center EPR model, with empirically derived parameters, to simulate the decaying probability of walking away from the centers. Combining empirical data and the EPR framework, we find that groups with higher walking times show a stronger tendency to take long-distance walks and explore more destinations. In general, walking behavior reflects both individual circumstances and residential context: walking durations are shorter among people without a public transport pass, car owners, and residents of low-density rural areas. These findings provide a basis for more targeted assessments of walkability and active-mobility-oriented urban design.

Title: Construction Contracts for Generated Embedded Domain-Specific Language Programs: A Measurement Protocol and a Conditional Effect
Author: Haowen Guo, Yangzhao Huang
Text_Content: A generated domain-specific program can be accepted by its host and still miss the reference construction. We measure the two events separately and test a short construction contract. The vehicle is Open Quantum Assembly Language (OpenQASM) 3. One 3-billion-parameter generator is run under seven conditions on 100 quantum approximate optimization (QAOA) and 100 variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) instances. Eighty of 100 QAOA signatures appear in some training split. Exact McNemar tests and 95% paired bootstrap intervals are used. The contract, a card, lists structural decisions, enters the prompt, and is checked without a simulator. Parse rates are 0.55 to 0.97 and full structural match is 0.02 to 0.87. On QAOA, at fixed weights, the card moves full match by +32.0 percentage points on card-trained weights (interval +22 to +42) and by -13.0 (-23 to -3) without that training. The +45.0-point difference is not a deployment contrast. The same-step plan-free gain is +23.0 (+13 to +33); the primary distributional score does not separate it. Against the earlier checkpoint the gain is +27.0 (+17 to +37), and the checkpoint also changes. A rule card is not separated from the learned planner, nor is a predicted-card compiler (0.760 vs. 0.780). On 20 QAOA rows outside every training split, the interval includes zero. Under this card, VQE adherence is 0.020 and full match stays near 0.03. Report the two checks separately. Insert a card only into a generator trained to read it, and only where a pilot shows adherence.

Title: Distributed Consensus, Optimization, and Learning under Communication Constraints
Author: Zheng Chen, Nicolò Michelusi, Themistoklis Charalambous, Kaibin Huang
Text_Content: Many modern engineering applications require distributed problem-solving in which multiple nodes in a network cooperate to achieve a common optimization objective. Numerous distributed optimization and learning algorithms rely on consensus-based distributed coordination to ensure network-wide agreement via iterative local interactions. In these algorithms, the accuracy, frequency, and reliability of information exchange among network nodes directly influence system performance, including convergence behavior, training delay, and model accuracy. This tutorial article adopts a bottom-up approach to present the fundamentals of consensus averaging and distributed optimization methods, and highlights the impact of network connectivity, information flow, and communication uncertainty on network cooperation and optimization performance. Building on these theoretical insights, we discuss key design principles for communication-constrained distributed learning across diverse network topologies and review common approaches to communication-efficient learning, particularly in wireless networks. Despite substantial progress, further efforts are needed to bridge the gap between theory and practice and fully realize the potential of cooperative and networked intelligence.

Title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control
Author: Xuemin Hu, Kaixin Li, Qingqing Xia, Yuxin Wang, Wei Xie, Bo Tang, Long Chen
Text_Content: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

Title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
Author: Corrado Calamita, Matteo Mendicini, Luca Ferrari, Riccardo Bertamini
Text_Content: Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.

Title: Deliberate Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
Author: Haobo Zhang, Qiannan Zhu, Yutao Zhu, Zhicheng Dou
