The detectors cover (A) QEC integrity over per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect-count, and repeated-syndrome rate; (B) decoder confidence over the margin between minimum-weight error explanations in distinct logical classes; (C) behavioral output divergence, flagging crosstalk-class and novel attacks by their effect on a victim's output relative to a matched control; (D) control-stack tampering via known-answer canary circuits, built to be indistinguishable to a resident implant, with a cross-job consistency statistic; and (E) compilation/execution integrity. Each gates on significance, so honest operation raises no alarm. We evaluate in faithful simulation and on three production IBM Heron processors, and bound the physical attack surface with a systematic negative map: most physical-layer attacks return statistically null, the exception an implemented, measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive. Every detector is also evaluated against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of it. To our knowledge this is the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC layer and classical control stack of a quantum computing system, demonstrated on production hardware.

Title: An Integrality-Gap Lower Bound of 1.2325 for Minimum Multiway Cut
Author: Dimitar Chakarov, Yury Makarychev
Text_Content: We prove that the integrality gap of the Călinescu-Karloff-Rabani relaxation for Minimum Multiway Cut is at least $1.2325$ when the number of terminals is large. By a result of Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008), it is therefore NP-hard, under the Unique Games Conjecture, to approximate Minimum Multiway Cut within a factor of $1.2325$. This improves the previously best known lower bound of $1.20016$ due to Bérczi, Chandrasekaran, Király, and Madan (2020).

Title: Cognitive Bias Signatures in Search-Equipped LLM Agents: A Stage-Resolved Analysis
Author: Yanru Xiao, Yingwei Yu
Text_Content: Search can help LLM agents correct mistakes, but their starting conditions may shape which evidence they find and use. Drawing on cognitive-bias paradigms, we develop a controlled search harness to examine result order, records of prior work, and initial hypotheses while holding each question and document collection fixed. Matched controls distinguish order effects from differences in document composition and the effects of failed work from context length. Across 10 models and 1,000 synthetic search worlds, we track queries, retrieved documents, document openings, and final answers. Our comparisons suggest that final answers are more sensitive to initial evidence order during active search than when all evidence is supplied in full. Dead-end histories can reduce strategy switching relative to matched neutral histories, indicating an effect beyond context length. Under wrong hypotheses, stage measurements distinguish reduced retrieval or opening from errors that persist after counter-evidence is opened. Exploratory interventions show that opening counter-evidence more often can coincide with lower accuracy, while accuracy can improve with little change in opening.

Title: Same Method, Different Task: What the Bitter Lesson Does Not License in Social Simulation
Author: Justin Downes, Robby Milletich, Newel Hirst
Text_Content: The bitter lesson holds that general methods leveraging computation defeat hand-encoded domain knowledge. We argue it carries a condition its popular reading omits: in every case Sutton cites, the general method was scaled against the same task the domain engineering was solving. Social simulation substituted across tasks instead, replacing hand-built agents with an artifact optimized for predicting text. The move is bitter-lesson-shaped, but the lesson does not license it. Prediction is a solitary act: the predictor bears no consequences from the interaction it models. Cooperation, defection, and norm enforcement are phenomena of interested parties; they do not exist for a disinterested observer at any scale. What is missing is not emergence, which LLM populations already show, but stakes. We show that several anomalies reported in prior work (excess cooperation that predates alignment training, collective agreement without individual fidelity, and population homogeneity) follow from this account. A 540-agent pilot with pre-specified hypotheses, which tests sensitivity to persistent consequences rather than cooperation, finds that consequences reshape strategies in two of three model families but never produce human-like heterogeneity. We argue for mixed-motive settings that shape agents rather than only test them, and ask whether agents should be pretrained differently from predictors.

Title: How Much Do Modern Embeddings Reveal? Inversion Attacks on Commercial Embedding Models
Author: Kareem Elaasar, Cristina Lopes
Text_Content: Text embedding inversion reconstructs source text from fixed-dimensional vectors, posing a privacy risk to systems that store embeddings instead of raw text. We adapt the vec2text framework (Morris et al., 2023) to support text-embedding-3-small and mistral-embed alongside GTR-base. We evaluate 800 samples per category across general instructions, Wikipedia passages, paraphrased instructions, health-related instructions, and short literal code snippets, using a common 60-80-character range and paired original and paraphrased instructions. Under the evaluated vec2text configuration, text-embedding-3-small achieves the highest exact-match rate in all five categories, including 47.4% on health-related instructions and 24.5% on general instructions under the evaluation's case-insensitive, whitespace-stripped matching rule. BERTScore F1 exceeds 87 on the 0-100 scale for every prose category and embedder, indicating high contextual similarity to the references. Short code snippets yield lower reconstruction scores. These findings characterize one attack configuration and the selected datasets; they do not establish attack-independent rankings or sensitive-attribute recovery rates. They nevertheless motivate explicit assessment of inversion risk and access controls for stored embeddings.

Title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Author: Tianming Sha, Junnan Li, Siqi Zhao
Text_Content: Deep search and long-horizon reasoning unfold as branching trajectories that pursue parallel sub-queries, abandon dead-end detours, and cross-check sibling findings. Yet modern serving engines, harnesses, and RL trainers execute episodes as flat, append-only sequences: stretching a context window leaves failed detours that dilute attention, in-place edits break KV caching and recurrent states, and all-layer cache splicing overwrites hybrid recurrent working memory and triggers hijacking. We introduce Octopus, a co-designed serving runtime, memory manager, and RL framework executing episodes as a GPU-resident DAG over radix cursors (89.6% KV hit rate). Agents coordinate via five primitives: fork shares parent KV prefixes in $O(1)$ with isolated 32K budgets, rewind restores recurrent checkpoints, read_thread mounts sibling KV pages in zero copy, and wait and done synchronize results. Octopus splices sibling KV pages only into full-attention layers under monotonic position offsets while recurrent layers skip mounted spans, retaining 92.2% of full-text answer information and cutting hijacking $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) with zero new KV pages. During RL, our packed DAG kernel and DAG-GRPO objective deduplicate shared prefixes via loss masks while keeping mounted KV edges differentiable, cutting rollout-training KL divergence $32\times$ and routing reader gradients into producer KV projections. Trained on Qwen3.5-4B with binary rewards, Octopus self-organizes a commander-worker hierarchy and latent KV mesh, lifting BrowseComp-Plus accuracy under BM25 from 26.0% (32K ReAct) and 32.1% (143K GRPO) to 49.6% (+17.5 pts; 51.2% on OpenResearcher), surpassing 9B context-editing RL (42.5%), matching o3 (49.3%), and outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger: Tongyi-DeepResearch (44.5%), DeepSeek-R1 (16.4%), Kimi-K2 (35.4%), GPT-4.1 (36.4%), and Claude 4 Opus (36.8%).

Title: CoReFlow: Consistency-Relaxed Flow Maps for Probabilistic Traffic Forecasting
Author: Pengnan Chi, Zhiguo Zhang, Xiaoliang Ma
Text_Content: Probabilistic traffic forecasting is essential for reliable Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as it captures uncertainties in complex road networks. Recent diffusion- and flow-based generative models have facilitated uncertainty modeling through a multi-step sampling process. However, beyond slow inference, this process is designed to capture complex multimodal distributions, which misaligns with the limited complexity of the conditional traffic data distribution, causing models to underperform deterministic baselines. To address this, we introduce the \underline{Co}nsistency-\underline{Re}laxed \underline{Flow} Map (CoReFlow) model, presenting the first effort to leverage the one-step generation capability of flow maps, known as solution operators of probability-flow ordinary differential equations. Besides, we improve accuracy using a concise training objective that supervises the model via interpolation endpoints over finite time intervals. Unlike existing methods (e.g., self-distillation and MeanFlow Identity) that maintain trajectory consistency to model multimodal distributions, our objective leverages conditional mean to restrict the consistency, thereby achieving higher accuracy in the probabilistic traffic forecasting task. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show CoReFlow achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy. It surpasses recent baselines, provides competitive uncertainty modeling, and reduces inference costs compared to existing generative baselines.

Title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin
Author: Lucian Bicsi, Adrian Budău
Text_Content: In the incremental minimum spanning forest problem, weighted edges arrive one at a time. After each insertion we must report the edge that leaves the minimum spanning forest, and queries ask for the bottleneck distance of two vertices: the smallest possible maximum edge cost on a path between them. Link-cut trees solve both in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. In 2021 we wrote the folklore BottleneckTree, a short competitive-programming structure that stores one parent pointer and one cost per vertex, and conjectured that it also runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. We show that this conjecture is false: on a family of inputs, its amortized cost per operation is $Ω(\sqrt{n})$. We then present a structure with the same state, two arrays and a single loop, and prove that it runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time per insertion and per query. Unlike the AM-tree of Ding, Gu and Sun, which attains the same bound, it stores no subtree sizes and maintains no balance invariant. For a connected graph with distinct costs, the structure can be viewed as an implicit link-cut tree on the Kruskal reconstruction tree: each rotation corresponds to exactly one preferred-child change, and each skip acts on a stale path-parent pointer. In experiments it is 1.3-2.1 times faster than the folklore BottleneckTree on insertions, up to 480 times faster on its adversarial input, and 6.3-16 times faster than an explicit link-cut tree.

Title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness
Author: Hector Tierno, Shuang Yang
Text_Content: The reachability diameter of a directed graph is the maximum finite shortest-path distance across all pairs of vertices. It has received recent attention under this name, although the underlying quantity has long played a central role in shortcut set and parallel reachability. Notably, Bals et al. establish hardness for every polynomial-factor approximation in nearly-linear time for weighted digraphs. Yet they give $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in the unweighted regime with nearly-linear running time, and their conditional lower bounds rule out certain constants only, leaving open whether polynomial loss is necessary. We give a randomized algorithm that estimates the reachability diameter of an unweighted digraph within a factor $n^{1/3+o(1)}$, with high probability, in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time. We complement our algorithm with a lower bound conditional on the 3-uniform Hyperclique hypothesis, ruling out an $n^{2/15-\varepsilon}$-approximation in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2/15)$, establishing the necessity of polynomial loss for nearly-linear time algorithms.

Title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
Author: Zhengtao Gao, Francesco Bombassei De Bona, Leonardo Alchieri, Ivana Kiprijanovska, Simon Stankoski, Bojan Sofronievski, Hristijan Gjoreski, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski
Text_Content: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

Title: Agents, Think Only When it Helps
Author: Min-Seon Kim, Seungdong Yoa, Sanghyu Yoon, Ye Seul Sim, Suhee Yoon, Dongmin Kim, Jung-Eun Kim
Text_Content: LLM agent distillation transfers agentic capabilities to student models by training on complete teacher trajectories that typically interleave thoughts and actions. We question how critical thought supervision is for agents' ultimate action performance. To answer this, we disentangle their impacts by independently perturbing teacher thoughts and actions during distillation. On widely adopted agent benchmarks across model scales, altering or discarding thoughts has little effect on student performance. We find, however, that thought supervision becomes important when information about the thought is not disclosed in the corresponding action during training. By identifying such discrepant cases, our findings challenge the common practice of distilling entire teacher trajectories for LLM agents, and offer a new insight that thought supervision can be a discernible choice for efficiency depending on whether the information of thought is disclosed in the action.

Title: Inventory and Assortment Optimization under General Choice: A Unified Approximation Framework
Author: Jacob Feldman, Heng Zhang, Yukai Huang
Text_Content: We study joint inventory and assortment optimization under general substitutable choice models. Before a selling horizon, a decision maker chooses initial inventories subject to a capacity constraint on total units stocked, and customers then arrive sequentially and choose among the offered products. We consider two settings, show-all inventory selection, in which every in-stock product must be offered, and dynamic assortment personalization, in which the decision maker observes each customer's type and may adapt the offered assortment to remaining inventory and purchase history. We develop a unified framework linking each setting to a static optimization problem. For show-all inventory selection, a polynomial-time $α$-approximation for cardinality-constrained static assortment optimization yields guarantees of $0.486α$ under deterministic or Poisson arrivals and $0.4328α$ under increasing-failure-rate (IFR) arrivals. For personalization, the same guarantees hold when $α$ is the approximation factor for the joint assortment and customization problem of El Housni and Topaloglu. Our approach combines a fluid relaxation, demand-dependent fractional inventory allocations, bounds on expected truncated demand, and dependent rounding. Notably, our personalized policy fixes one assortment per customer type before the horizon and then offers every in-stock product within it, so it requires no dynamic re-optimization despite competing against the optimal fully adaptive policy. Finally, we construct instances in which optimal show-all revenue approaches only one-half of the fluid bound under deterministic arrivals and $1-w\approx0.4328567$ under IFR arrivals, where $we^w=1$. With an exact static assortment oracle, our IFR guarantee approaches the latter factor arbitrarily closely.

Title: Neural networks and games
Author: Philip R. Neary
Text_Content: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

Title: Iterated Elimination of Dominated Mixed Strategies
Author: Federico Echenique, Amanda Friedenberg
Text_Content: This note compares two iterated dominance procedures, one based on eliminating mixed strategies and one based on eliminating pure strategies. It shows that, in compact and continuous games, the mixed-strategy procedure can trail the pure-strategy procedure by at most one round: If the pure-strategy procedure terminates at round $M$, the mixed-strategy procedure terminates at either $M$ or $M+1$, and this bound is tight. It also provides two characterizations of the mixed-strategy procedure that are round-for-round equivalent to it and that require checking for improvements only against opponents' pure strategies.

Title: Memory-Access Profiling for Early Multicore Interference Awareness in Embedded Systems
Author: Jean-Baptiste Lefoul, Ahmad Shahnejat Bushehri, Alaric Chan Lock, Felipe Gohring de Magalhaes, Gabriela Nicolescu
Text_Content: Applications executing on different multicore processors may interfere through shared resources. Such interference can introduce execution-time variability and complicate system integration, especially when applications that behave predictably in isolation are co-scheduled. This paper presents a profiling framework for early multicore interference awareness. The proposed approach captures source-level memory-operation traces from C applications with limited source-code modification and combines them with architectural parameters of the target platform. The framework maps memory accesses to cache sets and memory blocks, generates cache-occupancy profiles and heatmaps, and evaluates pairwise interference risks through a progressive three-stage analysis. First, a coarse-grained screening step classifies applications according to their non-stack memory-access behavior. Second, a static multicore cache-profiling step identifies cache sets whose combined footprint exceeds or approaches the hardware associativity. Third, a temporal footprint analysis tracks intervening unique blocks between consecutive accesses to the same memory block and computes Contention Potential Growth to identify execution windows vulnerable to cache eviction. The framework is evaluated using four benchmark pairings executed on a dual-core platform, with hardware performance counters measuring L2 cache misses used as validation references. The results show that the proposed analysis is consistent with the observed high- and low-risk cases and provides conservative warnings for near-capacity configurations. In particular, different applications pairs might produces up to 213.09% increase in L2 cache misses. These results demonstrate that memory-access profiling can provide practical and interpretable early indicators of cache-related multicore interference before exhaustive hardware testing.

Title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects
Author: Fernando Delbianco, Fernando Tohmé, Gustavo Bodanza
Text_Content: Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation. We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. In turn, a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Together they constitute a complete account of individual causal effects.

Title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council
Author: Rudrajit Choudhuri, Christian Bird, Carmen Badea, Anita Sarma
Text_Content: Qualitative data can tell software teams what their stakeholders need, yet rigorously analyzing thousands of qualitative responses takes expert time that few teams can afford or justify. Teams therefore often face a false choice: leave the responses unanalyzed, or hand them to a large language model and accept its interpretation and judgment. In this paper, we take a pragmatic approach to AI-assisted qualitative analysis and present TACT (Traceable AI Council for Thematic analysis), a procedure that enables such analysis at scale while keeping teams in control of interpretation and judgment. TACT comes in two variants: TACT-Lite, the core AI council procedure, and TACT-Full, which adds adversaries (models from other model families that critique each model's output) and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. We evaluated TACT on an independent dataset of 256 Stack Overflow threads qualitatively coded by other researchers. Against their labels, TACT's candidate codebook achieved an F1 of 0.75-0.77 and its final coding an F1 of 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between our own manual coding and TACT's coding was Cohen's $κ$ of 0.79-0.85. TACT is also economical: model calls cost \$13.77 (TACT-Lite) to \$33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads. Finally, drawing on our experience building and validating TACT, we identify pitfalls in AI-assisted qualitative analysis, describe safeguards to address them, and offer guidance for teams and researchers applying TACT in practice.

Title: Emission-associated energy deposition and Cherenkov-dose proportionality in megavoltage photon beams
Author: Xianghuan He, Yao Hao, Changyu Sun, Andy N. Wiles, Gregory B. Biedermann, Brian W. Pogue, Rongxiao Zhang
Text_Content: Background: Quantitative Cherenkov-to-dose conversion depends on beam spectrum, field size, depth, and material properties. Purpose: To distinguish dose contributions with and without accompanying Cherenkov production and assess their implications for calibration. Methods: Geant4 simulations paired dose and local Cherenkov distributions in water for flattened 6, 10, and 15 MV and flattening-filter-free (FFF) 6 and 10 MV beams with $3 \times 3$ and $10 \times 10$ cm$^2$ fields. Energy deposition was tagged by whether its transport step produced at least one Cherenkov photon. Component fractions were calculated over the phantom. Distributions were independently normalized within a shared reference region and compared using voxelwise ratios, lateral profiles, and spatial partitioning. Results: Emission-tagged fractions were 37%-61%, increasing with beam energy and lower for FFF beams. Fractions differed by less than 1.3 percentage points between field sizes. Emission-tagged ratios clustered near unity, with 98.4%-99.9% between 0.95 and 1.05 across the evaluated regions, whereas total and non-emission-tagged ratios varied with depth and lateral position. Emission-tagged profiles generally showed smaller residual differences. Conclusions: Emission-tagged deposition closely tracked local Cherenkov production. Departures of the total Cherenkov-to-dose ratio followed spatial variations in the emission-tagged dose fraction, indicating where calibration needs correction. The classification reflects actual photon production and depends on transport settings; dedicated electron-energy scoring is needed to isolate sub-threshold contributions.

Title: GeoDIVE: Geospatial Descent Informed by Value Estimation
Author: Hamza Iqbal, Dan Cher, Eric Xing, Pranavi Kolouju, Abby Stylianou, Robert Pless, Nathan Jacobs
Text_Content: Finding specific objects, structures, and spatial patterns supports critical work in agriculture, infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. These features, however, are often dispersed across very large regions and span dramatically different spatial scales, which defines a search space that is costly to embed, maintain, and search naively. We introduce GeoDIVE, a model that treats a multiresolution satellite image gallery as a forest and uses best-first traversal to determine which tiles to encode. At each visited node, a lightweight model then predicts an optimistic estimate of the best query similarity hidden among its descendants using the query and subtree representations. In evaluations with image and open-vocabulary text queries, GeoDIVE matches exhaustive search at 10% of the encoding cost for image queries and leads all tested baselines at every budget in both modalities. To support future evaluation of multiscale geospatial search, we also release object-level image and text queries for Git-10M, constructed from Microsoft building footprints and OpenStreetMap polygons with VLM-generated captions. Source code and models will be made publicly available.

Title: Demystifying Information Flow Downgrading using the Real--Ideal Paradigm
Author: Suraaj Kanniwadi, Andrew C. Myers
Text_Content: The real--ideal paradigm, an approach to security specification developed in the cryptography community, has the benefit that it can express sophisticated confidentiality and integrity requirements, even for decentralized systems. We show that this paradigm is the basis for a powerful and intuitive new semantic framework for language-based security. Our new framework cleanly and extensionally captures existing security definitions, including not only noninterference but also less understood information flow properties that involve downgrading, such as robust declassification and nonmalleable information flow. Past semantics for these properties have relied on intensional downgrading events. Further, we show that all of these properties can be enforced by a practical information-flow type system for a while-language that supports downgrading. Surprisingly, correctness of this type system is also characterized as a real--ideal simulation, with an important implication: the security of heterogeneous, decentralized systems with a strong (real) attacker can be understood by reasoning about a weak (ideal) attacker whose power is restricted to interaction with downgrading. This result explains the usefulness of nonmalleable information flow and related security properties. The results are fully formalized using the Rocq prover and are publicly available.

Title: Anchored Slice Propagation with Boundary Transport for 3D CT Segmentation from Three Orthogonal Annotated Slices
Author: Tushar Kataria, Md Rakibul Haque, Shireen Y. Elhabian
Text_Content: Sli2Vol propagates a binary mask through affinities between adjacent slices, but an error can persist because each prediction becomes the input to the next step. Three orthogonal annotations reduce dependence on any one chain, yet they offer more than three starting masks: where a chain crosses another annotated plane, the correct label is already known. Those labels could correct drift during propagation and indicate how much to trust each chain at fusion. Between annotated planes, the information carried by the chain may matter as well. A binary mask records foreground membership but discards distance to the boundary, a cue that could help follow gradual shape changes between slices.We address these two sources of error with a fixed pretrained affinity backbone. We anchor each chain by correcting its prediction where it crosses another annotated plane, then use its agreement with those labels to weight fusion. We compare this anchored mask with two ways of transporting boundary geometry: a truncated signed-distance field (SDF) propagated by dense affinity averaging, and a contour whose vertices follow motion cues from the same affinity. The contour tracker starts from a hand-crafted rule and learns a motion correction from supervoxel pseudo-objects in 506 CT volumes, without manual organ labels. On 2,091 held-out structure instances from approximately 403 CT scans spanning 17 abdominal structures, anchoring raises mean Dice from 0.737 with orthogonal mask propagation to 0.769 and improves every structure. Beyond the anchored mask, learned contour tracking improves Dice by 5.7\% for the esophagus and 5.9\% for the postcava, while SDF transport improves right-adrenal Dice by 2.8\%. The anchored methods have similar mean Dice (0.769--0.772); contour tracking performs worse on the kidneys, stomach, and hepatic vessel tree.

Title: A physics-informed neural network method for pressure-driven turbine-blade optimization
Author: Yuan Huang, Francesca di Mare
Text_Content: We develop a physics-informed method for aerodynamic shape optimisation of turbine blades, treating the flow field and blade geometry as coupled unknowns. The method translates prescribed surface-pressure distributions into geometric modifications through pressure-target continuation and alternating flow-geometry updates. A differentiable representation of the blade surfaces allows their positions and orientations to be optimised within the current flow field, followed by flow re-adaptation to the modified boundaries. The inverse formulation uses the two-dimensional steady compressible Euler equations as physics constraints and is evaluated on the LS89 turbine cascade using 28 pressure-target points derived from experimental data. Starting from a modified profile and a warm-started flow network, the final pressure-side and suction-side root-mean-square fitting errors are 1.13% and 2.21% of inlet total pressure, respectively. Independent forward verification with SharC reproduces the principal surface-pressure trends of the experimental measurements, with remaining differences near the trailing edge. These results demonstrate the translation of experimental-origin loading data into geometric blade modifications through coordinated optimisation of the flow field and moving boundaries.

Title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and $k$-NN Graph Building
Author: Tobias Rubel, Richard Wen, Guy Blelloch, Laxman Dhulipala, Lars Gottesbüren, Jakub Łącki, Vahab Mirrokni
Text_Content: Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) indexes such as HNSW and Vamana deliver state-of-the-art query performance at the cost of large indexing times. The recently introduced PiPNN method drastically accelerated index construction by way of a partitioning-based algorithm leveraging dense matrix multiplication and top-$K$ aggregation kernels. In this paper, we unlock the full potential of PiPNN's hardware-friendly algorithm design. We introduce PiPNN II, which optimizes multiple steps of the PiPNN recipe, giving up to $8\times$ speedups for graph-based ANNS index construction. In addition, we present GPiPNN, a GPU implementation which builds comparable ANNS indices up to $43.7\times$ faster than Jasper and up to $50\times$ faster than CAGRA. We also extend PiPNN II and GPiPNN to compute high-quality $k$-NN graphs directly, which unlocks massive speedups over methods used in many existing systems for clustering, anomaly detection, and more. For 10-NN graph building at $90\%$ recall, we obtain up to a $13\times$ speedup on CPUs and $6.6\times$ on GPUs as compared to the prior best methods. PiPNN II can build a billion-scale 10-NN graph in under 16 minutes. Common to both PiPNN II and GPiPNN is the use of quantization to reduce memory traffic and leverage fast low-precision matrix operations. Top-$K$ emerges as a new bottleneck, which we optimize with specialized code for specific $K$, and by fusing with the matrix kernel to avoid materializing the distance matrix to memory. On CPUs, we demonstrate further performance improvements by leveraging our matrix kernels in the RobustPrune procedure proposed in Vamana and used in PiPNN. On GPUs, we flatten recursive partitioning into segmented batches, use one fused top-$K$ abstraction for partitioning and leaf scoring, and prune with already-witnessed direct edges rather than new candidate-to-candidate scoring passes.

Title: TRUST-Stereo: Teacher-Assisted Robust Uncertainty-Guided Search and Transfer for Fast Stereo Matching
Author: Pouya Sohrabipour, Yihong Feng, Chaitanya Kumar Reddy Pallerla, Tuan Dang, Ngan Le, Dongyi Wang
Text_Content: Coarse-to-fine stereo matching enables efficient disparity estimation but remains sensitive to errors in propagated disparity, which may place ground-truth correspondences outside subsequent local search ranges. We propose TRUST-Stereo (Teacher-Assisted Robust Uncertainty-Guided Search and Transfer for Fast Stereo Matching), which addresses this limitation through an Uncertainty-Guided Residual Search Module (UGRSM). UGRSM estimates the reliability of propagated disparity and predicts residual offsets to adaptively relocate local cost-volume centers. Additionally, we introduce a two-stage Senior-Junior Teacher Assistant knowledge distillation strategy to transfer rich monocular representations from a large foundation model to a lightweight backbone to achieve fast stereo matching performance. Experiments on KITTI 2012, KITTI 2015, ETH3D, and Middlebury demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization. Using only 1.4M synthetic stereo pairs, TRUST-Stereo achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark metrics, outperforming competing efficient methods trained with substantially larger datasets, including real-world pseudo-labeled samples. Specifically, it achieves a KITTI 2015 EPE of 0.93, ETH3D Bad 1.0 of 2.13% and Middlebury Bad 2.0 of 6.79% while maintaining inference at approximately 50 ms per stereo pair.

Title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research
Author: Ying Zhang, Emily L. Kang, Shuo Li
Text_Content: Gaussian process regression is widely used for modeling responses in both physical and computer experiments. In practice, data from physical experiments may include replications and be subject to censoring due to equipment limitations or contextual constraints, and such datasets can be large, posing a scalability challenge for standard Gaussian process inference. Motivated by a real-world industrial research study, we develop a Gaussian process modeling framework that efficiently analyzes large replicated and censored data. Our approach integrates a Vecchia approximation for computational scalability with a likelihood-based formulation that fully exploits replication and rigorously incorporates information from censored observations, analogous to exact simulation from truncated distributions. Through experiments on synthetic data and a real case study from industrial research, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields improved predictive accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches, making it well suited for large-scale applications with structured replication and incomplete data.

Title: High-dimensional Four-Level Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis for Unbalanced Level Data with Application to Concussion Data
Author: Verena Werkmann, Alok S. Shah, Brian D. Stemper, Jaroslaw Harezlak
Text_Content: We implement the Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis (SFPCA) framework of Shou et al. (2015) in a four-level nested setting with arbitrarily unbalanced group sizes at every level of the hierarchy. While the SFPCA framework can in principle accommodate deeper hierarchical structures, practical implementations remain challenging when the number of curves is large and the hierarchy is highly unbalanced. Our contributions are twofold. First, we operationalize SFPCA for four hierarchical levels with arbitrary unbalancedness across units. Second, we propose a memory-efficient computational strategy that makes the analysis of large collections of curves feasible on conventional hardware. In particular, we construct the four design-specific matrices required for the Method of Moments (MoM) estimators of the level-specific covariance operators while controlling their memory footprint, which would otherwise grow prohibitively with the number of curves. We illustrate the approach using three subsets of the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium dataset (2014-2017).

Title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
Author: Maeve Côté
Text_Content: Background: The automatic identification of tree species from bark photographs is of practical interest for forestry inventory and the wood-processing industry, yet the design choices that govern the accuracy of deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some prior results may be inflated by leakage of images of the same trunk across training and test partitions. Methods: A systematic ablation study is conducted on the public BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species) under the established tree-level, leakage-safe partitioning scheme. Using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones, the following factors are varied in turn and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation: patch size, the strategy by which per-patch predictions are aggregated into an image-level decision, the training regime (single- versus two-stage), backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and the number of patches available at inference. Results: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically with patch size (from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px), and image-level accuracy rises in step, plateauing near 94.9% around 512 px. Learned aggregation exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp, an advantage that shrinks as patches grow and attention becomes near-uniform. Backbone capacity (pico to tiny) alters accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training offers no advantage over one-stage. Whole-image classification (91.9%) trails patch-based aggregation, since it admits no bag to average over; accuracy increases with the number of patches at inference, saturating around 64. Conclusions: The study yields a simple recommended configuration: patches as large as possible while leaving enough to average over (around 512 px here), with a nano backbone. It also quantifies the second-order role of learned aggregation and model capacity, providing a reproducible reference point for practitioners and future research

Title: Quadratic reset bounds for finite maximal prefix codes
Author: Samrath Singh Chadha
Text_Content: Let $C$ be a finite maximal prefix code of maximum codeword length $k\ge2$. We prove that, whenever the literal decoder of $C$ is synchronizing, it has a reset word of length at most $(k-1)(4k-5)$. The bound is independent of the alphabet and the number of decoder states. Its main ingredient is a short-detection theorem: a linear observation of the decoder, with terminal weight constant on states of depth $k-1$, is either identically zero or nonzero on a word of length at most $2k-3$. The proof uses a first-return decomposition in noncommuting variables and cancellation of a highest-degree coefficient. For codes whose codeword lengths are $k-1$ and $k$, we prove the sharper bound $2(k-1)^2-1$ and characterize equality. The binary code with the single short word $a^{k-1}$ attains this bound for every $k\ge2$; an age representation and a potential on circular arcs give the matching lower bound. Both upper bounds yield polynomial-time constructions in the explicit code size. The mathematical results and the algorithms are formalized in Lean, with polynomial work bounds in a specified binary cost model.

Title: How Do Artificial Agents Make Decisions in Light of Visual Data?
Author: Keyty Loza, Shayan Monadjemi
Text_Content: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.

Title: Inferring Factor Importance with Explainable AI Model for Macrophage Immune Cell Polarization
Author: Joseph Pateras, Gurseerat Kaur, D. Joshua Cohen, Barbara D. Boyan, Zvi Schwartz, Preetam Ghosh
Text_Content: Macrophages are highly plastic immune cells that dynamically shift between pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes in response to cytokines, transcriptional regulators, metabolic cues, and local microenvironment. Yet macrophage polarization is governed by nonlinear regulatory networks that are difficult to study experimentally. Here, we integrate mechanistic simulation, surrogate neural networks, and explainable machine learning to identify key regulatory drivers of polarization. We generated simulation data with a COPASI-based macrophage polarization model and used them to train an LSTM surrogate capable of reconstructing temporal macrophage marker dynamics across diverse macrophage activation states. SHAP, Individual Conditional Expectation, and Partial Dependence Plot analyses quantified feature importance, identified nonlinear response regimes, and characterized higher-order interactions among cytokines, transcription factors, and polarization markers. The model identified oxygen availability and IL10 as dominant anti-inflammatory regulators, consistently promoting M2-associated outputs such as ARG1 and VEGF. Conversely, IFN-γ, TNFα, IL12, iNOS, CXCL9, and mCXCL10 reinforced M1-associated inflammatory programs. STAT1-centered analyses identified iNOS, TNFα, and mCXCL10 levels as strong contributors to STAT1 outcomes, consistent with amplification of the IFN- γ/JAK/STAT1 inflammatory axis. VEGF negatively contributed to predicted STAT1 output, suggesting antagonism between M2 markers and M1 activation. SHAP, ICE, and PDP analyses also showed that STAT1 regulation is nonlinear and threshold-like: pro-inflammatory signals must accumulate before STAT1 rises sharply. Together, it demonstrates that the LSTM explainability framework can identify polarization drivers, uncover nonlinear regulatory thresholds, and prioritize pathways for experimental validation.

Title: The Harmonic Online $k$-Server Algorithm Is Poly(k)-Competitive
Author: Yichen Huang
Text_Content: The online $k$-server problem is one of the most fundamental problems in online algorithms. In this problem, $k$ servers are located in a metric space and serve a sequence of requests at points in the metric space by moving a server there. The Harmonic algorithm is a very natural algorithm: it chooses a server with probability inversely proportional to its distance from the request. It is also highly efficient, being memoryless and answering each request in $O(k)$ time. However, its competitive ratio has remained unsettled between the $O(2^k \log k)$ upper bound (Bartal and Grove, JACM 2000) and the $k(k+1)/2$ lower bound (Raghavan and Snir, 1994, IBM J. Res. Dev.). We prove that Harmonic is $2k^4$-competitive on every metric space against adaptive online adversaries. Our analysis uses a potential combining corrected electrical energy with the distances of online servers to their assigned adversary locations.

Title: Sundance: A Simple SMT Solver for Program Verification
Author: Amar Shah, Benjamin F. Jones, Can Cebeci, Jason Z. S. Hu, Lee A. Barnett, Rémi Delmas, Marijn Heule, Bryan Parno, Bruno Dutertre
Text_Content: We present Sundance, an SMT solver for program verification written in about 13,600 lines of Rust. Sundance combines the Cadical SAT solver with congruence closure, linear arithmetic, algebraic datatypes, and pattern-based quantifier instantiation. Sundance produces eDRAT proofs for every unsat answer. On 21,531 queries from Verus, Dafny, and F*, Sundance is comparable to existing solvers, with 26--38 times fewer lines of code than Z3 and cvc5. We further show that its components can be swapped for Z3's arithmetic solver, MiniSat, and the Semper e-graph. We have open sourced Sundance.

Title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning
Author: Xinkai Jiang, Jing Jiang, Hongyi Zhou, Pankhuri Vanjani, Ahmad Baki, Jakub Suliga, Ge Li, Zhuoyue Li, Gerhard Neumann, Rudolf Lioutikov
Text_Content: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.

Title: Revisiting Critic Estimation in Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms
Author: Jan Felix Kleuker, Koen Ponse, Aske Plaat, Thomas M. Moerland
Text_Content: Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is a widely used deep reinforcement learning algorithm that combines entropy regularization with an actor-critic architecture. Standard implementations rely on one-step temporal-difference learning of Q-functions, yet alternative critic design choices remain underexplored. In this work, we revisit three such choices: learning soft advantages instead of soft Q-values, the use of multi-step return targets, and the training of multi-step critics from replay buffer data. Keeping the policy objective fixed, we compare the six critic variants these choices generate: (i) advantage and (ii) dueling-advantage critics learned from one-step transitions, and $λ$-return and soft Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) critics learned either (iii, iv) on-policy or (v, vi) from replayed trajectory segments. Each variant is evaluated across an entire random hyperparameter search on fourteen tasks, treating the hyperparameters as part of the algorithm. Learning soft advantages instead of soft Q-values does not improve performance, and the soft GAE critic adds nothing over the simpler $λ$-return critic. What does improve performance, most clearly on continuous control, is training a $λ$-return critic on replayed trajectory segments, even without importance weighting or trace cutting. This extends earlier evidence that uncorrected multi-step targets work well under replay to the full soft $λ$-return, entropy terms included. By design, the underlying ideas studied here extend beyond SAC, and our empirical findings aim to encourage their application to a broader class of reinforcement learning algorithms.

Title: Construct Validity of Coding Benchmarks for LLM-based Agentic Coding Tools
Author: Alexander Berndt, Paul Ralph, Thomas Bach, Sebastian Baltes
Text_Content: Software developers increasingly adopt LLM-based agentic coding tools to assist them with development tasks. To provide developers with up-to-date information on these tools' effectiveness, prior work introduced benchmarks that enable comparisons across tools. Despite the widespread adoption of such benchmarks, however, recent work has shown that they suffer from issues threatening their validity. Aims. In this work, we aim to complement prior work by analyzing the construct validity of agentic coding benchmarks. Methodology. We analyze nine benchmarks commonly used to evaluate the effectiveness of agentic coding tools. We identify the constructs that the benchmarks claim to measure, the metrics used to operationalize them, and potential confounders that interfere with the measurement. Results. Our findings show that benchmarks commonly operationalize broad concepts such as coding capability with only a small set of metrics. The reported attributes that might confound the measurements vary between benchmarks, indicating a lack of standardization. Conclusions. We conclude with recommendations to strengthen construct validity in agentic coding benchmarks and encourage further empirical work to better understand the effectiveness of agentic coding tools.

Title: Combining Relevant Expert Knowledge Using Mixtures of Feedback Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
Author: Olaoluwa Adigun, Akash Kumar Panda, Bart Kosko
Text_Content: A neuro-symbolic system should combine only relevant answers from expert agents or other knowledge sources. Using only relevant experts for a given input query becomes ever more important for accuracy and scalability as the knowledge network grows and connects ever more knowledge sources. We extend the standard definition of relevance from the legal theory of evidence: An answer is relevant if and only if it is both probative and material for the matter at hand given the knowledge available. We apply this relevancy scheme to mixing the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps (FCMs) of real or artificial experts. The expert FCM directed causal graphs mix or combine into a common knowledge network. We compare the equilibrium limit-cycle predictions or answers of the experts to the answers of the mixture FCM and then estimate the probative status of answers by their difference or variation. A new Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge mixture into corresponding posterior-like FCMs that also allow relevancy-based comparisons. The result is a final set of relevancy mixing weights that produces a relevancy-mixed FCM knowledge network for the given query. So different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs. We demonstrate this relevancy approach using generated synthetic FCMs from an actual 13-node expert FCM that models the causes and feedbacks of ischemic-stroke risk.

Title: Grounded but Not Immune: Confirmation Bias in Agent-as-a-judge
Author: Drake Benjamin Brown, Khushbu Pahwa, Yubin Ge, Salvatore Romeo, Akhil Agnihotri, Yi Zhang, Xiaofei Ma, Daniele Bonadiman
Text_Content: Evaluating open-ended agent tasks increasingly falls to an Agent-as-a-Judge: an evaluator handed tools and the agent's full trajectory so it can verify a result against the environment. The premise is that a judge that gathers its own evidence should be grounded by it. We show that this grounding does not immunize the judge against confirmation bias: a single false pre-screening note, attributed to an authority and carrying no evidential bearing on the correct verdict, overturns up to 40% of a tool-using judge's correct verdicts across four judges and five datasets, even though the judge collects decisive evidence. The shift is driven by specific properties of the cue. We treat this cue as a controlled diagnostic of confirmation bias rather than an adversarial attack. Our central contribution is to explain how confirmation bias changes the judge's behavior in a trajectory. We classify changes in judge behavior and attribute changes to one of three failure modes: over-trust (verify, conclude correctly, then defer), hallucination (fabricate support for the flip), and under-investigation (stop at the first corroborating signal). For the two Claude judges, the failure is predominantly over-trust (67-75% of harmful flips), while smaller judges have error modes spread across all three. Lightweight mitigations blunt but never remove the bias.

Title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data
Author: Rebecca Anthopolos, Bo Cai, Lorna E. Thorpe, Hui Xie, Xiaochun Li, Sarah Conderino, David C. Lee, Hui Shao, Ibrahim Zaganjor, Marc Rosenman, H. Lester Kirchner, Muchiri E. Wandai, Levon Utidjian, Tessa Crume, Kristi Reynolds, Jasmin Divers, DiCAYA Study Group
Text_Content: Electronic health records (EHRs) are increasingly used for disease surveillance. However, data collected in EHRs may not be a representative sample of the target population for inference. Methods for EHR-based surveillance remain in their nascence. In addition to simple weighting approaches, researchers have used multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), a popular technique for finite population quantity estimation that remains understudied in EHRs. We are motivated by a US-based collaborative to modernize diabetes surveillance using EHR data from different health system centers across the country. To estimate type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence in children and adolescents, we propose and evaluate three Bayesian superpopulation models that are distinguished by how they account for two important features of EHR data: unobserved heterogeneity and data sparsity. The three models include an analysis of variance-inspired approach; a model with geographic effects varying by demographic subgroup; and MRP, which we consider as the reference model. We apply the models to estimate prevalence overall and in demographic- and geographic-based subgroups. Using plasmode simulations, we evaluate model estimation performance while preserving the complexity of the EHR data. Our results show that the superpopulation-based prevalence estimates were higher than those observed in the EHR sample alone, with the magnitude of the differences varying by health system center. The bias and coverage probabilities of MRP markedly worsened when the EHR sample size was smaller or the selection mechanism was more complex. Overall, the superpopulation model based on analysis of variance demonstrated the best estimation performance.

Title: AQUA - A Modular Authentication Quality Modeling Framework
Author: Alex R. Mattukat, Michael Zerbe, Krisa Carka
Text_Content: Authentication solutions are the key design, architectural, and implementation decisions that implement authentication security controls. An example is a password-based authentication solution. While researchers often examine authentication quality, existing approaches do not distinguish which effects on quality stem from which aspect of authentication. For example, multi-factor authentication solutions tend to be less usable because they combine multiple authenticators, whereas passkeys are more secure than passwords because of properties inherent to the authenticator itself. This paper presents AQUA, a modular quality modeling framework for authentication solutions. AQUA's core idea is to decompose authentication into four interrelated concepts, enabling modular specification of authentication quality and tracing quality effects back to their source. We demonstrate AQUA with initial definitional quality models that address the levels of authenticators, authentication techniques, and authentication solutions. We further illustrate the interrelations between these concepts through concrete examples and a usability metric, showing how quality propagates across the concepts and ultimately affects the overall quality of an authentication solution. Our results provide a foundation for future work, including designing assessment and prediction models for authentication solutions and automated quality assessments.

Title: Adaptive Domain Decomposition for Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks
Author: Sarah Helfert, Wanxin Chen, Amanda A. Howard, Panos Stinis, Alexander Heinlein
Text_Content: In this work, we present adaptive domain decomposition finite basis physics-informed neural networks (ADD-FBPINNs). The proposed method integrates Partition of Unity Networks (POUNets), a data-driven approach for learning domain partitions, with finite Basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs) to perform more efficient domain decomposition and achieve more accurate approximations. FBPINNs improve upon the accuracy of standard physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) through user-defined subdivisions of the computational domain. By adapting the domain decomposition based on the solution's features using a separable POUNet, the framework can automatically learn partitions that are stable and can be geometrically interpretable. We test this approach on the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation, two-dimensional Poisson equation with multiscale features, and viscous Burgers equation and observe improved accuracy compared with FBPINNs with fixed domain decomposition.

Title: Beyond Accuracy: Information-Theoretic Decoder Evaluation Under Latent Intent
Author: Tasha Kim, Benjamin Ballyk, Anson Lei, Ingmar Posner, Oiwi Parker Jones
Text_Content: A central challenge in assistive brain-to-robot control is decoding a user's latent intent from complex and noisy brain signals. Prior approaches evaluate decoders as single-trial classifiers with accuracy-based metrics, but this neglects the inherently sequential nature of assistive control. Since a planner must integrate intermittent, noisy decoder outputs over time, single-step accuracy can only be a proxy when predicting downstream task performance. We formalize brain-to-robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), and prove that there is a sharp phase transition: regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon as long as pairs of goals are all decoder-distinguishable, but grows linearly otherwise. We show that a single channel statistic, the worst-pair Chernoff information $Γ_{\min}$ sets this boundary. Then, we derive a closed-form regret predictor $U_{\mathrm{id}}(C)$, that can be computed from any confusion matrix in $O(K^2)$ time. Across two domains spanning orthogonal information channels, we show that $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy can explain. We then highlight a pathological accuracy trap, in which two decoders have identical validation accuracy 35.1% on real EEG data (BNCI2014001 subject 5) but result in a difference of $9.6\times$ in held-out regret, which $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts. Same-signal control confirms $U_{\mathrm{id}}$'s advantage with decoders that span independent feature channels. Ultimately, our work provides a drop-in diagnostic to evaluate and select sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control.

Title: When Are Two SAE Latents the Same Feature?
Author: Alexandra Suvorikova, Ilgam Latypov, Anton Trukhan, Yuriy Dorn
Text_Content: Comparing sparse autoencoders (SAEs) requires connecting feature correspondence, differences between whole dictionaries, and uncertainty from finite evaluation data. We develop a framework that connects these tasks through an energy-weighted optimal-transport plan under a specified similarity geometry. The same plan defines a dictionary-level discrepancy, decomposes it into latent contributions, and quantifies how each latent's mass is distributed across counterparts. We characterize relationships between decoder, activation, and first-order causal similarities; idealized models clarify the interpretation of splitting and absorption. For fixed trained SAEs, we derive joint asymptotic inference for transport costs and fractions, accounting for activation similarities and both energy marginals estimated from the same documents. A joint document bootstrap gives asymptotically valid simultaneous confidence bands. Experiments across four language models locate cross-seed discrepancy and separate context-dependent changes.

Title: Electron Kinetics in the Sheath of Atmospheric Pressure Plasmas in Helium and Helium:H$_2$O Vapor
Author: Uwe Kortshagen
Text_Content: The electron energy distribution function (EEDF) plays a central role in determining the rates of electron-induced reactions in the bulk plasma, the sheath, and at the plasma-surface interface. However, the electron kinetics within the sheath and near the surface are generally not well described by conventional Boltzmann solvers, which neglect the sheath electric field and electron losses to the surface. In this study, we investigate electron kinetics in atmospheric pressure plasmas in pure helium and helium-water vapor mixtures using a hybrid model that combines a fluid description of the collisional sheath with a particle kinetic Monte Carlo model for electrons. The floating wall potential is determined taking into account electron diffusion through the sheath and the non-Maxwellian EEDF. Our results demonstrate that electron kinetics within the sheath can exhibit both local and nonlocal behavior, even at atmospheric pressure. The transition between these regimes is governed primarily by the ratio of the electron energy relaxation length to the sheath thickness. At high plasma densities, where the sheath thickness becomes smaller than the electron energy relaxation length, the EEDFs approach the nonlocal limit, exhibiting significant changes in electron kinetic energy toward the wall. The addition of water vapor reduces the energy relaxation length and shifts the electron kinetics toward the local regime. In the nonlocal regime, the electron mean kinetic energy decreases substantially toward the wall, accompanied by reductions of more than an order of magnitude in electron-impact excitation and ionization rate coefficients. These findings demonstrate that modeling of electron-induced processes in the sheath and at plasma-surface interfaces requires accounting for nonlocal electron kinetics and electron losses to the surface, even at atmospheric pressure.

Title: Quantifying Trait-State Hierarchy in EEG Foundation Model and Signal Processing Embeddings
Author: Anusha Madapura, Aditya Kommineni, Shrikanth Narayanan
Text_Content: Electroencephalography (EEG) measures brain activity through recording electrical potentials of the scalp. EEG recordings capture two distinct sets of characteristics in the signal: (1) \emph{Traits} -- information that remains relatively constant over the course of a recording session, such as subject identity, age, and sex; (2) \emph{States} -- signatures that encode responses to external stimuli, including visual, auditory, and motor information. There is limited understanding of how different EEG modeling features (signal processing and foundation models) encode state and trait characteristics. In this work, we quantify state- and trait-level features captured by EEG embeddings using a hierarchy metric and kNN purity on Brain-Computer Interface dataset trials, and find that a majority of EEG features form a macro-trait hierarchy (embeddings form trait-level clusters with micro-states within). Our linear probe results indicate that this hierarchy structure leads to suboptimal state distinguishability, negatively impacting BCI performance of EEG foundation models. To mitigate this, we explore normalization techniques that reduce trait-specific information in embeddings and provide a $\sim$ 10\% improvement in balanced accuracy for state classification. Additionally, we observe that when fine-tuning models for downstream state decoding, embedding spaces transform from macro-trait to macro-state hierarchies, which in turn lead to better state decoding.

Title: A Sharp Additive Bound for the Threshold Rule in Repeated Rent-or-Buy
Author: Vasco Schiavo
Text_Content: Motivated by context management in LLM agents, we study a repeated rent-or-buy model with schedule-independent history growth and a fixed reset price $K$, a discrete form of dynamic TCP acknowledgment: every call pays as rent the history accumulated since the last reset, and a reset clears it. The classical threshold rule is $2$-competitive, and no deterministic rule guarantees a smaller ratio. We show that, measured additively, its loss is governed by the changes in the growth: if the growth is constant on $P$ runs, the threshold rule, knowing neither the runs nor the horizon, pays at most $(2P-1)K$ more than the optimal schedule chosen with hindsight, and the coefficient $2P-1$ is sharp. If the growth is only within a factor $1+\varepsilon$ of $P$ runs, the bound holds up to a factor $1+\varepsilon$ and an extra $\varepsilon K$. The proof is a potential argument built from the relative value functions of the single-rate problems. On two runs no deterministic rule guarantees a loss below $2K$. A rule that also resets when the growth decreases guarantees $2K$, while the threshold rule can lose arbitrarily close to $3K$.

Title: Predictability over Volatility: When simple strategies help households save on fuel
Author: Shahrzad Jamshidi, Ako Ogihara
Text_Content: What reasonable strategies can households use to save on gasoline or diesel purchases under different pricing functions? We assess basic strategies households might employ under a simplified model of a 10-gallon tank, fixed fuel consumption between refill opportunities, and price changes at each opportunity to refill. Purchases always fill the tank, and if the tank is empty, it must be refilled regardless of price. We explore three strategy types: price-independent (filling once the tank is below a specific level), price-dependent (filling when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average), and mixed (filling only below a set level, and then only when the price is below the last $n$ days or their average). We construct price functions from the nearest-in-time US weekly averages of regular gasoline and diesel, filling in higher-frequency values with a smoothing spline, linear interpolation, and random draws from normal and uniform distributions based on national averages. Additional simulations are built using Brownian motion. Together, these pricing models span a wide range of volatilities. We find that price-independent strategies are effective for the spline and linear functions, which have low volatility, while price-dependent strategies are effective for the normal and uniform distributions, which are highly volatile. Brownian motion, despite its mid-range volatility, admits no effective strategy. Our findings suggest that the predictability of price movements, whether prices trend or revert toward a stable level, matters more for household strategies than overall volatility: the random walk is volatile in the middle of our range yet offers households no usable signal. Policymakers can therefore assist households by addressing how prices move from day to day, not only the retail prices they face.

Title: Attributing Agent Failures to Their History Needs an Executed Counterfactual: Toward a Reporting Standard
Author: Egor Pakhomov, Erik Nijkamp
Text_Content: Published explanations of why long-horizon agents fail are commonly taxonomies labeled over completed trajectories: a judge reads a transcript and names the failure. We argue that a claim attributing an agent's behavior to its history should carry intervention-verified evidence, per instance or via a validated estimator: freeze an executable mid-trajectory state, alter only the history the agent sees, and continue - executed rather than inferred from the transcript, at a state whose restoration has been measured, with a replay certificate matched to the estimand. Each of the four manipulation classes we name has a precedent, and several methods already execute interventions from checkpoints, re-executed prefixes or recorded conversation states (for example DoVer, REFLECT, Min et al., Who&When Pro, Causal Agent Replay), but none reports a measured replay certificate. Two cautionary measurements, neither applying the standard, follow: a carrier taxonomy whose "concentration" could not be separated from benchmark construction (adjusted odds ratio 1.15, interval crossing 1), and hash-identical snapshots that, restored into identically seeded processes, agreed with one another in 24 of 24 states while differing from the live continuation in 9 and 20 of 24. Restoring the captured position of a random stream made all 24 agree with the live run.

Title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
Author: Dar-Yen Chen, Yi-Zhe Song
Text_Content: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

Title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films
Author: Seungwon Park, Jingyu Tang, Minsung An, Alan J. H. McGaughey, Lisa M. Porter, Robert F. Davis, Jonathan A. Malen
Text_Content: The thermal conductivities of (001) $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films deposited on $c$-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83 $^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ W/m$\cdot$K to 2.26 $^{+0.35}_{-0.40}$ W/m$\cdot$K as the thicknesses increase from 159 nm to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon-phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$-based electronic devices.

Title: ARIDA - Active railway infrastructure dataset annotation using neural network predictions
Author: Maximilian Dornik, Christian Sieberichs, Simon Geerkens, Alexander Braun
Text_Content: Modern railway perception requires large comprehensive image datasets, but creating them is slowed by manual labeling, especially for track polylines and other complex infrastructure geometry. This paper presents the Active Railway Infrastructure Dataset Annotation framework, a railway-specific semi-automated pipeline that converts instance predictions from a mask scoring instance segmentation network into bounding-boxes, polygons, polylines, and paired polylines. To keep automatic track geometry annotation reliable without ground truth, it applies confidence thresholds and an unique contour-agreement quality score as an acceptance gate. An active learning loop ranks remaining images by uncertainty and adapts the number of manual queries per cycle. This is achieved through a novel quantity control mechanism, in which easy images are auto-accepted and human effort targets hard cases. Experiments on disjoint, diverse imagery and time-sequential, redundant imagery quantify effort reduction and accuracy trade-offs, achieving about two thirds reduction in the disjoint regime and up to 93% in the sequential regime. The study also provides guidance for initial label budgets and stopping to avoid over-annotation.

Title: Data-Efficient Scaling-Law Discovery for Recommendation Systems via Coupled Hyperparameter Scaling
Author: John Martabano Landy, Louis C. Tiao, Yao Xuan, Luc Kien Hang, Rupinder P. Khandpur, Arvind M. Vepa, Srinidhi Raghavendran, Anirudh Agrawal, Xiaoyi Leo Liu, Jiang Liu, Peggy Yao, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic
Text_Content: Large-scale ranking and recommendation models of Web platforms benefit from increased compute much as large language models do, and their scaling behavior is broadly power-law in form. Yet ranking models have heterogeneous architectures which makes their scaling law less straightforward than that of LLMs. We address how to discover the scaling law of an arbitrary ranking model efficiently. We introduce a scaling layer, which groups primitive architecture parameters into semantically coherent groups and defines how they co-vary, inducing a mapping from a low-dimensional space of hyper-hyperparameters into the full architecture space. On top of it, Axia fits scaling-informed surrogates, selects configurations by a posterior-based acquisition criterion, and returns a Pareto frontier from which per-model operating points are validated -- replacing exhaustive sweeps with a small number of informative runs. A fleet-level evaluation protocol, computed on a fixed representative model set under matched trial budgets, makes refinements to either component measurable. Our contribution is an automated system that learns model-specific complexity-quality relationships and gives uncertainty-aware guidance for allocating compute across a heterogeneous model ecosystem. Across 34 model iterations in two development cycles on Meta's ads ranking and retrieval system, the workflow yielded a mean 0.66% offline normalized-entropy improvement and 0.36% cumulative online lift.

Title: Runway Characters: Serving a 57B Video Diffusion Transformer for Real-Time Conversation
Author: Rohan Agarwal, Robin Andeer, Alex Armbruster, Bennett Arthur, Michail Christos Doukas, Piero Esposito, Qiming Fang, Aron Filkey, Bryan Fox, Anastasis Germanidis, Jonathan Granskog, Corina Gurau, Robin Kahlow, Taras Khakhulin, Nasir Mohammad Khalid, Tomasz Łakomy, Mike Leisz, Kathleen M. Lewis, Daniil Merkulov, Nicolas Neubert, Ryan Phillips, Yining Shi, Axel Örn Sigurðsson, Erica Simmons, Mark Sturley, Ziyi Tang, Michail Tarasiou, Jamie Umpherson, Cindy Wang, Jimei Yang, Hudson Yeo, Wei Zhang, Zejia Zheng
Text_Content: Conversational video characters must generate video as fast as it plays, for one user at a time: at 24 fps, a sustained 166.7 ms per four-frame chunk at batch size one, with only a few chunks of buffering. We describe the system behind Runway Characters, which serves a $\approx$57B-parameter autoregressive video diffusion transformer (four denoising passes per chunk) at 704$\times$1088 and 24 fps on four H100 GPUs with a voice agent in the loop. Each chunk takes 240 attention calls, each reading a 5,788-slot KV cache in which only 757 tokens are new, and 29% of the original step was whole-cache work repeated in every call. We move that work to write time (a ring cache, RoPE and FP8 quantization applied once per write, and a delta rotation when positions reset), fuse the tensor-parallel all-reduce into the FP8 GEMM with in-switch reduction, and give the decoder that turns latents into video frames its own GPU. Without the fused kernel, our optimizations cut the diffusion step from 240.9 to 159.3 ms (1.51$\times$, 24.5 fps sustained) with no detected degradation in lip-sync scores; the fused kernel, rolled back once in production and since re-enabled, reaches 147.4 ms (1.63$\times$, 43% of FP8 peak). In seven weeks of production the worker averaged above 23.5 fps in 99.5% of sessions that streamed for at least a second, and our pipeline takes 0.49 s of a 2.1 s median conversational turn. On the same GPUs, the two open-source real-time video systems we benchmarked, at four denoising passes, miss real time or add over a second of latency (one by estimate), at a third to half of our resolution.
