Author: Artem V. Belopolsky, Florian Perdreau
Text_Content: Webcam eye tracking can greatly accelerate data collection in basic and applied research by reaching large, diverse samples of participants online. However, its spatial performance is considered well below that of hardware-based systems, limiting its use. We evaluated the first-generation Chiasm webcam eye tracker in a large online study ($N = 505$) spanning diverse participants, devices, and recording conditions. Chiasm achieved a mean spatial accuracy of 2.39 cm ($\approx 2.28^\circ$ at 60 cm), spatial precision (SD) of 1.05 cm ($\approx 1.00^\circ$ at 60 cm), and sample-to-sample precision (RMS-S2S) of 1.29 cm ($\approx 1.23^\circ$ at 60 cm). For the 91% of participants who met a 3 cm calibration criterion, spatial accuracy was 2.15 cm ($\approx 2.05^\circ$ at 60 cm). After three minutes of a task that encouraged head movement, spatial accuracy declined by 0.59 cm, while the gaze center at each target shifted by a mean distance of only 0.37 cm. On the validation block, the offset was 0.30 cm larger for men than for women. Age, region of residence, face luminance, and Michelson contrast showed no reliable relationship with spatial accuracy. A higher eye aspect ratio, a more open eye, was associated with a smaller offset. Wearing glasses decreased spatial accuracy on every validation block. In a comparison between a random subsample ($N = 101$) and a separate sample tested with the open-source tracker WebGazer ($N = 101$) using an identical protocol, Chiasm showed better spatial accuracy (2.18 vs. 4.51 cm) and spatial precision (SD; 1.01 vs. 1.55 cm). WebGazer showed better sample-to-sample precision (RMS-S2S; 0.79 vs. 1.26 cm), which likely reflects conservative, over-smoothed estimates rather than superior stability. These results suggest that Chiasm is narrowing the gap between webcam and hardware-based eye tracking, making large-scale gaze research "in the wild" a reality.

Title: Local Visibility Roadmaps in Continous Multi-agent Path Finding
Author: Kristýna Janovská, Pavel Surynek
Text_Content: We address the problem of smooth continuous multi-agent path finding (SC-MAPF), where agents move in a continuous environment along smooth curves in continuous time. The paths for individual agents are searched in local visibility roadmaps that consider obstacles and other agents. A new algorithm is proposed in this work, which combines the previous algorithm CE-CBS for high-level search with any-angle path finding for local single-agent planning, where agents are to avoid obstacles, both static and other agents. The new algorithm is tested and compared to CE-CBS, the algorithm building individual paths using RRT$^*$, and SMT-CCBS algorithm, an algorithm for MAPF$_R$. Experimental results show various advantages of the new algorithm over CE-CBS and SMT-CCBS in comparable settings.

Title: Learning Where to Look: Observation Policy Optimization for Thinking with Images
Author: Junfeng Wang, Jiawei Liu, Yongchao Xu, Tao Jiang, Jiangbo Ai, Jin Zhang, Chong Wang, Qixing Zhang
Text_Content: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.

Title: Residual Attribute Leakage Is an Interface: Auditing Privacy Evaluation After Text De-identification
Author: Tuan Thanh Duong, Joongmin Shin, Jeongho Yoon, Junyoung Son, Heuiseok Lim
Text_Content: A privacy evaluation of de-identified text asks a language model (the adversary) to guess a person's protected attribute. We introduce a prior-normalised clipped leakage score of its confidence gain on the true value and audit the conclusions drawn from it. Each verdict depends on an evaluation interface (the queried person, answer options, prior, adversary model and scoring rule), which we vary on fixed releases of three corpora. In a stress test, an editor that writes the opposite-sex form at the same spans a redaction editor would redact misleads the adversary about most people, yet ranks first among editors scored on the same MedQA entries under this score, as under attack accuracy and proper scoring rules read as privacy. A relabelling-invariant reading of AUC ranks that editor sixth of eight, and a rule-aware adversary recovers the attribute from the same text. On ordinary releases most verdict changes are gains or losses of separability; of six choices varied over all pairs, only the adversary reverses comparisons (5 of its 124 changes), and the query can target the wrong person. SACC, a traceable editor we build as the instrument, lets us ablate two editing principles and show where its advantage does not hold.

Title: HTNN-MSC: Multi-view Subspace Clustering with a Hyperbolic Tangent Tensor Low-Rank Surrogate
Author: Yiwen Dou, Yiqiang Ding
Text_Content: High-order dependencies among views can be modeled by tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in multi-view subspace clustering. However, the tensor nuclear norm often used with this framework assigns the same asymptotic marginal penalty to singular values of different magnitudes, which may excessively shrink dominant components that encode cluster structure. We propose HTNN-MSC, which replaces this norm with a bounded hyperbolic tangent tensor rank surrogate. The surrogate is strictly concave on the positive half-axis and has a Lipschitz continuous derivative. Its marginal penalty decreases as singular values grow. We develop an alternating direction method of multipliers solver in which the tensor subproblem decomposes into scalar frequency-domain shrinkage problems. Safeguarded multi-start Newton iterations and candidate-objective comparison implement the resulting hyperbolic tangent thresholding operator. The shape parameter is scaled by the input spectrum. We also establish o-minimal definability of the augmented objective. Under explicit boundedness, descent, relative-error, and exact-block conditions, the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz framework guarantees convergence of the full sequence to a KKT point. On 23 datasets, HTNN-MSC achieves a mean clustering accuracy of 0.8404 and an average accuracy rank of 2.78 against nine representative methods. Friedman tests and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon comparisons reveal significant overall differences, although several pairwise differences remain nonsignificant. HTNN-MSC records 19 wins, one tie, and three losses against the convex t-SVD-MSC skeleton. A same-skeleton ablation also shows that the proposed surrogate does not uniformly outperform alternative nonconvex penalties.

Title: Robustness Verification against Patch Attacks via Group-Lasso Semidefinite Relaxation
Author: Yukina Nakagawa, Takami Sato, Ken Kobayashi, Kazuhide Nakata
Text_Content: Robustness verification is essential for ensuring the safety and security of neural networks, but current methods focus heavily on norm-ball attacks, which do not adequately model typical real-world threats that present physical perturbations, known as patch attacks. A naive approach requires computationally prohibitive enumeration of all possible patch positions. To address the challenge, we propose a novel neural network verification method specialized to the patch-attack threat. Instead of enumerating patch locations, we first model the patch attack with group-wise sparsity and formulate its verification methods as a mixed-integer semidefinite program (MISDP) by applying SDP relaxation to the neural network. We then propose three relaxations, including Group-Lasso relaxation, that remove the integer variables while preserving the sparse, group-wise structure of the original attack, enabling substantially efficient verification. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that the proposed relaxations require less than 3% of the computation time of the original MISDP, while the Group-Lasso relaxation incurs only a 0.34\% average increase in the objective value over the original formulation. Furthermore, Group-Lasso achieves a verified rate of 91%, compared with under 70% for prior methods.

Title: The Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids
Author: Max Klimm, Paul Lippke, Philipp Warode
Text_Content: We study optimal contracts when an agent allocates continuous effort subject to polymatroid capacity constraints. Effort produces a linear expected reward and incurs a cost. With binary outcomes and limited liability, the principal chooses a single reward share. For linear costs, an optimal contract can be computed in polynomial time. For quadratic costs, the agent has a unique best response computable by polynomially many submodular minimizations, yet optimizing the principal's share is NP-hard even for explicitly represented cut-based rank functions. With $n$ activities, the best-response path can have $2^{n-O(\log n)}$ breakpoints even when each reward coefficient and each rank value is an integer representable in $O(n\log n)$ bits. The construction also answers a question of Allman, Lo, and McCormick on polynomial bit length for source-sink monotone two-parameter minimum cuts. Despite this complexity, an optimal contract for quadratic costs always exists with a share of at most $1/2$. Consequently, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ best-response computations suffice for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation. For rational quadratic costs on explicitly described rational polytopes containing zero, this gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. More generally, a share of at most $1/p$ suffices for continuous convex costs homogeneous of degree $p>1$, on any compact convex action set containing zero. For general convex costs with an exact value and bounded-subgradient oracle, we obtain an oracle approximation scheme using approximate best responses and a supplied lower bound on positive welfare.

Title: Generalized Lorentz Framework for Active Semiconductor Quantum Surface Plasmonics
Author: Wancong Li, Qiang Zhou, Runzhi Zou, Zi He, Pu Zhang, Hongwei Han, Shuangchun Wen, Xue-Wen Chen
Text_Content: Nanostructured semiconductors provide an actively tunable platform for light-matter interactions across a broad spectral range. As feature sizes shrink to the deep nanoscale (~10 nm scale), nonclassical carrier dynamics and surface plasmonic responses become prominent, creating substantial challenges for a rigorous and efficient theoretical treatment. Here we develop a generalized Lorentz framework for quantum surface plasmonics in nanostructured semiconductors with arbitrary energymomentum dispersion relations. The framework enables efficient quantitative treatment of carrier nonlocality, carrier surface accumulation and depletion, and nonlocal damping in three-dimensional semiconductor nanostructures, under electrical tuning and across a wide range of doping densities. Building on this framework, we further establish a rigorous quasinormal-mode analysis that provides transparent physical insight into complex surface plasmonic responses of multiscale semiconductor structures. We demonstrate electrically controlled deep-nanoscale carrier accumulation and depletion in a semiconductor nanoantenna, leading to pronounced plasmonic-response modulation that can be interpreted in terms of eigenmode shifts, creation, and annihilation. By quantifying and linking complex nonclassical carrier dynamics with plasmonic eigenmodes, our work establishes a comprehensive quantitative framework for active semiconductor quantum surface plasmonics and will foster the convergence of electronics and photonics at the deep nanoscale.

Title: VISTA: Vision-Language Integrated Semantic Triage Architecture for Online Face Clustering in Long Videos
Author: Jiashu Liao, Joanne Garde-Hansen, Sanjay Sharma, Tanaya Guha
Text_Content: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: https://github.com/SkyJiashu/VISTA.

Title: Modulating Merging Strengths via Joint Loss Estimation for LoRA-based Continual Learning
Author: Kun Gu, De Cheng, Zhipeng Xu, Lingfeng He, Di Xu, Nannan Wang
Text_Content: Continual learning (CL) aims to adapt models to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. Recently, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a representative Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has gained increasing attention in CL due to its efficiency and scalability. Several LoRA-based merging methods maintain a single inference model by scaling the newly learned LoRA update with one coefficient and merging it into the previous weights after each task. However, they usually control the whole update with a shared scalar factor, although different update elements may affect previous and current tasks in different ways. To address this issue, we propose Merging Strength Modulation via Joint Loss Estimation (M2LE). It consists of Hessian Information-guided Adaptive Merging (HIM) and Task Simulation Perturbation for Merging (TSP). Instead of searching for a global merge coefficient, HIM directly solves for the target merged update under a joint objective over previous and current tasks. Solving this objective gives an analytic solution that naturally takes the form of element-wise modulation over the current task LoRA update. To improve the stability of the learned update under subsequent merging, we introduce TSP which simulates different tasks interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that M2LE consistently outperforms existing PEFT-based continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/bbdeeer/M2LE_NeurIPS2026.

Title: Properly defining Erlang lists
Author: Albert Schimpf, Stefan Wehr, Annette Bieniusa
Text_Content: We define list types, distinguishing proper lists, which end in the empty list, from improper lists, which may end in any value. Both are encoded as recursive types of cons cells, implemented in etylizer. This work found one OTP compiler bug. We propose a one-line sound improvement to Dialyzer's list handling that finds six instances of dead code in the OTP code base. We compare BEAM VM type checkers and catalogue how other languages design lists and cons cells.

Title: The Nonlinear Physics and Statistical Field Theory of Twilight Clouds: Hovering Dynamics and Dynamic Inertia Emergence
Author: Mickaël D. Chekroun, Ilan Koren
Text_Content: Twilight clouds are small, optically faint warm clouds whose droplets fluctuate between haze and activated growth. We develop a nonequilibrium statistical field theory linking this regime to cloud-field organization through Köhler microphysics, supersaturation transport, and turbulent mixing. At parcel level, supersaturation rapidly tracks slow droplet growth with a finite lag. Mixing-induced supersaturation removal drives a saddle-node bifurcation, shifting the activation threshold and supporting intermittent hovering under turbulent fluctuations. Starting from turbulent transport of supersaturation coupled to droplet growth, we derive a droplet-supersaturation field system and formulate it within the Martin-Siggia-Rose framework. A Gurari-type variational reduction inspired by polaron theory eliminates the fast bath. Turbulence dresses the slow droplet field, shrinks the forbidden zone below the equilibrium curve, and raises the mixing threshold required to suppress activation. Each droplet population induces a screened supersaturation halo that couples neighboring cloud elements; its delayed adjustment generates dynamic inertia and temporally correlated noise. The resulting nonlinear, non-Markovian pseudoparabolic stochastic equation has a bounded frozen-background response at short wavelengths. Its long-wave coupling amplifies contrasts where the dressed slow manifold turns downward. Comparisons with the parent two-field system show that a spatially correlated Markovian closure preserves droplet-radius distributions and cloudlet organization. Near the activation fold, restoring residual-bath fluctuation memory improves recurrent-hovering frequency and patch extent without recalibrating the drift or fitting a correlation time. More broadly, the framework identifies how slow fields acquire interactions and inertia through the relaxing, diffusive environments they modify.

Title: PROSE: Preservation-Constrained Selective Editing for Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction
Author: Yimeng Wang, Zeyuan Tian, Xinyu Wang, Danyang Gao, Chenglei Shen, Zhongxiang Sun, Lei La, Weijie Yu
Text_Content: Legal judgment prediction models may retain a guilty verdict after a legally decisive condition has been altered such that the specified charge is no longer established. We study this guilty bias via selective repair over matched charge-established and charge-not-established cases, where the unsupported verdict should change while its supported counterpart remains stable. We construct CAIL-MC, a legally reviewed dataset of 11,478 matched pairs covering 261 Chinese criminal charges. Held-out activation interventions show that contrasts learned from correctly resolved pairs transfer to false-guilty cases, but target-reaching interventions can also damage matched supported-guilty decisions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce PROSE, which reconstructs case-specific targets from a training-derived residual geometry, aligns them with a local margin-descent signal, attenuates supported-guilty-sensitive components, and realizes bounded targets through a preservation-regularized low-rank parameter update. Across Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, PROSE achieves stronger pairwise safe repair and evidence sensitivity, while preserving standard single-pass inference.

Title: Metric Facility Location under Batched Random Order
Author: Fabrizio Grandoni, Stefano Leonardi, Matteo Russo
Text_Content: We study online metric facility location in the batched random-order model. An adversary partitions $n$ clients into $B$ nonempty batches, which arrive in uniformly random order. Each batch is revealed in full, and its clients must be connected to open facilities before the next batch arrives. Openings and assignments are irrevocable, and the objective is to minimize the total opening and connection cost. For both uniform and nonuniform opening costs, we prove that the tight competitive ratio is \[ Θ\!\left(\min\left\{\log(B+1), \sqrt{\log(n-B+2)}\right\}\right). \] Thus, the ratio is constant both when there is a single batch and when every batch is a singleton, but intermediate numbers of batches can require a $Θ(\sqrt{\log n})$ ratio. Our algorithms build on Meyerson's algorithm (2001) and do not need to know $n$ nor $B$. A key algorithmic novelty is that we process the clients in a batch one by one in uniform random order (hence neglecting the global properties of the batch). We present a novel analysis of this algorithm that hinges on the random order of the batches, as well as of the clients within each batch. We also provide a matching competitive ratio lower bound already for uniform costs, and even when the entire metric is known in advance.

Title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
Author: Kling Team, Dong Chen, Jialu Chen, Xinlong Chen, Yifan Dai, Haotian Dong, Binzong Geng, Yushuo Guan, Minghui Guo, Guanlin He, Guanxiao He, Jingyun Hua, Yanwei Huang, Yiyan Ji, Xueping Jia, Yizhuo Jia, Bozhou Li, Jiaze Li, Min Li, Shihao Li, Shujie Li, Shengyi Liao, Weihong Lin, Shiyuan Liu, Xinyu Liu, Siyang Mao, Xiaoru Qu, Dianmo Sheng, Yang Shi, Jiafu Tang, Longxiang Tang, Yuqi Tang, Chengzhuo Tong, Kuo Wang, Qixun Wang, Rui Wang, Tianduo Wang, Yuran Wang, Zekun Wang, Zihao Wang, Boyang Xia, Yifan Xu, Liu Yang, Zhenlong Yuan, Bohan Zeng, Mujin Zhang, Yuanxing Zhang, Zhicheng Zhang, Zhuoran Zhang, Yuanhong Zheng, Kun Gai, Chengru Song, Pengfei Wan
Text_Content: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

Title: Sorting in PRAM, Parallel Comparison Model and Parallel External Memory Model
Author: Gopalan Sajith, Manas Kumar Panda, Ranajit Senko
Text_Content: We study the problem of sorting on the Parallel Random Access Machine (PRAM), Parallel Comparison Model (PCM) and Parallel External Memory Model (PEM). On PRAM, we present a Concurrent Read Exclusive Write algorithm that runs in $O(\log n)$ time with $n$ processors; our algorithm is very different from Cole's Merge Sort. On PCM, we present the first optimal algorithm for sorting after AKS; our algorithm runs in $O(\log n/\logα)$ comparison rounds with $nα$ processors, for $1\leqα\leq n$. On PEM, we present a Concurrent Read Exclusive Write algorithm that sorts $N$ elements in $O\left(\log\frac{N}{B}\right)$ I/O rounds with $p\geq \frac{N}{B}$ processors.

Title: EP-LVMQA: Evidence-Preserving Coarse-to-Fine Localization for Low-Quality Long Video Moment Question Answering
Author: Guoning Chen, Zhexun Hu, Yifan Wei, Yixuan Weng, Bin Li, Yufei Zhao
Text_Content: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.

Title: MiCaDe: Online LiDAR-Camera Miscalibration Change Detection for Autonomous Driving
Author: Carlo Sgaravatti, Riccardo Pieroni, Matteo Corno, Sergio M. Savaresi, Luca Magri, Giacomo Boracchi
Text_Content: Reliable multi-sensor perception in autonomous vehicles requires accurate calibration between cameras and LiDAR. However, calibration drift is often unavoidable in long-term deployments: vibrations, thermal effects, and minor mechanical shocks may alter the relative pose between sensors, leading to systematic errors in downstream fusion tasks. We propose MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online solution detecting when the extrinsic LiDAR-camera calibration parameters are no longer accurate by means of sequential change detection. MiCaDe requires no calibration targets, or modification of the perception stack, providing low false-alarm rates with negligible computational overhead. Our key insight is that 3D and 2D bounding boxes produced by standard object detectors should remain geometrically consistent under correct calibration. By matching cross-modal detections, we derive geometric consistency metrics that serve as sensitive indicators of extrinsic drift. These metrics are aggregated into fixed-size batches and scored against a reference distribution, producing a likelihood stream that is monitored by a Change Point Model (CPM). Crucially, the CPM accumulates statistical evidence over time, enabling detection of subtle drifts that would otherwise go unnoticed. Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/MiCaDe.

Title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
Author: Sofia Blyufer, Amir Kleiner, Uri Peskin
Text_Content: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.

Title: Modeling runaway electron mitigation via passively driven plasma instabilities in a high-current tokamak
Author: R Datta, C Clauser, G Hu, A Braun, N Ferraro, R Sweeney, R A Tinguely
Text_Content: A critical challenge for tokamak-based fusion power plants is the formation of high-current, relativistic runaway electron (RE) beams during abrupt confinement loss events called disruptions. RE beams may significantly damage machine components if left unmitigated, jeopardizing the operational and economic viability of fusion power plants. We present the first self-consistent extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) computational study of RE mitigation with a passively driven RE mitigation coil (REMC) in a high-current tokamak. RE generation and transport are coupled with REMC-driven MHD activity in a 3D simulation that models the thermal and current quench phases of a mid-plane disruption, together with the vertical displacement and final termination of the plasma and RE beam on SPARC -- a high-field, high-current tokamak designed to achieve a fusion gain Q > 1. We demonstrate that REMC-driven magnetic stochasticity can reduce the RE current by over an order-of-magnitude when compared to unmitigated disruptions. The final termination is mediated via a post-thermal-quench "cold" vertical displacement of the plasma, which, together with magnetic stochasticity, increases RE losses via scrape-off once the plasma contacts the first wall. These results demonstrate a viable mechanism for RE mitigation using passively driven plasma instabilities on high-current tokamaks.

Title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
Author: Junsung Park, Sangwon Yu, Donghun Kang, Yeongtak Oh, Jaewon Jeong, Gyeongtae Yoo, Han Cheol Moon, Jungbeom Lee, Sungroh Yoon
Text_Content: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.

Title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
Author: Sungwoo Goo, Hwi-yeol Yun, Sangkeun Jung
Text_Content: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.

Title: Near-Linear Lower Bounds for Testing Directed Acyclicity
Author: Artur Czumaj, Pan Peng, Yuyang Wang
Text_Content: We study testing acyclicity of directed graphs in the bounded-degree incidence-lists model, where a tester can query the outneighbors of a vertex but not its inneighbors. Despite significant effort, no tester with $o(n)$ queries is known, while the best established lower bounds are $\widetildeΩ(n^{5/9})$ for one-sided testers (Chen, Randolph, Servedio, and Sun, 2022) and $Ω(n^{1/3})$ for two-sided testers (Bender and Ron, 2002). We show that a query exponent arbitrarily close to one is necessary: for every fixed $η\in(0,1)$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon_η>0$ such that, for every constant $d\ge2$, every randomized adaptive two-sided $\varepsilon_η$-tester for acyclicity of simple $n$-vertex directed graphs whose indegrees and outdegrees are at most $d$ makes $Ω(n^{1-η})$ queries. Our proof overcomes two barriers. First, in previous constructions, the acyclic part of the graph is easy to recognize, which helps an algorithm stay inside the cyclic part. We hide a high-girth cyclic core inside a hierarchy of acyclic masking regions, in which each region imitates the levels below it and can be told apart from them only through rare events, and an iterated information-theoretic argument shows that every exploration observes only small, low-diameter forest components of the core. Second, a two-sided tester may exploit the statistics of collisions without ever seeing a cycle, and at a near-linear budget collisions are unavoidable. We compare complete transcripts with those of an acyclic input built on a fixed core by counting injective embeddings of the observed forest: in high-girth cores, all connected collision patterns of bounded order contribute identically, which makes the two transcript distributions statistically indistinguishable.

Title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures
Author: Marco Bressan, Stefano Clemente, Giacomo Fumagalli, Daniel Paul-Pena, C. Seshadhri
Text_Content: A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible. We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time. We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

Title: Knowledge Graph Lakehouse: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Managing Enterprise Knowledge Graphs at Scale
Author: Bashar Ahmad, Christoph G. Schuetz, Loris Bozzato
Text_Content: Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse through metadata, indexes, and caching. Enterprise knowledge graphs (KGs) offer an alternative approach to such integration for the purposes of data analysis, but handling them at scale must address the Three Vs of big data: volume, velocity, and variety. Contextualized KGs (CKGs) meet part of that challenge by enriching facts with contextual information, yet many applications require only a context-specific subset of that knowledge. We propose the Knowledge Graph Lakehouse (KG Lakehouse), a cloud-native microservice architecture that adapts the data lakehouse paradigm for management of CKGs at scale. The KG Lakehouse indexes incoming source documents along configurable context dimensions and stores these documents in a data lake, from which application-specific CKGs are constructed on demand instead of maintaining a single, monolithic KG. We realize the proposed architecture as a proof of concept, with independently deployable services built from established cloud technology; context dimensions and format-specific document handling enter as configuration, leaving the architecture independent of the application domain. We evaluate the implemented system in experiments on a distributed cluster deployment.

Title: Local Distributed Computation under Crash Failures
Author: Diana Ghinea, Fabian Kuhn, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Zahra Parsaeian
Text_Content: We study deterministic algorithms for locally checkable graph problems in the synchronous LOCAL model with crash failures, where a crashing node may send messages to only some neighbors. We introduce consistent neighborhoods: partial radius-$R$ views that agree locally across surviving edges and are complete without crashes. For $R=T+\ell+1$, these views allow local simulation of $T$-round fault-free algorithms that remain correct on subgraphs, satisfying constraints wherever the radius-$\ell$ checking neighborhood contains no crash. On graphs with at most $n$ nodes and maximum degree at most $Δ\geq3$, we construct these views in $O(\min\{n,(Δ-1)^R,RΔf\})$ rounds when a crash bound $f\geq1$ is globally known; the first two bounds require no knowledge of $f$. For $Δ=2$ or girth greater than $2R$, including forests, $O(R)$ rounds suffice. Our upper bounds are essentially tight in suitable parameter regimes. One crash can force $Ω(n)$ rounds even for $R=3$ on diameter-two graphs. For each fixed $Δ\geq3$ and sufficiently large $R$, we prove a $(Δ-1)^{R-O(\sqrt R)}$ lower bound even with crashes restricted to round beginnings. We also prove an $Ω(ΔRf)$ lower bound when $R\geq4\lceil\log_{Δ-1}f\rceil+4$ and $n\geqΔRf$. For locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, we preserve $O(\log^* n)$ complexity under any number of crashes whenever this bound holds without faults on all graphs with a fixed degree bound. In contrast, we construct an LCL on graphs of maximum degree at most five with fault-free complexity $Θ(\log n)$ and crash-tolerant complexity $Θ(n)$. Finally, any fault-free sinkless-orientation algorithm can be transformed to tolerate any number of crashes with only one additional round, guaranteeing correctness even at surviving nodes adjacent to crashes.

Title: TapeSAC: Automated, Pareto-Optimal Fine-Grained Memory Management for Large Model Training
Author: Kaihui Ren, Yifan Zhao, Zejian Wang, Yingtong Xiong, Xiaoling Zhou, Daohong Xu, Chenhao Guan, Zhikang Mo, Jihu Guo, Zhuoru Ma, Yufeng Li, Lin Zhang, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song
Text_Content: Selective activation checkpointing (SAC) decides which activations to save for the backward pass and which to recompute: each choice is a point in the plane of peak memory and recomputation time, and the goal is that plane's Pareto frontier. Current practice falls short of this goal. Hand-tuned policies fix a single point that does not adapt when the model, batch or kernels change; PyTorch's SAC reruns each block's forward pass in program order, recomputing values the backward pass never reads; and the memory budget of torch.compile treats recomputation as free or forbidden and selects saved tensors by bytes alone, an assumption that fails for the custom kernels that produce many of a large model's activations. We present TapeSAC, which automates SAC in eager PyTorch without editing the model's forward code. TapeSAC records each block's forward pass at the dispatcher and, during backward, replays only the producers of the values autograd consumes, so saving a tensor eliminates every producer needed only for it. A planner selects the saved tensors from measured recomputation costs under a single limit on step-peak memory. On Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, replay alone reduces step time by 3.0% and 1.7% versus full checkpointing at no greater memory cost; memory-aware planning raises these gains to 6.3% and 13.9% under a 90%-of-device-memory limit. The evaluated hand-tuned policies fall short of this memory-recomputation frontier and, on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, run out of memory at larger batches. Over 500 steps on real data, TapeSAC reduces training time by 8-11%; on Qwen3.5-397B, it is 2.7% faster than a model-specific hand-tuned policy while using 14% less memory.

Title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
Author: ZhengXian Wu, Qianhao Nie, Zhuohong Chen, Junjie Gao, Yuyao Zhang, Yunyao Yu, Hangrui Xu, Cheng Cheng, Guiyu Ma, Jin Zhang, Xingzhong Xu, Kai Yang, Haoqian Wang
Text_Content: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

Title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
Author: Matteo Romilio Pasqual, Matteo Tomasetto, J. Nathan Kutz, Andrea Manzoni
Text_Content: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.

Title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
Author: Ziqing Zu, Ye Yuan, Tiejun Ling, Zhi Chen, Xiang Li, Zhiqiang Li, Qiang Wang, Jiangjiang Xia, Jiuke Wang, Yongjun Jia, Shinan Wang, Zhi-Yuan Zhang, Renbo Pang, Xiaojuan Lin, Yu Zhang, Huier Mo, Ang Li
Text_Content: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency. Overall pointwise accuracy summarizes forecast and reference agreement over all valid samples; physical consistency evaluates dynamical balances using model outputs alone; and distributional consistency evaluates distribution tails and multiscale spatial structures. Three AI models were deployed as representative testbeds in a unified operational environment. This comprehensive assessment shows that lower overall pointwise errors cannot preclude substantial dynamical imbalances and suppressed fine-scale variance. Conversely, higher pointwise errors may arise from spatial displacement of coherent structures rather than a poor representation of their amplitude. The results demonstrate that the evaluation of AI ocean forecasting models should be based on the multi-dimensional assessment of forecast trustworthiness, rather than solely relying on a single metric. The study provides a preliminary framework for AI model intercomparison, which is also informative for targeted model refinement and operational implementation.

Title: NP-Hardness and a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, with Applications to Dense Subgraphs
Author: Morteza Alimi, Tobias Mömke, Alexandru Popa, Michael Ruderer
Text_Content: Given intervals and points on a line, each point with a demand, and a budget $K$, Maximum Interval Multicover asks for at most $K$ intervals that satisfy as many points as possible, a point being satisfied if it lies in at least as many chosen intervals as its demand. One application is committee elections in which each candidate is approved by consecutive voters and voters have individual demands. Xu, Ran and Zhang introduced the problem and gave a $1/2$-approximation; the objective is not submodular when demands exceed one. Li, Tu, Zhang and Cao gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the minimization counterpart, unweighted partial interval multicover, and asked for its complexity. We prove that both problems are NP-hard, even for intervals of equal length; as their optima are integers bounded by the input size, neither has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We then give a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, also for arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing rewards for the coverage of each point. Building on a decomposition from Nonner's PTAS for Densest $k$-Subgraph on interval graphs, our scheme cuts the line into pieces at a small loss and solves every piece exactly. The key dynamic program handles intervals crossing a common point by choosing an interleaving of their left and right endpoints rather than sweeping along the line; it needs only two counters to track these intervals. The same algorithm yields PTASes on convex bipartite graphs for Bipartite Dense Subgraph, improving on the ratio $2/3$ of Backer and Keil for the subclass of bipartite permutation graphs, and on interval graphs for Maximum $k$-Vertex Cover and weighted clique counts.

Title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
Author: Yining Wei, Tianyuan Wu, Gu Gong, Yuechen Tao, Yinghao Yu, Xiaowen Chu, Wei Wang
Text_Content: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

Title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
Author: Renaud Lambiotte
Text_Content: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

Title: DLER: Dual-Logit Experience Replay for Online Continual Learning
Author: Huiwei Lin, Shanshan Feng, Kong Aik Lee
Text_Content: Online continual learning aims to continuously train neural networks on a non-stationary data stream in a single pass. Rehearsal-based methods alleviate catastrophic forgetting by replaying stored samples, but the imbalance between current and previous data often leads to predictions biased toward current classes. Many approaches have been proposed to overcome the forgetting problem by correcting the bias; however, they still need to be improved in an online fashion. By decomposing the dot-product logits into an angle factor and a norm factor, our analysis reveals that the angle factor efficiently captures novel knowledge but is particularly susceptible to prediction bias, whereas the norm factor helps preserve historical knowledge. Based on these observations, we propose Dual-Logit Experience Replay (DLER), which exploits dual-logits for both model optimization and memory management. Specifically, DLER learns current samples using cosine logits and incorporates additional dot-product logits when replaying previous samples to mitigate prediction bias. To strengthen dual-logit learning under limited replay memory, an auxiliary supervised contrastive objective promotes angular compactness within each class, extending corrections learned from limited replay samples to other samples of the same class. Meanwhile, we introduce a memory update strategy that preferentially retains samples for which dot-product prediction assigns a higher probability to the correct class than cosine prediction, aligning sample selection with dual-logit training. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DLER, particularly under limited memory budgets.

Title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
Author: Zehan Lin, Xiaowei Wu, Shengwei Zhou
Text_Content: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

Title: Reproducibility in open-source RISC-V HW flows
Author: Peter Kourzanov, Anmol Anmol
Text_Content: Open-source hardware is booming. To prevent fragmentation, encourage collaboration and reuse we propose the RISC-V to join forces with Reproducible Builds communities and concentrate innovation potential where its needed most: creation of new micro-architectures, IPs and their integration into new SoCs and applications. To facilitate this goal, we chose Guix, a rigorous solution for reproducible software artefacts. We apply it to dependency management & reproducibility problems in open-source hardware and show the validity of the approach, taking CVA6 as a running example. The end result - a fully reproducible collection of packaged tests, emulation, simulation and cycle-accurate models - shows a promising workflow that could (in future) scale to support larger RISC-V community with reusable software & hardware components for next-generation platforms.

Title: ScamWorld: An Interactive Environment for Evaluating Web Agents Against Online Fraud
Author: Yutao Wu, Xiao Liu, Ming Wen, Hanxun Huang, Jun Wang, Xingjun Ma
Text_Content: Web agents increasingly browse, shop, and manage accounts on behalf of their users. Prior work has shown that they can be misled by adversarial content, including prompt injections and deceptive interfaces. Beyond such attacks, agents operating on the open web also encounter online fraud designed to deceive humans, including fraudulent online stores, fake investment platforms, and advance-fee schemes. How web agents respond to such fraud during task execution remains underexplored, in part because scam websites are short-lived, making systematic evaluation difficult. To address this gap, we introduce ScamWorld, an interactive environment that reconstructs reported scam websites across diverse scenarios, fraud mechanisms, and languages. Each reconstructed website reproduces documented fraud mechanisms, making relevant signs of fraud observable before the agent's final action and enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation. Through an extensive study of web agents powered by six frontier LLMs, we find that baseline deception rates range from 11% to 35% across models. Agents proceed more readily with payments than with requests for credentials or wallet information. A closer analysis of agent trajectories shows that some agents acknowledge suspicious conditions yet proceed, at times treating the user's instructions as authorisation to accept additional terms imposed by the website. ScamWorld provides a reusable testbed for systematically evaluating and stress-testing web agents against real-world online fraud.

Title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
Author: Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu, Hengzhi Chen, Fei Shen, Li Zhuo, Zhiyong Wang, Tat-Seng Chua
Text_Content: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

Title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
Author: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust
Text_Content: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $λ$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6λ-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$. We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18λ-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $λ$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.

Title: Influence of Geometry and Tissue Damage on the Mechanical Behaviour of Skin Meshing
Author: Masoumeh Razaghi Pey Ghaleh, Denis O'Mahoney, Kevin Moerman
Text_Content: Skin meshing increases graft coverage, yet the clinically achieved expansion often falls below the manufacturer's nominal meshing ratio. Previous elastic analyses have demonstrated that mesh topology and skin anisotropy strongly influence graft expansion; however, the effect of progressive damage at larger deformation remains unexplored. This study therefore investigates how progressive damage affects the expansion and mechanical response of skin meshes. The performance of auxetic mesh geometries is compared with conventional Zimmer mesher (ZM) geometry. Human back skin was modelled using a one-term Ogden ground matrix and a Gasser Ogden Holzapfel (GOH) collagen network, with separate scalar Kachanov-type continuum damage variables for each constituent. The auxetic geometries, including 1st- and 2nd-order alternative slits (AS1 and AS2), I-shaped (IS) and H-shaped (HS) re-entrant patterns, and ZM, were analysed with Langer's lines oriented either parallel or perpendicular to the loading direction. Hyperelastic and damage-based formulations were compared up to 25% strain, and the damage-based simulations were subsequently extended to 40% strain. ZM was further loaded to 155% strain; the area ratios attained by HS at 40% strain were matched by ZM at 142.1% and 124.7% strain for Langer's lines parallel and perpendicular to loading, respectively. Results indicate that HS achieves greater coverage than ZM for a given stretch, whereas its damage advantage depends on the orientation of Langer's lines.

Title: OCR in the Foundation Model Era: From Specialist Models to Unified Models
Author: Zhiheng Li, Zongyang Ma, Jiaxian Chen, Cheng Cui, Yi Liu, Ziqi Zhang, Chunfeng Yuan, Bing Li, Xiang Bai, Weiming Hu
Text_Content: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/Awesome-OCR-in-the-Foundation-Model-Era.

Title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
Author: Zicheng Kong, Zhenbo Xu, Haoyan Zhang, Jinghan Yang, Zhenzhen Li, Yiwei Ru, Liuyu Xiang, WanTing Xu, Min Ren, Zhaofeng He
Text_Content: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

Title: Physics-Based Plausibility Assessment of AI-Predicted Vehicle Parameters for Automotive Radar in Pre-Crash Scenarios
Author: Rainer Engert, Patrick Zaumseil, Thomas Brandmeier
Text_Content: Automotive radar is a key sensing modality for safety-critical vehicle functions due to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent advances in AI-based radar perception enable the direct estimation of object parameters from a single radar measurement cycle. However, the internal decision process of data-driven models is typically not explicitly linked to the underlying radar sensing physics. Consequently, object estimates may achieve high statistical accuracy while remaining physically inconsistent with the measured radar signature, particularly in previously unseen scenarios. Such inconsistencies are especially critical for heading estimation, as they directly affect trajectory prediction and collision assessment in pre-crash scenarios. This paper presents a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating AI-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception. The proposed approach generates an expected radar signature from AI-estimated object parameters using a physics-based reference model that incorporates occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent RCS modeling, and characteristic wheel-induced MD signatures. The expected signature is compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based consistency metric computed from three complementary features: the spatial distribution of detections along object edges, the local detection count, and the radar reflection intensity. In this way, physically implausible object hypotheses can be identified and corrected independently of the underlying neural network architecture and without model retraining or architectural modifications. The proposed consistency module is integrated as a cascaded post-processing stage for vehicle heading estimation.

Title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
Author: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang, Jiafeng Xu, Shilong Wang, Yiqi Deng, Shaowen He, Xiaoqi Li, Qian Zhu, Ran Cheng, Hao Dong
Text_Content: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

Title: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough
Author: Zhanghao Hu, Linhai Zhang, Qian Zhao, Qi Zhu, Yuan Hua, Di Liang, Jiasheng Si, Xin Zhao, Yulan He, Zhumin Chen, Lin Gui
Text_Content: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.

Title: Geometric Obstructions and Sharp Genus Dependence in LCD Scalings
Author: Rahim Rahmati-Asghar
Text_Content: We study the least pole order of a rational function whose nonzero evaluations scale a prescribed code to a Euclidean LCD code. A residue-one differential yields an obstruction for odd-dimensional one-point AG codes in characteristic two: for $C=C_L(D,aQ)$ with $0\le a<n$ and odd dimension, the threshold is at least $n+2g-a-1$. The obstruction uses alternating Gram matrices and does not require the scaled code to be self-orthogonal. For the dimension-three codes $C_L(D,(r+1)Q)$ on Hermitian curves over $\F_{r^2}$, $r=2^e\ge4$, we obtain \[ n+2g-r-2\leτ_D(C;Q)\le n+2g-3. \] Consequently the leading genus contribution is asymptotically sharp even in dimension three. On the elliptic curve $y^2+y=x^3$ over $\F_4$, we prove the exact dimension-three threshold $6$ by an explicit multiplier. For repetition codes on the Hermitian family, the threshold equals the general interpolation bound $n+2g-1$. The upper bounds use information sets and hold for $q>3k$, and for $q>2k$ in characteristic two.

Title: Robust Aggregation of Quantile Statistics: from Median to Interval
Author: Mingyu Song, Yizhou Wang, Yuqing Kong
Text_Content: Quantile-based summaries, such as prediction intervals and medians, are commonly used in economic forecasting, climate science, and public health. For highly skewed samples, experimental evidence suggests that estimates of the mean can be biased toward the median, whereas estimates of the median are relatively accurate. This motivates aggregating explicitly elicited quantiles rather than reported means. We study robust aggregation of quantile reports for bounded outcomes under squared loss, minimizing worst-case regret relative to an omniscient Bayesian aggregator who knows the information structure and observes all private signals. Without restrictions on the information structure, no rule improves on the constant forecast at the range midpoint in worst-case regret. We therefore consider weak substitutes, a diminishing-returns condition on the value of information, and characterize optimal aggregation rules under this condition. For central prediction intervals with common nominal coverage $α$, the optimal rule, which we call regularized simple average for prediction intervals, shrinks the average reported interval midpoint toward the range midpoint, with a weight determined by $α$ and the number $n$ of experts. This optimal rule strictly improves on the constant baseline in worst-case regret when $α<1/\sqrt{n}$; at or above this threshold, the constant rule is optimal. The optimal worst-case regret is minimized at a unique interior coverage level, revealing a nonmonotonic relationship between coverage and aggregation performance. For median reports, regularized simple average for medians similarly shrinks the average reported median toward the range midpoint, assigning weight $1/n$ to the reported average and strictly improving on the constant baseline in worst-case regret for every finite $n\ge2$.

Title: Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents
Author: Yosef Zumer, Erel Segal-Halevi, David Sarne
