Title: Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations
Author: Chawit Kaewnuratchadasorn, Jiaji Wang, Xin Nie
Text_Content: High-fidelity simulation of dynamical systems is central to scientific discovery and engineering design, yet remains computationally demanding. Here we introduce the Implicit Neural Operator Solver (INOS), which learns the implicit solve and encodes a time integrator. INOS pretrains a neural operator from static equilibrium solutions and reuses it within Newmark-$β$ integration. At each time increment, the integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the pretrained neural operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state. Numerical examples in linear and nonlinear elastodynamics demonstrate accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision. Comparative results show that INOS, evaluated zero-shot, achieves higher predictive accuracy than neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. In addition, INOS delivers over 4,600$\times$ speedup in nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers. INOS natively accommodates changes in dynamic conditions and enables reuse of the pretrained operator across spatial and temporal discretizations. Further evaluation demonstrates a stable million-step rollout. These findings establish INOS as a reusable neural implicit solver for accurate, efficient, and robust dynamic modeling.

Title: RESTberus: Trace-Aware Benchmarking of Automated REST API Testing Tools Across Microservice Dependencies
Author: John Toniutti, Massimiliano Baldo, Marino Miculan, Vincenzo Riccio
Text_Content: Existing REST API testing benchmarks focus on isolated services, overlooking failures arising from interactions with downstream dependencies. In microservice systems, response bodies and entry-point operations alone cannot reliably distinguish failures, compromising tool comparisons. We present RESTberus, a Kubernetes-based benchmarking platform for black-box REST API testing tools on deployed microservice systems. By complementing API-level evidence with distributed traces, RESTberus can distinguish failures manifesting in the target service from those manifesting in downstream dependencies. Across six tools on two microservice benchmarks, our trace-aware deduplication strategy achieves 87.1% accuracy, outperforming baselines from prior work by 10-13 percentage points. Our empirical study shows that all tools expose downstream failures, accounting for 11.7% of estimated unique failures on average, which isolated-service benchmarks cannot expose. On single-service benchmarks, RESTberus produces statistically equivalent results to RESTgym, demonstrating that integration-level assessments can preserve compatibility with existing tools and comparability with prior evaluations.

Title: RadarFill: Observation-Constrained Gap Filling of Systematic Blind Zones in 3-D Weather Radar Reflectivity Mosaics
Author: Xin Huang, Haofei Sun, Wei Han, Yunfan Yang, Huaguan Chen, Xingtao Song, Dong Xiao
Text_Content: Ground-based weather radar mosaics contain systematic blind zones, especially at low altitudes, where missing reflectivity lacks corresponding complete observations for direct verification. We present RadarFill, an observation-constrained conditional diffusion framework for gap filling in three-dimensional radar reflectivity mosaics. RadarFill conditions on partially observed reflectivity and an observation mask, enforces available observations throughout reverse sampling, and preserves valid measurements in the final field. For training and controlled evaluation, structured synthetic missingness is designed from altitude-dependent missing-data statistics and the vertical nesting of blind zones in an operational 3-D radar mosaic product. Across 4,384 held-out test times and representative convective and typhoon cases, RadarFill recovers principal precipitation structures and moderate-to-strong echoes under extensive low-level missingness and generally outperforms conventional interpolation and a learning-based reference model. For real blind-zone evaluation, RadarFill model is applied directly to Fujian Province and compared with 90 matched volume scans from an independent phased-array radar. Within the principal 1-2 km low-level blind zones, RadarFill yields lower reflectivity errors than conventional interpolation, and the gap-filled precipitation structures show broad agreement with independent observations. In two controlled nowcasting experiments, improvements in RadarFill-initialized fields persist into subsequent forecasts, with the largest benefits at low altitudes and short lead times. These results provide complementary evidence from controlled synthetic missingness, independent radar observations, and downstream nowcasting, supporting the potential of observation-constrained conditional generation for gap filling in real 3-D radar blind zones.

Title: Testing for a Large Induced Expander: Sublinear Algorithms and Query Lower Bounds
Author: Pan Peng, Ranran Shen
Text_Content: Testing expansion asks to distinguish graphs of large conductance from graphs that are far from having large conductance. We study a relaxation in which only part of the graph is required to expand: does an $n$-vertex graph of bounded degree contain an induced expander on a constant fraction of its vertices, when the rest of the graph, including the edges leaving the expander, is arbitrary? Let $P_{α,φ}$ denote the property of containing an induced subgraph on at least $αn$ vertices with inner conductance at least $φ$. For every constant $κ\in(0,1)$, we give a tester that accepts graphs in $P_{α,φ}$ and rejects graphs outside $P_{κα,μφ^2}$, where $μ=Θ_{α,κ}(1/\log n)$, using $O_{α,κ}(\sqrt n\,φ^{-2}\log n)$ queries. For fixed $α\in(0,1]$, $κ\in(0,1)$, and $0<φ\le9/20$, we further show that distinguishing these two classes requires $Ω_{α,κ,φ}(n^{1/2+c_{κ,φ}μ})$ queries for every sufficiently large $n$ and every $0<μ\le1$, where $c_{κ,φ}>0$. The bound holds for adaptive algorithms, uniformly in $μ$. Hence, for testers with $\sqrt n\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ queries, the logarithmic loss in conductance is necessary up to a $\log\log n$ factor. The same tester also permits distance-based rejection at a weaker conductance while retaining the original core size. Our tester compares the endpoint distributions of random walks from different vertices with each other, rather than with the uniform distribution. Its analysis uses the trace chain, which observes the walk only at its visits to the unknown expanding core. Our lower bound builds on the noisy-parity construction of [CKK+18], using vector-valued parity labels in $\mathbb F_2^r$ to create many hidden classes, each too small to contain a qualifying induced expander.

Title: Selection instability and coefficient uncertainty in Cox modelling after Lasso selection
Author: Lena Schemet, Andreas Groll, Sarah Friedrich-Welz
Text_Content: After variable selection, uncertainty quantification often treats the selected model as fixed, although it may change under repeated sampling. We investigate whether this variability can be incorporated by repeating Cox-Lasso selection within a model-based bootstrap after unpenalised Cox refitting. We compare conventional post-selection Cox Wald intervals and a model-based bootstrap without re-selection, both of which keep the selected predictor set fixed, with two re-selection procedures: one retains the observed tuning-parameter value, whereas the other reapplies the cross-validation minimum (CV-min) tuning rule within each bootstrap sample. Against the data-generating coefficients, procedures holding the selected predictor set fixed frequently showed substantial undercoverage. Re-selection generally moved coverage closer to the nominal level, although performance varied across simulation regimes and coefficients. Sensitivity analyses evaluating coverage against the population Cox coefficients corresponding to each originally selected predictor set gave similar aggregate coverage for the primary interval comparison. In the NKI70 breast-cancer data, the four selected genes appeared together in only 0.6% of bootstrap samples under re-selection at the observed tuning-parameter value. These results suggest that selection instability can be an important component of post-selection coefficient uncertainty and that bootstrap re-selection can help incorporate this variability.

Title: Pixel-space video generation with U-JiT
Author: Théophane Vallaeys, Jakob Verbeek, Matthieu Cord
Text_Content: Latent diffusion and flow matching models are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art generative video models. While highly effective, relying on pretrained autoencoders to compress the data into a lower-dimensional latent space also comes with drawbacks. First, training proceeds in two stages: autoencoder pretraining, with compression and reconstruction objectives, followed by latent generative model training, precluding fully end-to-end training. Second, autoencoders also lead to an inherent loss of signal, and the trade-off between reconstruction quality and generative performance in the latent space is still an active area of research. In this paper we explore the viability of generative video models directly in pixel space. We analyze recent approaches in pixel-space generative modeling of images that rely on basic transformer designs, and identify several shortcomings that limit their effectiveness for the high-dimensional pixel-space video generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a UNet-like transformer architecture along with improvements to the training recipe and sampling strategy. We conduct controlled experiments, training latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600. For the standard frames-to-video task at 128 resolution, our U-JiT model improves generative FVD by 27% over prior state-of-the-art results, and by 14% against the JiT pixel-space baseline. Scaling to higher 256 resolution, we find the improvement over pixel-space and latent-based models grows as we increase the spatiotemporal compression rate up to $64 \times 64 \times 8$. Finally, we find that U-JiT improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models on class-to-video generation, with respectively 9% and 56% reduction in FVD.

Title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
Author: Raz Marshanski, Liran Nochumsohn, Mayank Jauhari, Boris N. Oreshkin, Omri Azencot
Text_Content: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25$\times$ reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.

Title: Beyond Local Refinement: Wide-Area Precise Cross-View Localization
Author: Qingguo Hu, Xinyu Ma, Yujie Lin, Yaoxiang Wang, Qi Shi, Zonghao Guo, Chi Chen, Jinsong Su
Text_Content: Fine-grained cross-view localization aims to precisely localize a ground camera against geo-referenced aerial imagery, but current methods typically assume a narrow geographic prior, substantially limiting their applicability when upstream localization remains coarse. To bridge this gap, we study this task over much larger aerial regions. However, this seemingly simple extension fundamentally changes the localization problem: the growing disparity in spatial extent between ground and aerial views makes reliable cross-view matching difficult to establish directly, while the increasing number of look-alike locations in larger regions introduces substantial visual ambiguity. To address these challenges, we propose RingMatch, a search-and-verification framework for wide-area cross-view localization. RingMatch first leverages predictive uncertainty to uncover plausible locations and progressively zooms into their surroundings to obtain increasingly fine-grained evidence, yielding a compact set of promising candidates. We then introduce the depth ring, a novel geometric representation that reveals subtle variations in the spatial layout around a location and serves as a view-shared spatial signature for an LVLM verifier to resolve residual ambiguity. To benchmark this setting, we construct VIGOR-Pro by composing VIGOR aerial tiles into contiguous regions with spatial extents of up to 400 m. Experiments show that RingMatch maintains strong localization performance as the aerial region expands, consistently outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.

Title: When Should an LLM Steering Edit Depend on the Input?
Author: Rachael Harkness, Konrad Rawlik
Text_Content: An activation steering edit should depend on the input exactly when the destination varies \emph{inside} the class a query requests, and that is measurable before any rule is fitted or applied. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) adds one fixed direction to every input, the difference of the class means. Conditioning it on the requested class accounts for the between-class variation in the required displacement and leaves the within-class variation untouched, which no rule that reads only the source state can express. We study the impact of increasing input-dependence in the steering edit, moving from a difference of means to a destination retrieved per query --- the mean of the $k$ stored states nearest the query, inside the requested class --- in which the two baselines are endpoints: at $k$ equal to the class size the retrieved rule \emph{is} the class-conditional difference of means. We measure input-dependent steering on six substitution corpora that vary in whether the edit changes a word or a clause, and on an external benchmark, and find that input-dependent steering outperforms fixed-direction steering when the destination varies within the class. Retrieval wins at every layer of every substitution corpus in two models, and the level of input-dependence needed governs how to apply it: word-level edits are best made in the first tenth of the network from a few neighbours, clause-level edits at any depth from the class mean. Where the class already determines the answer the class mean suffices and retrieval only matches it, though a fixed direction still fails there. Four quantities computed from the states alone identify the regime in which the edit should be applied.

Title: Non-Interfering Asymmetric AdamW Updates for Constrained Exploration of Equifinality in Hybrid Models
Author: Ekaterina Gikalo, Zavud Baghirov, Christian Reimers, Markus Reichstein, Martin Jung, Marco Körner
Text_Content: Hybrid models let neural networks supply the unresolved parameters of a process-based simulator, and are fitted to observations that constrain aggregate fluxes and storages but not the internal partitioning that produces them. Such a fit is equifinal: configurations indistinguishable in the observed aggregates can disagree substantially about the unobserved internals, and therefore about the mechanism they attribute to the same data. We study evapotranspiration, whose total flux is observed while its split into transpiration and evaporation is not. A model ensemble built from random seeds alone spans only a narrow band of the partitionings the data admit. We produce the spread deliberately, training members under auxiliary repulsion on transpiration, subject to the fit to observations not degrading. Non-interference is usually arranged by making the auxiliary gradient orthogonal to the main one, but under AdamW the applied step is a preconditioned momentum direction, so orthogonality between raw gradients no longer implies it. We introduce Non-interfering Asymmetric Network Optimization (NANO), an update whose first-order effect on the main loss is exactly that of the main objective alone, whose auxiliary step is bounded, and which concentrates repulsion in the coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.

Title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
Author: Sierra Bonilla, Fengyi Jiang, Chinedu Nwoye, Jingpei Lu, Kailey Reardon, Humphrey W. Chow, Francisco Vasconcelos, Sophia Bano, Adam Schmidt, Omid Mohareri
Text_Content: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

Title: Bounded AUKS: A Novel Evaluation Metric for Anomaly Detection via Bounded Area Under the Kolmogorov--Smirnov Curve
Author: Yanshuo Zhang, Juan Du
Text_Content: Recent literature widely used global metrics such as AUROC and AUPRO to quantify the detection performance. AUROC and AUPRO scores are approaching 100% in some public datasets such as MVTec AD dataset and VisA dataset, which misleadingly suggests that the pixel-level anomaly detection task has already been solved. Threshold-independent metrics represented by AUROC inherently ignore the threshold selection process, which is inevitable in practical applications. Although AUPRO restricts the False Positive rates (FPRs) to an acceptable range, extremely low FPRs can lead to increased false negative rates (FNRs). We argue that there is a lack of metrics capable of quantifying the separation between the anomaly score distributions of normal and anomalous samples, which hinders advancements in anomaly detection. In response, we propose the Bounded Area Under the Kolmogorov--Smirnov curve (Bounded AUKS), a partial integral metric that integrates the difference between TPR and FPR within a data-driven bounded range. Specifically, we introduce AUKS from KS integral as a direct measure of separability between the anomaly score distributions. The bounded range is determined only by score distributions of normal test samples. Lower bound excludes the uninformative high-FPR region. Upper bound avoids evaluation in extreme regions that aggressively push FPR towards zero, which result in a very low recall. Our experiments on 9 models across MVTec AD and VisA datasets show that Bounded AUKS can address the limitations of existing metrics and has a better performance in evaluating unsupervised anomaly detection models.

Title: Logarithmic Comparison-Query Complexity for EF1 Allocations
Author: Zehan Lin, Shengxin Liu, Biaoshuai Tao, Shengwei Zhou
Text_Content: We study the comparison-query complexity of computing allocations that are envy-free up to one item (EF1) for $n$ agents with heterogeneous additive preferences over $m$ indivisible items. In this model, the algorithm may only query which of two bundles an agent prefers, without ever observing numerical valuations or costs. Prior work established $O(\log m)$ query bounds for at most three agents, leaving open whether query complexity logarithmic in $m$ is achievable for every fixed $n \ge 4$. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for every fixed $n\ge2$, we design algorithms that compute EF1 allocations using $O(\log m)$ comparison queries, matching the known $Ω(\log m)$ lower bound. Our results hold for both chores with nonnegative costs and goods with nonnegative valuations.

Title: Nonlinearity-Induced Suppression of Dissipation in Bath-Coupled Floquet Topological Insulators
Author: Bhoomija Chaurasia, Sebabrata Mukherjee
Text_Content: Topological insulators can host chiral, disorder-robust edge states that dissipate energy when coupled to an external bath. We show that nonlinear interactions enable all-optical control over edge-state dissipation in a laser-written Floquet topological insulator periodically coupled to a photonic bath. Although moderate nonlinearity enhances dissipation due to mode mixing, increasing the nonlinear strength to an optimal value dramatically suppresses dissipation by forming highly localized traveling edge solitons. These results establish engineered system-bath coupling and nonlinear interactions as a route to suppress dissipation of chiral topological edge transport.

Title: What Does It Mean to Remove an Edge? Intervention-Aware Fidelity for Graph Neural Network Explanations
Author: Rocco Mattia Di Mauro, Marco Grassia, Giuseppe Mangioni
Text_Content: Graph neural network explanations are often evaluated via deletion fidelity, i.e., by deleting their top-ranked edges and measuring the resulting change in model output. Yet, in a message-passing GNN, "deleting an edge" does not specify a unique intervention. Structural deletion removes the edge from the graph and recomputes quantities such as degree normalization and attention, whereas message suppression leaves this structural context intact while blocking the message carried by the edge. The meaning of deletion fidelity therefore depends on what the intervention targets in the model computation. We formalize this distinction and derive sufficient conditions for exact equivalence. The two interventions coincide for additive message passing with edge-set-independent coefficients, but can diverge when aggregation depends on the presence of zero messages or when removing an edge changes the coefficients applied to surviving messages. We then construct intervention-specific edge attributions and evaluate each resulting ranking under both interventions, testing whether their relative fidelity changes with the evaluation intervention. Across nine datasets and a panel of GIN, GCN, and GATv2 models at depths 2--5, all nine GIN controls satisfy the equivalence predicted by the theory. On the target logit, the relative fidelity of the two rankings depends on the evaluation intervention in 10 of 11 reportable GCN and GATv2 cells, and in nine of them each ranking has the larger deletion area under the intervention it was built with. Deletion fidelity is thus not a property of an edge ranking alone. Evaluation protocols should explicitly report the intervention, output functional, target, and perturbation unit, and test alternative intervention semantics when the scientific question does not uniquely determine one.

Title: When Does Combining Software-Effort Estimates Help? Evidence from Four Public Project Datasets
Author: Azzeddine Ihsine, Sara Ihsine
Text_Content: Combining estimates can reduce individual prediction errors, but an ensemble may also dilute an unusually accurate estimator or repeat errors shared by its members. We study these competing effects on four archival software-effort datasets (Kitchenham: 145 projects, Desharnais: 77, China: 499, Maxwell: 63) with 100 repeated 70/30 training and test partitions per dataset. Three conventional models (parametric regression, analogy, and random forest) are combined with each other and, in Kitchenham, with a recorded human estimate. Out-of-fold calibration errors drive five combination rules: equal weighting, inverse-MSE weighting, a nonnegative simplex combination, signed Bates-Granger weighting, and Bates-Granger with covariance shrinkage. All preprocessing is learned within training folds. Model-error correlations range from 0.54 to 0.97. In Kitchenham, the human estimate dominates: equal weighting raises mean test log-MAE from 0.239 to 0.455, a loss that remains significant under a corrected resampled t-test with Holm adjustment, whereas the simplex rule limits the increase to 0.250. In Desharnais, China, and Maxwell, every rule lowers mean log-MAE (by 1.3 to 8.6%) and BG with shrinkage beats the calibration-selected individual on 75, 83, and 83 of 100 splits, but none of these gains is statistically distinguishable from zero once the overlap between repeated splits is accounted for. On a completion-year split of Desharnais, equal weighting becomes slightly worse and inverse-MSE is near the individual baseline, while simplex and shrinkage retain mean gains of about 5%. Combining correlated effort estimates is therefore a conditional decision: the harm of naive pooling next to a dominant source is clear, while the benefit elsewhere is small and uncertain.

Title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
Author: Ayush Patnaik, Nicolas Michel, Leonard Baursfeld, Davide Scaramuzza, Xinfan Lin
Text_Content: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.

Title: TAPES: Task-Aligned Joint Predictive Pretraining for Transaction Event Sequences
Author: Ruobing Zuo, Weiyu Han, Huilin He, Haoyu Jiang, Ze Zhao, Jie Sheng, Xiao Tan, Shuai Chen, Tianyi Zhang
Text_Content: Transaction event sequences support diverse prediction tasks in online commerce and digital financial services. The same transaction records can yield prediction targets with different semantics, including values, changes, and relations to past events. These targets impose different constraints on history representations, but their predictability alone does not establish the downstream utility of a target set. Moreover, target-wise prediction losses do not explicitly model conditional co-occurrence among targets. To address these challenges, we propose TAPES, a task-aligned joint predictive pretraining framework for transaction sequences. TAPES constructs a finite collection of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It selects a target set according to the downstream utility of representations learned through short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets. It then reinitializes the encoder and pretrains it on the selected targets through a joint likelihood parameterized by a shared discrete latent variable, before downstream supervised adaptation. Experiments in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that TAPES outperforms representative baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modeling.

Title: Perioperative shear wave elastography for the evaluation of spinal cord release in pediatric dysraphism: first experience in 21 patients
Author: Mathilde Gaume, Lou Richard, Claudio Vergari, Eleonore Blondiaux, Marius Buffard, Raphael Vialle, Timoth{é}e de Saint-Denis
Text_Content: OBJECTIVE Shear wave elastography (SWE) is a recent method for evaluating soft tissue stiffness. Its application to the spinal cord is limited by the ultrasound bone barrier. Spinal dysraphism can cause neurological symptoms impairing bladder, bowel, and lower limb function due to a mechanical stress known as tethered cord syndrome. Detethering of the spinal cord is a part of surgical treatment. This study aimed to assess the feasibility of intraoperative elastography to guide surgery in patients with spinal dysraphism involving traction of the spinal cord. METHODS This single-center retrospective study included all patients who underwent surgery for spinal dysraphism between November 2023 and July 2024. SWE was performed under general anesthesia with the patient in the prone position before and after spinal cord detethering. All SWE measurements were performed using the Aixplorer system. Demographic, clinical, and radiological data (age at surgery, neurological status, and MRI findings) were collected. RESULTS Twenty-one patients with a mean $\pm$ SD (range) age of 3.7 $\pm$ 5.3 (0--17.5) years were included. Etiologies included open saccular dysraphism (n = 3), spinal cord conus lipoma (n = 6), limited dorsal myeloschisis (n = 3), and fibrolipomatous filum (n = 9). In 85% of patients, at least 1 clip was of sufficient quality for analysis both before and after release. The mean $\pm$ SD (range) spinal cord stiffness at the beginning of surgery was 25.2 $\pm$ 9.2 (12.3--39.1) kPa and 11.2 $\pm$ 3.8 (6.2--16.5) kPa at the end of release, with a significant stiffness decrease (p = 0.018). No complications attributable to SWE were observed. CONCLUSIONS SWE of the spinal cord in patients with spinal dysraphism is a safe and feasible imaging method. This technique may assist in assessing the adequacy of untethering during surgery. However, no established normative SWE values for the pediatric spinal cord currently exist. Until it does, the intraoperative interpretability and clinical utility of this technique remain limited.

Title: Optimal (Randomized) Compact Routing Schemes
Author: Shiri Chechik, Avi Kadria, Gur Lifshitz, Liam Roditty
Text_Content: Compact routing schemes route messages along short paths while every vertex stores little information. We study the trade-off between the stretch and the storage of compact routing schemes in undirected graphs, in four models: labeled and name-independent schemes, with average or worst-case local storage. We improve the best known stretch in all four models. Our main result is a labeled routing scheme with expected stretch $2k-1$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ average local storage, in which only the routing is randomized. Under the Erdős girth conjecture, no scheme with this storage has stretch below $2k-1$, so our scheme is optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors in the storage. With deterministic routing, we obtain stretch $\approx2.47k$, the best known deterministic stretch with average storage. Worst-case local storage is the classical setting of compact routing. The leading coefficient $4$ in the stretch $4k-5$ of Thorup and Zwick~[SPAA'01] was improved only by Chechik~[PODC'13], to $\approx3.68$ in unweighted graphs. In unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(\frac83k+O(1),O(k))$, and deterministic stretch $\approx3.05k$. Name-independent routing is harder, since the source knows only the name of the destination. The best known stretch with $\widetilde O(n^{1/k})$ local storage in unweighted graphs was $96k$, by Abraham, Gavoille, and Malkhi~[DISC'04]. We improve it by more than a factor of $8$. With average storage, we obtain expected stretch $4k-5$, which matches the labeled scheme of Thorup and Zwick. With worst-case storage in unweighted graphs, we obtain expected stretch $(8k+O(1),O(k))$. All our schemes for unweighted graphs extend to weighted graphs with a small loss in the stretch, and still improve the previous unweighted bounds.

Title: Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Criteria Network Design Problems
Author: Mehrshad Taziki, Ali Vakilian
Text_Content: Min-max multi-criteria optimization asks for a single feasible solution minimizing the maximum of its costs under $\ell$ nonnegative cost functions, a formulation that captures both fairness across groups and robustness across scenarios. It has proved hard to approximate even for basic problems: for robust shortest paths, polylogarithmic approximations are known only in quasi-polynomial time. For network design, the best known guarantee is an $\ell$-approximation, which is tight for the natural LP relaxation. We show that exponentially better and nearly optimal guarantees are achievable for two fundamental network design problems. For multi-criteria connectivity augmentation (MC-CAP), which asks to increase the edge connectivity of a given undirected graph by one, we give a randomized polynomial-time $O(\log \ell)$-approximation algorithm. Applying our augmentation procedure iteratively and analyzing its randomized choices jointly across iterations yields an $O(\log k \log \ell)$-approximation for the multi-criteria $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph (MC-$k$-ECSS) problem, for every $k \geq 2$. We complement these algorithms with a nearly matching lower bound: for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, MC-CAP admits no polynomial-time $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} \ell)$-approximation, even when the underlying graph is a star, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}\bigl(n^{\log^{O(1)}n}\bigr)$. The same hardness extends to the MC-$k$-ECSS problem.

Title: A RISC-V Simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix Architecture
Author: Nick Brown, Daniyal Arshad
Text_Content: RISC-V based AI accelerators have become popular and not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Tenstorrent are one example, and whilst they document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present Wolfpine, a community developed RISC-V simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack. Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, Wolfpine is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.

Title: Smallest Multiplicative Stretch for an $α$-APASP Below $\widetilde O \left(n^ω\right)$ Runtime
Author: Lakshay Saggi, Ariel Sapir
Text_Content: Dor, Halperin and Zwick [FOCS'96; SICOMP'00] showed that $(2-\varepsilon)$-APASP is at least as hard as BMM for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$. Zwick [FOCS'98; JACM'02] gave a $2$-APASP algorithm in $\widetilde O(n^{ω+o(1)}\log W_{\max})$ runtime, where $W_{\max}$ is the maximum edge weight. Bringmann, K{ü}nnemann and W{ę}grzycki [STOC'19] removed this logarithmic factor. Using OpenAI's recent bound $ω\leq\frac{9}{4}$ gives $\widetilde O\left(n^{\frac{9}{4}+o(1)}\right)$ time. We present two weighted undirected $2$-APASP algorithms. The first uses $(\min,\max)$-products. Earlier rectangular FMM bounds of Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'24] and Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu and Zhou [SODA'25] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.36999465})$ runtime, below the previous $ω\leq2.371177$ of Dupont, Eisenberger, Kozlovskii, Mehrabian, Ruiz, See, Zhou, Alman, Vassilevska Williams and Balog [arXiv'26]. Current rectangular FMM bounds give $\widetilde O(n^{2.34549151})$, independent of $W_{\max}$. For integer weights, our second algorithm has $\widetilde O(n^{ω-\frac{(ω-2)^2}{ω-1}+o(1)}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$ runtime, with exponent below $ω$ whenever $ω>2$. The rectangular bounds of Uzna{ń}ski [arXiv'26] or of Amanov, van den Berg and Zuiddam [arXiv'26] give $\widetilde O(n^{2.17157288}\log^{O(1)}W_{\max})$.

Title: TEXMET: A Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction
Author: Muhammad Hamza Zafar, Davit Gigilashvili, Jon Yngve Hardeberg
Text_Content: The reconstruction of fragmented historical textiles presents a significant challenge in computational archaeology. The Oseberg ship burial, dating to 834 CE, yielded hundreds of degraded textile fragments that have resisted systematic computational analysis. While deep learning has revolutionized image-based puzzle solving, progress on archaeological textiles has been limited by the lack of domain-specific datasets and systematic evaluation of modern architectures. To address this gap, we present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection, representing the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle-solving research. Using TEXMET, we conduct a systematic evaluation of three state-of-the-art puzzle-solving models: JPDVT, FCViT, and DiffAssemble. Our experiments reveal that the transformer-based models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalize to textiles, but domain-specific fine-tuning proves highly effective. The graph-based DiffAssemble model, when fine-tuned on TEXMET, achieves 85.89% puzzle accuracy on textile data. Most significantly, applying this fine-tuned model to 45 highly degraded Oseberg fragments yields a performance increase from 26.67% to 64.44% puzzle accuracy. These results establish TEXMET as a new benchmark for textile reconstruction and demonstrate that domain adaptation is essential for applying puzzle-solving methods to imagery of real archaeological materials.

Title: Tree Covers for Directed Graphs: Distance Oracles, Routing Schemes and Spanners
Author: Shiri Chechik, Gur Lifshitz
Text_Content: In a seminal work [STOC'01; JACM'05], Thorup and Zwick showed that every weighted undirected graph admits a tree cover where each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ trees in expectation, and every pair has a path of stretch at most $2k-1$ in some tree. In this paper, we extend this structural property to directed graphs with nonnegative edge weights. Let $\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v) = \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + \mathrm{dist}_G(v \to u)$ denote the roundtrip distance. For every integer $k$, we construct a collection $\mathcal{T}$ of tree-pairs, each consisting of an in-tree and an out-tree rooted at the same vertex. Each vertex belongs to $O(kn^{1/k})$ tree-pairs in expectation, and for every ordered pair $(u, v)$ some tree-pair $T_{in}\cup T_{out} \in \mathcal{T}$ satisfies $\mathrm{dist}_{T_{in}\cup T_{out}}(u \to v) \le \mathrm{dist}_G(u \to v) + (k-1)\mathrm{dist}_G(u \leftrightarrows v).$ We call this a \emph{$k$-strong (roundtrip) tree cover}. While prior techniques partition distances into geometric scales and build separate structures for each scale, our construction handles all distances simultaneously within a single, unified hierarchy. This yields the first directed tree cover for general $k$ matching the classic Thorup-Zwick stretch-size trade-off. Our cover immediately implies improved constructions of roundtrip spanners, path-reporting distance oracles, and compact routing schemes, as well as their source-wise and prioritized variants. We also provide faster algorithms for these structures: for general $k \ge 4$, all the above objects can be constructed in $\widetilde{O}(\min\{mn, n^{2.5}\})$ expected time, breaking the $mn$ barrier in dense directed graphs.

Title: Finding Integer Roots of Polynomials in Nearly Optimal Time
Author: Yansong Feng, Itamar Nir
Text_Content: Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients of absolute value less than $2^b$. Using Pan's approximate factorization theorem, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds all distinct integer roots of $f$ in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations. This matches the bit size of the input up to logarithmic factors and does not require $f$ to be square-free. Since we were unable to verify parts of the running time analysis of Pan's theorem, we also give a self-contained deterministic algorithm with running time $\widetilde O(nb+\min(n,b)^3b^2)$, which is $\widetilde O(nb)$ whenever $b\leq n^{1/4}$. This answers a question of Harvey and Hittmeir (2022), who asked whether integer roots can be found deterministically in quasilinear time, conditionally on Pan's theorem, and unconditionally for $b\leq n^{1/4}$. The fastest previous deterministic algorithm, due to Nir, takes $\widetilde O(n^{3/2}b)$ bit operations and works only for square-free polynomials. Instead of $p$-adic lifting, we combine approximate complex root finding with exact polynomial evaluation. We first approximate the complex roots of the polynomial formed by the top $\min(n,b)+1$ coefficients of $f$. Every integer root $r$ of $f$ with $|r|\geq 2$ lies within distance $2$ of some complex root of this truncated polynomial. Rounding the real parts of the approximate roots therefore gives a list of $O(\min(n,b))$ candidate integers that is guaranteed to contain all integer roots of $f$. Although a single candidate can have up to $b$ bits, a bound via the Mahler measure shows that the bit lengths of all candidates sum to $O(b)$. This allows us to test all candidates by exact multipoint evaluation in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations.

Title: SPOD: Recovering Suppressed Temporal Evidence in Video-LLMs via Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition
Author: Yangguang Lin, Quan Fang, Xiaoyan Liu, Zefan Xu
Text_Content: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.

Title: Self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation requires linear time
Author: Joel Rybicki
Text_Content: Synchronising the clocks of processes is a fundamental problem in distributed computing. We consider message-passing systems in which processes start in an arbitrary initial state (self-stabilisation) and up to $f$ processes may be non-transiently faulty. It is well known that synchronising clocks \emph{exactly} is at least as hard as consensus and requires $Θ(f)$ time. In contrast, without self-stabilisation, clocks can be synchronised \emph{approximately} much faster, in time independent of the number of non-transient faults [Srikanth and Toueg, JACM 1987; Welch and Lynch, Inf. Comput. 1988]. In this work, we show that deterministic self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks require $Ω(f)$ time to stabilise. This gives the first non-trivial time lower bound for these tasks, whose time complexity has remained open for over two decades [Dolev and Welch, JACM 2004; Dolev, Függer, Schmid and Lenzen, JACM 2014]. In particular, this answers the open question whether self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks are as hard as consensus or as easy as approximate agreement [Lenzen and Rybicki, JACM 2019]. The results show that guaranteeing \emph{both} transient and non-transient fault-tolerance simultaneously is expensive even for approximate synchronisation tasks. The lower bounds hold in a very strong model: the faulty processes can only crash, the local clocks of processes have no clock drift, and the message delay is bounded and known to all processes. The proof is based on a combinatorial topological argument showing that no fast finite-state protocol can ensure that the clocks behave consistently across all executions. To our knowledge, this is the first use of topological arguments to prove time lower bounds in the self-stabilising setting.

Title: Pure Differentially Private Query Release via Laplace Input Smoothing
Author: Zongrui Zou
Text_Content: We study the offline release of a public family of $k$ statistical queries on a database of $N$ records from a public universe of size $d$, under pure $\varepsilon$-differential privacy. We give an efficient algorithm that, with probability at least $1-β$, answers all queries simultaneously to error $$O\left(\min\left\{1,\sqrt{\frac{\log(d/β)\log k}{N\varepsilon}}\right\}\right).$$ The output is a synthetic histogram on the data universe, and its running time depends polynomially on $N,d$ and $k$. This resolves a conjecture of Nikolov and Ullman (2021) with an efficient, polynomial-time construction. Fitzsimons (2026) recently established the same square-root error scale via an information-theoretic construction that relies on a computationally intractable Lipschitz envelope over the exponential space of possible outputs. In contrast, we introduce an input-side smoothing approach: we run a selection-only multiplicative-weights process after a single sparse Laplace perturbation of the input histogram. Departing from standard first-order stability analyses, we investigate the stability of stability by establishing a uniform lower bound on the second-order log-derivatives of the output transcript across $T$ rounds of multiplicative weight updates. We then develop an analytic smoothing principle showing that this curvature bound allows a sparse, coordinate-wise perturbation to guarantee pure differential privacy globally, attaining optimal utility through a conceptually simple, polynomial-time pure-DP mechanism.

Title: OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
Author: Feng Cheng, Yu-Hsuan Huang, Fengyi Wang, Chaofan Zhou, Zhennan Zhu, Huan He, Bo Zhang, Ruoqi Zhang, Zhanfeng Mo, Ziwei Liu, Lanyi Li, Yifeng Pan, Junhua Long, Ziqiu Zhou, Yue Lin, Shaowei Liu
Text_Content: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

Title: Bayesian-optimized magnetic-field-gradient sensing with a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate
Author: Shixiang Chen, Juan Wang, Yan Li
Text_Content: Building on our previous study of the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate, we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient sensing that relates the maximum rotational deflection angle of the spin-density distribution to the magnetic-field gradient. We analyze the dependence of the sensing performance on key parameters and perform a systematic parameter optimization. A Bayesian optimization algorithm is introduced to efficiently identify the optimal parameter combination, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of magnetic-field-gradient sensing. Numerical simulations under the adopted noise model show that, compared with the parameter set used in our previous work, the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work provides a new route for magnetic-field-gradient sensing and offers a reference for machine-learning-assisted quantum precision measurement.

Title: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking via Automated Adversarial Chain of Thoughts Discovery
Author: Masoud Poorghaffar Aghdam, Göktuğ Serdar Yıldırım, Sinem Sav
Text_Content: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks by generating explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, but the safety implications of this intermediate reasoning surface remain underexplored. We demonstrate that the reasoning trace itself is a powerful attack vector. Safety alignment in large models is substantially less robust to malicious reasoning embedded in the context than to direct imperative prompts. We introduce BrainwashedLLM, a weak-to-strong adversarial framework that automates the discovery of reasoning-based jailbreaks. First, we use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm, with a multi-objective rule-based reward to fine-tune a small, white-box source model to generate adversarial reasoning traces. Crucially, the reward is computed entirely over the source's own reasoning trace. Second, we show that these traces transfer in a zero-shot manner. When traces are injected as input prefixes, they steer larger black-box LRMs to continue the adversarial reasoning and produce harmful outputs, without requiring prompt optimization, gradient access, or any form of output feedback from the target model. Across four state-of-the-art LRMs that span distinct architectures, BrainwashedLLM achieves ASR@5 between 0.74 and 0.98 across targets, within 16 points of query-based baselines, without querying the target during attack construction. To our knowledge, this is the first framework to use RL to directly optimize the CoT of LRMs as an attack surface without any target feedback, and the first to demonstrate zero-shot weak-to-strong transfer of reasoning traces. Our results suggest that exposed CoT is a vulnerability in LRMs and motivate architectural defenses that isolate the reasoning buffer. Warning: This paper contains potentially offensive and harmful text.

Title: ZeroGR: Filtering-First Constrained Decoding for Generative Recommendation
Author: Xiangrui Yang, Jiawei Yang, Liang Zeng, Daqian Ding, Ziqian Liu, Bing Tian, Cheng Peng, Yunfeng Zhao, Fangyu Zhang, Jiaqiang Liu, Xiao Liang, Yiming Qiu
Text_Content: Generative recommendation is gaining traction in production, retrieving items by generating their identifiers one token at a time. The generated sequences must identify relevant catalog items, so constrained decoding couples relevance scoring with validity filtering. Because most possible sequences are invalid, scoring before filtering wastes computation on candidates that will be discarded. Our evaluation shows that filtering first can avoid this work with negligible impact on recommendation quality. We present ZeroGR, a filtering-first constrained decoding system for generative recommendation. ZeroGR uses a step-sliced filtering index to reduce GPU memory use by tailoring data representations to each decoding step. Its execution engine adopts shared-slot execution to accelerate data exchange across stages and hybrid projection to adapt computation to workload patterns, thereby reducing execution overhead. During index refreshes, ZeroGR applies layout-guided streaming construction to speed up updates and limit serving interference. Extensive evaluation shows that ZeroGR accelerates the filtering and scoring pipeline by up to $9.9\times$ over representative baselines while reducing GPU index memory use and accelerating index reconstruction.

Title: Leakage-aware acoustic drone detection: fusing hand-crafted and pretrained audio features in a stacking ensemble
Author: Zahid Iqbal
Text_Content: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation exposes the optimism of random splits and gives a reliable benchmark, and fusing hand-crafted with YAMNet features consistently improves detection in real time on one CPU thread.

Title: VISAGE: Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration via Dual-Stream Diffusion for Arbitrary 3D Heads
Author: Jeremias Krauß, Pragati Jaiswal, René Schuster, Didier Stricker
Text_Content: Recovering identity-faithful, physically based surface appearance for 3D human heads from sparse images remains challenging. Existing methods often rely on UV-based pipelines, introducing seam artefacts, or operate in image space, limiting surface consistency. We present VISAGE, Vertex-based Intrinsic Surface Appearance GEneration, a surface-based conditional diffusion framework that synthesises per-vertex albedo and roughness directly on arbitrary mesh topologies, without requiring consistent UV parameterisation at training time. VISAGE combines global spectral processing with local geodesic K-Nearest-Neighbour refinement, enforcing structural coherence while restoring detail beyond the truncated spectral basis. Multi-view RGB images condition the network via visibility-aware cross-attention, enabling occlusion-robust synthesis across the full head surface. Region-specific modules specialise in semantically demanding and distinct areas (eyes, mouth, skin and hair), while a tangent-space output projection recovers fine iris detail. We further introduce a scalable procedural augmentation pipeline that enriches raw geometry scans with physically plausible albedo, roughness and normal maps for training. The predicted attributes render directly as a single RGBA vertex-colour channel. VISAGE reduces FID by 42.7% on NPHM and 22.5% and 4.4% on zero-shot FaceVerse and i3DMM, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, with a 7.2M-parameter core network.

Title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
Author: Qinglin Yang, Jiepeng Wang, Yuxing Huang, Haibin Huang, Kai Xu, Chi Zhang, Ruizhen Hu, Xuelong Li
Text_Content: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

Title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
Author: Carlo Sgaravatti, Daniele Kopyshevskiy, Davide Secco, Giacomo Boracchi
Text_Content: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.

Title: Learning from Unlabeled Photographs for General Oral Image Analysis
Author: Zhong-Shi Zhang, Zi-Li Yu, Xiao Xiao, Huan Liu, Gui-Song Xia, Cui Huang, Meng-Xun Li
Text_Content: Oral photographs contain rich clinical information and hold significant potential for artificial intelligence applications; however, most models are trained for individual tasks and rely on costly expert annotations. We hypothesized that self-supervised training on unlabeled oral photographs could produce transferable visual representations for heterogeneous vision tasks. To test this hypothesis, we developed DOVE (Dental Optical Visual Encoder) by domain-adaptive self-supervised pretraining on approximately 530,000 unlabeled oral photographs collected from publicly accessible sources. DOVE was benchmarked against 3 established baselines across 5 classification datasets and 4 segmentation datasets, covering both frozen backbone evaluation and end-to-end finetuning. DOVE achieved the strongest overall performance, ranking best in few-shot transfer and label efficiency on most benchmarks. Under the 20-shot frozen-backbone protocol, DOVE outperformed the second best DINOv3 by 4.37 percentage points in mean macro-F1 across classification datasets and by 4.49 percentage points in mean macro-Dice across segmentation tasks. Under end-to-end finetuning, DOVE achieved at least 80% of the strongest full-data baseline's performance across most evaluation datasets using only 10% of the labeled training data. Qualitative retrieval and feature analyses further indicated better organization of image-level and spatial representations. These findings support DOVE as a generalizable and label-efficient backbone for oral vision research.

Title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
Author: Dimitrios Bekris, Marios Glytsos, Panagiotis P. Filntisis, Niki Efthymiou, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
Text_Content: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.

Title: Methodological Assessment of Instrumented Indentation for Spatially Resolved Mesoscale Stiffness and Creep in Short Fiber-Reinforced Injection-Molded PBT Components
Author: Eduard Klatt, Natalie Rauter
Text_Content: Instrumented indentation enables assessment of local mechanical properties in heterogeneous polymer systems, but specimen preparation and the selected indentation protocol significantly influence the quantitative interpretation of the measured response. This study develops and evaluates an experimental methodology for spatially resolved mesoscale characterization of both unreinforced and short fiber-reinforced composites. An unreinforced material system is used as a reference material to systematically examine the effects of indentation spacing, surface preparation, maximum indentation load, temporal loading parameters, and unloading evaluation. Indentation loads of 500, 1000, and 1750 mN are investigated in complementary experimental campaigns. The apparent indentation modulus exhibits moderate sensitivity to indentation load and loading time within the studied ranges. In contrast, indentation depth and the creep-related depth increment display greater sensitivity to the applied load history. Surface polishing minimizes topographical disturbances and enables reliable identification of residual indentation profiles and pile-up. Based on these methodological findings, a final load-hold-unload protocol with an indentation load of 1750 mN, a loading time of 6 s, a holding period of 300 s, and an unloading time of 4 s is applied to both unreinforced material and short fiber-reinforced composites. The mean apparent indentation modulus increases from 2.91 GPa for unreinforced material to 6.65 GPa for short fiber-reinforced composites, while the mean depth of indentation creep decreases from 2.36 to 1.91 microns. The coefficient of variation also increases for both quantities, indicating that short-fiber reinforcement enhances mean local stiffness and introduces pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both stiffness-related and time-dependent mesoscale indentation responses.

Title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies
Author: Flavio Tuteri, André Freitas
Text_Content: Turbulence is defined by a set of emergent and singular phenomena: a constant-flux energy cascade, intermittency, a dissipation rate that survives the vanishing of viscosity, and the spontaneous loss of determinism of the inviscid limit. Which physical ingredients produce them remains unclear, because in fluids they always come together with incompressibility, spatial structure and vortex dynamics. Here we show that a hierarchy of inertia, coupled by the purely geometric nonlinearity of rigid constraints, is enough. A planar chain of rigid pendula whose lengths and masses decrease geometrically, coupled only through nearest-neighbor constraints, develops a far-from-equilibrium cascade that replaces thermal equipartition, with statistically local and time-irreversible energy transfer despite intrinsically nonlocal coupling. Its fluctuations are intermittent, yet self-similarity is restored by a hidden scale symmetry. As the viscosity vanishes, the dissipation rate saturates at a finite value, and thermal noise consistent with fluctuation-dissipation balance is amplified from the smallest to the largest scales within a fraction of a large-scale period. Because the hierarchy can be tuned and the same dynamics can be realized mechanically or electrically, turbulence becomes a property that can be designed and measured in the laboratory.

Title: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
Author: Hui Xuan Tan, Stefanos Chaliasos, Alastair F. Donaldson
Text_Content: A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, typically Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. The proof covers the compiled binary, so a miscompilation can make a correct zkVM produce a valid proof of a computation that differs from the developer's source. We present the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to zkVM guarantees, on the production zkVMs SP1 and Jolt. We assemble 88 known rustc and LLVM miscompilations with Rust reproducers, using an LLM agent to recover Rust triggers for 60 of 124 LLVM bugs reported only as LLVM IR. Many of the bugs carry over to zkVMs: 48 of the 88 make a guest commit a wrong output on SP1 and 46 on Jolt, including the same 15 rustc bugs on both. Most bugs that do not reproduce never reach the faulty code on the zkVM's target, e.g. because they need an instruction-set extension. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident. Across 13 guests of 10 popular SP1 projects, the buggy and the fixed compiler produce byte-identical binaries in 447 of the 552 guest-bug pairs that build, and the other 105 have the same code or agree on every input we ran. An attacker who contributes code to a guest, however, can trigger these bugs on purpose. For about $40 per project, an LLM agent found patches that look like ordinary optimisations, preserve the behaviour of the guest's source, and expose a known bug in 12 of 366 project-bug pairs, across 11 of 20 projects. In four cases the guest commits a wrong output, including an Ethereum client that rejects a valid block, and in the other eight it fails on a valid input. Reviewing or formally verifying the zkVM or the guest's source cannot catch such a patch, because both are correct. zkVM projects should treat their compiler as part of their trusted base and track the known bugs of their toolchain.

Title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
Author: Pavle Tepavčević, Dušan Jakovetić, Miloš Savić
Text_Content: Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order. In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-α}$, $α\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2α-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=Ω(nm\cdot m/n^{2α-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

Title: Glauber Dynamics for Sampling Colorings: Rapid Mixing above $(1+1/\mathrm{e})Δ$ via Hidden Hard-Core Models
Author: Xiongxin Yang
Text_Content: We show that for every $γ>0$ and every sufficiently large $Δ$, the Glauber dynamics for proper $q$-colorings of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $Δ$ has spectral gap $Ω_γ(1/n)$, and hence mixing time $O_γ(n^2\log q)$, whenever $q\ge(1+1/\mathrm{e}+γ)Δ$. Our proof establishes a Bochner-type inequality by exploiting the spectral gaps of hard-core models hidden in the color classes. The constant $1+1/\mathrm{e}\approx1.368$ comes from the uniqueness threshold $\approx\mathrm{e}/Δ$ of the hard-core model on the infinite $Δ$-regular tree.

Title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
Author: Rounak Sen, Divya Kumari, Deeksha Varshney
Text_Content: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

Title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
Author: Simon Savukoski, Tatu Pinomaa
Text_Content: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

Title: Rate-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff for Vector Gaussian Sources with Limited Common Randomness: Exact Characterization and Approximate Universality
Author: Wentao Wang, Shuo Shao, Ruibin Li, Jingjing Qian, Jun Chen, Bin Xia
Text_Content: The distortion-rate-common randomness-perception (DRCP) theory characterizes how limited common randomness (CR) improves reconstruction fidelity under perceptual constraints, thereby providing an information-theoretic foundation for generative compression. In this paper, we characterize the DRCP tradeoff for vector Gaussian sources with limited CR under the squared-error distortion measure and the squared Wasserstein-2 perception measure. Specifically, we first establish a generalized reverse waterfilling characterization of globally optimal allocations. Second, we derive an analytical upper bound on the DRCP function through sequential greedy allocation of rate and CR. For fixed rate and CR budgets, the resulting representation is independent of the perception threshold. Finally, we establish its approximate universality through uniform performance guarantees: the achievable distortion exceeds the optimal distortion by at most $2ρ^*\approx0.2897$ times the total source variance, whereas the optimal-to-greedy distortion ratio is at least $η^*\approx0.7517$.

Title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
Author: Atikkhan Faridkhan Nilgar, Manuel Dietrich, Kristof Van Laerhoven
Text_Content: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges.
