We develop a systematic approach to extract the history kernel of a fixed sphere in spatially uniform, unsteady flow from axisymmetric Navier-Stokes simulations of finite-duration acceleration and deceleration ramps at initial Reynolds numbers from 0.2 to 200. The resulting kernel surface recovers the Basset limit at short lags and in the creeping-flow limit and is continued beyond the resolved lags using far-wake asymptotics. At higher Reynolds numbers, the kernel develops non-monotonic behaviour at intermediate lags, associated with delayed adjustment of the boundary layer and wake. For the cases tested, the present kernel substantially improves history-force predictions for finite ramps, oscillatory forcing and non-periodic composite velocity histories relative to the literature formulations considered, without case-specific adjustment. These findings indicate that lag and Reynolds number capture the dominant memory response.

Title: Sparse-View 3D Coronary Reconstruction from Vessel Segmentations Using a Diffusion Prior
Author: Tianyuan Wang, Kenan Niu, Stefano Stramigioli
Text_Content: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) coronary anatomy from sparse angiographic views could support percutaneous coronary intervention, but limited angular coverage and imperfect vessel segmentations introduce substantial geometric ambiguity. We propose a vessel-specific reconstruction framework combining a learned 3D diffusion prior, visual-hull initialization, and projection-based data consistency. The unconditional diffusion model is trained on coronary vessel masks without paired 2D--3D data and reused across different view counts without retraining. During inference, a scaled visual hull initializes reconstruction, while projection-based updates constrain diffusion refinement using patient-specific vessel observations. We evaluated the framework on simulated angiograms derived from ImageCAS computed tomography angiography volumes using two, four, and eight views at two contrast levels. Across 50 evaluation coronary-tree cases, the proposed method achieved higher mean Dice and clDice than visual hull, deep image prior (DIP), and hash-grid implicit neural representation (INR) at all view counts under reduced contrast. With eight views, improvements over DIP, the best-performing baseline at lower contrast, were approximately 0.13 in Dice and 0.22 in clDice. At higher contrast, performance remained competitive with hash-grid INR, the best-performing eight-view baseline. The preferred diffusion starting timestep depended on observation quality and view count, with excessive refinement reducing accuracy at higher contrast. Projection guidance improved both metrics across all conditions. Averaging stochastic reconstructions further improved accuracy, while sample disagreement localized errors with average-precision gains of 0.14--0.21 over error prevalence. These findings support diffusion-prior reconstruction from sparse vessel observations, although clinical validation remains necessary.

Title: SCANO: Restoring Boundary-Condition Completeness in Sampled Meshes with a Sliced-Cross-Attention Neural Operator for 3D Thermal Fields
Author: Tianyu Li, Zhiwei Cao, Qingang Zhang, Ruihang Wang, Binyang Song, Yonggang Wen
Text_Content: Training neural operators on million-cell meshes can exceed GPU memory limits. Models are therefore trained on subsamples and deployed on whole meshes or selected regions. However, subsampling can distort boundary information, degrading accuracy. We ask when boundary conditioning under sampling stays consistent with whole-mesh training, and how to aggregate and inject boundary data. Representing the solution as an integral of boundary data against type-dependent measures, we show that subsampling distorts this conditioning in three ways: incomplete boundary coverage or a sample-dependent global state, face weighting by count rather than area, and compression of boundary inputs into a low-dimensional vector. This analysis yields four measurable consistency conditions checkable before training. We satisfy them with two backbone-agnostic modules. Boundary Quadrature Attention (BQA) aggregates all boundary faces, typed and area-weighted, into slice tokens that every query point reads at every layer. Anchored Global State (AGS) estimates the global state from anchors independent of the sampled points. Adding both to a scalable message-passing and slice-attention backbone yields SCANO. We evaluate the approach on controlled and public benchmarks and a data-centre thermal simulation dataset (DCTS) containing million-cell meshes. On both benchmarks, BQA improves every backbone, reducing whole-mesh error up to 15-fold. On all three datasets, AGS aligns regional with whole-mesh predictions, cutting regional error at least tenfold for most backbones on the public benchmark. Together, the modules nearly halve the best original backbone's whole-mesh error on both benchmarks. SCANO predicts a room-scale field in under one second, over 100 times faster than whole-room anchor self-attention.

Title: How Python Audio Libraries Change Across Releases: Module Structure and Documentation
Author: Mateusz Modrzejewski, Michał Rokita, Łukasz Neumann
Text_Content: Developers who upgrade a Python audio library need to know what changed in the code they import and whether the release notes say so. Release notes and breaking changes have been mined for general software, but the module structure of audio libraries and its documentation have not been studied together. We mine 56 audio repositories used in machine learning workflows: the import graph of 49 packages at 1,395 releases, joined to 20,864 release-note and changelog entries, labeled by three open-weight language models and checked against two human coders. We find that (1) the set of a package's top-level modules is unchanged in 86.1% of consecutive release pairs, while the set of module files is unchanged in 61.4%. (2) A major increment changes the top level 5.2 times as often as another increment, and major and 0.x minor increments together account for 48.7% of the observed changes. (3) When a release removes modules, its notes name 8.9% of the removal units under a lexical match, an estimated 4.3% after a hand check of the matches. (4) Longer notes are more likely to contain an entry labeled as structural, and within each length band this proportion is also higher for releases with module removals. We intend to release the aligned dataset and the pipeline

Title: Estimating "Realized" Skewness using Convolutional Neural Network
Author: Haozhe Jiang, Ostap Okhrin, Michael Rockinger
Text_Content: We propose a new estimator of low-frequency skewness (monthly) that exploits high-frequency data (5 min) through a direct functional mapping consisting of layers of Convolutional Neural Networks followed by Multi Layer Perceptrons. Monte Carlo experiments involving stochastic volatility models, with and without jumps, show that the estimator reduces finite-sample bias relative to existing realized-skewness estimators and remains accurate under model misspecification. Empirically, our estimator exhibits temporal stability and delivers cross-sectional performance in actual skewness-sorted portfolios. We characterize the finite-sample bias of conventional plug-in skewness estimators and establish risk consistency properties of the proposed NN estimator under standard regularity conditions.

Title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
Author: Anita Yang, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Yohan Jung
Text_Content: Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.

Title: Directional Statistics in Signal Processing: A Geometry Driven Overview of Models, Learning, and Applications
Author: Anders S. Olsen, Kanti V. Mardia, Dimitri Van De Ville, Morten Mørup
Text_Content: Many signal-processing objects are defined by periodicity, normalization, sign or global-phase ambiguity, basis invariance, or positive-semidefinite constraints and therefore cannot be modeled faithfully in ordinary Euclidean space. This paper develops a geometry driven framework for directional statistics in signal processing, connecting signal representations to their natural manifolds or quotient spaces and to probability models compatible with their invariances. After reviewing instances of directional statistics in the signal processing literature, we review circular, toroidal, spherical, projective, Stiefel, Grassmann, and covariance-valued distributions, emphasizing their statistical assumptions, computational requirements, and dimensional limitations relevant to signal processing. We describe various modeling and estimation strategies, including analytical and gradient-based maximum likelihood, structured low-rank parameterizations, mixtures and hidden Markov models (HMMs), score-based and contrastive estimation, and geometry-aware K-means. To exemplify the consequences of geometry-aware modeling, we study multivariate phase coherence in synthetic data and functional neuroimaging, comparing toroidal phase vectors to projective, Grassmann, and positive-semidefinite representations. We also study speaker separation in a car environment, showing that directional representations outperform a standard Euclidean model. These examples demonstrate that when the geometric representation, statistical distribution, inference method, and computational regime are considered together, they have the potential to lead to improved models across a broad range of signal processing applications.

Title: Rondo: Controlling Reordering in High-Throughput Packet Spraying
Author: Xizhi Zhang, Zhongjie Chen, Yang Zhang, Fengyuan Ren
Text_Content: Modern datacenter applications demand high network bandwidth, motivating packet-level multipath transport to exploit the aggregate capacity of multiple paths. However, packet reordering under packet spraying poses challenges for hardware transports. Excessive packet reordering makes it difficult to infer packet loss, imposes substantial pressure on NIC resources, and ultimately degrades performance. Existing transports either prioritize throughput without controlling packet reordering, or mitigate reordering by restricting transmissions, which leaves available path capacity unused. In this paper, we identify two fundamental sources of packet reordering: transient inter-path queueing differences caused by control dynamics, and persistent path-delay differences due to path heterogeneity. These observations motivate a joint design of a multipath controller and a packet scheduler to address transient and persistent delay differences, respectively. We present Rondo, a packet-level multipath transport that achieves both high throughput and low packet reordering. Its multipath controller uses ACK-based per-path capacity estimation and probing to maintain stable path loads, while its packet scheduler adjusts packet transmission order to compensate for persistent delay differences. Testbed experiments and large-scale simulations show that Rondo reduces the maximum out-of-order degree by up to 97.5% while maintaining high throughput. With constrained receiver buffers, Rondo achieves up to 8.51 times higher goodput.

Title: System-level performance in massive ISAC networks
Author: Emanuele Mengoli, Nahuel Soprano-Loto
Text_Content: We propose a dynamic stochastic geometry framework to model and evaluate large-scale integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) networks. Base stations are distributed according to a homogeneous Poisson point process, while user equipments and sensing objects undergo localised random motion around their serving base station. Full spectrum reuse with a common waveform generates mutual interference that couples the two functionalities. Communication performance is characterised through downlink queues whose service rates are governed by the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) via the Shannon capacity. Sensing performance is captured by a Kalman filter (KF) whose measurement noise covariance depends on the sensing SINR, yielding a non-classical state-dependent filtering problem. We define system-level performance metrics under the Palm distribution of the base station process and prove the consistency of their empirical estimators. We then prove that, for a typical base station, communication and sensing metrics are associated, so that operating regimes favourable to one functionality tend to benefit the other. The proof combines the monotonicity of the queue and filter recursions in the configuration of interferers with the Harris--FKG inequality for Poisson functionals. We also show that the excess association ratio of the two interference levels decays as the inverse of the network density. Simulations based on a ray-tracing channel model corroborate the analysis.

Title: SparseGraph-I2P: Consistency-Guided Hypothesis Selection for Efficient Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration
Author: Ziyang Yu, Xiang Li, Qiong Chang, Jun Miyazaki
Text_Content: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud (I2P) registration risks discarding correct but ambiguous patch pairs, while retaining more candidates repeats fine matching over overlapping patches. SparseGraph-I2P aims to improve registration recall by increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver, using sensor or monocular depth. A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips pixel--point comparisons covered by an ancestor patch paired with the same point-cloud region. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve. With monocular depth, depth or inverse depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering. SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency among the compared methods on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth. With predicted depth, it retains the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. Code will be released.

Title: Can Network Models of Science Do Without Pluralist Agents?
Author: Jonas Hallgren, David Hyland, Mahault Albarracin
Text_Content: Science is a process of useful models being proven wrong time and again, but despite its many flaws, it somehow works. Why is this? Paul Feyerabend argued that it works because people dare to hold and defend incompatible rival theories against the accepted one, since a theory's failures often lead to its abandonment in the presence of a more accurate or simpler alternative. He called this view theoretical pluralism. We introduce a theoretical and experimental model in which this can be examined. It compares communities of pluralist agents, which can hold rival theories side by side and maintain beliefs within and between those theories, with communities of monist agents, which can only incorporate what they hear or observe into a single model of their own. In a multi-agent variational inference setting, our experimental demonstrations illustrate how communities with rival theories can go through periods of uncertainty followed by a shift in the theories they hold true, how the information that is communicated between communities affects beliefs when those communities make different observations about the world, and how sharing support for theories and sharing beliefs within them contribute differently to collective belief dynamics.

Title: Conditional independence and graphical models for rankings
Author: Aritz Pérez
Text_Content: Ranking models define probability distributions over rankings and are fundamental in applications such as preference learning and decision-making. Without structural assumptions, these models are intractable due to their factorial complexity. Although independence assumptions are key to reducing complexity and enabling interpretability, standard notions of conditional independence must account for the mutual exclusivity constraints inherent to rankings. We introduce relative rank models, a probabilistic framework based on structured coarsenings of the ranking space that relax these constraints while preserving relative order information. This representation enables a well-defined notion of conditional independence for rankings and allows rankings to be modeled using Bayesian networks. As a result, standard methods for learning and probabilistic inference can be applied to rankings, with interpretable representations based on conditional independence. We further show that two prominent ranking models based on independence assumptions tailored to rankings arise as special cases, providing a unifying framework for independence in ranking models.

Title: A reliability data aggregation method for fusion-oriented research facilities
Author: Helena Ortiz, Juan Eloy Ruiz-Castro, Christian Acal, Karol Kowal, Juan Chiachío, Ana María Aguilera
Text_Content: This paper aims to develop a statistical method for integrating multiple incomplete data sources to improve the estimation of the failure-rate probability distribution of fusion-specific devices. The data aggregation approach proposed in this work is to support the Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Inspectability (RAMI) studies for fusion-oriented research facilities. This work focuses on developing a procedure for handling missing or incomplete data from multiple sources, as well as formulating a statistical framework for combining data from different sources that refer to the same equipment type and failure mode. Specifically, a Bayesian result is adopted under the assumption of a constant failure rate over time. This framework motivates the use of the Gamma distributions to model the failure-rate parameter of each device. Subsequently, two alternative procedures are introduced to approximate, using a single Gamma distribution, the weighted mixture formed by combining Gamma distributions corresponding to the same equipment type across multiple data sources. The proposed method is validated through an extensive simulation study and further illustrated by application to the accelerator systems of the IFMIF-DONES facility. Finally, the proposed algorithm has been implemented in the open-source software R to facilitate its use in the nuclear fusion community.

Title: Multi-Path Mamba Diffusion for 3D Point Cloud Semantic Scene Completion
Author: Li Liang, Naveed Akhtar, Jordan Vice, Anwaar Ulhaq, Ajmal Saeed Mian
Text_Content: 3D semantic scene completion plays a critical role in enabling various downstream tasks within autonomous systems by estimating both missing geometric structures and semantic information in scene data. In this work, we introduce a unique neural framework that integrates state space modeling with diffusion-based generative approaches to enhance 3D point cloud semantic scene completion. We propose \textit{MPath Mamba} diffusion network, leveraging a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations within multi-path data to efficiently process long-sequence data for feature extraction. The proposed method operates in the conditioned latent space of a variational autoencoder, enhanced by a state-space mechanism to improve 3D point cloud representation and reconstruction. Extensive experiments conducted on the SemanticKITTI benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive performance for 3D point cloud semantic scene completion.

Title: Confidence-Aware Aggregation for Multimodal Audio Reasoning
Author: Michel Olvera, Paraskevas Stamatiadis, Ga{ë}l Richard
Text_Content: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) enable generative reasoning over complex acoustic scenes but often exhibit prediction instability. We show that this variability can serve as a reliability metric via inference-time self-consistency and confidence-aware aggregation. Using a log-probability--based scoring framework, candidate answers are weighted by model likelihoods, leveraging reasoning diversity and self-certainty without additional training. Experiments on four LALMs, including Qwen3-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, demonstrate that confidence-aware aggregation improves accuracy and calibration, with additive methods like Borda voting outperforming classical Majority Vote, especially under high disagreement. This approach transforms LALM variability into a source of reliability for scalable and robust multimodal audio understanding. Project code is available at https://github.com/michelolzam/lalm-self-consistency.

Title: FreeForm Harness: A Mobile-Native Agent Harness for Open and Composable Extensions
Author: Bo Zhang, Pengbo Zhang, Jiaxin Jiao, Yue Liu
Text_Content: Mobile phones support many everyday agent tasks, but current mobile agents bundle capabilities into monolithic pipelines with no open recombination point. Users and third parties cannot publish, install, and compose new behaviors, leaving personalized daily-life requests underserved. We argue that the missing piece is a substrate: although phones are the Web's dominant access point, open publication and composition under decentralized authorship stop at the agent harness. We present FreeForm Harness (FFH), a mobile-native agent harness for open, composable extensions. A frozen base and a permanence-aware required layer handle mobile constraints, including location, proactive triggering, and scarce channels. A uniform plugin contract makes independently authored extensions composable, checkable, and replaceable over a frozen socket set. FFH also supports end-user authorship through a tiered commissioned-authoring path. When no existing extension matches a user's intent, a Web coding agent generates a candidate artifact, which is validated and admitted on device under the same contract as other extensions. An Android prototype spans device, market, and cloud. Evaluation shows that architectural boundaries are enforced at runtime; realistic daily-life requests fit the declared composition space without widening it; and user intent reaches on-device execution through retrieval or commissioned authoring, with final trust decisions remaining device-local. FFH advances the agentic Web from "everything is a plugin" toward "everyone is a developer" on mobile.

Title: Impedance-controlled Laser Dynamics in Near-Zero Index Media
Author: Adrien Debacq, Andrei V. Lavrinenko, Elizaveta Semenova, Olivier Deparis, Michaël Lobet
Text_Content: Near-zero-index (NZI) media have been explored for controlling spontaneous emission, but their impact on stimulated emission and lasing properties remains unexplored within their different classes, i.e., epsilon-near-zero (ENZ), mu-near-zero (MNZ), or epsilon-and-mu-near-zero (EMNZ). Here, we show theoretically that lasing emission depends on the class of NZI medium and can be controlled through its impedance. The major difference, as compared to conventional laser media, arises from the incorporation of dispersive electric and magnetic properties in the derivation of the Maxwell Boch equations. In this framework, the analysis of laser rate equation reveals that the ENZ class, with high impedance, can reduce the lasing threshold through enhanced electric-field interaction. Numerical simulations further show that the NZI class also governs the spectral response: whereas ENZ and MNZ classes suffer from multimode emission, the EMNZ class preserves single-mode emission.

Title: The Lovász Local Lemma Is Sharp for the Hat Guessing Number
Author: Thomas Delépine, Matthieu Rosenfeld
Text_Content: In the hat guessing game on a graph $G$, each vertex is occupied by a player wearing a hat whose color is chosen from a set of $q$ colors. Each player knows the graph and their position in it and sees only the hat colors of their neighbors. The players may agree on a strategy beforehand but must simultaneously try to guess their own hat colors without communicating. They win if at least one player guesses their own hat color correctly. The hat guessing number of $G$, denoted by $\textrm{HG}(G)$, is the largest integer $q$ for which the players have a strategy that guarantees a win for every assignment of hat colors. A direct application of the symmetric Lovász Local Lemma shows that $\textrm{HG}(G) < eΔ$ for every graph $G$ of maximum degree at most $Δ\ge 1$. We prove that this bound is asymptotically sharp: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every sufficiently large $Δ$, there exists a graph $G$ of maximum degree at most $Δ$ with $\textrm{HG}(G) \ge (e - \varepsilon)Δ$. This answers a question of Alon et al., disproves the conjecture $\textrm{HG}(G) \le 2Δ(G)$ of Bosek et al., and improves on the construction of Latyshev and Kokhas, which achieves $\textrm{HG}(G) = 4Δ(G)/3$. The hat guessing number thus provides a natural combinatorial problem in which the Lovász Local Lemma is asymptotically tight.

Title: ValQID: Learning the Net Value of Semantic Query Groups for Web Device Identification
Author: Yifan Yang, Zhen Huang, Weijia Shi, Xichen Tan, Zhihuang Liu, Xionglve Li, Zhiping Cai
Text_Content: Web interfaces are widely used to access network services and manage networked devices. Identifying the vendors and types of devices behind Web interfaces is a critical step in asset inventory, security management, and risk assessment. Device identity cues are dispersed across page text, configuration fields, and management functions, and interpreting them often requires linking related Web objects. Responses and objects require different amounts of semantic analysis, so exhaustively processing all candidate content can introduce unnecessary computation. We present ValQID, which uses a relation graph to combine dispersed device identity cues, evaluates semantic questions efficiently with DSEJEV, and accounts for complementarity among semantic questions when estimating computation value. Based on the current identification state, ValQID weighs each question group's expected identification benefit against its execution cost and adaptively allocates computation to identify device vendors and types. Evaluation on real Web response data shows that ValQID achieves relative gains of up to 47.1% in joint macro-F1 and up to 82.1% in macro-F1 for low-frequency vendors over a state-of-the-art method. DSEJEV speeds up semantic processing by up to 8.58 times compared with general-purpose language models.

Title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations
Author: Daniel A. Moroz-Broitman, Eliya Nachmani
Text_Content: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.

Title: Identifying the determinants of soccer coach turnover by competing risks models: a case study on Italian League Serie A
Author: Francesco Porro, Marialuisa Restaino, Juan Eloy Ruiz-Castro, Mariangela Zenga
Text_Content: This paper investigates the determinants of head coach turnover in the Italian Serie A over the period 2010-2019 by explicitly accounting for multiple exit mechanisms within a competing risks framework. Four mutually exclusive exit types are considered: end of contract, mutual consent, resignation, and sacking. To identify robust predictors of turnover, we combine classical cause-specific Cox models with a variable selection procedure based on forward selection, LASSO regression, and Random Survival Forests. The results show that performance-related variables are the primary drivers of coach turnover, while personal characteristics play a limited role once performance is controlled for. Short-term performance indicators, such as points per match until turnover, strongly influence the risk of dismissal. Conversely, cumulative poor performance substantially increases dismissal risk: a higher proportion of losses over a coach's tenure raises the hazard of sacking by more than four times. Season timing also plays a crucial role, as sackings and mutual-consent terminations are significantly more likely to occur during the season, whereas contract expirations concentrate at the end of the season. Overall, the findings highlight that clubs differentiate between short-term performance shocks and longer-term performance trajectories when deciding how and when to replace a head coach. By distinguishing among exit mechanisms and adopting a conservative variable selection strategy, the study provides a robust and nuanced assessment of managerial turnover dynamics in the most important Italian professional football league.

Title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
Author: Andrea Cenzato, Lukas Karch, Andre Luckow, Yoran Pichon, Francesco Pasqua, Abouzar Ghasemi, Rishikesh Ranade, Ira Shokar, Julia Kowalski
Text_Content: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets. The dataset is available for download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/andreacenzato/Ground-Wing

Title: Setting the Stage: Enhancing Music Recommendations with Spoken Introductions to Stimulate Serendipity
Author: Brett Binst
Text_Content: People like to keep their music listening fresh and interesting, but recommender systems often struggle to support this need. Even when a recommended song is potentially refreshing and enriching, listeners may not perceive it as such. Building on Silvia's appraisal theory of interest, this paper studies whether enhancing recommendations with spoken introductions, immersive or informative, can stimulate two distinct flavors of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening (sparking interest in music outside one's typical preferences) and taste-deepening (deepening interest in music within one's typical preferences). Results from a large-scale user study show that both introduction types stimulate taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening is most effectively stimulated through transportation (absorption in a narrative world), whereas taste-deepening is most effectively stimulated through cognitive elaboration (learning something new about the artist or the social context in which the music emerged). We discuss how these findings could be translated into practice through curated taste-broadening playlists, where both introduction types appear promising, and taste-deepening playlists, where informative introductions seem particularly effective.

Title: Abelian embeddings make useful promises: approximation of detrivialised equations
Author: Tamio-Vesa Nakajima, Zephyr Verwimp, Stanislav Živný
Text_Content: We study the following family of search problems: given a system of equations $x+y+z\equiv 0\pmod p$ promised to admit a solution that is nonconstant on every equation, find a $c$-colouring of the variables that makes no equation monochromatic. For $p\in\{2,3\}$, the problem recovers known tractable Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs). For $p > 3$, we obtain a complete complexity classification: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $c \geq 4$, yet even its decision version is NP-hard for $c = 3$, and it is not well-defined for $c = 2$. Our main conceptual contribution is a general tractability framework for PCSPs based on Abelian embeddings, a notion introduced by Bhangale, Khot, and Minzer [STOC 2022] in the study of quantitative approximation of satisfiable CSPs. We show that suitable Abelian embeddings yield polynomial-time PCSP reductions realised by singleton algorithms in the sense of Zhuk [FOCS 2026]. On the hardness side, the promise relation is far removed from the reconfigurable regime covered by the conditional hardness framework of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima [LICS 2026]; our proof instead relies on a new additive-combinatorial rigidity theorem classifying special $3$-colourings of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

Title: A research world model of power engineering learns its dynamics and reveals what-ifs
Author: Fanping Sui, Ying Zhang, Liwei Lin
Text_Content: Decisions about the direction of research in power engineering determine which technologies mature and, through them, shape infrastructure that lasts decades, yet their consequences cannot be observed before they are taken, and existing forecasts of research fields extrapolate a single trajectory. Here we introduce research world models, which treat a research field as a dynamical system that can be acted upon, and establish one for power engineering from 1.1 million papers. A distilled language model reads each paper into role-typed concepts, two sophisticated, high-fidelity graph-temporal neural network cores learn how the resulting concept network evolves, and operators learned from natural experiments in the publication record estimate the effects of interventions. In temporally held-out tests, the model forecast years ahead which concepts would grow and which method-target pairs would be joined for the first time, outperforming tuned machine-learning baselines in most settings, and its estimated intervention effects tracked those realized in natural experiments it had not seen. Its training scheme and three of its operators replicated in two fields withheld from development. Questions posed in natural language are compiled by a domain-specialized 27-billion-parameter language model into executable actions and answered as paired simulations with and without the intervention. The answers were rated 4.1 of 5 for faithfulness by an independent language-model judge. By revealing the latent dynamics of a research field and its response to interventions, research world models offer a new way to simulate and test research decisions before they are made.

Title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
Author: Jirko Rubruck, Alice Zhang, Andrew Saxe, Christopher Summerfield
Text_Content: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

Title: Optimized size, shape and orientation of rhombic transposition flaps and excisions by gradient-based methods
Author: Niels Aage, Brandon Marshal Parks
Text_Content: This work presents a new method for gradient-based optimization of the rhombic transposition flap and the excision it closes, which set the strain of the skin after closure. Previous studies swept at most three parameters. Here, using structural optimization methods, up to eight variables, two flap angles, two cut lengths and the size, shape and position of the rhombic excision, are optimized under up to 32 geometric and stress constraints. The skin is a pre-stretched, incompressible hyperelastic membrane that wrinkles instead of carrying compression. Smoothed level-sets on a fixed grid represent the cuts, and springs between interpolated points the sutures, so designs change without remeshing and the adjoint method gives the sensitivities. The energy the surgery adds to the skin is minimized, and the model reproduces the energies of a published 48-design sweep with a median deviation of 5%. The optimal flap angles, $(-23^\circ, 31^\circ)$, lie outside the swept range and add 63% less energy than the Limberg flap and 15% less than the best swept design. Under unequal in-vivo tension, the optimal flap turns with the direction of the tension. Fitting the excision to the lesion and its margin lowers the energy by a further 35%, and with all eight variables it is 78% below the Limberg flap. This optimum is the same for finer grids, narrower cuts and wider undermining, although wider undermining reduces its gain. Lowering its suture-line stress by 41% costs only 2.3% more energy.

Title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
Author: Benedikt Bollig, Patricia Bouyer-Decitre, Matthias Függer, Dhrubajyoti Ghosh, Thomas Nowak, Nathalie Sznajder
Text_Content: Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories. More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense. In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

Title: Distributionally Robust Search: The Power of Information and the Limits of Moments
Author: Nicole Megow, Cliff Stein, Jose Verschae
Text_Content: We study binary search for a target drawn from a distribution on $n$ ordered elements. The cost is the expected number of comparison queries. In our distributionally robust framework, the algorithm knows only an uncertainty set containing the distribution and minimizes its worst-case approximation ratio against an optimal strategy that knows the distribution. Collections of uncertainty sets capture different forms of information: quantiles, moments, general linear measurements, or approximate CDFs. This framework quantifies how much and what form of information is needed for near-optimal search. Our main result separates moments from general linear measurements. Although $n-1$ moments determine the distribution exactly, for every constant $δ\in(0,1)$, the first $n^{1-δ}$ exact moments can be as uninformative for search as no information: the worst-case approximation ratio remains $Ω(\log n)$. In contrast, for every constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $O(n^\varepsilon\log^4 n)$ suitably chosen linear measurements suffice for an $O(1/\varepsilon)$-approximation. The limitation lies in the measurements chosen, rather than linearity itself. Using LP duality and polynomial bounds of Rakhmanov and Bernstein, we construct distributions with identical moments and mass concentrated at different positions. For the upper bound, we combine dyadic sketches and Johnson--Lindenstrauss embeddings with a truncated median-search algorithm that converts uniform CDF approximation into search guarantees. Measuring information in bits, we prove a lower bound of $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ on the approximation ratio for summaries of any form using at most $\frac12 n^\varepsilon\log n$ bits, for every sufficiently small constant $\varepsilon>0$. Quantiles match this within constant factors. For Kolmogorov balls of radius $n^{-\varepsilon}$ the optimal approximation ratio is $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$.

Title: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Reveals Grotthuss Transport in Concentrated Electrolytes
Author: Øystein Gullbrekken, Sondre Kvalvåg Schnell
Text_Content: Proton transfer is responsible for the anomalous high conductivity in acidic or basic aqueous solutions. Yet, the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the conductivity of concentrated aqueous solutions is unknown. In this work, we compute the transport properties of KOH(aq) systems with different concentrations, using Molecular Dynamics simulations with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIP), which includes proton transfer. We quantify the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the diffusivities of hydroxide ions and water molecules, and the ionic conductivity and transport numbers of the electrolytes. The contribution is substantial at lower concentrations, but diminishes at very high concentrations.

Title: Inter-Agent Influence: Evaluating Persuasion, Deception, and Coercion in Multi-Agent Systems
Author: Chandler Smith, Qi Guo, Cecilia Elena Tilli, Sophia Hatz, David Demitri Africa, Patricia Paskov, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Philip Torr, Lewis Hammond
Text_Content: The deployment of AI agents in multi-agent settings enables inter-agent influence, whereby agents can strategically steer each other's behaviour towards an intended outcome. Such capabilities pose novel risks, as malicious agents could direct others towards harmful actions. In this work we investigate three such capabilities - persuasion, deception, and coercion - across five realistic evaluation environments and a variety of agents instantiated with frontier language models. We observed significant inter-agent influence capabilities; in oversight environments, all tested models shifted overseer decisions from rejection to approval through persuasion, deception, or coercion. We also observed successful influence in non-hierarchical 'peer-to-peer' settings through redirection of a peer's safety research trajectory. As multi-agent deployments become increasingly commonplace, these results point to a pressing need for work on mitigating the risks from inter-agent influence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Cooperative-AI-Foundation/inter-agent-influence.

Title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
Author: Zhan-He Wang, Zi-Yang Lang, Yi-Yang Li, Qing-Yu Lan, Yun-Song Piao
Text_Content: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

Title: SEEK-VAU: Towards Evidence-Faithful Video Anomaly Understanding via Agentic Search
Author: Minghe Wang, Weijun Zeng, Dapeng Luo, Xinyue Wang, Nong Sang
Text_Content: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.

Title: An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case
Author: Gleb Shishaev, Anton Shirokov, Shadfar Davoodi, Mohammed Al-Shargabi, Vasily Demyanov, Daniel Arnold
Text_Content: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.

Title: Mutual-Coupling-Aware Joint Precoding and Antenna Positioning for Movable-Antenna MU-MIMO Systems
Author: Wei Guo, Tianyi Liao, Zixin Wang, Shenghui Song, Jun Zhang, Khaled B. Letaief
Text_Content: Movable antennas (MAs) improve wireless communications by adapting antenna positions to the propagation environment. However, antenna movement also changes the mutual coupling (MC) among elements of the transmit and receive arrays, which affects the performance of MA-enabled systems. In this paper, we investigate MC-aware joint precoding and antenna positioning for a downlink multiuser multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) system with MAs at both the base station and users. We establish an MC-aware system model by combining field-response propagation with a circuit-based representation of the transmit and receive arrays. Based on this model, we formulate a weighted sum-rate (WSR) maximization problem that jointly optimizes multi-stream precoders and antenna positions. The problem is challenging because the precoders and positions are coupled through the propagation channels and position-dependent MC matrices. To address this challenge, we reformulate the problem in the antenna-current domain to to efficiently handle the MC matrices and develop a current-domain weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) framework for alternating optimization. Furthermore, we handle the nonconvex position updates within the framework by using majorization--minimization (MM) and solve the resulting convex subproblems with a dedicated conic alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed design improves the WSR over both an MC-aware fixed array and a movable-array design that ignores MC during optimization.

Title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
Author: Simone Betteti, Matteo Martin, Morten Gram Pedersen, Sandro Zampieri, Giacomo Baggio
Text_Content: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.

Title: Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes
Author: Benjamin Bachmayr, Mohamed Youssef, Oliver Bimber
Text_Content: Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) enables drones to observe forest canopies by warping and averaging multiple displaced views at a common depth. However, occlusion is suppressed rather than eliminated, causing poorly observed regions to appear occupied and leading to systematic biomass overestimation. The Deep Forest project cannot distinguish reconstruction artifacts from real vegetation because its training data relies on measured reflectance points, excluding empty space and preventing the network from learning explicit occupancy boundaries. This thesis addresses the problem by modifying training labels rather than the imaging process. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal-stack generation and as 550 depth-clipped slabs derived from scene geometry to provide occupancy labels, explicitly representing void space as a negative class. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural forest stands containing 80-200 trees across three species. A pretrained Pix2Pix model translates rendered RGB images into a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces aligned focal stacks of 550 planes across three channels. Four architectures were evaluated on a held-out scene. The plain 2D U-Net achieved an IoU of 0.6290, outperforming the volumetric 3D U-Net (0.5707). Established reconstruction methods performed substantially worse: COLMAP achieved 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959, both after their respective optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture achieved the highest IoU of 0.6514 without dilation or per-scene calibration. These results highlight the limitations of conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.

Title: Are LLM Assistants Regulatory Ready? Answers from regenold's 2026 EU AI Act Q&A Challenge
Author: Marco Virgolin, Thomas Haszprunar, Maximilian Regenold
Text_Content: Large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly proposed for regulatory affairs, yet their reliability in regulatory tasks remains unclear. We introduce the EU AI Act Q&A Benchmark, an expert-curated benchmark of 110 open-ended questions about the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Each question comes with an exemplary answer, question-specific correctness criteria, and expected references. Evaluation measures answer correctness, reference quality, conciseness, tone, and latency, with a multi-turn ``hard mode'' testing responses to simulated user pushback. We also present the results of the 2026 EU AI Act Q&A Challenge, based on the benchmark, where three off-the-shelf baselines and five purpose-built assistants (from four commercial developers and one academic entrant) were tested. Only two of the five submitted assistants consistently outperformed the baselines; one achieved high scores across all evaluated metrics. These results show that specialist development alone does not guarantee better performance and highlight the critical importance of LLM assistant evaluation in regulatory affairs. The benchmark code is openly available at https://github.com/regenold-GmbH/eu-ai-act-benchmark-2026/.

Title: Coercive at the equilibrium, monotone nowhere: exact convergence certificates for learning in first-price auctions
Author: Benjamin Lubin
Text_Content: The Bayes-Nash equilibria of an auction are the solutions of a variational inequality, and for standard auctions its operator fails every monotonicity notion, so the theory of monotone operators is unavailable to learning in auctions. We show what replaces monotonicity for the first-price auction: a certificate that is strong but local. For uniform values the single-population operator has an exact closed form and an exact Minty identity at the equilibrium; for two bidders its Gateaux derivative there is $L^2$-coercive with best constant exactly one in every piecewise-linear bid space with $m$ pieces, while the Minty inequality holds only on a ball whose radius decays like $m^{-5/2}$. The decay is exact: $m^{5/2}$ times the radius converges to $1/(8 \cdot 3^{1/4})$, and the worst perturbations converge to an alternating geometric profile with ratio $-(2-\sqrt{3})$. Refinement shrinks the ball, not the constant; independent learners see the same constant. For a general prior and bidder count there are two certificates, at the true equilibrium and at the equilibrium of the finite-dimensional bid space a learning algorithm runs in. The first is an explicit weight $w_F$, positive for every log-concave prior, equal to the second exactly for the value distributions $F(v)=v^a$. Otherwise the learners' certificate differs by knot masses, because the discretized equilibrium's slopes oscillate with a law proved for two and three bidders, and for four under a computer-verified bottom layer. The limit of the learners' certificate is proved in closed form, a function of the prior alone, and characterizes positivity: positive uniformly in $m$ in the limit exactly when that minimum is positive, with a known rate; for one prior at every $m$ by interval arithmetic. For more bidders the limit is conjectured. The exact identities and leading-order inequalities are machine-checked in Lean.

Title: CANDO: Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization for Residual Reinforcement Learning
Author: Zeyu Gao, Chengkai Hou, Chaoyue Li, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Yao Mu, Peng Jia, Li Zhang, Shanghang Zhang
Text_Content: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on https://cando-rl.github.io/.

Title: Wavefront engineering with atomic Huygens' surfaces made simple
Author: K. E. Ballantine, J. Ruostekoski
Text_Content: Atomic arrays provide a cooperative platform for light-mediated interactions in nonlocal metasurfaces which can operate in the quantum regime without nanofabricated optical elements or intrinsic material absorption. We present a minimal atomic implementation to harness wavefront engineering and create a near-ideal intrinsic atomic Huygens' surface. A simple bilayer square lattice with a two-atom unit cell, not limited to small lattice spacings, provides near-unity reflectionless transmission and a full $2π$ phase control of transmitted light without the localized site-dependent level shifts of previous proposals. This simplification is achieved through nonlocal radiative excitations that provide the familiar electric-dipole response with even radiation parity as well as an odd-parity radiation channel whose leading multipolar interpretation combines magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions in atoms exhibiting only electric dipole transitions. This eliminates the need to simultaneously excite pure electric-dipole and magnetic-dipole responses with exactly matched radiation. We derive a two-mode model for this response and show that it accurately captures full coupled-dipole simulations near the optimal lattice spacings. Because of the wide applicability of coupled-dipole models, the relevance of our microscopic analysis extends beyond atomic physics to nanostructured metasurfaces. Moreover, the same platform also connects directly to established subradiance-protected single-photon storage protocols, suggesting a route toward combining wavefront engineering, storage, and retrieval in a simple atomic bilayer.

Title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models
Author: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
Text_Content: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.

Title: Machine learning emulators of dynamic global vegetation models for fast gridded carbon budget predictions
Author: Piyu Ke, Xiaofan Gui, Stephen Sitch, Zhu Liu, Xun Li, Jiang Bian, Pierre Friedlingstein, Philippe Ciais
Text_Content: The land carbon sink explains most of the variability of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate, but the Global Carbon Budget estimates it with dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) run once a year. Emulators could provide it sooner if they reproduce each model outside its training period. Here we show that convolutional neural network emulators of 19 of these models, driven by ERA5 climate and their own past predictions, reproduce the global land sink of these models and its spread over two years not used in training. Global monthly net biome production (NBP) anomalies were reproduced with a median R^2 of 0.81. The error of the multi-model mean annual NBP was at most 0.23 GtC yr^-1. At the grid-cell level, the median R^2 of monthly anomalies was 0.30, partly because of errors that accumulate in the emulated NBP history.

Title: A Universal Raw-IQ Radar Encoder for Cross-Sensor Human Sensing
Author: Jonas Leo Mueller, Dario Zanca, Sebastian Hoefler, Jan Petermann, Thomas Altstidl, Naga Venkata Sai Jitin Jami, Emmanuelle Salin, Bjoern M. Eskofier
Text_Content: Radar-based human sensing typically relies on end-to-end task-specific models trained on hand-chosen signal projections, which generalize poorly across unseen users, tasks, and hardware. We argue that the dominant signal processing choice, the micro-Doppler spectrogram, is a poor starting point for transfer because it keeps the Doppler axis, which carrier frequency rescales, and discards the angular axis, which carrier frequency leaves unchanged. We instead pretrain a convolutional beta-VAE without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from four platforms spanning 60 and 77 GHz and 4 to 12 virtual antennas, aligned by a unified spectral interpolation grid. For every downstream benchmark the encoder stays frozen, and only a small supervised temporal classifier is trained on its embeddings. We compare against supervised models trained end to end on each benchmark and a pretrained radar foundation model across ten settings covering activity, gesture, sign-language, and gait recognition. When the test users and the radar are seen during training, our encoder is best on all five benchmarks. For users never seen in training, it leads on three of four benchmarks, by 4.8 to 23.2 points. On subject-disjoint gait recognition, it is best for each of the four held-out subjects and 8.3 points above the strongest baseline on average, even though its pretraining excluded every recording of this radar. Excluding the test radar from pretraining costs at most 5.3 points on any benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/jonasmueler/UniversalRadarEncoder_WACV.

Title: A Systematic Comparison of In-Context Learning Strategies for Peptide Property Prediction in Low-Data Regimes
Author: Jiantao Zhao, Andrei Voinea, Mathijs F. J. Mabesoone
Text_Content: Peptide sequence-property relationships are often highly non-linear, but can be learned with machine learning models and exploited for the design of new materials and bioactive compounds. Various methods based on transformer architectures have become available for molecular property predictions. These foundation models promise straightforward inference and prediction of properties of new materials through in-context learning. Benchmarks of individual model architectures exist, but a systematic comparison of various foundation models against classical baselines on similar datasets is lacking. Here, we provide a systematic evaluation of the predictive performance of various in-context learning strategies. We compare several large language models, tabular foundation models, and typed decision models against an XGBoost baseline. We evaluate predictive performance on binary and multiclass classification tasks on pH-dependent surface activ-ity, IR spectral signatures, self-assembly, and anti-cancer activities. Our results show that ICL is competitive, yet does not significantly outperform classical baselines, and performance varies between models and tasks. Our findings further suggest that language models use both in context examples and knowledge acquired during pretraining to infer properties of unseen samples. This finding indicates that pretrained models can leverage the existing literature for predictions, but may also bias their predictions towards established sequence-property relationships.

Title: The Price of List Replicability: Tight Bounds for Bias Estimation
Author: Michael Chen, Atieh Bastan, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
Text_Content: We study the sample complexity of list replicable algorithms for estimating the biases of $d$ coins. An algorithm is $(k,\varepsilon,δ)$-list replicable if for every bias vector $\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^d$, there is a set of outputs $L_{\mathbf{p}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of at most $k$ elements such that every $\mathbf{y}\in L_{\mathbf{p}}$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\rVert_\infty\leq\varepsilon$, and the algorithm output is in $L_{\mathbf{p}}$ with probability at least $1-δ$. Prior work gave a $(d+1,\varepsilon,δ)$-list replicable algorithm with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^3}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, but no nontrivial sample complexity lower bound was known. We establish the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for this problem and give an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors. Together, these results determine the optimal sample complexity for list size $d+1$ to be $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, showing that the quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors. More generally, for every $k\in[d+1,2^d]$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds of $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log k}\right)$ on the total sample complexity.

Title: A New Bound on Light-by-Light Scattering in the Low-Energy Regime
Author: Aimé Matheron, Michal Šmíd, Felix Karbstein, Sebastian Göde, Willi Hippler, Robert Lötzsch, Naser Ahmadiniaz, Michal Andrzejewski, Sergey Antipov, Carsten Baehtz, Christina Bömer, Victorien Bouffetier, Erik Brambrink, Jakub Bulička, Samuele Di Dio Cafiso, Rafael Celestre, Jaromír Chalupský, Thomas E. Cowan, James P. Edwards, Sebastián Franchino-Viñas, Holger Gies, Jörg Grenzer, Travis Griffin, Věra Hájková, Jens Hauser, Thomas Heinzl, Uwe Hernandez Acosta, Peter Hilz, Hauke Höppner, Alžběta Horynová, Lingen Huang, Oliver Humphries, Šimon Jelínek, Libor Juha, Pooyan Khademi, Ben King, Christian Kohlfürst, Dietrich Krebs, Alejandro Laso-García, Alexander J. Macleod, Berit Marx-Glowna, Masruri Masruri, Nikita Medvedev, Anthony Mercuri-Baron, Elena A. Mosman, Motoaki Nakatsutsumi, Gerhard G. Paulus, Jennifer Popp, Thomas R. Preston, Isabella Probst, Sripati V. Rahul, Lisa Randolph, Ralf Röhlsberger, Thomas Roth, Sakshath Sadashivaiah, Felipe C. Salgado, Roland Sauerbrey, Alexander Sävert, Hans-Peter Schlenvoigt, Sebastian M. Schmidt, Ulrich Schramm, Ralf Schützhold, Jan Patrick Schwinkendorf, Frank Seiboth, Daniel Seipt, Georgiy Shoulga, Thomas Stöhlker, Minxue Tang, Abha Thazhathe Peedika, Monika Toncian, Toma Toncian, Maksim Valialshchikov, Vojtěch Vozda, Edgar Weckert, Colin Wessel, Jan Wild, Andreas Wipf, Ulf Zastrau, Matt Zepf
Text_Content: The superposition principle at the heart of optics states that electromagnetic fields do not interact in vacuum. This principle is not universal, instead electromagnetic fields couple weakly via quantum vacuum fluctuations. Striking consequences are light-by-light scattering and vacuum birefringence. Experimental results from colliding X-ray free-electron and optical high-intensity lasers combined with dark-field detection and polarimetry for background suppression are reported. This approach yields the most stringent bound for light-by-light scattering in the low-energy regime achieved to date -- improving upon previous experimental limits by ten orders of magnitude -- and paves the way for precision measurements.

Title: Learning to Falsify: Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning for High Resolution AI-Generated Image Detection
Author: Haoran Chen, Daiqi Gao, Xinyuan Li, Yongwei Wang, Lei Zhu, Rui Cai, Jianfeng Dong
Text_Content: Recent advances in generative models have made synthetic images increasingly photorealistic, posing growing challenges to reliable and generalizable detection of AI-generated images. Existing methods typically rely on holistic image-level classification, which may overlook local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images. To address this limitation, we formulate this task as a falsification-driven multiple instance learning problem, where a single fake patch can falsify the whole image, while a real image requires all patches to be authentic. Based on this formulation, we propose \textit{Learning to Falsify (LTF)}, a hierarchical multiple instance learning framework that models an image as multiple bags of instances across different spatial levels and aggregates their predictions under the falsification-inspired principle. We further introduce Cross-Shuffle during training to encourage the model to learn local artifact evidence rather than image-level shortcuts. Furthermore, we propose the \textit{Falsification-driven Test-time Aggregation Strategy (FATAS)}, a plug-and-play module that extends the same falsification-inspired principle to existing detectors by aggregating patch-level predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTF achieves strong generalization and robustness across multiple benchmarks, while FATAS substantially improves representative detectors in high-resolution scenarios without retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/HuiGuanLab/LTF.git

Title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models
Author: Jaehyeong Jo, Sangwon Jang, Sihyun Yu, Seonghyeon Ye, Yekyung Nah, Hojung Jung, Kimin Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
Text_Content: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

Title: E2I-Flow: EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Wavelet-Temporal Cross-Attention and Conditional Flow Matching
Author: Haowei Pan, Hwa Hui Tew, Junn Yong Loo, Fuad Noman, Hernando Ombao, Chee-Ming Ting
Text_Content: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based visual decoding and reconstruction aims to recover visual information from non-invasive brain signals. But there are challenges due to the complex temporal-frequency characteristics of EEG signals and the difficulty of discrete denoising framework in mapping neural activity to meaningful visual representations. Here, we propose E2I-Flow, an EEG-to-image decoding and reconstruction framework that combines a novel EEG encoder for time-frequency representation learning from EEG features, and conditional flow matching for visual decoding. A stationary-wavelet frequency branch and a temporal-mixing branch are integrated through bidirectional cross-attention and adaptive fusion, with the resulting EEG representations aligned to ground-truth image embeddings using contrastive and mean-squared-error loss supervisions. The aligned EEG representation is then used as a condition for a Transformer-based flow-matching model to predict the corresponding visual embedding for image synthesis. Experimental results show strong zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval and improved visual reconstruction performance, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines.

Title: Action Intent as a Bridge: Transferring Manipulation Knowledge from Human-Centric Videos to Robots
Author: Zhiqian Xia, Lianyang Ma, Haifeng Xia, Siyu Xia, Wei Wang, Xiaochun Cao
Text_Content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.

Title: Estimating the generator of matrix exponential time-series
Author: Jonáš Fuksa, Jens Eisert, Ingo Roth
Text_Content: The achievable precision in estimating the spectrum of a time-series signal that is promised to be sparse in Fourier space deteriorates rapidly as the spectral peaks get closer together, as soon as we introduce noise. Here, we study the related task of generator estimation: estimating the generator of a matrix exponential time-series and its eigenvalues.
